news.titleEn: Universal Migrator helps closing startups offboard customers and reduce legal risk
news.titleZh: Universal Migrator 帮助关闭中的初创公司完成客户迁移并降低法律风险
news.summaryZh: 管理不善的关闭可能带来重大风险，如客户声称数据丢失、未获合理机会取回数据或导出不完整。Universal Migrator 提供文档化的迁移流程，帮助初创公司在关闭时履行对客户的义务，降低法律风险。该平台支持超过170种法律和商业应用的数据迁移，包括实践管理、文档管理、CRM、计费等系统。它使公司能够依赖迁移专家和成熟工具，而非从零构建导出系统，从而提高效率，改善客户体验。
news.bodyHtml:
A poorly managed shutdown can create significant risk. Customers may claim that they lost access to data, were not given a reasonable opportunity to retrieve it, or received exports that were incomplete or unusable.

While no technology can eliminate legal risk, a documented and organized offboarding process can demonstrate that a company took reasonable steps to protect its customers and fulfill its obligations.

Universal Migrator helps startups:

  • Extract customer data before systems are decommissioned.
  • Deliver information in structured, accessible formats.
  • Support migrations into replacement platforms when appropriate.
  • Create a consistent process across the entire customer base.
  • Reduce dependence on a shrinking internal engineering team.
  • Document the steps taken to return or transfer customer information.

This can help founders, investors, and wind-down teams close the company without leaving unresolved data issues behind.

Keeping Engineers Focused on the Wind-Down

As a startup approaches closure, employees may leave, infrastructure may be reduced, and engineering resources may become increasingly limited. Building and supporting custom export tools can consume time that the remaining team needs for security, billing, vendor termination, compliance, and other shutdown responsibilities.

Universal Migrator allows the company to rely on migration specialists and proven tooling rather than creating a new offboarding system from scratch.

The result is a more efficient process for the startup and a better experience for customers who need access to their information.

Support for More Than 170 Applications

Universal Migrator supports migrations involving more than 170 legal and business applications, including practice management, document management, CRM, billing, accounting, and related systems.

That broad connector library allows Universal Migrator to support a range of shutdown scenarios, whether customers need their data exported for safekeeping or transferred directly into another application.

About Universal Migrator

Universal Migrator is a migration platform built for consultants, technology professionals, and software companies that need to move customer data between business applications.

Its growing library of connectors and migration tools helps teams accelerate conversions, improve repeatability, and reduce the manual work involved in extracting, transforming, and transferring complex data.

For startups preparing to close, Universal Migrator provides a practical way to make customer offboarding part of a responsible wind-down—helping protect customer relationships, reduce potential disputes, and give founders greater peace of mind.

news.titleEn: LexisNexis opens New York customer innovation lab as AI development cycles compress
news.titleZh: LexisNexis开设纽约客户创新实验室，AI开发周期缩短
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis Legal & Professional于8月4日宣布在纽约市开设客户创新实验室，作为法律AI构建和交付的新模式。实验室中，法律专业人士、LexisNexis工程师及OpenAI、AWS等AI合作伙伴将并肩工作，在数小时内解决工作流程痛点并制作原型。实验室启动时有约30人，其中20人专职，其余从内部调动，未来还将轮换其他4000名工程师。过去需要数月或数年完成的工作现在数周即可完成，模型提供商每六至八周发布新模型，客户面临如何吸收AI的挑战。实验室旨在让工程师更贴近客户，消除中间层。在一小时内根据客户反馈三次修改产品。开发重点为法律AI助手Protégé，客户反馈不会立即成为产品，但会在一周内与10至20个客户测试。实验室已与Am Law前50强及前10强中的部分律所合作，成果包括客户管理的Protégé Vault，可分析多媒体材料，律师可在几分钟内分析两小时的证词并定位关键事实。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today (4 August) announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City – describing it as a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped.  

Within the Lab, legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI collaborators like OpenAI and Amazon Web Services will “build side by side”, solving workflow pain points with prototypes “in hours”. 

The Lab launches with around 30 people, made up of engineers, AR scientists and productivity UX specialists, of which 20 are fully dedicated to the Lab. They have been hired in as well as moved internally, with the anticipation that LexisNexis will also cycle through its other 4,000 engineers and technologists.  

Speaking to Legal IT Insider about the Lab, LexisNexis executive vice president and chief technology officer Greg Dickason said that it is a reflection of the speed of change, observing: “What was done in months and years in the past is now being done in weeks.” 

Advertisement

With model providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI releasing models every six weeks to eight weeks, Dickason observed that “what we’re really seeing is that our customers are struggling with how do they absorb all of this AI, not just from the model providers, but also across the board from all the different vendors out there.” 

The idea of the Lab is to bring LexisNexis engineers closer to the customer, with “none of this middle layer.” It is hoped that this will help customers to get a handle on how to cut through the noise as well as help to build products live. 

Dickason says: “We did one this week, which I was pretty excited about. The customer gave us feedback, we iterated, they gave us more feedback, reiterated, and essentially in one hour, we had changed the product three times.  

“For me, that’s the real sort of signal of how the Lab can work, is that we can [not only] understand customer problems, but put them right with the people who can build the solution, which is the engineers.” 

Much of the development will focus on legal AI assistant LexisNexis Protégé, and asked how LexisNexis will streamline customer demands, Dickason said that “when you get that feedback from one customer, that doesn’t immediately become a product. It gives us really good ideas as to where we should be going. And then we can test it with a second set of customers and a third set. But very quickly, within a week or so, we would have tested it with, say, 10 or 20 different customers and got real ideas to what’s going to make a difference for them.” 

He adds: “The Lab’s really helping us crystallise what’s most important.”  

 LexisNexis via the Lab is already engaging with associates and CIOs and technology leaders. It is already working with a few of the Am Law top 50 firms and a couple of the Am Law top 10 firms. 

Examples of ideas that have come to fruition include an advanced, customer-managed Protégé Vault for analysing complex multimedia materials. Legal professionals will be able to store and analyse documents, videos, images, audio files, and other matter materials. A lawyer could, for example, analyse a two-hour deposition in minutes with Protégé, pinpoint the exact moments when key facts emerge, and trace findings directly to the timestamps and source materials. 

Interestingly, as we enter a period in which a lot of the largest law firms are looking at leveraging their own ecosystem rather than buying a product off the shelf, and even training their own models, Dickason says the Lab helps “because it helps them conceptualise.”

“I see it as educational,” he says. “So it’s not just about coming and us getting all the benefit of it. It’s also for them to get other benefits to come in, understand how we think about fine tuning, where we see fine tuning models make sense and where you should still be using foundation models. We use a blend of models across all the major vendors, but also fine tune our own. And I think it really comes down to what’s the right use case for your particular need , what you need to do.”  

While the Lab is currently a physical space in New York, LexisNexis will also be looking at rolling out in other major centers around the world.  

Dickason says: “I think you get so much more when people are in one room and they can actually see and interact. You get far more when people can see the response. And say ‘okay, that worked. That didn’t work.’ You don’t get that over Teams, et cetera.”  

“Congratulations to LexisNexis on the launch of its Customer Innovation Lab,” said Scott Liska, VP AWSI, Amazon Web Services in a statement. “Bringing trusted AI into professional work requires both rapid innovation and a strong technology foundation. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with LexisNexis as it advances secure, authoritative AI capabilities for legal professionals.”  

At the time of publishing, LexisNexis was looking for a director of software innovation, if you think that has your name on it, you can take a look at that role here: https://www.builtinnyc.com/job/director-software-engineering-customer-innovation-lab/9690097

news.titleEn: LexisNexis Opens Customer Innovation Lab in New York to Bring Customers, Engineers and AI Companies Together to Build Legal AI in Real Time
news.titleZh: LexisNexis在纽约开设客户创新实验室，汇聚客户、工程师与AI公司，实时构建法律AI
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis Legal & Professional宣布在纽约市开设客户创新实验室，这是一个实体空间，法律专业人士、LexisNexis工程师以及包括OpenAI和亚马逊网络服务在内的AI技术合作伙伴并肩工作，共同设计、原型制作和测试新的法律AI能力，有时在一小时内多次迭代想法。该实验室实际上已运营约1.5个月，提供了一种构建和交付法律AI的新模式。实验室不是内部开发AI能力然后让客户事后验证，而是让客户参与工作会议，LexisNexis工程师根据他们的具体痛点实时构建。通过公司质量、准确性和安全标准的原型可以推进到开发阶段，成为LexisNexis代理平台的能力，或为特定客户定制，或通过Lexis+ with Protégé扩展。实验室缩短了了解问题的人与构建解决方案的人之间的距离，使技术人员真正理解问题，从而加速响应市场。传统方法每次迭代可能需要数周或数月，而实验室将循环缩短至几分钟。上周，一个解决方案在一小时内因客户反馈被修改了四次。实验室团队约20人，与约4000人的工程组织交接原型。对于功能级功能，从实验室原型到实际产品的路径可能不到一个月。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City, a physical space where legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI technology partners including OpenAI and Amazon Web Services work side by side to design, prototype and test new legal AI capabilities – sometimes iterating on an idea multiple times within a single hour.

The company says the lab – which actually opened about 1.5 months ago – offers a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped. Rather than developing AI capabilities internally and asking customers to validate them after the fact, the lab brings customers into a working session, where LexisNexis engineers build against their specific pain points in real time.

Prototypes that clear the company’s standards for quality, accuracy and security can advance into development as capabilities within the LexisNexis agentic platform, either customized for the customer or scaled across Lexis+ with Protégé.

“For me, the biggest thing is we’re collapsing the distance between the people who know what the problem is and the people who can build the solution,” Greg Dickason, chief technology officer of LexisNexis Legal & Professional, told me in an interview for my LawNext podcast, which will air later this week.

“Putting them in the same room means that our technologists really understand the problems, which means that our ability to respond very quickly to where the market’s going is hyper-accelerated.”

A Different Approach to Customer Input

Over the years, I have sat through any number of company briefings – including by LexisNexis – in which executives told me that customer involvement was a core tenet of how the company develops products. So I asked Dickason to explain what is actually different with the lab.

His answer, in a nutshell, was cycle time. The traditional approach – which involves interviewing customers, going and building something, bringing it back for feedback, and then repeating the process – could take weeks or months per iteration, he said. In the lab, that loop collapses to minutes.

“Literally in the session in the lab, the customers are telling us their problem. We’ve already got the first solution, because we’ve listened and we’ve already pulled that together. We show that to the customer. They say to us, ‘Yeah, but it would work slightly better if this happened or that happened.’ And then we tweak it live in the lab,” Dickason said.

Just last week, he said, he saw a solution get changed four times in one hour as a result of customer feedback.

The idea is for everyone to be hands-on in real time, Dickason said. While one or two LexisNexis staff talk with the customer, engineers sit alongside, listening and coding, often using agentic coding tools such as Claude Code integrated into the LexisNexis product. At some point, they turn their laptops around and ask, “Is this what you meant?”

Dickason said the lab has been quietly operating for about a month and a half ahead of today’s launch, with the company using that time to refine its working cadence, including how a lab team of roughly 20 people hands off prototypes to an engineering organization of some 4,000.

For functionality-level features, he said, the path from lab prototype to live product “can be less than a month.” 

Already Out of the Lab

The lab has already produced prototypes and designs that LexisNexis says are advancing into Lexis+ with Protégé capabilities, including:

  • A customer-managed Protégé Vault for multimedia materials, allowing legal professionals to store and analyze documents, video, audio and images together. Using this tool, Dickason told me, a customer could upload a two-hour video deposition and ask when the witness showed surprise and what was being discussed at that moment, with findings traced to timestamps and source materials.
  • Protégé Workrooms, secure shared spaces where teams can bring together documents, analyses, skills and AI-assisted work on a matter with outside counsel, clients, experts and other authorized participants, governed by permissions and access controls.
  • LexisNexis-developed legal AI models, purpose-built for legal work using the company’s content and expertise.

The vault work, Dickason said, originated from a gap the company had heard about from customers, then took shape when customers came into the lab and described the actual queries they would run. He said that one of LexisNexis’s core technology providers, which he declined to name, was in the room with the customers, helping define what was technically possible. 

Drafting As A Priority

LexisNexis says that the lab’s current top priority is legal drafting. The company cites research showing lawyers spend 40 to 60 percent of their time drafting and reviewing documents, more than on any other task.

Existing tools, Dickason said, get lawyers only 80 or 90 percent of the way there, leaving hours of work to reach a final product. The gaps he identified included conforming drafts to a firm’s own style, precedents and playbooks; flagging risk against a customer’s own standards; carrying context across related documents so a primary document and its supporting materials line up; verification of citations surfaced directly in the draft; and layering in litigation and judicial analytics.

Frontier Models, For Now

With Thomson Reuters recently announcing that its own proprietary model will begin replacing general-purpose models for certain tasks, I asked Dickason whether LexisNexis sees itself heading the same direction.

“Never say never,” he said, but for now the company’s view is that frontier models — he specifically mentioned Claude Opus 5 — combined with LexisNexis’s knowledge graph, retrieval infrastructure and prompting deliver state-of-the-art results.

The company has evaluated models continuously since its work with Amazon on Bedrock more than three years ago, he said, and already uses fine-tuned models for certain parts of the legal workflow.

“We’re going to make sure the highest quality is for us the number one bar,” he said.

Dickason also sees an agent-driven future in which AI agents increasingly act on behalf of lawyers — “disintermediating the user,” as he put it — and said LexisNexis is working on agent-to-agent and MCP interfaces to participate in that ecosystem.

Notably, he does not want third-party agents browsing raw content inside Lexis+ with Protégé, arguing that raw retrieval without the company’s grounding and tuning “generally doesn’t work.”

Who Gets In

Participation is open to “effectively anybody,” Dickason said, from CIOs and partners to junior associates, small firms, solos, and even judges, and whether or not they are current customers.

LexisNexis owns the IP in what comes out of the lab, which participants acknowledge before joining. Dickason said the lab is also set up for a separate track in which large firms building their own internal AI platforms can explore how LexisNexis might plug in.

Now that the lab has launched as an ongoing operation in New York, LexisNexis plans to expand it globally as well as to conduct on-site lab sessions at ILTACON and at customer locations. Firms and legal departments can learn more at www.lexisnexis.com/lab.

My full interview with Dickason will air later this week on LawNext.

news.titleEn: Breaking news: BigHand acquires Ayora
news.titleZh: 突发新闻：BigHand 收购 Ayora
news.summaryZh: BigHand 于8月4日宣布收购法律AI定价专家Ayora，标志着其AI战略进入新阶段。Ayora利用历史数据帮助律师和定价团队实时制定事务定价，其代理技术有望在BigHand产品组合中广泛应用。双方上季度建立合作，市场反响积极，加速了收购进程。收购后，Ayora的技术和八人团队将并入BigHand，首阶段重点整合Ayora与BigHand事务定价，未来AI能力将扩展至资源管理和商业智能等领域。Ayora的数据增强层可将非结构化事务所数据转化为结构化情境情报。Ayora于2023年在Mishcon的MDR实验室孵化，其联合创始人Stefan Ciesla表示，公司利用LLM和专有技术构建数据增强系统，以解决律所数据利用难题，例如通过分类事务帮助律所快速响应客户查询。Ayora的代理层将定价提升至新水平，帮助律所依赖数据而非直觉进行准确费用估算。
news.bodyHtml:
BigHand today (4 August) announced the acquisition of legal AI pricing specialist Ayora, in a move that it says marks the next phase in its AI strategy. 

Ayora uses historic data to help lawyers and pricing teams create real time matter pricing, but within the breadth of the BigHand portfolio, it is anticipated that its agentic technology can be used well beyond that.  

BigHand partnered with Ayora last quarter and says that the response from customers and the wider legal market has been overwhelmingly positive, highlighting the growing demand for AI-powered pricing solutions. While the partnership was formalised this year, the pair have worked together for 18 months, and chief marketing officer and EMEA revenue officer Briana McCrory told Legal IT Insider that while acquisition was on the cards, it was accelerated due to the response and need from the market. 

The acquisition brings Ayora’s tech and eight-strong team into BigHand, with the first phase focused on integrating Ayora with BigHand Matter Pricing. Over time, AI capabilities will be introduced across BigHand’s wider portfolio, including resource management and business intelligence. 

Advertisement

Underlying all of this, Ayora’s data enrichment layer transforms unstructured firm data into structured, contextual intelligence. Ayora, which was incubated in Mishcon’s MDR Lab in 2023, featured in Legal IT Insider’s Startup Corner in October 2023. Co-founder Stefan Ciesla told Legal IT Insider: “You probably know from the days that we’ve done this Startup Corner review that we’ve been obsessed with this idea that law firms are sitting on a ton of pent-up data that could be used for a multitude of better purposes to better run the business.” One example is timesheets, which contain “insane records of experience” but are messy and not good enough for use at scale. As AI has taken off, this has become a bottleneck for firms, with Ciesla using the “garbage in, garbage out” analogy. 

“What we have done at Ayora is built data enrichment. We built a system which uses LLMs and our own proprietary tech to profile matters.” 

He says that if you go to any firm and ask “Hey, what have you done for HSBC”, they usually don’t have a central record. “They would have to call a bunch of people up and ask them,” says Ciesla, adding, “We solved that issue.” 

Ayora classifies matters across a multitude of vantage points and this “really important breakthrough” led to firms including Harneys signing up. But given the hoops that companies need to go through to get access to sensitive data, deployment became a bottleneck for Ayora in itself.  

Of the acquisition, Ciesla says: “From our point of view it just made sense because like we can go 100 times faster and benefit from all the amazing work that the team has been doing for many years.” 

BigHand has been mapping data models across law firms and already has large client relationships, which Ciesla says means that instead of a painful IT project it will become a case of, “Ok, this is a button, let’s switch it on.” 

While there is some overlap with the work that BigHand does with matter pricing, chief product officer Rob Stote said that Ayora takes pricing “to the next level, which is they now take an agentic layer and wrap that around what we’ve done with our software.” 

This will be important as firms increasingly wrangle with fixed prices or even just being increasingly held to accurate fee estimates, where they need to rely on data, not instinct. 

Going back to the breadth of the impact of the acquisition, Stote says: “I want to stress that for me, it’s not just about matter pricing. If we think about how firms make decisions, if we think about how what’s important for firms is the entire commercial spectrum, the entire operational spectrum. The technology that we’re bringing on board, overlaid on top of a lot of our products, will offer that agentic layer in the resource management space or the BI space. The way that Stefan and Gordon, the co-founder and CTO have built this technology, it allows us to very quickly put that on top of some of our other products and offer that value.” 

The value of the deal isn’t public and nor is Ayora’s ARR, so all we really know for sure is that it raised a pre-seed round in 2024 of $1.6m.

news.summaryZh: LawSHIFT公司发布了新书《预接案问题：当受伤者在寻找答案时，人身伤害律师却缺席对话》，该书由Nick Kringas和Lydia Flocchini合著，于7月1日出版。书中定义了“预接案问题™”，即受伤者在咨询律师前试图了解事件、权利和下一步行动的阶段。AI在此阶段影响力日益增强，人们使用消费级AI平台提问、评估索赔并选择律师。律师事务所在接案后的流程上投入巨大，却忽视了接案前的关键时期。LawSHIFT建立了“人身伤害预接案AI™”类别，并开发了“AI for PI Index™”，追踪AI平台如何解读、引用和推荐律所，覆盖256个市场的1500多家律所，并每周发布洞察。律所声誉需转化为AI可识别的信号，这标志着新法律推荐经济的开始。
news.bodyHtml:
New mini-book examines how AI is influencing injured people before they ever speak with an attorney

NEW YORK — July 2026 — LawSHIFT, the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, announced the launch of The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation. This new mini-book co-authored by Nick Kringas and Lydia Flocchini examines how artificial intelligence is changing the earliest stage of the legal client journey.

Published July 1, the book defines the Pre-Intake Problem™ as the period when injured people are trying to understand what happened, what their rights may be, and what to do next before speaking with legal counsel. LawSHIFT argues that AI is becoming increasingly influential during this window as people use consumer AI platforms to ask legal questions, evaluate potential claims, and decide which attorneys they may trust.

“Personal injury firms have spent decades competing for visibility after someone searches, calls, or fills out a form,” said Nick Kringas, Founder and CEO of LawSHIFT. “The most important decisions are increasingly being shaped before intake and before a lawyer ever speaks with the injured person. That is the pre-intake problem.”

Law firms have traditionally built client acquisition strategies around referrals, advertising, reputation, and search visibility. Those channels remain important, but LawSHIFT believes the client journey is being rerouted as injured people increasingly seek AI-generated guidance before contacting a firm.

“The first legal conversation is no longer always with a lawyer. Increasingly, it is with AI,” Kringas said. “The legal industry has invested heavily in improving intake once someone reaches a firm, while paying far less attention to the period when that person is still trying to understand their situation and decide whom to trust.”

LawSHIFT was built around the question of what happens before an injured person ever calls an attorney. The company has established Pre-Intake AI for PI™ as a category focused on that previously difficult-to-measure stage and has developed the AI for PI Index™, an ongoing research initiative tracking how leading AI platforms interpret, cite, and recommend personal injury firms across hundreds of U.S. markets. Drawing on data from more than 1,500 firms across 256 markets, with visibility into approximately 20,000 firms, the company publishes weekly insights examining how AI is reshaping legal visibility, authority, and client acquisition.

 

Lydia Flocchini, Partner and Legal Category Designer at LawSHIFT, said, “The client journey has already changed. A law firm’s reputation used to live in the market. Now it must also be legible to machines. Authority has to be translated into signals AI can recognize, trust, and recommend. This is the beginning of a new legal referral economy.”

“AI is not replacing personal injury attorneys, but it is increasingly shaping what injured people believe, which questions they ask, and which attorneys they consider first,” Flocchini said. “Our mission is to help close the distance between that early search for answers and trusted legal counsel.”

The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation is available now on LawSHIFT’s Substack.

 

About LawSHIFT

LawSHIFT is the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, building AI systems, visibility infrastructure, and pre-intake tools for the personal injury legal market. Founded in 2013 and headquartered in New York, the company brings together more than 50 years of combined experience across personal injury marketing, legal technology, category design, and growth strategy. LawSHIFT’s technology includes the AI for PI Index™, CASETIMATOR™, and its proprietary AI Authority Protocol™, all developed around its mission to help injured people move from early questions and AI-assisted research toward trusted legal counsel.

Media Contact
Name: Lydia Flocchini
Email: lydia@lawshift.ai

news.titleZh: 网络研讨会回放：律师事务所AI准备度的现实
news.summaryZh: 本次网络研讨会由OneAdvanced法律与专业服务高级副总裁Doug Hargrove及法律科技咨询公司Lights-On董事总经理Stephen Brown共同主持，探讨了AI在律师事务所应用中的现实挑战。讨论基于OneAdvanced年初发布的第十份法律趋势报告，并对比了七个月后的进展。议题涵盖数据问题、云迁移、AI成功衡量、网络安全风险、微软技术终止支持的影响，以及律所是否充分重新设计工作方式并提供足够培训。
news.bodyHtml:
AI can expose poor data, fragmented workflows, legacy systems, weak training, cyber risk and unclear ROI. In this webinar with OneAdvanced’s SVP for legal and professional services, Doug Hargrove, together with the managing director of legal tech consultancy Lights-On, Stephen Brown, we looked at look at some of the findings of OneAdvanced’s 10th legal trends reports at the start of the year, and how they stack up seven months on.

Are firms really ready to change the way they work, or are they still trying to bolt new technology onto old operating models? What are the data challenges firms are facing when they are looking to leverage AI solutions? How are they progressing in their cloud journeys? How are they measuring AI success? What are the unintended cyber security ramifications of AI? What are the risks around Microsoft end of lifing tech (including Outlook Classic) for firms? And are law firms sufficiently reimagining the way they work and managing the consequences of that? Are they providing enough training?

Join us for a candid conversation on all of these topics as well as some practical insights into the opportunities and realities of AI adoption today.

You can listen and watch the full webinar replay below:

news.summaryZh: 其内部自建的大型语言模型在性能上已能与全球最佳通用AI模型竞争，并发布了首批基准测试结果。7月31日，首席技术官Joel Hron和AI研究主管Jonathan Schwarz在公司创新博客上分享了名为Thomson的专有模型的早期基准数据，该模型自2024年收购AI研究初创公司Safe Sign Technologies以来一直在开发。在一系列法律和通用基准测试中，Thomson与Anthropic的Claude Opus 4.8表现相当，并领先于OpenAI的GPT-5.5、Anthropic的Claude Sonnet 5和Google的Gemini 3.1 Pro。Hron和Schwarz写道：“最强大的AI模型不再只来自前沿AI实验室。现在有一个来自汤森路透。
news.bodyHtml:
Thomson Reuters says the large language model it has been quietly building in-house now performs competitively with the best general-purpose AI models in the world, and it has released its first benchmarking results to back up the claim.

In a July 31 post on the company’s innovation blog, Chief Technology Officer Joel Hron and Head of AI Research Jonathan Schwarz shared early benchmark data for Thomson, the eponymously named proprietary model the company has been developing since its 2024 acquisition of the AI research startup Safe Sign Technologies.

Across a range of legal and general-purpose benchmarks, they wrote, Thomson performed competitively with Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5, and Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro.

“The most capable AI models no longer come only from frontier AI labs,” Hron and Schwarz wrote. “One now comes from Thomson Reuters.”

I’ll go into what the numbers actually show, how the tests were run, and what remains unverified, but first, some background on Thomson.

What Thomson Is

“Launching later this summer, Thomson is the newest layer of the Thomson Reuters AI strategy, and a demonstration of what becomes possible when authoritative content, expert judgment, professional tools, and model development come together,” Hron and Schwarz say in their post.

According to the post, Thomson starts from an open-source foundation model and is then trained, using what they describe as state-of-the-art mid-training and post-training techniques, on decades of proprietary content from Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint and Reuters.

Hundreds of subject-matter experts evaluated outputs, identified failure modes, and validated the model’s reasoning, they say, adding that customer data is never used in training.

Notably, they say that less than 10% of Thomson Reuters’ proprietary content has been used in training so far – suggesting there is plenty of room for Thomson’s capabilities to further improve.

The model’s first deployment will come in August, when Thomson becomes the default model powering Tabular Analysis in CoCounsel Legal.

Hron and Schwarz say they chose Tabular Analysis because that type of high-volume, structured document review offers a clear, measurable accuracy standard where a purpose-built model’s advantage should be immediately visible. Over the next year, they write, Thomson Reuters will integrate the model across its legal and tax product portfolio.

The Numbers

The benchmark that drove the headline pits Thomson (technically called Thomson-1-Large) against Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5 across three legal benchmarks and four general-domain composites. Thomson took the top score in three of the seven rows:

Legal domain:

  • Stanford LegalBench: Thomson 0.823 – behind Gemini 3.1 Pro (0.843) and GPT-5.5 (0.832), ahead of Opus 4.8 (0.818).
  • PrBench Legal Hard: Thomson 0.352 – best in class, ahead of GPT-5.5 (0.333), Opus 4.8 (0.315), and Gemini (0.293).
  • Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark: Thomson 0.857 – a close second to Opus 4.8 (0.869), and well ahead of Gemini (0.555).

General domain:

  • Instruction following (IFEval + FollowBench): Thomson 0.914 – best in class.
  • Reasoning (GPQA Diamond, HLE, MMLU-Pro): Thomson 0.684 – behind Gemini (0.748) and Opus (0.737).
  • Coding (SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1): Thomson 0.399 – last place, well behind Opus (0.598).
  • Long context (Infinity Bench plus internal TR benchmarks): Thomson 0.753 – best in class, by a hair over Gemini (0.750).

In their blog post, Hron and Schwarz write, “Thomson matches the best. And beats the rest.” Taking the benchmark scores at face value, that is a fair characterization, particularly given that Thomson is a fraction of the size and operating cost of the frontier models it was up against. For a domain-specific model built by a legal information company, this is a notable achievement.

But the results are more mixed than the headline suggests. Thomson did not win a majority of the rows. Gemini and GPT-5.5 both beat Thomson in the best-known legal benchmark, LegalBench. Anthropic’s Opus edged Thomson on the Harvey agentic benchmark and beat everyone on coding.

In addition, the “fine print” in the above graphic reveals that the test conditions were not entirely equal. Thomson used test-time scaling — which gives it more time and computing power. Gemini and Opus ran in the more-powerful reasoning mode, but GPT-5.5 was tested in non-reasoning mode.

While non-reasoning mode is faster and more efficient for routine tasks, it is typically less capable when handling complex, advanced or multi-step challenges. That suggests that the benchmark may have understated OpenAI’s performance.

Some Benefit to Thomson

Through a Thomson Reuters spokesperson, I asked Hron about this. He said that Thomson did, in fact, benefit from test-time scaling on certain tasks, but that the overall effect was minor. “Its grand average increased from 0.787 without test-time scaling to 0.789 with it,” he said, “and the conclusions from the benchmarks would not have materially changed without it.”

With regard to the use of non-reasoning mode for GPT-5.5, Hron said that the reasoning-mode evaluation took substantially longer to complete, and that those results were not ready in time for publication.

“We expect reasoning mode to improve its performance but based on the results we have seen so far, not dramatically,” Hron said. “We are continuing to run those evaluations and plan to include the results in the technical report.”

Hron said it is also important to note that reasoning mode and test-time scaling are not necessarily direct analogs.

“A model operating in a mode described as ‘non-reasoning’ may still benefit from test-time scaling or other inference-time techniques implemented behind the provider’s API,” he said. “Because external providers generally do not disclose the full details of those systems, we cannot know precisely which techniques were applied.

“We made a best effort to ensure a fair comparison based on the information available and disclosed Thomson’s use of test-time scaling in the interest of transparency.”

The Retrieval Test

In a second evaluation, Hron and Schwarz compared Thomson’s performance when integrated with Thomson Reuters’ proprietary content with leading frontier models given unrestricted access to the web.

Specifically, they tested completeness and factuality on 53 legal research queries written by Thomson Reuters’ internal subject-matter experts. Thomson was connected via an in-house agentic harness to Westlaw and Practical Law, while the competing frontier models were given unrestricted web access through the Brave search engine.

Completeness was scored against SME-written rubrics listing every element a good answer would require. Factuality was scored by extracting each claim in a report and checking whether the cited sources actually supported it. Scoring was done by LLMs as judges, calibrated against expert scoring.

Unsurprisingly, Thomson-plus-Westlaw beat frontier-models-plus-web-search on both dimensions.

I say “unsurprisingly” because this is less a test of the models than of the retrieval sources behind them. It seems fair to assume that, for legal research questions, a model grounded in Westlaw and Practical Law should beat a model fishing the open web. It also seems that would be true regardless of whether the model was Thomson, Opus or GPT.

In that sense, the evaluation was not so much of the Thomson model itself, but of the value of Thomson Reuters’ content it drew on. What it does not tell us is what would happen if the frontier models were given the same Westlaw access.

As Anthropic, OpenAI and others push deeper into legal workflows, and as tools such as MCP connectors make it increasingly feasible to pipe authoritative legal content into general-purpose models, that is a comparison I would like to see.

Here again, I asked Hron about this. Here is his response:

“We did test other frontier models with access to Thomson Reuters content across dimensions including factuality, completeness, conciseness, understandability, relevance and coherence. Importantly, these tests did not use the CoCounsel Legal harness, which includes a more sophisticated combination of models, tools and capabilities. Instead, we tested each model using a simpler agentic harness with native search access to our content.

“Across the four models compared, overall scores ranged from 0.81 to 0.91, with Thomson scoring 0.89. This reinforces our view of the value of authoritative Thomson Reuters content, while also demonstrating that Thomson is broadly competitive with frontier models under equivalent conditions.”

Caveats and Context

Needless to say, these benchmark results are entirely self-reported on the part of Thomson Reuters, with no mention of any independent third-party verification. Undoubtedly, as Thomson is put into wider use, there will be independent evaluations.

Hron acknowledges this in a statement the company provided: “Internal evaluations are necessary because they allow us to test against the real workflows, failure modes and quality standards our customers encounter. We also recognize the importance of credible third-party validation and expect that to be an important part of how Thomson is evaluated over time.”

When I interviewed Thomson Reuters CEO Steve Hasker in June, he talked about the development of Thomson and said one of the reasons for building it was that it provided the company with a degree of flexibility beyond reliance on the flagship LLMs.

He also talked a lot about the concept the company has been emphasizing of delivering “Fiduciary-Grade AI,” and Hohn and Schwarz use that phrase twice in their post, positioning Thomson as a development that is in furtherance of that commitment.

It might also be a signal of where the legal AI market is headed.

“These results show that the most capable AI for professional work does not have to come onlyfrom the largest frontier labs,” Hron said. “Thomson is a fraction of the size and cost of many leading models, yet it performs competitively with the strongest models available and outperforms leading models in several evaluated categories. That is what becomes possible when you build the model around the work.”

news.titleEn: When 'Agentic AI' Meets Data Protection Laws: A Fundamental Mismatch?
news.titleZh: 当“代理式人工智能”遇上数据保护法：根本性错配？
news.summaryZh: 代理式AI在金融、医疗、物流和机器人等领域已获应用，主要开发者提供预建工作流模板以加速转型。然而，其兴起揭示了机器自主性与现有法律框架之间的深刻且日益扩大的错配。GDPR和CCPA等法规的核心假设被代理式AI颠覆：个人与非个人数据的严格区分在AI交互中崩溃，同意和目的限制等原则因代理意图无法预先确定而失效。GDPR基于静态数据处理模型，要求控制者预先明确收集目的，但代理系统动态生成步骤，无法预知意图。例如，代理爬虫基于广泛目标自主导航，实时决定收集范围，使事前声明成为法律虚构。此外，AI代理持续重新利用数据，如从健身追踪器生物数据推断心理健康状况，构成未经授权的“进一步处理”，而代理无法在执行中暂停进行兼容性评估。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Agentic AI represents a seismic shift toward autonomous, goal-directed systems that can pursue open-ended objectives, create their own workflows, and adapt in real time with limited human oversight. This development poses fundamental challenges to modern privacy and data protection laws, which depend on assumptions about consent, purpose limitation, and the distinction between personal and non-personal data. This post argues that agentic AI requires a rethinking of privacy law and invites policymakers, regulators, and technology companies to consider how data protection rules should evolve for a world of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Modern agentic AI introduces a distinct paradigm shift in data protection. Agentic AI refers to autonomous, goal-seeking systems capable of pursuing open-ended objectives and adapting continuously without persistent human direction. From a cognitive perspective, AI agents are capable of learning dynamically from their environment, revising their own goals, and making decisions with minimal human oversight and control. Adaptive AI agents are already gaining traction across sectors as diverse as finance, healthcare, logistics, and robotics. To accelerate this transition, major AI developers are providing pre-built workflow templates that automate complex sequences or empower users to build custom-designed agentic architectures. However, the rise of agentic AI reveals a profound and growing mismatch between the realities of machine autonomy and the well-established legal frameworks designed to govern digital systems and protect personal privacy. Crucially, agentic AI defies the foundational assumptions underpinning data protection regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). This tension is best illustrated by two systemic challenges. First, the rigid dichotomy between personal and non-personal data (a distinction central to regulatory scope) collapses within context-hungry, AI-mediated interactions. Second, core principles governing data processing, such as consent and purpose limitation, become functionally obsolete when the fluid, indeterminate, and unpredictable intent of an autonomous agent cannot be determined ex ante. Europe’s flagship data protection regulation, the GDPR, is built on an ambition to restrain the unchecked exploitation of data. The EU aimed to empower individual consumers and curb the surveillance-capitalism models that defined the commercialized Internet. The GDPR mandates a lawful basis for processing personal data while establishing robust safeguards for data subjects such as explicit consent, lawful basis, and purpose limitation. Under this “consent and control” framework, data subjects “relinquish” absolute privacy in exchange for an enforceable regime of “data protection.” This framework relies on a fundamentally static model of data processing, wherein a human data controller pre-determines what data is collected, how it will be utilized, and when it will be deleted. As such, the GDPR operates on the assumption that controllers can clearly articulate these discrete purposes to data subjects at the point of data collection. That assumption no longer holds in the age of AI. Agentic AI systems undermine these well-established legal principles. First, autonomous systems lack a fixed, pre-programmed operational path, rendering traditional purpose-limitation rules meaningless. AI agents follow open-ended objectives and dynamically generate their own intermediary steps, workflows, and data-gathering strategies. Simply put, the actual intent and action trajectory of an AI agent cannot be known or predicted ex ante, and this characteristic of the technology is by design. This systemic unpredictability of intent can be illustrated by modern automated web intelligence, or data scraping, practices. Unlike legacy scrapers that execute deterministic scripts targeting specific data fields, an agentic crawler operates autonomously in a browser based on broad goals, such as “map regional market sentiment” or “find the top 10 trending items on Amazon.” It independently navigates the web, uses adaptive machine learning to overcome operational frictions, and dynamically decides which pathways or unindexed forums to harvest. Because its retrieval logic evolves in real time, the controller cannot know ex ante whether it will ingest personal data or cross-reference anonymous profiles. In this setting, ex ante declarations of data access intent risk becoming a legal fiction because the agent itself determines relevance and collection scope mid-execution. Second, AI agents continuously repurpose data. Their core utility lies in reapplying ingested knowledge across fluid, evolving contexts. For example, an agent with access to an individual’s biometric data from a fitness tracker might begin by monitoring step counts, but later infer a user’s mental health status, burnout levels, or cardiac conditions. Neither the developer nor the user could have predicted this outcome ex ante. Although such synthesis may be an engineering breakthrough, it may constitute an unauthorized “further processing” the GDPR was designed to prevent. Because an autonomous agent reasons non-linearly and in real time, it cannot pause mid-execution to conduct an Article 6(4) compatibility assessment before shifting the purpose of its processing.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论代理式AI对数据保护法（如GDPR和CCPA）的挑战，属于法律与AI交叉领域，核心关注法律框架如何适应AI技术，因此高度相关。

news.titleEn: IRS Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) Issues AI Guidance: Tax Professionals Also Face AI Ethics and Compliance Obligations
news.titleZh: IRS职业责任办公室发布AI指南：税务专业人士同样面临AI伦理与合规义务
news.summaryZh: 美国国税局职业责任办公室于2026年6月发布《联邦税务实践中负责任使用AI的入门指南》（警报2026-19），阐明现有《通告230》义务如何适用于使用生成式AI的税务从业者，包括律师、注册会计师和注册代理人。该警报未制定新的AI特定规则，而是将现有义务应用于AI使用，确认AI可辅助专业判断但不可替代。税务专业人士必须独立验证AI生成的内容，确保事实、引文和计算的准确性，并将AI输出视为草稿进行专业审查。此外，专业能力要求从业者理解AI系统的运作机制、局限性和风险，以避免不当建议或错误申报。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! For much of the past two years, discussions regarding generative artificial intelligence (AI) in professional services seems to have focused on lawyers, and perhaps for good reason. Courts have sanctioned attorneys who submitted briefs containing fabricated case citations. In response to these and other mishaps, several state bars issued ethics opinions often applying existing professional obligations to AI such as technological competence, confidentiality, supervision, and billing. Those same themes, however, are increasingly relevant to other professional service providers, such as tax professionals, including employee benefit plan advisors in some cases. The IRS has now made clear that ethics and compliance obligations extend well beyond litigation and the legal profession generally. In June 2026, the Internal Revenue Service’s Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) issued Introductory Guidelines for Responsible AI Use in Federal Tax Practice (Alert 2026-19), explaining how existing Circular 230 obligations apply when tax practitioners, including attorneys, certified public accountants (CPAs), and enrolled agents, use generative AI. Specifically, the Alert arises out of IRS Circular 230 which governs practice before the IRS and establishes standards of competency, diligence, ethical behavior, and procedures for discipline. Rather than creating AI-specific rules, the Alert applies these existing obligations to the use of AI. It confirms an emerging regulatory principle likely to apply across virtually every licensed profession: AI may assist professional judgment, but it may not replace it. The work of tax professionals extends well beyond Form 1040 preparation (individual federal tax return preparation). By way of example, professionals working on corporate tax issues, payroll taxes, estate taxes, and the qualified plan rules for employee benefit plans may all need to consider Alert 2026-19 when incorporating AI into their practice. The Alert offers a roadmap for ethical AI use that such professionals can adapt when performing tax-related services and advising clients. One of the central themes of the Alert is that AI-generated work must always be independently verified, a principle familiar to every practicing attorney. When using GAI, practitioners must thoroughly review all AI-created documents and language incorporated into writings before delivery to a client or submission to the IRS. Due diligence requires verifying the accuracy of facts, citations, and calculations produced by AI. Practitioners cannot rely solely on AI; human scrutiny and editing are essential to ensure correctness and compliance with IRS expectations. In short, AI-generated content should be treated as a draft requiring professional review rather than as a final work product, whether that content is a tax return filed with the IRS, a tax memorandum to the client, or a benefit plan communication addressing tax consequences. The IRS also emphasizes that professional competence increasingly requires understanding the technology itself. Practitioners must understand both the law and the technology used in their representation of clients before the IRS, including AI systems’ operational mechanics, limitations, and risks. They must understand how AI develops content, recognize the potential for bias or errors, and be able to evaluate whether AI outputs are suitable for use in IRS matters. Lack of technological competence could lead to improper advice or flawed filings. This mirrors a growing consensus among regulators and professional organizations that technological competence is no longer optional. news.titleEn: Can Government Contractors Use AI? A Legal Guide to AI Compliance and Disclosure Requirements
news.titleZh: 政府承包商能否使用人工智能？AI合规与披露要求的法律指南
news.summaryZh: 人工智能正迅速改变政府承包商的工作方式，但使用ChatGPT等工具引发法律与网络安全问题。承包商通常可使用AI，除非合同、招标、机构政策或法律禁止。联邦采购条例未全面禁止AI，但个别项目已出现限制，如2026财年国防授权法禁止使用中国深度求索的AI系统。承包商需评估合同要求、保护政府信息、遵守网络安全义务，并了解披露要求。AI使用需根据合同条款、工作性质、信息类型及机构政策判断。低风险应用如起草提案、总结文档等，在适当保障下风险较低；但用于核心合同要求时需确保满足质量要求并有人工监督。承包商对合同履行负最终责任。目前无政府层面的AI工具清单，选择工具需考虑数据敏感性，处理受控非密信息或机密数据时需更严格防护，甚至禁止使用外部AI服务。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming how government contractors develop proposals, manage contracts, write software, analyze data, and perform countless other functions. Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini promise significant gains in efficiency and productivity, but they also raise complex legal, contractual, and cybersecurity questions. As federal agencies continue to develop agency-specific AI policies and procurement requirements, contractors are increasingly asking whether they can use AI at all, whether generative AI tools are permitted under federal contracts, and what compliance obligations accompany their use. So, can government contractors use AI? The short answer is yes. Government contractors generally may use AI, including generative AI, unless a contract, solicitation, agency policy, or applicable law prohibits or limits its use. However, the legal analysis rarely ends there. Contractors must carefully evaluate contract and solicitation requirements, protect government information, comply with cybersecurity obligations, and understand when AI use may need to be disclosed to the government. In most circumstances, government contractors are permitted to use AI in performing federal contracts. Neither the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) nor most agency supplements impose a blanket prohibition on AI technologies. That said, categorical restrictions tied to specific AI systems are beginning to appear in individual acquisition programs. For example, Section 1532 of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) bars DoD contractors from using certain “covered artificial intelligence” — including AI systems developed by China-based DeepSeek — when performing on DoD contracts, showing that agency- or program-specific prohibitions can arise even without a government-wide ban. Instead, AI should be viewed like any other business technology. Whether its use is appropriate depends on the terms of the contract, the nature of the work being performed, the type of information involved, and any agency-specific policies governing contractor performance. Many contractors already use AI to draft proposal content, summarize large volumes of technical documents, analyze procurement data, generate software code, review contracts, assist with research, create reports, and automate administrative tasks. These applications often present relatively low legal risk when implemented with appropriate safeguards. Using AI to fulfill core contract requirements, however, requires considerably more scrutiny. If AI assists with engineering, software development, cybersecurity operations, technical analysis, medical services, financial decisions, or other mission-critical functions, contractors should ensure that the technology satisfies contractual quality requirements and that qualified personnel continue to provide appropriate oversight. Ultimately, contractors — not AI providers — remain responsible for contract performance. There is no government-wide list of approved or prohibited AI tools for federal contractors. Whether a contractor may use a particular platform depends on several factors, including agency guidance, contractual restrictions, information security requirements, licensing terms, and the sensitivity of the information being processed (see, e.g., The Government’s Attempted Anthropic Ban: What Government Contractors Should Be Doing Now). Many contractors use commercially available AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and enterprise AI solutions that operate within secure environments. Increasingly, organizations are also deploying internally hosted large language models that never transmit sensitive information to public AI services. The appropriate tool often depends on the data involved. Public AI platforms may be appropriate for drafting marketing materials or brainstorming internal documents, while contracts involving Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), classified information, export-controlled data, proprietary government information, or personally identifiable information typically require significantly greater safeguards — or may prohibit the use of certain external AI services altogether.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦政府承包商使用AI的法律合规问题，涉及联邦采购法规、国防授权法限制、合同义务及数据安全，属于法律与AI交叉领域，与法律AI高度相关。

news.titleEn: Alabama State Bar Issues AI Ethics Guidance for Lawyers: Key Questions and Practical Answers
news.titleZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会发布AI伦理指南：关键问题与实务解答
news.summaryZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会发布正式意见2026-01，就律师使用人工智能提供指导。该意见未创设新的道德义务，而是解释现有职业行为规则如何适用于生成式AI及新兴代理型AI工具。意见强调AI不产生新义务，而是重新定义现有义务，如能力、保密、监督、沟通、坦诚及合理收费。阿拉巴马州认可AI提升效率、降低成本及扩大法律服务获取的潜力，并指出技术能力日益包含对AI工具的理解。核心原则是律师对最终工作成果负责，即使AI协助完成。意见还涉及能力要求，包括理解AI运作方式及其能力与风险。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The Alabama State Bar has joined a growing number of jurisdictions providing formal guidance on lawyers’ use of artificial intelligence. Formal Opinion 2026-01, Artificial Intelligence Use: Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules, does not create new ethical obligations. Instead, it explains how longstanding duties under the Rules of Professional Conduct apply when lawyers use generative AI and emerging agentic AI tools in practice. Below are answers to some of the most important questions for law firms and legal departments. The opinion recognizes that AI has rapidly moved from an experimental technology to an everyday tool used to draft documents, summarize evidence, conduct research, analyze contracts, and communicate with clients. Rather than waiting for disciplinary issues to arise, the Alabama State Bar sought to explain how existing professional conduct rules govern these technologies. Importantly, the opinion emphasizes that AI does not create new ethical duties. Instead, it “recontextualizes” existing duties—including competence, confidentiality, supervision, communication, candor, and reasonable fees—in light of AI-assisted legal practice. No. To the contrary, the opinion recognizes AI’s potential to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and expand access to legal services. Alabama acknowledges that AI is becoming an ordinary component of modern legal practice and that lawyers should understand both its benefits and its limitations. The opinion also notes that as AI becomes more integrated into legal education and practice, technological competence increasingly includes understanding AI tools. The opinion consistently returns to one central principle: Lawyers remain responsible for the final work product—even when AI assisted in creating it. Among the practical expectations discussed are: The opinion explains that competent representation now includes understanding how AI works sufficiently to appreciate both its capabilities and its risks.

research.titleEn: LegalPincite: Multi-level Legal Information Retrieval Dataset
research.titleZh: LegalPincite：多层级法律信息检索数据集
research.abstractEn: A common task in legal Information Retrieval (IR) is to find relevant legal sources from case-law collections. While legal practice often requires pinpoint citations (pincites) to specific case paragraphs, most existing public legal IR datasets lack paragraph-level citation annotations. Yet, publicly available datasets with such information contain data leakage in the query text and exclude paragraphs that are neither citing nor cited from the corpora, creating an unrealistic and oversimplified retrieval setting, potentially leading to inflated performance. To address these limitations, we contribute a large-scale legal IR dataset constructed from Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) judgments. The dataset contains: (i) masked case/paragraph queries, with removed citation information; (ii) a corpus that includes all paragraphs; and (iii) case- and paragraph-level ground-truth citations, with partial human expert validation. Our dataset supports both the development and rigorous evaluation of legal IR methods, at multiple query-document levels (case-to-case, paragraph-to-case, and paragraph-to-paragraph retrieval). Link to dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite
research.abstractZh: 法律信息检索（IR）中的一个常见任务是从判例法集合中查找相关的法律来源。虽然法律实践通常需要针对特定案件段落的精确引用（pincites），但大多数现有的公开法律IR数据集缺乏段落级别的引用注释。然而，具有此类信息的公开数据集在查询文本中存在数据泄漏，并且将既未引用也未引用的段落排除在语料库之外，这造成了一种不现实且过度简化的检索环境，可能导致性能虚高。为了解决这些局限性，我们贡献了一个基于欧盟法院（CJEU）判决构建的大规模法律IR数据集。该数据集包含：（i）掩码的案件/段落查询，其中移除了引用信息；（ii）包含所有段落的语料库；以及（iii）案件级和段落级的地面真值引用，并经过部分人类专家验证。我们的数据集支持法律IR方法在多个查询-文档层级（案件到案件、段落到案件、段落到段落检索）上的开发和严格评估。数据集链接：https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite

news.titleEn: Three accounts from one wartime morning in Russia
news.titleZh: 俄罗斯战时一个早晨的三份说法
news.summaryZh: 8月2日，关于鄂木斯克附近早晨的三份说法进入公共记录，战争研究所（ISW）未加协调地转述了全部三份。其中，鄂木斯克炼油厂烟雾的报道未被标记为地理定位，而其他地点如萨拉托夫、乌法、恩格斯基地等则引用了地理定位视频。鄂木斯克州长称无人机残骸引发火灾，巴什科尔托斯坦领导人称防空击落无人机后起火，而军事博主称乌克兰无人机未到达炼油厂。俄官方反复使用“残骸坠落”等措辞，避免承认乌方打击成功。乌克兰空军记录到俄方发射133架无人机，击落109架，24架击中19处地点。网络安全、信息治理和电子发现专业人士应将其视为案例研究，关注俄方是否封锁Telegram、官方与实测进展差异、AI生成战场影像检测及官方与非官方说法分歧。

Editor’s Note: Three claims about one morning near Omsk reached the public record on Aug. 2, and the Institute for the Study of War relayed all three without reconciling them. Elsewhere in the same assessment ISW cited geolocated footage. For Omsk it did not, and that one distinction carried the whole claim.

Cybersecurity, information governance and eDiscovery professionals should read this as a case study rather than as war coverage. The failure modes are ones they already audit for: severity language drifting from the underlying artifacts, escalation paths that reward the expected answer, synthetic media offered as proof of events that did not happen, and platform-hosted evidence facing a government block with no preservation plan behind it.

Four things to watch. Whether Russia moves from charging Telegram’s founder to blocking the platform, which would put a deadline under anyone collecting from it. Whether Russia’s claimed advances keep diverging from measured ones, given that ISW puts even Moscow’s own claimed rate at about footpace. Whether AI-generated battlefield footage keeps being caught by visual analysis rather than detection tooling. And whether official and unofficial Russian accounts of the same incident keep diverging as they did here.

Industry News – Geopolitics Beat

Three accounts from one wartime morning in Russia

ComplexDiscovery Staff

Footage published Aug. 2 reportedly showed smoke rising from the Omsk Oil Refinery. The regional governor said falling drone debris had caused a fire in a field near Omsk City.

A Russian milblogger said Ukrainian drones did not reach the refinery at all. Three claims from one morning, and the Institute for the Study of War relayed all three without reconciling them.

How ISW handled them is the story. Among the sites for which its Aug. 2 assessment cited geolocated footage were a fire near the Saratov Oil Refinery, smoke at the Bashneft refinery in Ufa, a fire near the Engels-2 strategic bomber base, and smoke at a Wildberries warehouse in Samara Oblast. For Omsk, the same document said only that footage reportedly showed smoke rising from the refinery. One qualifier separates footage ISW described as geolocated from footage it only relayed, and it carries the entire evidentiary weight of the claim. Look again at the three claims and the line gets finer still. They are not even about quite the same thing. A field near Omsk City is not the refinery, and smoke is not a strike.

Where a euphemism becomes the record

Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko said drone debris caused a fire in a field near Omsk City. Radiy Khabirov, who heads the republic of Bashkortostan, said air defenses had turned back a major drone attack and downed a single drone above an industrial area of Ufa, and that a fire started afterward. Note the grammar in both. Something fell, something burned, and nobody struck anything.

Khabirov had said much the same thing the day before. On Aug. 1, after Ukraine’s security service reported striking three Bashneft refineries in Ufa, he said forces had repelled a drone strike but that a downed drone hit the city’s industrial zone. Same official, same construction, two consecutive days, two separate strike reports. ISW characterizes such claims from Russian officials as repeated, and wire copy out of Russia has carried the construction for months. A phrasing that survives that kind of repetition is not a description. It is a policy.

The complaint about it now comes from inside. On Aug. 2, a Kremlin-affiliated military blogger, or milblogger, faulted the authorities for refusing to describe the country’s situation candidly in public. His specific objection was to the vocabulary. Officials keep attributing damage to wreckage falling from intercepted drones and missiles, he said, rather than saying that Ukrainian strikes had succeeded. He added that Ukraine’s long-range strikes had not decreased for a second month running, and that a high interception rate was no guarantee of safety for infrastructure behind the lines.

What makes the euphemism effective is that debris is real. Ukraine’s own air force logged debris falls at three locations on the night of Aug. 1 to 2, when Russia launched 133 drones and loitering munitions, a mix ISW itemized as Shahed, Gerbera and Italmas strike drones, Banderol loitering munitions and Parodiya decoys. Ukrainian forces downed 109, and 24 struck 19 locations. Falling wreckage is a real category of harm, which is precisely what makes the phrase serviceable. The defect is not the word. It is using an accurate category to absorb a different event, which is harder to detect than a fabrication and considerably harder to correct later.

Records professionals should recognize the mechanism, because it does not require a war. A euphemism repeated across enough reports stops being a word choice and becomes the data. Incident reports that say “service degradation” when they mean “intrusion” produce trend analysis measuring vocabulary rather than risk. Security teams have a familiar version: severity shaved by one grade at each escalation, “no evidence of exfiltration” standing in for “we did not have the telemetry to look,” and a quarterly summary that reaches the board describing a well-managed quarter, assembled in perfect good faith from documents each defensible on its own. The corrective is unglamorous and specific. Audit the language of your incident record against the underlying artifacts on a sample basis, and treat a downgrade between tiers as an event needing its own justification rather than a routine act of summarization.

A reporting chain optimized for the answer above it

The deeper finding landed on July 31. Restating it in the Aug. 2 assessment, ISW wrote that Russia’s Northern Grouping of Forces and high military command “are likely lying to the Kremlin about the extent of Russian gains in northern Ukraine in order to further the narrative that Russian forces are actively advancing across the entire theater.” The section of front at issue has barely moved in nearly two years. Battlefield evidence does not back the claimed gains in northern Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts, ISW assessed, and Ukrainian troops have been counterattacking in some of the places Russia says it captured.

ISW assessed that the Kremlin then uses those inflated internal claims outward, as part of an effort to persuade Ukraine’s partners that the war is lost and their support is wasted. Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov described the capture of Mohrytsya, a village with a reported prewar population of about 850, as a strategic success.

The next day’s assessment put numbers to the gap. Russian forces advanced in 37.85 square kilometers of Ukraine in July 2026, an area ISW notes is smaller than Manhattan, for an average of 1.22 square kilometers a day. Counting infiltrations as well, the figure reaches about 121.56. ISW’s own year-over-year comparison is the starker one: even that combined figure is a fraction of the 455.74 square kilometers Russian forces seized in July 2025. The Ukrainian General Staff put Russian losses for July at 42,860, a monthly high for the war, which works out to 1,132 casualties for every square kilometer seized. Every derived figure in that assessment reconciles against its own base values when you run the arithmetic, which is worth saying plainly about a source this article leans on heavily.

Against that record, the Russian Defense Ministry and the Kremlin newswire TASS spent July 31 making what ISW called exaggerated claims about how many settlements had been taken in the month. Counting every advance, every infiltration and every assertion together, ISW put the rate at 18.49 square kilometers a day, and then did the thing the whole article is about. It stated what the claim would have to mean. “But even the Kremlin’s most extensive claims do not have Russian forces advancing faster than footpace, a rate of advance far slower than the Kremlin would need to collapse Ukrainian lines and rapidly seize the areas Moscow reportedly aims to capture by the end of 2026,” the Aug. 1 assessment says. The exaggeration is not manufacturing a breakthrough. It is manufacturing a slightly faster walk. ISW also assessed that the effort likely aims in part to persuade Russians that the casualties, the economic strain, the Ukrainian strikes inside Russia and the censorship have been worth it.

What makes this instructive rather than merely damning is who joined the challenge. Ukrainian formations disputed the Russian claims, as you would expect. Kremlin-aligned military bloggers did too, refuting their own side’s account in public. ISW documented the same phenomenon in January 2026 around Kupyansk, where pro-war bloggers complained about what they called beautiful reports, meaning polished claims of progress sent upward that ground conditions did not support. The consequences they described were operational: countermeasures based on a false picture, coordination failures, and casualties in the hundreds.

That is the part worth carrying into a compliance review. A reporting chain that rewards the answer leadership wants will supply that answer, and the damage does not arrive as an obvious lie. It arrives as resource allocation built on a map that no longer matches the ground.

Proof manufactured to order

The fabrication has moved past wording. On July 27, Russian sources circulated video purporting to show a Russian servicemember raising a flag at Bilyi Kolodyaz in Kharkiv Oblast, offered as confirmation the settlement had been taken. ISW assessed the footage was likely generated or altered using artificial intelligence.

The open-source research project GeoConfirmed said it identified the manipulation, and the Ukrainian mapping project DeepState reported the settlement remained under Ukrainian control. The indicators analysts described were mundane rather than exotic. The soldier vanished partway through the clip, and one researcher put his apparent width at roughly three meters before he disappeared. In a second video attributed to Khrystoforivka, analysts flagged a soldier without a helmet, a flag unfurling in the absence of wind, and a figure whose head disappeared before the rest of him did.

This is not new, and that is the point. ISW reported in May 2026 that Russian sources were increasingly distributing AI-generated flag-raising videos as offensive progress slowed, and in June assessed that flag-raising footage from Kostyantynivka and the nearby village of Dovha Balka may have been AI-generated.

Russia is working the same broad class of technology in the opposite direction at the same time, though the evidence for it is thinner and should be read that way. ISW reported on July 29 that a Ukrainian commander said Russian forces were attempting to equip Molniya fixed-wing first-person view drones with machine vision and AI-enabled targeting. On Aug. 2 it relayed an assessment by the Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, drawn from recently published photographs, that Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 drones had been reworked to house an optoelectronic guidance system, alongside a fixed camera that open-source analysts identified as a Chinese 180-degree wide-angle unit. Neither is a confirmed fielded capability. One reported line of Russian effort seeks to equip machines to identify targets from real imagery. Another circulates imagery made to be believed rather than verified. Both are running at once. That is roughly where authentication sits in ordinary commercial matters now too.

Evidence on a clock, cargo on a manifest

On July 29, Russia’s Federal Security Service charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with aiding terrorism under Article 205.1 of the Russian Criminal Code, an offense carrying a possible life sentence, and placed him on an international wanted list. The FSB said Telegram had failed to remove channels that it said Ukrainian intelligence services used to organize sabotage, killings and fraud inside Russia. Telegram declined to comment at the time. Durov has previously called comparable allegations a pretext for suppressing privacy and speech.

ISW assessed that the Kremlin is continuing to set conditions to block Telegram and to close off the open internet in Russia, and that the move may also support efforts to manage public backlash should compulsory mobilization follow. Those qualifiers are ISW’s, and they belong in any restatement of the claim.

Follow the sequence. The military reporting chain produced claims its own supporters could not accept. Those supporters said so on Telegram. The state is now positioning to remove Telegram. Whether or not suppressing that dissent is a motive, a block would have that effect, and it would arrive as a preservation problem with a deadline. Content on a platform a government is setting conditions to block is evidence on a clock. Anyone whose matters touch this record should be collecting it now, with provenance captured at collection rather than reconstructed later.

Classification does comparable work in physical logistics. Samara Oblast’s governor and the Wildberries press office both confirmed that Ukrainian forces hit one of the company’s warehouses on Aug. 2. Wildberries is a major Russian online marketplace, which ISW calls the country’s closest equivalent to Amazon, and by ISW’s count the strike was the 17th against its facilities since July 18. Separately, ISW relayed a claim from Ukrainian officials on July 30 that Wildberries logistics centers supply the Russian military with drone components and navigation equipment. Nothing in the reporting establishes that the warehouse hit in Samara Oblast held any such goods, and nothing here should be read to suggest it did. But whether a given warehouse is retail infrastructure or military logistics is a records question before it becomes a targeting question, and the answer lives in shipping documentation. Compliance teams running dual-use screening against commercial logistics data are working that same problem with lower stakes and better lawyers.

When the vacuum fills itself

The pattern repeated on Aug. 1 in central Moscow, where an improvised explosive device detonated at Balzi Rossi, an Italian restaurant on the ground floor of a Stalin-era tower. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee put the toll at three: the woman who brought the device in, wrapped as a present, a security guard, and a diner. Twenty-one people were hurt. No identities were released, and no responsible party was named.

Baza, a Russian outlet with ties to Russian law enforcement, then reported that two of the wounded had died, which put the count at five. That higher figure came from Russian media and law-enforcement-linked Telegram channels rather than from an official announcement, and Russian reporting later settled there, according to Kyiv Post and Ukrainska Pravda. The unofficial figure arrived first and held. The business daily Kommersant reported that security at the party was heavy, and that Federal Protective Service officers were there off duty. Insider Russian sources said the intended target may have been Russian Aerospace Forces Commander Col. Gen. Alexander Chayko, reportedly marking his 55th birthday. His condition went unstated for two days while those sources speculated. The Moscow Times reported on Aug. 3 that he was alive and unharmed.

Then the vacuum filled from an unexpected direction. On Aug. 3, the day this article published and a day after the assessment it draws on, the Russian Embassy in Rome blamed the bombing on what it called Kyiv terrorists, saying the attack was meant to frighten Italians working in Russia. It offered no evidence, and Ukrainian authorities had not commented. The embassy also gave a casualty count of five killed and 19 injured, a figure that does not match the 21 wounded Russia’s own National Antiterrorism Committee had reported two days earlier.

Watch what just happened to the record. For two days the official account was accurate as far as it went and silent past that point, and unofficial channels filled the silence with a death toll that later held. On the third day a diplomatic mission filled the remaining gap with an attribution and a revised injury count, neither evidenced, neither from the investigators. Incomplete records do not stay incomplete. They get completed by whoever is willing to fill them, and the filler sets the terms.

What a defensible record actually looks like

Set the Russian reporting chain beside ISW’s and the contrast is procedural rather than ideological. Every assessment carries the same published methodology statement: “ISW does not receive any classified material from any source, uses only publicly available information, and draws extensively on Russian, Ukrainian, and Western reporting and social media as well as commercially available satellite imagery and other geospatial data as the basis for these reports.”

ISW provides endnote references for the sources used in each assessment. Uncertainty is signaled through estimative language, words like likely, possibly, claimed and confirmed, so a reader can tell an observation from an inference. ISW publishes no formal confidence scale; the discipline is in the vocabulary. And each assessment states plainly what it does not cover, disclosing that ISW does not report in detail on Russian war crimes, giving its reason, and condemning those violations even while declining to document them. Publishing the boundaries of your own coverage costs almost nothing, and it is worth adopting in any reporting that someone will rely on later.

None of this is exotic. It is the same discipline behind the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations, which the Human Rights Center at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights launched in English in December 2020 and issued as a United Nations publication in 2022. It sets out how investigators should collect, assess and preserve digital open source material in cases involving international criminal, human rights and humanitarian law. It is guidance rather than law. Its value is that it made the expectations explicit, which is exactly what an organization cannot do after the fact.

Applying the same test to these sources

Fair use of that standard requires turning it on this article. ISW is not a neutral instrument; it is a Washington-based research institution with a declared position on the war, and its assessments are arguments as well as records. The milbloggers whose dissent carries much of the argument above are not auditors either. They are a pro-war constituency who want the war prosecuted harder, which gives them a motive to publicize failure that has nothing to do with candor. Ukrainian strike claims here come from Ukrainian commanders, and DeepState is a Ukrainian project. Each source is useful. None is disinterested.

Retrieval provenance matters as much. This article draws on five consecutive daily assessments, July 29 through Aug. 2. The Aug. 1 and Aug. 2 were read as raw text. The July 29, 30 and 31 assessments came through a tool that summarizes pages rather than returning them, so their wording is a paraphrase of a paraphrase. That is why nothing from those three days appears here inside quotation marks, and why all three quoted passages come from the two documents read in full. A prepublication review against the primary assessments found that same layer had stripped qualifiers from several technical claims; they were restored before publication. Figures and assessments here are current as of ISW’s Aug. 2, 2026 assessment, except for the Aug. 3 developments in Moscow, which are dated in the text. A reader is entitled to know which claims rest on which footing, and the distinction is invisible unless someone writes it down.

Which brings the question back to Omsk. Somewhere a file now records that a fire started in a field, and that record will outlive everyone’s memory of the morning. Every organization has an Omsk: an incident where the official file says one thing, the people closest to it say another, and no one reconciles the two. So the question to carry into your next audit is not whether your reports are accurate. It is whether anyone in your reporting chain is rewarded for saying so when they are not.

He added that Ukraine’s long-range strikes had not decreased for a second month running, and that a high interception rate was no guarantee of safety for infrastructure behind the lines. What makes the euphemism effective is that debris is real. Ukraine’s own air force logged debris falls at three locations on the night of Aug. 1 to 2, when Russia launched 133 drones and loitering munitions, a mix ISW itemized as Shahed, Gerbera and Italmas strike drones, Banderol loitering munitions and Parodiya decoys. Ukrainian forces downed 109, and 24 struck 19 locations. Falling wreckage is a real category of harm, which is precisely what makes the phrase serviceable. The defect is not the word. It is using an accurate category to absorb a different event, which is harder to detect than a fabrication and considerably harder to correct later.
