news.titleEn: Entegrata Hires Simpson Thacher AI Leader Andrew Baker To Head New AI Enablement Product Line
news.titleZh: Entegrata 聘请 Simpson Thacher AI 负责人 Andrew Baker 领导新 AI 赋能产品线
news.summaryZh: 法律数据公司 Entegrata 聘请 Andrew Baker 担任其首位首席 AI 与数据战略官，负责领导面向律所的新 AI 赋能产品线开发。Baker 此前在 Simpson Thacher & Bartlett 领导应用 AI 与数据科学超过五年。Entegrata 的数据湖仓平台帮助律所将分散的数据整合为单一可信源。公司正快速增长：前三年签约前10家客户，而最近六个月又签约10家，其中包括 Cleary Gottlieb、Mayer Brown、Wilson Sonsini、Mintz、Kilpatrick Townsend 和 Winston Taylor 等全球大型律所。Baldwin 于2023年创立 Entegrata，旨在解决律所数据在数十个业务系统中的碎片化问题。Baker 的加入将公司使命从商业智能扩展到支撑全所 AI 的数据层。Baker 与 Baldwin 曾在 Reed Smith 共事，Baker 后来在 Seyfarth Shaw 创立了行业首个法律技术创新办公室，并开创了法律解决方案架构师角色。他还在 HBR Consulting 共同领导法律转型与创新实践，之后在 Simpson Thacher 工作了五年半，推动数据科学与新兴技术的应用。离开律所加入供应商是为了“在行业中构建重大且持久的东西”，并指出从外部解决律所面临的共同挑战比从内部更为可行。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal data company Entegrata, whose data lakehouse platform helps law firms consolidate siloed data into a single source of truth, has hired Andrew Baker, who for more than five years led applied AI and data science at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, as its first chief AI and data strategy officer, where he will lead development of a new product line focused on AI enablement for law firms.

The appointment, announced today, comes at a time of rapid growth for the company, founder and CEO Tom Baldwin told me during an interview this week with him and Baker. “It took us three years to sign our first 10 customers,” Baldwin said. “It’s taken six months to sign the last 10.”

Among those recent signings are some of the largest firms in the world, including Cleary Gottlieb, Mayer Brown, Wilson Sonsini, Mintz, Kilpatrick Townsend, and Winston Taylor.

As I reported last year when Entegrata raised $4.5 million in seed funding, Baldwin — the former CIO or CKO at firms including Cadwalader, Reed Smith and Sheppard Mullin — founded the company in 2023 to address the fragmentation of law firm data across dozens of business systems, consolidating it within a purpose-built data lakehouse.

With Baker’s hire, the company is extending that mission from business intelligence into the data layer that underpins firm-wide AI.

A Reunion Two Decades in the Making

For Baldwin and Baker, the hire is something of a reunion. The two worked together at Reed Smith in the early 2010s, when Baldwin was running pricing, legal project management and other functions there and, as he tells it, went looking for “a unicorn in the form of a JD black belt” in process improvement, and found Baker’s profile on LinkedIn.

Baker later returned to Seyfarth Shaw, where he had previously worked, to help launch that firm’s innovation program. There, he founded what Entegrata says was the industry’s first legal technology innovations office and pioneered the legal solutions architect role.

He went on to co-lead the legal transformation and innovation practice at HBR Consulting (now Harbor) before joining Simpson Thacher, where he has spent the last five-and-a-half years advancing the firm’s use of data science and emerging technology. Along the way, he earned a master’s degree in applied data science.

“I’ve been hunkered down at this intersection of law, data, tech and strategy for quite some time,” Baker said.

So why leave what he called “probably one of the cooler jobs in a law firm that you could ask for” to join a vendor?

“It’s really about the opportunity to build something big and lasting in the industry,” Baker said. “I spent a lot of time in pretty much every vendor tool that’s out there, a lot of time working with teams to build custom solutions within our firm, and I feel like I have a pretty clear understanding of where the hard edges are on each of those. And we keep running into the same challenges over and over.”

Solving those challenges from inside a single firm is daunting, he said, but it is a different ballgame from the outside.

“When you think about where you want to put your time and energy if you’re doing technical work in a law firm, it’s not on the plumbing and the data ecosystem,” he said. “It’s building the cool, exciting, creative things.”

What ‘AI Enablement’ Means

In his new role, Baker will own Entegrata’s AI roadmap across engineering, product and customer experience, with his central focus on a new product line the company describes as AI enablement.

To date, Baker said, Entegrata has been adjacent to the AI story — its data could be put to creative use, but AI was one step removed from the core product.

“This next chapter in the book brings Entegrata straight to the coalface on everything AI-related,” he said. Whatever firms are pursuing — model routing, autonomous agents, custom development — “none of those can be executed very well without the right kind of content or context to make that happen.”

The goal, he said, is “providing a framework and layer to help people truly do that, and moving beyond theory into pragmatism.”

Baldwin says the product vision centers around what he calls the four Cs: content, context, cost control and choice. The idea is to give AI tools richer content and context drawn from across a firm’s systems, provide firms observability into AI costs, and preserve their ability to swap in new models and tools as the market shifts, without starting over each time.

“To be clear, we are not building yet another AI model or product,” Baldwin said. “We’re enabling deeper context and giving more content to the existing tools firms have” — he named Harvey, Legora and Deep Judge as examples — “and creating that downstream off-ramp to different tools as they become available.”

Central to the effort is an ontology for legal data that the company is currently building, layered on top of a schema that Baldwin said already contains some 5,000 fields. (When I wrote about the company last year, that schema had 3,500 fields.)

The ontology is designed to capture the full web of relationships within a firm — the “360-degree view” that connects a document to a timekeeper, the timekeeper to a matter, the matter to a client, and outward to industry, jurisdiction, judge and opposing counsel.

“You lose all of that context the minute you take a document out of the DMS and manually upload it into an AI tool,” Baldwin said. “We bring that all back and throw an ontology on top of it.”

He drew a comparison to the much-discussed partnership between Kirkland & Ellis and Palantir. “Long term, this is going to be an offering that’s going to feel very Kirkland-esque in terms of the capabilities, but at a fraction of the time and cost that it’ll take to implement something like Palantir.”

The Data Layer as the Bottleneck

Both men agree that the data layer has become the choke point for firms trying to move beyond their first wave of generative AI deployments.

In the early rush, Baldwin said, firms were under enormous pressure simply to get AI up and running, in part so they could say they were using it.

Now that firms have had time to settle into it, he said, the next stage of maturity is “moving beyond the disconnected download-documents-out-of-the-DM, upload-them-manually-into-an-AI-tool” workflow toward AI that can run on the firm’s full data estate. He said the last six firms Entegrata signed all characterized their moves as being about AI readiness and enablement.

The challenge for law firms, Baldwin said, differs from other industries. “The challenge isn’t in depth and speed. We don’t have petabytes of real-time streaming from one or two ERP sources. Our challenge is width. It’s stitching together data from 20 or 30 systems.”

Baker made a similar point about leading practice-of-law AI platforms. “The Harveys and Legoras of the world are fantastic for helping firms move quickly,” he said. “The challenge you run into is that they all have hard edges.” Firms whose practices do not fit neatly within those boundaries — or that want to rethink a practice’s economics or go-to-market approach — quickly find themselves breaking through them.

“Right now, there are a number of solutions that are focused on retrieval, and some of them do a really good job,” Baker said. “But that next hop over — how do we analyze, synthesize and create anew — it’s hard to get the data in the right structure for that. And we think we can do that in a way that others really can’t.”

As an example of what this can mean for customers, Baldwin said that for one of its largest customers, a 2,000-lawyer firm, Entegrata is building an AI tool for just three people in firm leadership designed to answer the questions that, as he put it, the people who sign everyone’s checks care about.

“It’s the opposite of, ‘I’m a third-year associate grinding through this asset purchase agreement draft,'” he said. “It’s, ‘I’m the chair of the firm and I want to know directionally where the firm’s headed.'”

Baker’s Remit

Baldwin described Baker’s mandate as spanning three buckets. First and foremost is architecting the new AI enablement product line. Second, with law firms increasingly hiring for net-new data and AI leadership roles, Baker will offer his playbook as a service to firms just standing up applied AI functions — drawing on his consulting experience at Harbor in making what works at one firm portable to many. Third, he will take over much of the data strategy engagement work that Baldwin has been leading himself.

“Andrew has lived this problem from inside one of the most prestigious firms on the planet, so he knows what it takes to make AI dependable across a real practice,” Baldwin said.

“His mandate is simple: prepare firm data and context so any model or tool it chooses actually delivers. That is the layer most of the industry is still missing, and it is what Andrew will build for our clients.”

Baker will be at ILTACON in Nashville, Aug. 23-27, where he hopes to meet with firms to discuss the intersection of data strategy and AI.
news.bodyText: The legal data company Entegrata, whose data lakehouse platform helps law firms consolidate siloed data into a single source of truth, has hired Andrew Baker, who for more than five years led applied AI and data science at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, as its first chief AI and data strategy officer, where he will lead development of a new product line focused on AI enablement for law firms. The appointment, announced today, comes at a time of rapid growth for the company, founder and CEO Tom Baldwin told me during an interview this week with him and Baker. “It took us three years to sign our first 10 customers,” Baldwin said. “It’s taken six months to sign the last 10.” Among those recent signings are some of the largest firms in the world, including Cleary Gottlieb, Mayer Brown, Wilson Sonsini, Mintz, Kilpatrick Townsend, and Winston Taylor. As I reported last year when Entegrata raised $4.5 million in seed funding, Baldwin — the former CIO or CKO at firms including Cadwalader, Reed Smith and Sheppard Mullin — founded the company in 2023 to address the fragmentation of law firm data across dozens of business systems, consolidating it within a purpose-built data lakehouse. With Baker’s hire, the company is extending that mission from business intelligence into the data layer that underpins firm-wide AI. For Baldwin and Baker, the hire is something of a reunion. The two worked together at Reed Smith in the early 2010s, when Baldwin was running pricing, legal project management and other functions there and, as he tells it, went looking for “a unicorn in the form of a JD black belt” in process improvement, and found Baker’s profile on LinkedIn. Baker later returned to Seyfarth Shaw, where he had previously worked, to help launch that firm’s innovation program. There, he founded what Entegrata says was the industry’s first legal technology innovations office and pioneered the legal solutions architect role. He went on to co-lead the legal transformation and innovation practice at HBR Consulting (now Harbor) before joining Simpson Thacher, where he has spent the last five-and-a-half years advancing the firm’s use of data science and emerging technology. Along the way, he earned a master’s degree in applied data science. “I’ve been hunkered down at this intersection of law, data, tech and strategy for quite some time,” Baker said. So why leave what he called “probably one of the cooler jobs in a law firm that you could ask for” to join a vendor? “It’s really about the opportunity to build something big and lasting in the industry,” Baker said. “I spent a lot of time in pretty much every vendor tool that’s out there, a lot of time working with teams to build custom solutions within our firm, and I feel like I have a pretty clear understanding of where the hard edges are on each of those. And we keep running into the same challenges over and over.” Solving those challenges from inside a single firm is daunting, he said, but it is a different ballgame from the outside.

news.titleEn: LexisNexis posts fastest growth in its history, powered by AI products
news.titleZh: LexisNexis 创历史最快增长，AI 产品驱动业绩
news.summaryZh: RELX 旗下 LexisNexis Legal & Professional 公布创纪录半年业绩，基础收入增长 7%，调整后营业利润增长 9%，调整后每股收益增长 11%。LexisNexis 是 RELX 增长最快的部门，基础收入增速从 2025 年的 9% 提升至上半年的 10%，创历史新高。收入达 9.59 亿英镑，高于去年同期的 9 亿英镑；调整后营业利润增长 13% 至 2.08 亿英镑。90% 的新业务来自 AI 相关产品，主要驱动力是 Lexis+ with Protégé，Protégé 品牌已包含 15 个生成式 AI 产品。增长覆盖所有地区，多模型方法和自有专有数据集是关键差异化因素。LexisNexis 拥有无截止日期的记录、数据源和法院链接，可借助小型模型获得更优结果并有效管理成本。在技术供应商转向按用量计费模式的趋势下，LexisNexis 无此计划，其代币成本占比不足 1%，客户偏好订阅制。客户满意度而非股价才是关键指标，公司专注于打造优质产品，这是公司历史上增长最快的产品，利润率和增长均在提升。
news.bodyHtml:
RELX, the parent company of LexisNexis Legal & Professional, today (23 July) announced record half-year results, with underlying revenues up 7%; adjusted operating profit up 9%; and adjusted earnings per share up 11%.  LexisNexis was RELX’s fastest-growing division, with underlying revenues accelerating from 9% in 2025 to 10% in the first half, the fastest growth rate in its history. LexisNexis revenues reached a record £959m, up from £900m in the same period last year. In dollar terms, it added about $78m in the period or $156m on an annualised basis. Adjusted operating profits increased 13% to £208m.  

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, Sean Fitzpatrick, CEO of LexisNexis for North America, UK and Ireland, said that 90% of new business for LexisNexis came from AI related products. The primary driver is Lexis+ with Protégé, but LexisNexis continues to grow the Protégé brand, which now includes 15 generative AI products, including Intelligize and PatentSight.  

Advertisement

Fitzpatrick says that growth came across all geographies and that the real differentiator has been LexisNexis’ multi-model approach, which it has taken from the beginning. “We use the model that gives the customer the best answer,” he said.  

Also key has been LexisNexis’ ability to leverage its own proprietary data set. Fitzpatrick said that LexisNexis’ has unparalleled records, data sources and court links “with no cut off dates” and continuous updates. “Because we have that repository, we can get better results with smaller models,” he said. “You don’t have to search every corner of the internet, and we can manage our costs more effectively.” 

Advertisement

What this is driving towards, as tech vendors move to a consumption rather than subscription model for token use, is that LexisNexis is not under pressure to do the same, with token costs representing less than 1% of its costs. 

“While others are talking about moving to a consumption model, we don’t have any plans to do that, and our customers really like that,” Fitzpatrick said. Customers are inevitably worried about the impact of financial unpredictability, and Fitzpatrick references one conversation where the customer had anticipated costs of $300,000 from one vendor but ended up with a bill of $500,000. “That can have a big impact and we don’t have the need to do that at this point,” he says. 

In terms of what ‘at this point’ might mean, Fitzpatrick points out that LexisNexis is entering three-year contracts with customers that provide subscription-based billing, which in term terms is about as much of a cushion as you’re ever likely to get. 

Taking a high level view of today’s announcement, results can be a double edged sword in a world where tech vendors are accused of charging too much money. What they will do is reassure the market that customers are voting with their wallets, even if you can’t always see it.  

The results will also be welcome following a drove of headlines around LexisNexis’ stock price plunging in the aftermath of Anthropic launching its own legal tool. “The indicator we need to worry about is customer satisfaction, not the stock price,” says Fitzpatrick. “We are focusing on creating great products for customers, and this is the fastest growing product in the history of the company. We’re seeing an increase in growth and profit margins. Stock prices are based on the present value of future cashflow and everything we’re doing will translate to a good stock price.” 

The stock market plunge led to a vast number of conversations around the durability of LexisNexis data moat and a focus on its partnerships with Anthropic and Harvey, which were two of the developments in the year to cause perhaps the most headlines. How have they impacted on financial performance?  

Fitzpatrick says: “We’ve been working with Anthropic since the beginning, in fact I think the first invoice they issued was to LexisNexis. We have a special relationship and we get access to their models and engineers so that we can use their technology in our products and get the legal skills they are building. We can take those skills and rebuild them in Protégé, grounded in our authoritative content. If you just use those skills from Anthropic, you will just be getting the information from their LLM with a cut off date, and it’s way more powerful in our system.” 

With regard to Harvey, Fiztpatrick says: “We have a Harvey agreement and we also for that matter have a Luminance agreement. They are licensing not our content but our AI technology. If you are a Luminance Lumi customer, you can go to Lumi and ask a legal research question that will be encrypted and sent to Protégé, then answered back in Lumi, so that the attorney can see it, but Lumi can’t because it’s encrypted. 

“We want customers to have access to our content wherever they may be.”   

With so much market focus on legal tech companies that are borrowing (and spending) VC money hand over fist, it is no surprise that LexisNexis is shouting about its financial position today.

Paul Abrahams, chief communications officer of RELX told Legal IT Insider: “RELX generated $3bn of cashflow after we invested capex in new product and after a spend of $2.5bn in IT. This is a hugely profitable organisation able to fund itself without debt or equity markets and without relying on incredibly fickle VC investors.”

news.titleEn: Choosing Between U.S. and Chinese AI Models: The Export Control Risks on Both Sides
news.titleZh: 选择美国还是中国AI模型：双方的出口管制风险
news.summaryZh: 随着企业面临越来越多的AI解决方案选择，AI模型的监管限制与其能力同等重要。在G7峰会上，马克龙警告美国可能随时切断AI供应，而6月12日美国商务部确实通过未公开信函要求Anthropic暂停其前沿AI模型Fable 5和Mythos 5的全球访问，援引《出口管制改革法》和EAR军事-情报最终用途管制。后续信函允许部分可信合作伙伴访问，但Mythos仍限于美国机构。与此同时，中国实验室持续发布模型：7月16日Moonshot AI发布Kimi K3，成为首个在主要编程排行榜上超越Fable 5和GPT-5.6的中国模型；Z.ai的GLM-5.2以MIT许可证开放权重，被NIST评为当时最强大的开放权重模型。中国模型虽在能力上仍有差距，但更便宜、可下载且不受美国开关控制，然而它们受制于另一套未知风险。若企业涉及美国出口管制，使用DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM或Kimi等中国模型本身可能产生违规风险。中国开放权重模型已从新奇事物变为默认基础设施：2026年中，中国模型处理OpenRouter约61%的token，阿里Qwen系列下载量超10亿，占Hugging Face新衍生模型的40%。美国政府对DeepSeek的评估显示其下载量自2025年1月增长近1000%。NIST发现DeepSeek V4 Pro落后前沿约8个月，GLM-5.2与约6个月前发布的美国模型相当。结构性差异在于：美国领先模型通过API封闭访问，可被开发者或美国政府限制或切断；中国领先模型可下载并托管于全球任何地方。美国和中国控制约90%的前沿AI开发算力，以及全部50个顶级基础模型。2025年美国发布59个显著模型，中国35个，其他国家均不超过8个。法国Mistral是唯一接近前沿的第三方实验室，但其当前旗舰模型仅为强开放权重模型，而非前沿模型。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As companies choose between an increasing range of AI solutions, the regulatory restrictions on the AI model may be as important as the capabilities of the AI model. At the G7 summit in June, over a lunch attended by President Trump and the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI, President Macron warned that if the United States “from one day to the next can turn off the switch,” it would damage not only the economies building on American AI, but also the American AI companies themselves. He was not speaking hypothetically. On June 12, the Commerce Department used export controls to order Anthropic to suspend access to its newest frontier AI models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, just days after their release. The order came not as a rule or a published directive but as an unpublished letter requiring export licenses before the models could be made available to any foreign person worldwide, reportedly invoking the Export Control Reform Act and the EAR's military-intelligence end-use controls.[1] A follow-up letter on June 26 carved out “certain trusted partners,” and access to Fable returned on July 1 with additional safeguards, while Mythos remains limited to approved U.S. institutions. Nothing about the episode ever appeared in the Federal Register. For three weeks, the most capable AI models ever released were switched off for most of the planet, and the switch was flipped by a letter. Meanwhile, the Chinese labs keep shipping. On July 16, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, which became the first Chinese model to top a major coding leaderboard ahead of both Fable 5 and GPT-5.6; Moonshot has promised to open source full model weights by July 27. That release follows Z.ai's GLM-5.2, released mid-June with open weights under an MIT license, which NIST's own AI evaluators judged “probably the most capable open-weight AI model” at its release. Whatever those models still lack against their U.S. counterparts, they compensate for by being cheaper, downloadable, and free of an American off switch. They are not, however, free of switches. They come wired to a different panel, in a different capital, with its own set of unknown risks. Additionally, if your business has U.S. export control exposure, how your company interacts with a Chinese AI model like DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi can itself create violation risk. Being model agnostic is not, by itself, an answer. U.S. models and Chinese models each come with a distinct set of legal tripwires, and the right procurement decision depends on which set your operations can tolerate. Chinese open-weight models have gone from novelty to default infrastructure in the last eighteen months. In mid-2026, Chinese models account for roughly 61% of tokens processed on OpenRouter, a major model-routing platform, and Alibaba's Qwen family has passed one billion downloads and forms the base of roughly 40% of new derivative models on Hugging Face. The U.S. government's own evaluation of DeepSeek noted that downloads of DeepSeek models had grown nearly 1,000% since January 2025. Whether Chinese models have “caught up” depends on who is doing the measuring, but the gap is now months, not years, and it is narrowing at the top. NIST’s CAISI found DeepSeek V4 Pro roughly eight months behind the frontier in May 2026, and in July 2026 judged GLM-5.2 comparable overall to a U.S. model released about six months earlier (Opus 4.6). Kimi K3’s leaderboard results suggest an even shorter end of that range. What is not contested is the structural difference: the leading U.S. models are closed and accessed through APIs that their developers (and, increasingly, the U.S. government) can condition or cut off. The leading Chinese models can be downloaded and hosted anywhere on the globe, which changes both the risk profile and the legal analysis. If you are holding out for a third option wired to neither D.C. nor Beijing, we have unhelpful news. The United States and China control roughly 90% of the computing power used for frontier AI development, and, by one count, all 50 of the top-ranked foundation models. Stanford's AI Index credits U.S. organizations with 59 notable model releases in 2025 and China with 35, with no other country reaching more than eight. France’s Mistral is the only third-country lab consistently described as near-frontier, but its current flagship evaluates as a strong open-weight model, not a frontier one.

news.titleEn: AI Agents A Top 2026 Cybersecurity Threat
news.titleZh: AI代理被列为2026年顶级网络安全威胁
news.summaryZh: 网络安全公司Forrester发布《2026年顶级网络安全威胁》年度报告，预测组织面临的最关键风险。AI模型广泛可及、AI工具与代理能够摄取海量数据并高速学习与运作，是威胁的根源。这些能力使网络攻击自动化与规模化、影子AI超出组织治理范围、供应链风险加剧，进而引发合规问题、削弱控制力并增加整体网络风险。实施稳健的AI治理计划是2026年的关键战略优先事项。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Cybersecurity firm Forrester recently issued its annual report, Top Cybersecurity Threats in 2026, which outlines “the most critical risks organizations need to plan for.” The report predicts the top threats that organizations will face in 2026 based on recent trends and observations. The top five threats expected in 2026 include: The threats listed above stem from the widespread accessibility of AI models and the ability for AI tools and AI agents to ingest vast amounts of data, learn from it, and operate at unprecedented speed and scale. These capabilities enable the automation and expansion of increasingly sophisticated cybersecurity attacks, the use of shadow AI beyond an organization’s governance and visibility, and heightened supply chain risks. Together, these challenges create significant compliance concerns, reduce organizational control, and increase overall cybersecurity exposure. news.titleEn: New PTAB Challenge Targets Zhuhai CosMX Battery Patent
news.titleZh: 新PTAB挑战针对珠海冠宇电池专利
news.summaryZh: 2026年7月22日，专利审判与上诉委员会（PTAB）收到一份新的多方复审请求（IPR2026-00401），针对珠海冠宇电池有限公司的专利。该案件涉及电池技术专利纠纷，对能源存储和电子供应链企业具有影响。具体专利号、权利要求、请求人及无效理由需待申请材料公布。该复审请求依据35 U.S.C. §§ 102和/或103，要求PTAB基于在先专利和出版物重新评估已授权专利的有效性。电池领域的IPR案件因技术发展迅速且商业竞争激烈而尤为重要，PTAB的立案决定可能影响平行诉讼、许可谈判、供应商关系及自由实施评估。专利从业者应关注该案件，以了解电池技术中的显而易见性论证、专家证言处理方式及可充电电池市场的竞争态势。
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要报道PTAB的专利无效程序，涉及电池技术专利，但未聚焦法律AI或法律科技，仅与专利法律程序相关，属于法律领域但非AI或科技核心。

news.titleEn: Meta Seeks Ninth Circuit Stay of District Court Proceedings During Appeal
news.titleZh: Meta寻求第九巡回法院在上诉期间暂停地区法院诉讼程序
news.summaryZh: Meta Platforms已向第九巡回法院提交“暂停诉讼程序动议”，要求在上诉期间停止地区法院的诉讼活动。该动议旨在维持现状，避免在地区法院继续推进诉讼（包括证据开示、动议实践或实体审理）造成不可弥补的损害，尤其是当上诉涉及管辖权、豁免权、可仲裁性或关键中间命令的可上诉性等门槛问题时。法院通常评估四个因素：上诉胜诉可能性、无暂停时的不可弥补损害、暂停对其他当事人的损害以及公共利益。该动议揭示了Meta认为具有决定性意义的上诉问题，并可能影响和解谈判、证据开示时间表、案件预算及相关案件。在科技诉讼中，证据开示成本高昂且敏感，暂停动议成为重要战略战场。此案提醒律师，上诉动议实践可能决定案件是加速进入实体裁决还是在关键转折点暂停。
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论Meta在第九巡回法院寻求暂停地区法院诉讼程序的法律动议，属于一般诉讼程序策略，未涉及法律AI或法律科技内容。

news.titleEn: Legal Data Governance Startup Entegrata Hires Simpson Thatcher, Seyfarth Alum for AI Role
news.titleZh: 法律数据治理初创公司Entegrata聘请Simpson Thatcher和Seyfarth前高管担任AI职务
news.summaryZh: 法律数据治理与分析公司Entegrata宣布任命Andrew Baker为首席人工智能与数据战略官。Baker此前担任Simpson Thatcher & Bartlett的分析与AI应用总监，并曾在Seyfarth Shaw、Reed Smith等律所以及HBR和LexPredict咨询公司任职。在新职位上，Baker将负责领导Entegrata的AI赋能产品线，与工程、产品和客户成功团队协作，帮助律所客户以更利于利用AI系统的方式存储和结构化数据。加入Entegrata能让他解决工作中遇到的工具孤岛和缺乏统一数据基础等问题，这些限制了AI系统的投资回报。他还将负责监督Entegrata的AI路线图，重点帮助律所更好地利用非结构化数据。Entegrata于2025年3月完成450万美元种子轮融资，并于2026年3月发布了Admin App平台。

# Legal Data Governance Startup Entegrata Hires Simpson Thatcher, Seyfarth Alum for AI Role

Andrew Baker will help law firm customers with AI enablement in a position that spans engineering, product and customer success responsibilities.

3 minute read July 23, 2026 at 06:00 AM

By

![Image 18](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b683f4b314e480bc994cab5d8feb663b?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Benjamin Joyner](http://www.law.com/author/profile/benjamin-joyner/)

## What You Need to Know

*   Legal data governance company Entegrata announced the appointment of Andrew Baker as chief AI & data strategy officer.
*   Baker previously worked at Simpson Thatcher, Seyfarth Shaw and Reed Smith.
*   He will be responsible for leading Entegrata's AI roadmap and helping law firm customers with AI enablement.

![Image 19: Entegrata logo.](https://images.law.com/assets/28/77/41d59b7b433fac2072d0894fb414/entegrata-jpg767x505.jpg)Entegrata logo.
Legal data governance and analytics company Entegrata announced Thursday the appointment of Andrew Baker as chief artificial intelligence and data strategy officer. Baker was most recently director of applied analytics and AI at Simpson Thatcher & Bartlett and previously worked at firms Seyfarth Shaw and Reed Smith, and consultancies HBR and LexPredict.

In his new role, Baker will be responsible for leading Entegrata’s AI enablement product line, working with engineering, product and customer success teams. He will be tasked with helping the company’s law firm customers store and structure their data in ways that allow them to better leverage AI systems.

Baker told Law.com that it was a hard choice to leave Simpson Thatcher, but the position with Entegrata represented a synthesis of work he’s done over the past decade relating to the interaction between data and AI, describing the opportunity as “a unique moment in time, unique problem set, and a unique platform to create some real meaningful change in in the market.”

He added that working with Entegrata would allow him to help firms tackle issues he’s seen in his work, which include siloed tools and a lack of a common data foundation that limits the return on investments from AI systems.

“You've got a situation where you've got an archipelago of disconnected tools that are spread out, and there really should be some connecting tissue in the background from a data standpoint that allows firms to get more from their use of generative AI and have that compounding effect through use over time,” he said.

As part of his position, Baker will be tasked with overseeing Entegrata’s AI roadmap, part of which will focus on helping firms make better use of data not included in structured data sources many AI tools draw on today.

“We're going to move into semi-structured and unstructured data in a more direct manner, and that requires drawing additional meaning from that content and getting it prepped and ready for applications,” he said. “It's going to be a little bit of both centralizing and trying to create a more consistent pool to draw from, but also adding structure to that ... to allow not just people to pull back and find data that's relevant, but actually conduct analysis on top of that.”

Entegrata [raised](https://www.law.com/2025/03/21/legalweek-2025-pre-show-news-rundown-entegrata-raises-45-million-sterne-kessler-launches-ai-patent-drafting-tool-and-more-/) a $4.5 million seed funding round in March 2025 and [released](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/03/09/legalweek-2026-pre-show-news-rundown-relativity-announces-brand-refresh-epiq-expands-agentic-ai-suite-and-more-/) Admin App, a centralized platform designed to connect law firm systems, in March of this year.

news.summaryZh: DecoverAI于2026年6月发布的工作论文测试了九种大语言模型在100份文档响应性分类任务中的表现。结果显示，最昂贵的模型（Anthropic的claude-opus-4-8，每份文档0.0813美元）F1得分仅为0.760，排名倒数第二；而最便宜的模型（DeepSeek V4 Pro，每份文档0.0027美元）F1得分为0.815，被论文指定为价值操作点。得分最高的模型是Qwen 3.6 Plus（F1=0.868，每份文档0.0205美元）。在10万份文档规模下，最高价与最低价模型之间的成本差为7860美元，相当于约52小时合同律师质量控制费用。买家为高价模型支付的是品牌溢价而非性能。然而，该基准测试仅基于100份文档的单次运行，论文自身标注为“指示性，未经审计”。论文未公布数据集、标注协议、分类指令、模型设置、推理路径、token计数、原始预测或重复运行结果，因此排名和成本无法独立复现。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A vendor benchmark landed in June with a finding built to unsettle procurement assumptions: the highest-cost model among nine tested for legal document classification finished second to last, while models costing a fraction of its price clustered near the top. DecoverAI’s working paper argues that review architecture, not model capability, sets the accuracy ceiling, an interpretation its single-pipeline design cannot prove, and two other provider studies offer related though limited support.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, the stakes are concrete. Inadvertent production of privileged material can implicate Federal Rule of Evidence 502, and amended Rule 26(f)(3)(D), effective Dec. 1, 2025, requires early views and proposals on privilege claim timing and method, which means model choice and validation evidence may surface in meet-and-confer sessions. The paper also leaves questions open, from its 100-document single-run sample and unpublished methodological details to the governance implications of routing privileged material to models from Chinese developers.

Watch for privilege-specific benchmarks, court scrutiny of AI-assisted privilege logs, and controlled validation runs to become standard requests in the year ahead.

Industry News – eDiscovery Beat

On a 100-document responsiveness test, model price did not predict accuracy

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

The highest-cost model tested in a new nine-model legal AI benchmark finished next to last. The cheapest one, priced 68 times lower, landed 0.075 behind the leader on the study’s F1 score.

Those results anchor a working paper published in June 2026 by DecoverAI, a San Mateo, California-based eDiscovery vendor, and they carry an uncomfortable message for legal teams that equate model price with review quality. On this test, the paper concludes, buyers of the top-priced option were “paying a premium for brand rather than performance.”

What the benchmark measured

Decover Research Working Paper 2026-02 tested nine large language models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Anthropic on a fixed 100-document responsiveness classification task with a gold-labeled answer key of 27 responsive and 73 nonresponsive documents. The vendor ran its own two-step production pipeline for every model, changing only the model underneath, and metered cost from actual token usage at June 2026 prices.

Eight of the nine models landed inside an 11-point F1 band, from 0.76 to 0.87, across a per-document cost spread from $0.0012 to $0.0813. Qwen 3.6 Plus posted the best F1 score, 0.868, at $0.0205 per document. Anthropic’s claude-opus-4-8, the highest-cost model tested at $0.0813 per document, scored 0.760, second-lowest in the study and below models costing 30 times less. DeepSeek V4 Pro delivered an F1 of 0.815, with precision and recall balanced at 0.815 each, for $0.0027 per document, which the paper designates its value operating point.

At 100,000 documents, the paper calculates, the spread between that value option ($270) and the highest-cost model ($8,130) is $7,860, which it equates to roughly 52 hours of contract attorney quality control at $150 per hour.

Read the fine print before repeating the numbers

The caveats deserve as much attention as the rankings. The benchmark is a single run over 100 documents, which the paper itself labels “indicative, not audited.” Small samples produce wide confidence intervals, and a handful of borderline documents could reorder the middle of the table.

The paper also does not publish the dataset, the labeling protocol, the classification instructions, model settings, the inference route, token counts, raw predictions or repeated-run results. Without those materials, neither the observed rankings nor the per-document costs can be independently reproduced.

The scope note contains a larger qualification: this is a responsiveness benchmark, not a privilege benchmark, despite the paper’s title. Privilege calls are harder and more judgment-intensive, and Decover acknowledges model rankings may differ on a privilege-specific gold set, which it says it is building as a follow-on study.

The design limits run deeper than sample size. Because the test held Decover’s pipeline constant and compared no alternative architectures, it shows only that most models clustered within this pipeline on this 100-document set. It does not establish that architecture caused the clustering, that the observed F1 range transfers to other collections, or that a model upgrade could not improve performance elsewhere. And Decover sells the pipeline credited with producing the plateau, which gives its preferred interpretation, that architecture rather than model choice sets the accuracy ceiling, a commercial interest. Buyers should treat the paper as vendor-published research making a testable claim, not as an audited independent evaluation.

The precision finding is the practical headline

For privilege review, the paper’s most useful contribution may be its warning about precision. One model, Anthropic’s claude-sonnet-4-6, achieved the highest recall in the study at 96.3 percent but flagged 58 documents as responsive when only 27 were, a precision score of 0.448. Fewer than half of its positive calls were correct.

That figure is responsiveness precision measured on this one set. It does not establish what the model’s precision would be on privilege classification, and the paper’s model-specific privilege recommendations remain hypotheses awaiting a privilege-labeled test. The conceptual point survives the caveat, though, because the error asymmetry is specific to privilege work. A missed privileged document risks inadvertent waiver, though Federal Rule of Evidence 502(b) protects against waiver where the disclosure was inadvertent, the holder took reasonable steps to prevent it, and the holder promptly took reasonable steps to rectify the error. An over-inclusive model creates the opposite problem: it can produce a privilege log padded with improper withholding claims, inviting entry-by-entry challenges and, in some circumstances, sanctions requests. The paper argues a reasonable recall rate paired with high precision produces a more defensible log than maximum recall at low precision, and recommends avoiding any model with precision below 0.75 for privilege classification without attorney review of every positive call.

Two other provider studies offer related evidence, with limits

Neither supporting study is disinterested; both come from companies with products in the fight, and each supports a narrower proposition than Decover’s. Percipient, a legal services provider, gave 10 model variants a 78-document review task that included responsiveness, privilege coding and production of a privilege log, graded by experienced attorneys. Nine of the 10 scored within eight points of one another on that composite task, though gaps widened to as much as 37 points on insurance coverage analysis, a reasoning-intensive assignment. “The industry’s conversation has largely focused on model size, speed, and cost,” Chad Main, Percipient’s founder, said in the study’s announcement. “What this research demonstrates is that the next phase of competition will be won by systems that reason better, not simply systems that generate text faster.”

LegalOn Technologies makes an adjacent argument from its 2026 contract review benchmark of 11 models, a vendor-run study in which the publisher’s own system ranked first. “The model matters, but the harness matters too,” Daniel Lewis, LegalOn’s chief executive, wrote in a sponsored thought-leadership article for Artificial Lawyer. “For contract review, that can be the difference between a system that is impressive in a demo and a system that is reliable enough for daily legal work.” LegalOn’s claim is that a purpose-built harness can beat raw foundation-model use, which is adjacent to, not proof of, Decover’s convergence thesis.

The open question sits in the privilege detail. Percipient’s composite score included privilege coding and still converged, but the study published no separate precision and recall figures for the privilege calls, so whether model performance converges on privilege specifically remains unresolved by these studies. Privilege determination, with its fact-specific judgments about legal advice, dual-purpose communications and third-party waiver, plausibly sits closer to the reasoning-heavy end where Percipient found divergence. That is this article’s analysis, not a finding of either study.

Model provenance is the question the paper skips

The governance question a chief information security officer will ask first goes unaddressed in the paper. Six of the nine model entries come from Chinese developers: Qwen 3.6 Plus, MiniMax M3, the two DeepSeek models and the two Kimi models from Moonshot AI. Several are distributed as open weights that legal teams can self-host or run on infrastructure in a jurisdiction of their choosing, but the paper does not say where its test inference ran or what deployment it assumes for client matters.

For privileged attorney-client communications, that silence is the gap to close before any cost comparison matters. Legal teams should confirm where inference occurs, what the model provider or host retains, whether outside counsel guidelines and protective orders permit the routing, and whether client consent is needed. A model that saves $7,860 per 100,000 documents buys nothing if the deployment breaches a confidentiality obligation.

New privilege log rules raise the stakes

The timing gives the debate procedural teeth. Amendments effective Dec. 1, 2025 revised Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f)(3)(D) to require that the discovery plan state the parties’ views and proposals on issues about privilege claims, including the timing and method for asserting them, and revised Rule 16(b)(3)(B)(iv) to permit the scheduling order to adopt those provisions. Privilege logging moves from a late-stage task to an early negotiation. When AI-assisted classification forms part of a proposed privilege process, model selection, validation evidence and quality control protocols may become subjects of those discussions, and a party that cannot explain why it selected a given model, or produce validation results on its own document population, will be poorly positioned if the question arises.

That points to the paper’s most defensible advice: validate a proposed system against a representative, gold-labeled sample from the matter’s own document population under a documented protocol rather than relying on a vendor benchmark. Demand precision figures alongside recall, because a recall-only quote conceals the false-positive rate that inflates privilege logs. Run the cost arithmetic at the matter’s real volume, where the difference between $0.003 and $0.08 per document is trivial at 1,000 documents and decisive at 500,000. And treat model savings as budget for attorney quality control on escalated documents rather than as margin.

The paper packages its recommendations into four proposed buyer profiles: Qwen 3.6 Plus for maximum accuracy, DeepSeek V4 Pro for value, claude-haiku-4-5 for precision-first work and DeepSeek V4 Flash for first-pass review at extreme volume. These are Decover’s hypotheses, not validated privilege-review guidance, and the precision-first designation contains an internal inconsistency: the paper calls claude-haiku-4-5’s 0.875 precision the highest in the study, but its own results table shows Qwen 3.6 Plus higher on precision (0.885) as well as recall, F1 and accuracy, leaving a $0.001 per-document cost edge as the Haiku model’s only listed advantage. The paper’s architecture-floor test, the idea that a platform demonstrating F1 between 0.81 and 0.87 on a controlled sample has made model selection a pure cost decision, should be read the same way: a score below that band could reflect collection difficulty, class prevalence, labeling disagreement, criteria design or model configuration as easily as architecture.

Model pricing will keep shifting, and the specific rankings in any single-run benchmark will age quickly. The durable question for legal teams is different: when opposing counsel asks how you validated the AI that built your privilege log, what will your answer be?

news.summaryZh:
美国职业棒球大联盟（MLB）限制休息区iPad功能，引发对AI治理的广泛关注。MLB在发现球队使用AI工具实时支持换人、投球呼叫等战术决策后，禁用了定制平板标签。联盟的担忧并非针对技术本身，而是维护实时比赛中允许的数据访问与自动化战略建议之间的界限。AI改变了决策支持的速度、规模和性质，使联盟必须回答哪些工具公平、何种自动化程度可接受、谁对决策负责等问题。

MLB的举措表明，组织采用AI时需要明确的使用边界，而非笼统的“使用技术”许可。治理必须具体规定系统可访问的内容、使用时间、依赖者以及哪些决策必须由人类主导。无论是棒球休息区、交易台、医院还是招聘场景，同样的原则适用：AI虽强大，但缺乏深思熟虑的护栏，可能从有用工具变为改变规则的力量。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Major League Baseball’s (MLB) move to restrict dugout iPad functionality is a reminder that AI governance is showing up everywhere, including in the middle of professional baseball games. According to reports, MLB disabled custom tablet tabs after concerns that teams were using AI-powered tools to support real-time decisions on substitutions, pitch calling, and other in-game strategy. The league’s concern appears less about technology generally, and more about preserving the line between permitted data access and automated strategic recommendations during live competition. That line matters. Sports have always evolved with analytics, video, scouting systems, and performance data, but AI changes the speed, scale, and nature of decision support. A tool that helps a team review video before a game feels very different from one that recommends the next pitch in real time. Once AI starts influencing live decisions, leagues must answer harder questions: What tools are fair? What level of automation is acceptable? Who is accountable for the decision? And how can rules keep pace when technology moves faster than the rulebook? The takeaway extends well beyond baseball. Organizations adopting AI need clear use-case boundaries, not just broad permission to “use technology.” MLB’s crackdown shows why governance must be specific: what the system can access, when it can be used, who can rely on it, and which decisions must remain human-led. Whether the setting is a dugout, a trading desk, a hospital, or a hiring situation, the same principle applies: AI may be powerful, but without thoughtful guardrails, it can quickly move from helpful tool to rule-changing force. news.titleEn: Technological Shifts Compel New Executive Orders for AI and Quantum Computing
news.titleZh: 技术变革推动人工智能与量子计算新行政令出台
news.summaryZh: 数千名经济学家和研究人员签署声明，警告人工智能系统可能以前所未有的速度和更短的时间重塑经济。6月2日，白宫发布《促进先进人工智能创新与安全》行政令，要求前沿模型在向可信合作伙伴发布前最多30天向联邦政府提供访问权限。该行政令还建立了分类基准和自愿框架流程，以确定可提前访问前沿模型的“选定可信合作伙伴”，并明确这不是许可要求。随后，白宫发布《国家安全企业人工智能》情况说明书，旨在加速人工智能在国家安全领域的应用。作为延伸，上周二宣布了“金鹰倡议”，以利用前沿人工智能促进公私部门合作共享可操作的威胁和补救信息。此外，6月还发布了两项关于量子计算的行政令，强调量子计算与人工智能和网络安全在国家安全方面的重叠。近期发生了一起前所未有的网络安全事件：一个代理型人工智能威胁行为者利用多个软件漏洞，将其串联并执行勒索软件攻击和勒索通知，受害者公司身份尚未披露。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! “We must act now.” That was the clarion call last week by thousands of economists and researchers that signed a statement warning that AI systems could reshape the economy at unprecedented speed and on a vastly shorter timeline. “We must act swiftly to remain ahead.” That was the call-to-action last month as a follow-up to guidance issued in May. These statements arrive on the heels of unprecedented events in June and July, when frontier models publicized the cybersecurity capabilities of new models, pre-released them to a select few and were forced to withdraw them for national security reasons based on an Executive Order signaling federal priorities and foreshadowing potential new legal duties. For an administration that had previously taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, its current approach has been a sudden shift. Given the way AI has accelerated the speed, scale and sophistication of cyber threats, we explain below how recent federal actions on AI and quantum computing and AI-driven cyber incidents are reshaping what “reasonable security” means. On June 2, the White House released an Executive Order titled Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security. The most notable section of the order is the requirement by frontier models to provide the federal government with access “for a period of up to 30 days before they plan to release such models to other trusted partners.” Last month’s AI order, under the subheading “Secure Frontier Model Deployment,” also outlined the establishment of a classified benchmarking and voluntary framework process for determining “select trusted partners” that will have early access to covered frontier models. The order expressly points out that this process is not a permitting requirement. A few days after the order, the White House released a fact sheet titled AI in the National Security Enterprise, aimed at accelerating AI adoption for national security. As an extension of the order and fact sheet, the Gold Eagle Initiative was announced last Tuesday to leverage frontier AI for public and private sector collaboration of actionable threat and remediation information. Also in June, two executive orders relating to quantum computing were released, each signaling an overlap with national security concerns like those with AI and cybersecurity: Both orders reflect a familiar framing: quantum is a powerful tool and a major area for commercial growth, and the United States should seek to develop it before other world powers. Just as AI systems become more autonomous and integrated into critical workflows, the security supporting quantum computing systems also becomes more consequential.1 In the AI and quantum computing contexts, policymakers are not rejecting the underlying technology; they are recognizing that the same tools that create commercial and strategic advantage can also compress risk timelines, lower barriers for adversaries and require organizations to revisit assumptions that previously seemed sufficient. Unprecedented cybersecurity incidents have also happened this month. Three weeks ago, an agentic AI threat actor exploited several software vulnerabilities, made decisions on how to string them together and executed a ransomware attack and demand note. The identity of the victim company has not been disclosed, but the attack details have.

news.titleEn: Caught in the Middle: When State AI Laws and Federal Consumer Protection Law Collide
news.titleZh: 夹在中间：当州AI法律与联邦消费者保护法冲突时
news.summaryZh: 2025年12月11日，特朗普总统签署第14365号行政令，指示联邦贸易委员会（FTC）发布执法政策声明，处理州法律要求修改AI模型准确输出与《FTC法案》要求之间的冲突。FTC于2026年7月1日发布拟议政策声明，将AI行业视为合规问题的事项重新定义为消费者保护问题。消费者对AI系统有合理期待，即系统应忠实准确地实现用户目标，不受未披露的意识形态议程影响。违反这一期待构成《FTC法案》第5条下的欺骗行为。FTC直接针对为遵守州法律而调整AI输出的公司，警告即使出于合规目的，欺骗性调整仍可能违反联邦法律。FTC强调《FTC法案》未提供州法安全港，公司必须同时遵守第5条。FTC特别关注科罗拉多州AI立法，该法要求AI公司避免输出导致不同影响，并可能因客户使用产品造成的歧视性结果承担责任，从而激励公司优先考虑公平而非准确性，且不向用户披露。这种未披露的调整构成欺骗。其他州类似法律也可能使公司陷入法律困境。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI companies operating across the United States are increasingly finding themselves pulled in two directions at once. On one side, a growing patchwork of state laws purports to govern what AI systems can and cannot output. On the other, the Federal Trade Commission has made clear that navigating those state requirements the wrong way could expose companies to federal liability under one of the oldest consumer protection statutes on the books. On December 11, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14365, directing the Commission to issue an enforcement policy statement addressing how state laws requiring alterations to the accurate outputs of AI models can conflict with the requirements of the FTC Act. The FTC responded on July 1, 2026 with a proposed policy statement that reframes a question the AI industry had long treated as a regulatory compliance matter into something far more familiar territory: a consumer protection problem. The Commission’s starting point is the reasonable expectation consumers bring to AI systems, namely, that those systems aim to produce the best output possible, faithfully and accurately achieving users’ stated objectives, free from undisclosed ideological agendas. That expectation, the FTC argues, is not merely a philosophical position. It is the foundation of Section 5 of the FTC Act, and the Commission takes the position that violating it, regardless of why, constitutes deception. The FTC’s proposed policy statement takes direct aim at companies that steer or alter their AI systems’ outputs to comply with state law, warning that doing so may deceive consumers in violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act, and that this is true even if the deceptive steering is done in an effort to comply with state laws. The Commission has emphasized that Congress did not provide state-law safe harbors in the FTC Act. Even where a state’s laws shape the provision of products or services, companies must still comply with Section 5. The legal framework the FTC is invoking is well-established. Under the Commission’s 1983 Policy Statement on Deception, the FTC will find a violation where there is a representation, omission, or practice that is likely to mislead a consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances, to the consumer’s detriment. This analysis examines whether the practice is material and whether it is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer. Federal courts have consistently applied these same principles and have recognized that the Commission’s deception authority covers not only overt misrepresentations, but also implied misrepresentations, half-truths, and instances where only a significant minority of consumers are misled. What is notable here is not the legal framework itself. It is the context to which the FTC is applying it. The agency is essentially arguing that an AI system’s implicit promise of accuracy and neutrality is itself a consumer-facing representation, and that secretly undermining that promise to satisfy a state regulator is no different from any other form of undisclosed deception. The FTC’s statement focuses particular attention on Colorado’s AI legislation. The original version of Colorado’s Artificial Intelligence Act imposed a broad duty on AI companies to avoid output that might lead to disparate impacts in various contexts, including where a customer’s foreseeable use of that output could itself create a disparate impact. The revised version of the law explicitly provides that AI companies can be held liable for discriminatory outcomes caused by their customers’ use of their products, creating a predictable incentive for AI companies to prioritize objectives such as equity over accuracy to avoid state liability, without disclosing these tradeoffs to users. That scenario (a company quietly adjusting outputs to sidestep state liability without telling users) is precisely what the FTC is targeting. The Commission takes the position that AI companies that steer the outputs of their systems toward unexpected objectives, and away from the objectives set by or reasonably expected by users, are likely to deceive consumers in violation of Section 5, because they have made both explicit and implicit representations that their systems aim to produce outputs that achieve users’ objectives as faithfully and accurately as possible. Importantly, Colorado is not uniquely situated. The growing number of enacted and proposed state AI laws threatens to create a patchwork of regulatory regimes and compliance challenges for American companies, including laws that regulate the outputs of AI models and effectively require companies to embed ideological bias within those models. Any state law that creates an incentive for AI companies to quietly alter outputs could, under the FTC’s theory, put those companies in a legally untenable position.

news.titleEn: AI Legislation- 2026 Legislative Wrap-Up
news.titleZh: 人工智能立法——2026年立法总结
news.summaryZh: 随着2026年各州立法会议接近尾声，人工智能监管已从新兴领域转变为主流合规义务。Epstein Becker Green持续追踪各州已颁布的AI立法，按三大政策领域（综合法案、医疗与生命科学、就业）分类，并在其“趋势议题”页面提供交互式地图。在联邦全面AI法规缺失的背景下，各州填补了空白，形成了不同的监管哲学：一些州制定了广泛的消费者透明度框架，要求在使用AI进行重大决策时进行披露；另一些州则采取针对性方法，聚焦于医疗保健覆盖决定或就业筛选工具；少数州采用基于风险的框架，对高风险应用施加更严格义务。企业可能同时面临来自同一州的三种不同监管制度。2026年综合AI法规继续扩展，加州、科罗拉多州和犹他州最为活跃，新法规细化了先前框架。一个显著趋势是针对生成式AI和大语言模型的要求，多个州颁布了基于规模阈值的披露义务。医疗保健领域仍是AI监管最活跃的领域，重点在于事先授权：多个州加强或澄清了禁止AI作为拒绝承保唯一依据的规定，要求人工审查AI辅助决定。第二波立法针对AI生成的患者通信，要求医疗机构披露通信是否由AI生成，并确保患者可获取人工替代方案。就业领域的AI监管已显著成熟，从第一代披露要求转向第二代审计、报告和反歧视义务，要求雇主证明其AI系统不产生歧视性结果。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As 2026 state legislative sessions draw to a close, one theme dominates the policy landscape: artificial intelligence (AI) regulation is no longer an emerging frontier but a mainstream compliance obligation. Epstein Becker Green continuously tracks enacted state AI legislation, organizing laws across three policy domains (Omnibus (affecting every sector), Health Care and Life Sciences, and Employment) and makes its interactive map freely available on the firm’s Trending Issues page. With 2026 legislative sessions now closing across the country, this wrap-up provides a comprehensive overview of what was enacted, what patterns emerged, and what compliance obligations businesses should prioritize heading into the second half of the year. In the continued absence of a comprehensive federal AI statute, states have filled the void with laws reflecting sharply different regulatory philosophies. Some states have enacted broad consumer-facing transparency frameworks that require disclosure whenever AI is used in a consequential decision. Others have taken a targeted approach, focusing narrowly on health care coverage determinations or employment screening tools. A few states have adopted risk-based frameworks that impose more demanding obligations on higher-risk applications while permitting lighter-touch treatment of lower-stakes deployments. The result is a patchwork of compliance obligations that vary by jurisdiction, sector, and use case. A business that uses AI to screen job applicants, generate patient-facing communications, and make automated coverage determinations may face three distinct regulatory regimes simultaneously—potentially from the same state. This complexity is precisely what the Epstein Becker Green AI Enacted Bills Map is designed to navigate. Omnibus AI statutes continued to expand in 2026. These laws impose broad transparency, disclosure, risk assessment, and accountability requirements that apply across industries and use cases, often requiring businesses to notify consumers when AI or automated decision-making affects them, to document training data and model behavior, and to establish liability frameworks for AI-caused harm. California, Colorado, and Utah remain the most active states in this space, with new legislation refining and extending the frameworks those states established in prior sessions. A notable trend in 2026 is the emergence of requirements specifically targeting generative AI and large language models. Several states enacted or proposed disclosure requirements that are triggered by the deployment of generative AI systems above specified scale thresholds, a category of obligation that did not exist in most state frameworks even two years ago. Businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing applications should evaluate whether these new requirements apply to their deployments. Health care remained the most active arena for AI regulation in 2026, driven by persistent concerns that automated systems are influencing clinical and coverage decisions without adequate human oversight. The primary focus of enacted legislation in this category was prior authorization: multiple states strengthened or clarified prohibitions on AI serving as the sole basis for coverage denials, requiring human review of AI-assisted determinations and mandating documentation sufficient to support appeals. A second wave of health care AI legislation targeted AI-generated patient communications, requiring health care organizations to disclose when a communication was generated or substantially drafted by an AI system and to ensure that patients can access a human alternative. States active in this area include California, Colorado, and New York. Smaller states that had not previously enacted health care AI legislation began moving in this direction in 2026 as well, suggesting that the sector-specific frameworks pioneered by early-mover states are now being adopted more broadly. State regulation of AI in the employment context has matured significantly in 2026. The early generation of employment AI laws focused primarily on disclosure requirements—obligating employers to notify applicants and employees when automated decision-making tools were used in hiring or performance evaluation. That first wave is now largely enacted. The 2026 session has seen states move to a second generation of requirements: auditing, reporting, and affirmative anti-discrimination obligations that require employers not just to disclose AI use but to demonstrate that their AI systems do not produce discriminatory outcomes.

news.titleEn: Harvey Deepens Microsoft Relationship
news.titleZh: Harvey深化与微软的合作关系
news.summaryZh: Harvey向微软的企业、外部和法律事务部（CELA）提供其法律AI平台，同时自身扩大对Microsoft 365和Microsoft 365 Copilot的内部使用。微软CELA团队本可使用自有工具，但选择了Harvey平台。CELA使用Harvey是双方长期关系的重要一步，表明全球领先的法律团队正将AI作为核心运营方式。很高兴扩大与Harvey的合作，以帮助团队更高效地工作并专注于复杂高影响力的工作。
news.bodyText: Harvey has deepened its engagement with Microsoft, in this case via providing its legal AI platform to the tech giant’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) group; with the legal AI pioneer in turn ‘expanding its use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot internally’. At present Copilot uses multiple models, having moved beyond its initial reliance on OpenAI’s ChatGPT LLMs and now also uses Anthropic’s offerings. And it’s worth noting that Microsoft is also developing its own ‘Legal Agent’, staffed by former Robin AI team members. I.e. the CELA team possibly could have used a lot of their ‘own brand’ tools, but have chosen to use Harvey. The legal tech company said that ‘as part of this collaboration, CELA will use the Harvey AI platform to support its work and enhance how teams operate. This reflects Microsoft’s continued investment in applying AI to improve efficiency, streamline workflows, and enable high-quality outcomes at scale’. AL asked Winston Weinberg, CEO of Harvey, about a couple of aspects, including what the deepening relationship meant to him and the company; and also how this has come about: ‘It means a lot. Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization using Harvey is an important step in our long-standing relationship with Microsoft. More broadly, it signals that the world’s leading legal teams are making AI a core part of how they operate.’ ‘We’ve built a strong relationship with Microsoft over many years, and this announcement reflects the next chapter in that collaboration. Like any enterprise deployment, CELA also went through a thorough evaluation process before deciding to use Harvey.’ Weinberg also added: ‘Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team. ‘Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.’ And Antony Cook, Corporate Vice President and Deputy General Counsel at Microsoft, said: ‘We’re pleased to expand our work with Harvey as part of our broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into our operations. This collaboration will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.’ — Two Major Legal Innovators Conferences this November Come and join us in New York and London this November at Legal Innovators!

news.titleEn: The Innovators – ‘Press Conference’
news.titleZh: 创新者——‘新闻发布会’
news.summaryZh: 凯蒂站在管理合伙人办公室门外，像犯错的学生。蒂姆清退了其他人，独自紧急头脑风暴。其他人在无人发言的“卢比孔河项目”新闻发布会后台紧张等待，同时回避记者关于发布会何时开始的追问。律所创新主管深呼吸，自问是否引发了危机，并承认是自己所为但别无选择。蒂姆让她进门后，表示虽想承担责任但并非自己导致混乱，他们只有五分钟挽救律所声誉。凯蒂等待下一步指示，但管理合伙人沉默。最终凯蒂询问对策，蒂姆却让她去面对记者，吸收所有攻击和尖锐问题，用演讲挽救律所声誉。凯蒂虽不认同其归咎，但意识到争论无益，在辞职与抓住机遇之间选择了后者。
news.bodyText: Katie stood outside the managing partner’s door like a naughty student. Tim had sent everyone else away so he could have a solitary, emergency brainstorm. Meanwhile, the others were now standing nervously at the back of the currently speakerless Project Rubicon press conference, wondering if anyone from the firm would ever take the podium, while deflecting questions from the annoyed journalists about when things would start. The firm’s head of innovation breathed in deeply, as she had been taught at yoga. ‘Did I cause this crisis?’ Katie asked herself. ‘Yes, you did. But you had no choice,’ replied another part of her. ‘You can come back in now,’ Timothy Marks intoned from within. When she had shut the door behind her, he began, not waiting for her to sit. Much as he wanted to take responsibility for this mess, he explained, he had not caused this fiasco. Right now they had about five minutes to save the firm’s reputation. His as well, he added. Katie nodded in agreement and waited for the next bit. But Smyth & Marmalade’s elected leader, this primus inter pares of the equity partners, seemed to have nothing else to say. They stared at each other across the huge desk. The seconds ticked painfully by on the clock behind the managing partner. Eventually the silence was too much. ‘Sir? What are we going to do?’ ‘We?’ he replied with a grin that she didn’t like very much. ‘You are going to go out there and you will absorb the poison. Every arrow. Every barbed question. You are going to talk the firm’s reputation out of the jaws of ridicule – if I am allowed such a metaphor.’ ‘Me?’ ‘You’re the head of innovation, aren’t you? Go and innovate a speech. You’re obviously brilliant at thinking up devastating things at the last minute. You got us into this predicament, you get us out of it.’ She gulped. Disagreed profoundly with his take on the situation, but ascertained an argument about blame would have to wait. Katie took another long, deep breath and in that instant realised she stood half-way between resignation and a fantastic opportunity. She chose the latter.

news.titleEn: Flank Launches ‘Record’ – Agentic Contract Truth System
news.titleZh: Flank 推出 'Record'——自主合同真相系统
news.summaryZh: 柏林法律科技公司 Flank 发布 Flank Record，这是一套自主代理合同记录系统，可大幅减少人工输入需求。该系统通过代理连接客户现有系统，整合合同存储位置，并在签署时从已执行文件中捕获准确元数据，确保记录“通过构建而非纪律”实现准确。代理持续维护记录，并由合格律师通过 Flank 的监督层进行核查。联合创始人 Jake Jones 解释，该系统将代理置于数据层之下而非之上，代理负责“图书馆员工作”：监控合同实际存放位置（电子签名、邮件、共享驱动器、旧 CLM），抓取已签署文件，提取最终版本的元数据，归档、标记、识别修订并更新记录，每日持续进行。传统合同管理系统依赖人工维护，数据易漂移，而 Flank Record 是首个不依赖任何人记忆操作的准确记录系统。该产品即日开放候补名单，并推出面向企业的设计合作伙伴计划，部署包括由代理主导的现有合同资产迁移。
news.bodyText: Flank, the agentic legal tech company focused on inhouse teams, has launched Flank Record, an autonomous agentic contract system of record, which greatly reduces the need for manual input. As Berlin-based Flank told AL, ‘agents connect to the customer’s existing systems, consolidate contracts wherever they live, and capture accurate metadata from each executed document at the point of signature, so the record is accurate by construction, not by discipline. The agents then maintain the record continuously, and a qualified lawyer checks their work through Flank’s supervision layer’. ‘Flank Record closes [the] gap by putting agents underneath the data layer rather than on top of it,’ they added. This site then asked co-founder, Jake Jones, some more about this approach. He explained: ’Think of it as two different jobs an AI can have in relation to your contracts.’ ‘The ‘data layer’ is just the pile of facts: the contracts themselves plus everything recorded about them, like renewal dates, counterparties, and values. Every tool you use sits on top of that pile and reads from it. ‘Agents on top is what almost everyone else builds. You point a chatbot or copilot at your existing contract store and it answers questions from whatever it finds. In this case the AI is a reader. It doesn’t touch the underlying data, so if the pile is wrong, and it so often is, the AI confidently answers from garbage. Ask “what expires this quarter?” and it reads a renewal date that was logged at drafting and changed twice in negotiation. You get a fast, fluent, wrong answer, in spite of how smart the asking layer is. ‘Agents underneath means the AI’s job is to make and keep the data true, not to interpret it. Flank’s agents do the librarian work: they watch wherever signed contracts actually land (e-signature, email, shared drives, the old CLM), grab each executed document, extract the real metadata from the final signed version rather than the draft, file it, tag it, spot amendments and update the record, and reconcile duplicates, continuously, every day. Optionally, a lawyer on the Flank side checks their work. In this case the agents are the maintenance workforce for the record itself.’ (Below are some screenshots.) Alistair Maiden, who recently joined as ‘growth leader’ at Flank, added: ‘I spent a decade implementing contract management systems, and the uncomfortable pattern is that the interface sits unused while the data drifts from the day it’s set up. Buyers were promised a reliable record, and a model that depends on sustained human upkeep structurally can’t deliver one. This is the first system of record I’ve seen where accuracy doesn’t depend on anyone remembering to do anything.’ Flank Record launches today with a waitlist, and also with a design-partner programme for enterprises. Deployment includes a full agent-led migration of the existing contract estate, they added. More about Flank Record here. —

news.titleEn: Willkie Farr partners with OpenAI to develop proprietary AI platforms and solutions
news.titleZh: Willkie Farr与OpenAI合作开发专有AI平台与解决方案
news.summaryZh: Willkie Farr律师事务所宣布与OpenAI合作，加速开发和部署“下一代AI解决方案”，涵盖法律和业务运营，包括在全所范围内推广ChatGPT Enterprise。Willkie是首批与OpenAI合作、专注于在自身环境中加速开发和部署专有AI平台与解决方案的国际律师事务所之一。该合作基于Willkie的AI与创新组织Willkie Works，该组织已开发出一系列专有AI平台。OpenAI的前沿模型将助力这些平台的下一代升级，加速新AI驱动能力的测试与部署。合作还涉及OpenAI Codex，Willkie计划通过Willkie Works将其集成到AI开发环境中，以加速专有平台、工作流程和客户解决方案的设计与部署。借助OpenAI的前沿模型和Codex，Willkie能够将专业知识和创意转化为贴合律师工作方式和服务客户的工具。此次合作正值律所面临选择：是采用现成的法律AI工具，还是自行构建。律所的关键差异化因素在于知识结构、工作流程连接、律师验证和改进输出的方式，以及在模型之上构建的专有客户体验。若底层大语言模型日益商品化，律所的优势将体现在编排层和围绕其构建的领域专业知识上，但需注意AI公司转向按token消耗计费模式可能带来的高昂成本。
news.bodyHtml:
Willkie today announced a collaboration with OpenAI that it says will accelerate the development and deployment of “next-generation AI solutions” across the firm’s legal and business operations, including a firmwide rollout of ChatGPT Enterprise.

Willkie is among the first international law firms to join forces with OpenAI to focus on accelerating the development and deployment of proprietary AI platforms and solutions within its own environment. As we wrote in December last year, others include Dentons.

Advertisement

The collaboration builds upon Willkie Works, the firm’s AI and innovation organization, which is focused on developing proprietary technologies and integrating them into legal and business workflows.

Through Willkie Works, the firm has developed a portfolio of proprietary AI platforms, including:

  • Wendell Intelligence – Willkie’s enterprise AI platform, providing a unified interface to AI-powered legal and business workflows
  • Wendell Financial Insights – a firmwide financial and matter intelligence platform supporting operational and client-service decision-making
  • Wendell Horizon – an AI-powered professional development and attorney training platform
  • Wendell Private Funds Secondaries Platform – a specialized solution supporting complex private funds and secondaries workflows
  • Wendell Class Action Claimant Platform – a technology-enabled platform supporting claimant analysis and litigation workflows

Willkie says that OpenAI’s frontier models will help power the next generation of these platforms, enabling Willkie to accelerate the design, testing and deployment of new AI-driven capabilities across legal and business functions.

Thomas Cerabino, Willkie’s chairman said: “AI is changing the practice of law. We have been through pivotal transformations before and are embracing this generational shift, supporting our position as a leader in the AI evolution. The opportunity AI presents is not simply to work faster, but to rethink how legal services are delivered, how institutional knowledge is leveraged and how clients are served. At Willkie, we are achieving this through combining exceptional legal talent with transformative technology to best meet our clients’ needs.”

The collaboration also extends to OpenAI Codex, which Willkie expects to integrate into its AI development environment through Willkie Works. These capabilities will help accelerate how the firm’s AI engineers design, test and deploy the next generation of proprietary platforms, workflows and client solutions.

“The future of legal will be shaped by firms that can put the power of coding directly into the hands of their lawyers and technologists,” said Jason Boehmig, head of product for the legal vertical at OpenAI. “With OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex, Willkie can turn its expertise and ideas into tools designed around how its professionals work and serve clients. That ability to build is genuinely new, and we’re excited to support their innovation.”

The collaboration comes as law firms increasingly look at whether they should be adapting off the shelf legal AI tools or building their own. A key differentiator for firms now is how the firm’s knowledge is structured; how it is connected to workflows; how lawyers validate and improve outputs; and what proprietary client experience the firm builds on top of the models. If underlying LLMs are increasingly a commodity, the firm’s advantage lies in the orchestration layer and the domain expertise wrapped around it. This is with the big caveat that with AI companies moving to a consumption model for tokens, the costs may end up being prohibitive.

news.summaryZh: NetDocuments 为 ndMAX Studio 新增六款 AI 驱动应用，旨在帮助法律团队简化商标诉讼和原告方诉讼流程。ndMAX Studio 现有预构建应用总数增至 39 款。这些应用可直接部署，专为特定法律工作流设计，无需从零开始。商标诉讼应用针对截止日期驱动的文件提交、重复性 Office Action 答复及预提交审查等常规但耗时任务。另有三款关联应用支持原告方业务，帮助律所将数百页医疗记录转化为结构化时间线，并生成索赔函草稿，无需使用第三方应用。新应用即日起可用。
news.bodyHtml:
NetDocuments has added six new AI-powered apps to the ndMAX Studio, designed to help legal teams streamline trademark prosecution and plaintiff-side litigation. They expand the ndMAX Studio to 39 pre-built apps.

ndMAX Studio apps are ready to deploy and purpose-designed for a specific legal workflow, meaning legal teams don’t have to start from scratch.

Advertisement

The trademark prosecution apps address deadline-driven filings, repetitive Office Action responses and pre-filing reviews – routine but time-intensive tasks that demand speed and precision from senior practitioners. Three new connected apps also support plaintiff-side practice. They enable firms and legal teams to transform hundreds of pages of medical records into a structured chronology, and to create a draft demand letter, without needing to use third-party apps. See below for the details.

The ndMAX Studio continues to grow with connected, pre-built AI-powered apps that help legal teams move from one stage of a matter to the next. This covers key tasks including preparing filings and responding to Office Actions, building chronologies, drafting demand letters, and preparing for litigation.

Advertisement

The six new apps are available to use immediately.

For Trademarks:

  • The Trademark Pre-Filing Registrability & Risk Review App analyzes proposed word marks and goods/services descriptions to identify pre-filing registrability risks, descriptiveness concerns, disclaimer sensitivity, and scope drafting issues in a structured, memo-style review.
  • The Trademarks USPTO Office Action Response App reviews USPTO trademark Office Actions, extracting structured examiner findings and generate playbook-driven response strategies and draft reply sections for trademark practitioners.
  • The USPTO Trademark Prosecution Deadlines App extracts, calculates, and tracks USPTO trademark prosecution deadlines from DMS-stored documents using AI-assisted analysis with human review before any data is saved.

Plaintiff case-building:

  • The Medical Chronology App summarizes and extracts key events from medical records into a structured memo for efficient chronological review.
  • The Demand Generator App extracts facts, causation evidence, and itemized damages from medical records and case documents to draft jurisdiction-appropriate demand letters for personal injury, employment, and insurance bad faith matters.
  • The Expert Witness Profile Builder App builds structured expertwitness profiles from CVs, transcripts, and published works, extracting credentials, prior opinions, and case history while flagging testimony inconsistencies and cross-examination vulnerabilities.
