news.titleEn: Built By Lawyers, For Lawyers: DingDuff Is A Free Claude Connector That Its Founders Say Rivals The Legal Research Giants
news.titleZh: 由律师为律师打造：DingDuff 是一款免费 Claude 连接器，其创始人称可与法律研究巨头媲美
news.summaryZh: 德克萨斯州奥斯汀的两位执业律师开发了一款名为 DingDuff 的免费 MCP 连接器，可将 Claude 直接接入数百万份法院意见、法规、条例和法院规则，以及通过 PACER 获取的联邦法院文件。在内部测试中，该工具的表现匹配甚至有时超越其律所付费的 Westlaw AI 账户。连接 DingDuff 的普通 Claude 账户生成的研究备忘录质量与律所提供的法律专用 AI 产品相当。两人最初为自身执业需求构建该工具，未计划成立公司，但在获得出乎意料的结果后决定与其他法律专业人士分享。限制因素并非 AI 的智能，而是其对数据的访问权限。
news.bodyHtml:
Two practicing lawyers in Austin, Texas, have built a free connector that plugs Claude directly into millions of court opinions, statutes, regulations and court rules, along with federal court filings via PACER — and they say that, in their own testing, it matches and sometimes beats the Westlaw AI accounts their firms pay for.

The tool is called DingDuff, and it is an MCP connector — short for Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets an AI assistant call outside tools and data sources. That means there is no separate application to learn. The lawyer works in Claude, asks a legal question, and Claude searches the actual primary sources and answers with citations the lawyer can open and check.

The founders are Kyle Dingman, a plaintiff-side mass torts lawyer, and Stephanie Duff-O’Bryan, a commercial litigator and former Consumer Financial Protection Bureau enforcement attorney. They built DingDuff — the name is a mash-up of their surnames — for their own practices, and say they never set out to build a company.

They decided to share it with other legal professionals after a result that surprised them. Dingman keeps a small set of test prompts that he reruns as models and products change, and in those comparisons, he said, an ordinary Claude account connected to DingDuff was producing research memos that matched the output of the legal-specific AI products available through their firms.

“It turns out memos that are basically as good as Westlaw’s,” Dingman told me in a recent interview. “We weren’t trying to build some sort of competitor to Westlaw.”

It is a claim the founders now make publicly on their website, where they say DingDuff outperformed their firms’ Westlaw AI accounts so consistently that they both eventually stopped using them.

Granted, that is their own assessment, not an independent benchmark. Still, it goes to a larger question the legal AI market has been debating these days, which is how much value comes from a purpose-built legal AI platform as compared to simply giving a general-purpose model such as Claude or ChatGPT direct access to reliable legal sources.

From A Raspberry Pi In A Closet

The tagline on DingDuff’s GitHub page emphasizes its origin story: “Built by lawyers, for lawyers.” It grew out of the mix of anxiety and fascination that swept the profession after ChatGPT’s release in late 2022.

“I got kind of obsessed with AI,” Dingman said. “I was like, ‘Oh God, the robot’s going to replace me.’ But also I was super excited by it.”

Founders Stephanie Duff-O’Bryan and Kyle Dingman. (Composite image generated from separate headshots by ChatGPT.)

He read everything he could about how the models worked, bought a $10,000 computer, and spent a weekend at the home of his father, a retired software engineer, trying to figure out whether he could train specialized legal AIs.

The machine soon sat gathering dust as the frontier models improved faster than anything he could build. But he said the experiments taught him something about legal AI. The limiting factor was not the AI’s intelligence, he concluded, but its access to data.

So Dingman began downloading cases from Harvard’s Caselaw Access Project and compiling them into a database, which he ran on a $35 Raspberry Pi tucked away in his closet.

Why the $35 computer and not the $10,000 one? “If I accidentally break it with some bad Python code, I can just buy another,” Dingman explained

Duff-O’Bryan joined the project in mid-2025, after the DOGE-era upheaval at the CFPB froze her investigations and sent her back to private practice. Neither founder is a professional coder, so both learned as they went. Duff-O’Bryan said she opened her computer’s terminal for the first time since a high school C++ class.

Their case law source changed to CourtListener, the Free Law Project’s open database of court opinions, after they reached out to its co-founder Mike Lissner. Rather than mirror CourtListener’s enormous and constantly changing corpus, DingDuff accesses it through API calls. DingDuff later added its own database of federal and state statutes and rules.

The DingDuff team has since grown to include two developers: Dingman’s brother Brady, a former naval submarine nuclear operator who curates the statutory database, and Julia Teleki, a software developer.

The company has no investors, and the service is free. “I have zero investors to appease,” Dingman said. “I am perfectly happy running this with a tip jar indefinitely.”

Getting Out Of The AI’s Way

The DingDuff website sums up the design philosophy in six words: A legal connector that “gets out of the AI’s way.”

“The tool itself is just a pipe from the law to Claude,” Dingman said. “It doesn’t tell Claude how to go analyze a legal issue. Claude’s actually pretty good at it out of the box.”

“There’s a lot that you want to do as an attorney that goes beyond writing a memo,” he said. “… What I really want to do is just interact iteratively with the AI as I’m working on a memo or a brief.” The model surfaces its assumptions about the law, he said, and the lawyer can challenge them, redirect the research, or ask it to pursue a competing argument.

Dingman is particularly interested in work that is impractical for a human researcher on an ordinary litigation budget, such as tracing back an entire line of case law so that he can better understand it and perhaps even algorithmically process all the cases. No associate has the hours for that, and it is a much different job than producing a polished one-shot memo.

An AI legal research product such as Westlaw does not allow that sort of interaction, he said. “It feels like they don’t trust the attorney because they guide it so much.”

He is also critical of Thomson Reuters’ recently released CoCounsel MCP connector, which I have written about here. Rather than giving Claude access to the industry’s largest corpus of legal content, he said, it only lets Claude request a research report from CoCounsel’s own AI.

“It seems to defeat the purpose of having an MCP server,” he said. “An actually really useful server would give it access to the corpus directly and let Claude figure out the answer.”

Adding Statutes to Case Law

Given that CourtListener now has an MCP server of its own, which I have also written about and discussed on my LawNext podcast, I asked how DingDuff differs.

The clearest difference, Dingman said, is statutory coverage. CourtListener’s connector reaches its case law collection, PACER and RECAP data, citation networks and more, but not statutes. DingDuff adds statutes, regulations and rules of procedure and evidence for the federal system and all 50 states plus the District of Columbia.

That layer matters more than it might sound, Dingman said. Give Claude only opinions, and it will infer what a statute says from cases quoting it. But a court may quote only the subsection relevant to its dispute, omit a critical exception, or discuss a version that has since been amended or repealed.

In one of Dingman’s recurring test questions, the model, without access to statutes, found older cases discussing a repealed statute and treated it as current law.

Building the statutory database proved harder than the founders expected. Some states offer clean APIs; others required scraping every section while tracking hierarchy, cross-references and amendments over time.

“Nobody actually has a complete corpus of all the laws,” Dingman observed. “You would think that somewhere there would just be some source you can go to for all of the laws, even for just a state. But there’s really not.”

Dingman credits the Supreme Court’s 2020 decision in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, which held that Georgia could not copyright its annotated code, for clearing the way to add statutes from states such as Vermont and Arizona, whose codes are published by Lexis and Westlaw respectively.

A second difference is design. Where CourtListener’s tools mirror its API endpoints – a structure, Dingman said, well suited to the academic research the API was built for – DingDuff’s various tools carry task-oriented names that map to the stages of legal research an attorney actually performs, such as search opinions, retrieve opinion text and browse statute hierarchy.

That structure, Dingman believes, cues the model’s intuitions about how to conduct research without heavy prompting.

The Lawyer Is The Guardrail

DingDuff’s hands-off design also means the tool will sometimes get things wrong, the founders admit. Their answer is not to construct more guardrails, but to limit access to licensed attorneys, who must confirm their status in the terms of service. The guardrail is the lawyer reading and checking the output.

The founders say they have never seen the tool fabricate a case or statute when working from DingDuff’s sources. “As long as it has access to the cases, it won’t give you made-up cases,” Dingman said. “All of the cases will be real, but it’ll misunderstand cases.

“The kinds of mistakes it makes are the kinds of mistakes associates make. They’re actually very human kinds of mistakes.”

Dingman offers the real-life example of a major law firm partner who emailed him asserting that his claim was time-barred under a one-year limitations period. The partner based his email on a case quoting a statute, but the statute had since been amended.

“I got to write them a very fun email back pointing out that you have to pull the actual statute,” he said.

DingDuff has built that type of verification directly into the product. Alongside the connector, it offers free downloadable skills for legal research, legal analysis and citation formatting, along with what may be its most distinctive feature: a deterministic citation checker.

DingDuff offers four supplemental skills that enhance its performance for specific tasks.

After a lawyer drafts a memo or brief, the checker downloads every cited case and statute, pairs each claim in the document with the passage in the source that supports it, and opens a side-by-side review panel where the attorney marks each citation verified, in need of attention, or rejected.

In a demonstration during our interview, the checker tracked 79 citation instances in a draft memo. Where it verified a citation, it displayed the source text with the supporting language highlighted. Where no copy of a cited authority could be retrieved, it flagged the citation in red and told the reviewer to obtain the source and rerun the check, rather than silently approving it.

Because the text matching is done by code, not by the AI’s memory, a made-up or misremembered quotation cannot slip through as verified. What the checker cannot do is decide whether a source actually supports the proposition, or whether the authority remains good law. That judgment stays with the lawyer.

Even so, Duff-O’Bryan said she is still not comfortable filing anything without reading the cases herself and running a separate citator check. “The AI would just have to be bulletproof, and we’re not there yet.”

From a confidentiality standpoint, DingDuff’s servers see the tool calls Claude sends them, but not the surrounding conversation, and the company’s privacy policy says tool-call parameters are retained for no more than seven days.

The Benchmark: Outperforming CoCounsel and Protégé

In a benchmark published on DingDuff’s website, it gave Claude and ChatGPT, armed with the DingDuff connector, the same legal research assignment as it gave Thomson Reuters CoCounsel and Lexis Protégé, and then graded the resulting memos based on their substantive legal accuracy and their citation accuracy.

The bottom line was that Claude Fable, Claude’s latest model, with DingDuff scored a perfect 11/11 on legal accuracy and had every citation correct, outperforming all the other models they tested.

More details on the benchmarking can be found on DingDuff’s website.

DingDuff v. Claude Alone

This is somewhat of a side note, but this morning, in search of a good screenshot example, I submitted a legal question to Claude. It appeared to me that, in generating the answer, it did not use the DingDuff connector I therefore asked Claude to re-run the query, but this time to use DingDuff.

Notably, after running the same query through DingDuff, Claude changed its answer. Here is how Claude put it: “Running it through DingDuff’s case-law tools surfaces the same authorities but sharpens the doctrine in a way worth flagging — and corrects something in my first answer.”

Notably, by reading the actual case, Claude found that something it had first described as a common-law qualified privilege was not that — and that, in fact, the majority opinion had expressly declined to opine on the common-law rule. Rather, the opinion upheld the lower court based on a finding that the trial judge had acted within a broad measure of discretion.

During our interview, I had asked Dingman whether I need to tell Claude to use DingDuff or whether it would know to use it.

He said Claude would look at its available tools and decide which is best to answer the particular question. But if you have multiple legal research engines connected, it might try to pick one.

To avoid any confusion, Dingman has created a general instruction that can be used to tell Claude to use DingDuff when it is answering a legal question.

His recommended instruction, which you would add to your general Claude settings, is: “When I ask a legal question, always use the DingDuff connector and rely only on the DingDuff database. Tell me the jurisdiction you searched and include citations.”

Taking Back The Profession

DingDuff is supported by a tip jar on its website, and the founders said their costs are low enough to keep it free. (The terms of service do reserve the right to introduce fees in the future, on at least 30 days’ notice.) Usage is growing steadily. They told me they add one or two new users a day, and can watch power users run the roughly 100 tool calls it takes to research and write a brief.

For Dingman, the free model is based on his own experience. He spent time as a solo practitioner representing tenants and consumers in small cases, work that could never support a $500-a-month AI research subscription. Before Westlaw’s AI even existed, he had contemplated buying a stack of cheap MacBooks, loading each with his legal database, and handing them to legal aid attorneys.

His stated fear, only half-joking, was that Westlaw would eventually release “some kind of Death Star AI” priced so that only large firms could practice with computer assistance, distorting the law itself.

“I wanted something that would just always be there,” he said. “I’m pretty sure DingDuff will keep up with it, because DingDuff gets better as Claude gets better, and Claude keeps getting better and better.”

“There’s the sense that the billionaires are quickly taking everything, including maybe the law,” said Duff-O’Bryan. “And it’s like — actually, no. We can build this and we can share it for not very much money.” As lawyers, she said, they are keeping the profession’s tools in the profession’s own hands.

To me, DingDuff’s story demonstrates something every legal research incumbent should find unsettling: Two lawyers with a frontier AI model, an open case law database and a homegrown statute collection can now create a credible legal research alternative — and give it away for free.

(Instructions for installing DingDuff in Claude can be found on its GitHub page.)

news.titleEn: HAN LLP Selects iManage to Bring Order to Complex Commercial Legal Work
news.titleZh: HAN LLP 选择 iManage 以规范复杂商业法律工作
news.summaryZh: iManage 宣布，业务律师事务所 HAN LLP 已选择 iManage 平台，以集中管理文档、加强版本控制并支持内部团队与外部方的安全协作。HAN LLP 专注于商业房地产和商业诉讼，其工作需要对复杂交易和法庭程序中流通的文档版本进行严格控制。随着事务所发展，跨多个存储环境管理文档带来了版本准确性、文件连续性和外部文件共享方面的风险。该事务所选择 iManage 是因为其文档识别能力、直观界面以及将法律内容整合到单一受控环境中的能力。关键优先事项包括：改善文档可追溯性、外部协作以及运营连续性。HAN LLP 正在与 iManage 实施合作伙伴合作完成上线。上线后，iManage 将作为事务所所有业务领域的文档管理、版本跟踪和安全外部协作的中心环境。
news.bodyHtml:
New York and Los Angeles business law firm selects iManage to improve document traceability, external collaboration, and operational continuity across a growing team

CHICAGO — July 16, 2026 — iManage, the company dedicated to Making Knowledge Work™, today announced that HAN LLP, a business law firm with offices in New York City and Los Angeles, has selected the iManage platform to centralize document management, strengthen document version control, and support secure collaboration across internal teams and external parties.

HAN LLP practices commercial real estate and commercial litigation – work that requires strict control over document versions circulated during complex transactions and court proceedings. As the firm has grown, managing documents across multiple storage environments created risk around version accuracy, file continuity, and external file sharing. The firm selected iManage for its document identification capabilities, intuitive interface, and ability to consolidate legal content into a single, governed environment that teams can reliably adopt.

Key priorities driving the selection include:

  • Document version control: Maintaining accurate document identification across commercial lease negotiations and litigation matters, where multiple versions circulate among clients, co-counsel, and opposing parties
  • Centralized, secure file sharing: Replacing fragmented approaches to external document production and discovery with a single, governed environment for sharing large document sets with co-counsel and external parties
  • Ease of adoption: Selecting a platform the broader team can use confidently as the firm scales, replacing a fragmented mix of storage tools that lacked consistent document identification and governance
  • Operational continuity: Ensuring legal work and knowledge can be accessed and continued seamlessly as the team grows and matters develop over time

“Documentation is the foundation of everything we do,” said Chris Han, Founding and Managing Partner at HAN LLP. “When you’re managing commercial leases with dozens of redlined versions in circulation, or coordinating production across hundreds of documents in litigation, you cannot afford to lose track of what was sent, what changed, and which version is current. iManage gives us the document identification, the structure, and the central workspace we need to hold strict control over our work – and share it securely with the people who need it.”

We are pleased to support them as they put that foundation to work.”

news.bodyHtml:
UK listed law firm Gateley yesterday (22 July) announced that CEO Rod Waldie is stepping down from 1 August for health reasons, following revelations first revealed by Roll on Friday of “sweeping cuts” to business services roles. Gateley, which has put up to 40 roles at risk, becomes the latest firm to make such cuts – others in the last 12-24 months include Clifford Chance, A&O Shearman, Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner and Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath. 

At Gateley, Martin Pike will be appointed interim CEO with effect from 1 August 2026, working closely with the senior leadership team. Pike spent nearly 30 years at Willis Towers Watson where he led the EMEA risk consulting and software business and was a member of the global leadership team. He joined Gateley in April 2025 as an independent non-executive director and chair of the audit committee.

Advertisement

In June Gateley announced that it expects revenue for the year ended 30 April 2026 to be approximately £193 million, a 7% increase year-on-year and above consensus, with underlying operating profit anticipated between £21 million and £22 million, in line with expectations.

Interestingly, it noted that it remains focused on margin improvement including from its system investments, such as Jylo, the AI platform, and returns from selective hiring in key growth areas, whilst continuing to actively manage its cost base, with a clear focus on continuing to maximise utilisation across the business and gaining operational efficiencies in FY 27.

news.titleEn: When AI Becomes the Third Party - Courts Divide Over Privilege and Work Product Protection
news.titleZh: 当AI成为第三方——法院在特权与工作成果保护问题上出现分歧
news.summaryZh: 在美国诉赫普纳案中，纽约南区联邦地区法院首次裁定，与公开可用人工智能平台的通信不受律师-客户特权或工作成果原则保护。被告赫普纳在收到大陪审团传票并得知成为联邦调查目标后，使用生成式AI平台Claude准备涉及可能指控、辩护和法律策略的材料，随后与律师分享。Claude并非律师，通信不具保密性，且赫普纳自愿将信息提供给第三方AI提供商，其隐私政策允许收集和保留用户输入输出并允许向第三方披露。此外，律师未指示赫普纳使用Claude，材料创建时未反映律师策略。法院未排除律师指示使用AI且技术作为律师代理人的情形下可能不同分析。此前，密歇根州联邦法院在华纳诉吉尔巴科案中裁定，自诉原告使用ChatGPT协助诉讼准备属于受保护的工作成果。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! In United States v. Heppner, No. 25 Cr. 503 (JSR), 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 32697 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 17, 2026), the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York addressed a question of first impression: whether communications with a publicly available artificial intelligence platform, made in connection with a pending criminal investigation, are protected by the attorney-client privilege or the work-product doctrine. The court answered “no.” The defendant, Bradley Heppner, used the generative AI platform Claude after receiving a grand jury subpoena and learning that he was a target of a federal investigation. He used the platform to prepare materials addressing possible charges, defenses and legal strategy, which he later shared with his attorneys. The court held that the communications were protected by neither the attorney-client privilege nor the work-product doctrine. Attorney-Client PrivilegeUnder Second Circuit law, the attorney-client privilege protects communications that are: (1) between a client and an attorney; (2) intended to be, and actually kept, confidential; and (3) made for the purpose of obtaining or providing legal advice. United States v. Mejia, 655 F.3d 126, 132 (2d Cir. 2011). The court found that Heppner’s communications with Claude failed these requirements. Claude was not an attorney, and discussing legal issues with a nonlawyer platform did not create an attorney-client relationship. The communications were also not confidential because Heppner voluntarily transmitted information to a third-party AI provider whose privacy policy permitted the collection and retention of user inputs and outputs and allowed certain disclosures to third parties. The court further held that, even if Heppner entered information that he had originally received from counsel, any privilege was waived when he disclosed that information to the AI platform. The materials did not later become privileged merely because Heppner shared them with his attorneys. Finally, Heppner’s counsel did not direct him to use Claude. Although Heppner claimed that he created the materials to assist later discussions with counsel, the court focused on the purpose of the communications when they were made. Heppner independently sought assistance from Claude, which the provider expressly disclaimed providing formal legal advice. Work-Product ProtectionThe work-product doctrine generally protects materials prepared by or at the direction of counsel in anticipation of litigation and is intended to safeguard an attorney’s mental impressions, legal theories and litigation strategy. Although Heppner created the documents while anticipating criminal charges, his attorneys did not direct him to use Claude. He acted independently, and the documents did not reflect counsel’s strategy when they were created. The fact that the materials may have later influenced counsel’s strategy was insufficient to establish work-product protection. The court did leave open the possibility that a different analysis could apply where counsel directs the use of an AI system and the technology functions as an agent assisting counsel. However, the court did not decide whether an AI platform could qualify as such an agent. Other Courts Take a Different ApproachShortly before Heppner, a federal court in Michigan reached a different result in Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc., 820 F. Supp. 3d 629 (E.D. Mich. 2026). There, the court held that a pro se plaintiff’s use of ChatGPT to assist with litigation preparation was protected work product.

news.summaryZh: 纽约州议会于2026年6月通过《人工智能劳动信息法案》（S.8706B/A.9581B），要求雇主每年报告AI使用对招聘、裁员、工时及工作任务的影响。该法案由州参议员Michelle Hinchey提出，待州长Kathy Hochul签署。若生效，将成为美国首个强制性AI劳动影响报告要求。法案适用于在纽约运营且员工超50人的企业及所有上市公司，须每年3月1日前向州劳工部提交报告，内容包括因AI使用而失业、受雇、工时增减的员工数量，因AI空缺的职位数，AI执行的任务及人工监督措施。未报告者每日罚款最高500美元。此前版本曾包含对因AI裁员企业的直接税，但因资金去向不明被删除。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! New York may soon require employers to answer one of the central questions in the debate over artificial intelligence and work: what is AI actually doing to jobs? In June 2026, the New York State Legislature passed the AI Labor Information Act (S.8706B / A.9581B), a bill that would require covered employers to report annually on how their use of AI is affecting hiring, layoffs, hours, and workplace tasks. The legislation, introduced by New York State Senator Michelle Hinchey, now awaits signature by Governor Kathy Hochul. If signed, it would create the first mandatory AI labor-impact reporting requirement of its kind in the United States. The bill requires employers to disclose information to the state about how AI is being used and how that use is affecting workers. The bill is premised on a simple proposition: before lawmakers can decide how to regulate AI’s effect on the labor market, they need reliable data about what is actually happening. “AI is here, and there are important, beneficial ways to use it, but there’s also a real downside, especially given how fast it’s moving in the labor market,” said Senator Hinchey, the author and sponsor of the bill. The AI Labor Information Act would apply to any business entity operating in New York with more than 50 employees, as well as any publicly traded entity regardless of size. Covered businesses would be required to submit annual reports to the New York State Department of Labor by March 1 of each year. The required disclosures would include estimates of the number of employees who were displaced or hired, or whose hours increased or decreased, due in whole or in part to the employer’s use of AI. Employers would also have to report the number of positions left unfilled because of AI, describe the tasks being performed by AI systems, and explain what human oversight measures, if any, are in place. Failure to report can result in penalties up to $500 per day. The bill that passed the Legislature contained significant changes from a prior bill Senator Hinchey first introduced in 2025, which included a direct tax on companies that reduced their workforce due to AI replacement. “Originally, we wanted a corporate tax on businesses that displaced workers with AI, with that revenue going to help cover the gap it created,” Senator Hinchey said. “But the honest question we kept getting back was, if you raise that tax, where does the money actually go? We didn’t have a clean enough answer, so we took that piece out.”

news.bodyText:
The Shower Curtain Fallacy (And Why You Are Burning Your Vitality)

I’ve just published the July issue of the _Personal Strategy Compass_ newsletter, and it centers on a physical metaphor that hit me during my recent Q3 Personal Quarterly Offsite (PQO).

I caught myself spending far too much analytical energy on a minor home logistical transition and over-architecting (to put it mildly) a task that required almost zero strategic thought. It made me realize how often high-achieving professionals commit what I call the **Shower Curtain Fallacy**.

A shower curtain rod requires basic, “good enough” installation. A bathroom grab bar, on the other hand, requires flawless structural engineering for safety. Yet most of us spend our days treating administrative shower curtains like routine vendor choices, travel bookings, and low-stakes scheduling (“does this time work for you?”) with the precise, exhausting energy required for safety grab bars.

In this issue, I explore:

- **The Billable Ghost:** Why we use administrative over-engineering as a defense mechanism to avoid bigger, messier human realities.

- **The Vitality Firewall:** How accepting “good enough” on minor mechanics protects the biological capital you need for real crisis.

- **The White Space Trap:** Why clearing your plate often tempts you to invent new, performative work.

If you are using your summer recovery to over-architect routine logistics, this issue offers a concrete 3-2-1 framework (3 insights, 2 action items, 1 reflection prompt) to help you reset your boundaries.

# The AI Arms Race in Private Equity: What the Kirkland–Palantir Deal Means for the Rest of the Market

There is a clear logic to Kirkland's approach. A proprietary build gives the firm complete control over its architecture, allows the platform to be trained on decades of the firm's own precedent and partner judgment, and keeps a potential competitive advantage in-house. For a firm with Kirkland's scale and resources, building rather than buying is a rational bet.

4 minute read July 22, 2026 at 02:03 PM

By

Esther Chiang

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

![Image 18: Palantir at 100 Hamiliton in Palo Alto (Photo: Jason Doiy/ALM)](https://images.law.com/assets/2f/9c/8ebb25174f38bf66c45201397b30/palantir-7231-jpg767x505-1.jpg)Palantir at 100 Hamiliton in Palo Alto (Photo: Jason Doiy/ALM)
When news broke that Kirkland & Ellis had partnered with Palantir to build a proprietary AI platform for private fund formation, the legal industry took notice. The system is reportedly designed to handle complex fund documentation, side letters and compliance obligations—some of the most nuanced and high-stakes work in private capital.

The announcement settles a question that has hung over the industry for the past two years: can generative AI reliably handle the sophisticated, judgment-intensive work of private equity fund formation? When the market's dominant fund formation practice commits its own capital, precedent, and reputation to the answer, that answer is effectively yes.

There is a clear logic to Kirkland's approach. A proprietary build gives the firm complete control over its architecture, allows the platform to be trained on decades of the firm's own precedent and partner judgment, and keeps a potential competitive advantage in-house. For a firm with Kirkland's scale and resources, building rather than buying is a rational bet.

But the announcement also raises questions that the broader market—law firms, general partners, and limited partners alike—will now have to work through.

The first is data governance. Private equity runs on discretion: LP identities, bespoke deal structures, and valuations are among the most closely guarded information in finance. Palantir brings deep engineering expertise in large-scale data integration, which is precisely what makes some market participants enthusiastic and others cautious. GPs and LPs will reasonably want to understand how their information is segregated, who can access it, and what happens to it over time—questions they would ask of any AI architecture, proprietary or otherwise.

The second is what happens to the rest of the market. Every law firm partner reading the headlines is likely asking their technology committee some version of "where is our answer to this?" Very few firms—even within the Am Law 100—have half a billion dollars in discretionary R&D capital, or a decade of senior partner judgment sitting in a well-structured data lake ready for a large language model.

For those firms, the choice is not simply build or don't build. A middle path has emerged in the form of vertical AI platforms built specifically for legal and private-capital workflows, which allow firms to ingest their own precedent and expertise without constructing infrastructure from scratch. Each route carries trade-offs: proprietary builds offer maximum control at maximum cost; third-party platforms offer speed and lower investment but require diligence on security, customization, and vendor stability. The right answer will differ by firm size, practice mix and risk tolerance.

The third question is raised by a related trend: reports that elite firms intend to license their AI tools to other firms. This would be a genuinely novel development—law firms becoming software vendors to their own competitors—and it introduces strategic considerations the market has not faced before. Will a mid-market firm be comfortable routing its clients' deal flow through a rival's technology stack? Will GPs want their data embedded in a single law firm's proprietary ecosystem if it makes changing outside counsel technologically costly? These are open questions, and how firms and clients answer them will shape which distribution models succeed.

What seems most likely is that the market will not converge on a single model. Some firms will build. Some will license from rivals. Many will turn to independent platforms. Clients, for their part, will increasingly ask pointed questions about data sovereignty, portability, and conflicts before their information enters anyone's system.

Kirkland and Palantir have demonstrated that AI can operate at the highest level of fund formation practice. The more consequential story is what comes next: whether the resulting capabilities remain concentrated within a handful of walled gardens, or become an operating standard available across the ecosystem. For the $50 trillion private capital market, that outcome matters far more than any single partnership.

**Esther Chiang**_is the CEO of SmartEsq, a legal AI company serving the private capital market._

# Why We Decided to Become an ABS Firm

The model is only as trustworthy as the people operating within it, which means treating expanded permission as expanded obligation. Firms operating this way have a responsibility to demonstrate that non-lawyer ownership and rigorous legal ethics aren't in conflict.

6 minute read July 22, 2026 at 11:45 AM

By

Matt Freund

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

![Image 18: Matt Freund, with ClaimsHero. Courtesy photo](https://images.law.com/assets/08/9b/606dda524081b53ad9ea60d2c822/matt-freund-jpeg767x505.jpg)Matt Freund, with ClaimsHero. Courtesy photo
When we started ClaimsHero, we weren't chasing scale for its own sake. We started with a question: how do we help Americans assert legal rights they already have but rarely exercise?

Most people don't pursue these rights because the legal system typically requires upfront financial resources to participate. When potential recoveries are modest, or a plaintiff can't afford billable hours, even well-intentioned lawyers often can't take the case.

The result is that firms decline these matters, not out of indifference, but because the economics don't work. Multiplied across millions of people, this creates a category of legal rights that exist on paper but are effectively unenforceable in practice.

## **A Different Kind of Firm**

This is the gap the Arizona Supreme Court's Alternative Business Structure (ABS) framework was designed to address, by permitting non-lawyer ownership of law firms. It's also why our firm exists: to expand access to the legal system.

Early on, we considered focusing on people harmed by corporate negligence at scale, starting with the effects of digital addiction techniques used by social media platforms. We quickly ran into a structural problem: millions of minors and young adults had been affected, but traditional law firms are built around a lawyer's finite capacity: the number of hours in a workday sets a hard limit on how many clients one lawyer can serve.

We concluded that expanding access meant removing friction between individuals and the legal system, and that technology could let lawyers represent more clients than a traditional model allows without replacing the attorney-client relationship. Building that properly, with real legal supervision at every level, meant developing the technology in house rather than buying it off the shelf.

That approach also shaped who we needed to hire. Traditional law firms can bring on skilled engineers, but the technologists who could build this well expected the same equity stake that senior attorneys expect. The ABS structure was the only way to offer both.

In practice, that meant recruiting technologists from regulated industries (trust and safety, insurance, financial services) where working within professional constraints is already familiar. They work alongside our lawyers on incremental changes to the legal workflow, without altering the substance of legal representation itself. Under our structure, a client can always reach a lawyer, every interaction is attorney-supervised, and our legal team is involved in both client engagement and technology development.

## **Governance Built for This Model**

We recognize the skepticism in parts of the legal profession toward applying a start-up mindset to law. That skepticism is reinforced by how the “move fast and break things” approach at some tech companies has caused real harm to minors and other users of social media. Startups often treat legal requirements as an obstacle to work around rather than a factor to build into their operations from the outset.

Avoiding that outcome meant building a fully integrated, regulated team of lawyers and technologists within a single entity, with governance to match. The ABS framework's entity-level licensure, biennial renewal requirements, and protections for attorney independence were built for exactly this kind of structure.

As a non-lawyer CEO, my role is to align our legal and technical work while ensuring attorneys retain independent legal judgment. The ABS framework keeps everyone, including me, accountable to professional standards, with attorney oversight extending from the CEO down to every technologist on the team.

## **What Scale Teaches You**

Operating at this scale has surfaced a few consistent lessons. Client communication has to be continuous: when someone signs up with us, it marks the start of what is often a multi-year relationship, and they need to understand what's happening, what's outstanding, and what comes next. Treating communication as an afterthought to the legal work, rather than part of it, puts that relationship at risk.

Edge cases also become far more common than they'd first appear: changes in a client's circumstances, unusual documentation requests, a parent acting on behalf of a minor. Individually, each looks like an exception. Across a large client base, these situations recur often enough that they've shaped how we build our systems: infrastructure that handles standard cases reliably, but that our team can also configure to incorporate what we learn from edge cases.

We've also learned that small error rates don't stay small. A process that works correctly the vast majority of the time can still leave a meaningful number of people affected by the remainder. A firm handling a handful of matters can catch errors by hand; that approach doesn't hold at scale. So reliability isn't incidental: every claim record needs to be accurate, traceable, and recoverable, because errors compound with the number of clients affected.

These aren't just operational details. They shape the quality of the legal services we provide. Technology can expand access, but it can compound mistakes just as efficiently.

## **Different Structure, Greater Responsibility**

We didn't set out to invent a new kind of law firm. We started by asking what kind of company would let consumers actually exercise their legal rights, and concluded that the answer required lawyers, engineers, operators, and capital to operate within the same entity, with accountability built in.

We think the credibility of the ABS model depends on how firms like ours behave, and we try to hold ourselves to that standard. The model is only as trustworthy as the people operating within it, which means treating expanded permission as expanded obligation. Firms operating this way have a responsibility to demonstrate that non-lawyer ownership and rigorous legal ethics aren't in conflict.

Not every firm needs an ABS structure. Not every legal matter should be standardized, and not everything about representation can or should be automated. But as the harms consumers face increasingly happen at technological scale, we think they deserve legal representation that can operate at the same scale on their behalf.

The mission shaped who we needed to hire, and that shaped the structure we built.

**Matt Freund**_is co-founder and CEO of ClaimsHero, an ABS (Alternative Business Structure) a legal technology platform that connects consumers and law firms to pursue mass action legal claims more efficiently and transparently._

news.summaryZh: 一起新的集体诉讼在联邦法院提起，指控三家律师事务所使用AI语音向潜在的大规模侵权客户拨打营销电话，违反了《电话消费者保护法》和德克萨斯州类似法律。AI代理询问其可能的伤害，但消息不适用于她；她多次回答“不”，AI代理仍继续推销法律服务。原告未同意接听电话，且电话使用了自动拨号器和“人工语音”。诉讼指控四项违法：违反TCPA（需同意接收含人工语音的电话，FCC已确认AI语音属于人工语音）；违反德克萨斯州“迷你TCPA”；三家律所未注册自动销售电话，违反德州电话推销员注册法；违反德州禁止律师通过电话招揽法律业务的法律。案件尚待审理，但提醒使用AI代理的电话项目需审查合规性。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! A new class action lawsuit filed in federal court under both the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and a similar Texas state law takes issue with AI-generated voices in marketing calls. The case was brought against three law firms that used AI voices to call potential mass-tort clients. As a reminder and as we have written previously, the FCC’s position is that an AI-generated or AI-cloned voice counts as an “artificial voice” under the TCPA. In this case, the AI agent asked individuals about their possible injuries. According to the recently filed suit, the plaintiff alleged the messages she received did not apply to her. And, that she replied “no” multiple times but nevertheless, the AI agent continued to attempt to sell her legal services. She also stated in the complaint that she had not provided consent to receive the call and that the call was made using an automated dialer and contained an “artificial voice.” She argued that this violated four different laws. First, she alleged a violation of TCPA, which requires consent to receive calls that contain artificial voices. The FCC has confirmed that AI voices count as "artificial voices" under the statute. Second, she alleged violations of a similar Texas law, Texas’s “mini-TCPA”. Third, she alleged that the three law firms failed to register to make automated sales calls, in violation of the Texas telephone-solicitor registration statute. That law requires registering before making solicitation calls. Finally, she alleged a violation of a Texas law that prohibits lawyers from soliciting legal employment by telephone. Putting it Into Practice: This case is still pending. However it is a reminder that plaintiff’s attorneys are not hesitating to use state laws when bringing suit for alleged call violations. Thus, even where we may see some reprieve under TCPA interpretations, that does not mean that the lawsuits will necessarily slow down. Now is a good time to review compliance with call laws if you are using AI agents as part of your call programs. news.titleZh: 当召回失控：AI驱动的召回欺诈的影响
news.summaryZh: 召回欺诈是一种日益严重且复杂的问题，不法分子利用在线召回流程获取不应得的补救措施，增加企业合规成本，削弱合法召回项目的有效性。2026年4月15日，美国消费品安全委员会（CPSC）就召回欺诈及其影响发布信息征询（RFI），征求制造商、进口商、分销商、零售商、召回管理员、消费者权益倡导者及公众的意见。RFI重点关注人工智能生成的虚假提交和协调赎回计划，并邀请就现有欺诈检测工具和技术（包括AI能力）提供反馈。在2026年6月15日截止的评论期内，CPSC收到20份来自制造商、行业组织、个人及召回管理公司的意见。核心主题包括：AI驱动的欺诈及向认证捕获的转变、产品退货作为预防召回欺诈的最安全有效方式、以及召回欺诈的成本。生成式AI被提及最多，它通过伪造图像、收据、序列号和身份文件，提升了欺诈的复杂性和规模，使欺诈从孤立机会主义转向有组织的系统层面。多数行业参与者同意将欺诈检测转向捕获点，基于实时照片及其元数据（如地理位置和图像特征）评估真实性，而非事后验证。尽管存在技术可在家验证召回产品，但多个评论者强调物理退货仍是最安全有效的预防方式。历史上及未来防止召回欺诈的首要方法始终是实际退回召回产品。玩具协会和Sedgwick也支持物理退货，认为这不仅能防止欺诈，还能增强消费者安全，并降低召回产品被转售的风险。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Recall fraud[1] is a growing and increasingly sophisticated problem that occurs when bad actors exploit online recall processes to obtain remedies to which they are not entitled. This illicit activity increases compliance costs for companies, undermines the effectiveness of legitimate recall programs, and results in heightened requirements to submit a legitimate request for a recall remedy. On April 15, 2026, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) issued a Request for Information (RFI) on recall fraud and its impact, seeking information from manufacturers, importers, distributors, retailers, recall administrators, consumer advocates, and the public. The CPSC’s RFI sought input on the following four issues: 1) observed recall fraud; 2) impacts of recall fraud; 3) fraud mitigation measures, and 4) potential Commission actions. The RFI specifically calls out Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated fake submissions and coordinated redemption schemes as key concerns. The CPSC also invited feedback on existing fraud detection tools and technologies used to address evolving organized fraud schemes, including AI capabilities. During the RFI comment period, which ended on June 15, 2026, the CPSC received twenty comments from manufacturers, industry organizations, private individuals, and recall administration and logistics companies that provide support to recalling companies. A few central themes emerged in these comments, including: 1) concerns over AI-fueled fraud and the shift to authenticated capture, 2) product return as the safest and most effective way to prevent recall fraud, and 3) the costs of recall fraud. 1. AI-Fueled Fraud and the Shift to Authenticated Capture Generative AI emerged as the most frequently referenced topic among recall administrators and technology vendors involved in recall logistics. Generative AI has fundamentally transformed the recall fraud landscape by making it easier to fabricate images, receipts, photographs, serial numbers, and identity documents. More troubling, industry participants noted that generative AI has increased both the sophistication and scale of recall fraud, with trends suggesting that fraud now operates on an organized, systemic level rather than as isolated consumer opportunism. For example: It seems that most industry participants agree on a shift toward fraud detection at the point of capture, assessing authenticity based on a photograph taken in real time along with its metadata (such as geolocation and image characteristics) instead of post-submission verification of eligibility for the recall. These comments reflect a broader understanding that traditional recall verification methods are no longer sufficient in an AI-enabled environment, and that proactive, risk-based detection must become standard practice. 2. Returning the Product as the Safest and Most Effective Way to Prevent Recall Fraud Although technology and software exist to authenticate and verify recalled products from consumers’ homes, several commenters emphasized that physically returning the product to the recalling company is still the safest and most effective way to prevent recall fraud. Recall Results, a recall management partner, emphasized this point, stating that “[t]he number one way to prevent recall fraud and abuse has historically been, and will continue to be, the actual return of the recalled product to the recalling company or to their recall administrator for destruction.” An anonymous comment reiterated that recalling companies should physically obtain the recalled product—either by mail or in-person drop-off facilities—as this will not only prevent fraud but bolster consumer safety. The Toy Association maintained this position in their comment as well, stating that the most effective way to prevent recall fraud is to require the return of the product or the smallest critical component to the recalling company. Sedgwick commented similarly, recommending “physical returns where feasible.” Product return also reduces the risk that a recalled product will be re-sold by the consumer, even after receiving a refund—an issue that the CPSC is particularly concerned about.

news.titleEn: AI Bills of Materials (AI-BOMs) and Model Provenance: Contracting for Cybersecurity in AI-Enabled Manufacturing Supply Chains
news.titleZh: 人工智能物料清单（AI-BOM）与模型溯源：AI赋能制造业供应链中的网络安全合同策略
news.summaryZh: 制造商部署AI检测工具后，供应商模型更新导致漏检。问题可能源于模型漂移、数据污染、组件漏洞或第三方API。若合同未明确模型、数据集及依赖项，制造商难以定位故障。AI物料清单（AI-BOM）借鉴制造业BOM和软件SBOM概念，记录模型、数据集、软件依赖、API等组件。模型溯源则追踪模型与数据的来源、修改、验证及变更历史。两者使团队能在事件前后评估AI系统。AI风险不限于供应商网络，生产系统可能含开源库、云推理等多层依赖。传统问卷无法揭示底层组件，缺乏可见性则无法监控风险。NIST指出攻击可针对训练数据、模型参数或通过微调投毒、提示注入等。溯源记录有助于区分数据污染、模型篡改或漂移。合同应明确：1. 定义AI-BOM内容，包括模型、依赖、数据集等，若无法披露则要求替代方案；2. 要求模型溯源包，记录来源、训练历史、验证及安全测试；3. 将透明度作为持续义务，更新时需通知重大变更。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! A manufacturer deploys an AI-powered inspection tool on a production line. After a vendor model update, the system begins missing defects. The cybersecurity question is immediate: did the failure result from ordinary model drift, corrupted training data, a compromised model artifact, a vulnerable open-source component, an insecure model serialization format, or an undisclosed third-party API? If the contract and documentation do not identify the model, datasets, software dependencies, and update history, the manufacturer may not be able to answer that question when production is disrupted, sensitive operational data is exposed, or a customer demands an explanation. That problem builds directly on two prior pieces. Our Foley colleague’s recent article on 5 Strategies for Reinforcing Supply Chain Cybersecurity addressed foundational cybersecurity practices such as vendor oversight, incident response planning, and security-by-design. Our earlier series article on Contract Strategies for AI Predictive Maintenance in Manufacturing and Supply Chains explained why AI vendor agreements often fail to reflect manufacturing realities. This article addresses one area of overlap between these topics in more detail. For AI-enabled manufacturing systems, the next cybersecurity contracting challenge is whether the manufacturer can see enough of the AI supply chain to identify, verify, and preserve evidence of the system’s components, data lineage, and model history. An AI-BOM adapts a familiar manufacturing and cybersecurity concept to AI systems. Manufacturers already understand a bill of materials as a list of parts that go into a product, and cybersecurity teams increasingly use software bills of materials (SBOMs) to identify the software components and dependencies inside digital products. In 2026, CISA and its G7 partners issued guidance applying similar supply-chain transparency principles to AI systems. Under that approach, an AI-BOM documents the key components and dependencies that influence how an AI system functions, including models and model versions, training and fine-tuning datasets and their provenance, software and infrastructure dependencies, APIs and external services, and other elements relevant to cybersecurity, risk management, and supply-chain transparency. Model provenance is the companion concept. In plain terms, it is the chain-of-custody record for the model and its data: where they came from, who modified them, what validation or security testing was performed, and how changes were tracked over time. Together, these records turn an opaque AI tool into something procurement, legal, cybersecurity, and operations teams can evaluate before and after a cyber incident. AI cybersecurity risk does not stop at the vendor’s network perimeter. A production-facing AI system may include a vendor application, a pre-trained model, open-source libraries, cloud-hosted inference, customer-provided operational data, and periodic vendor retraining. Each layer can introduce a different cyber exposure, including vulnerable code, insecure integrations, opaque data flows, or dependencies controlled by subcontractors or other third parties. A traditional vendor questionnaire may describe the vendor’s security program, but it may not reveal the open-source model, image-labeling service, third-party dataset, external API, or cloud inference layer embedded in the AI product. Without that component-level visibility of an AI bill of material, manufacturers may not know which dependencies to monitor, which vulnerabilities require remediation, or which supplier relationship created the risk. Model provenance addresses the related integrity problem. NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2, January 2024) recognizes that attackers may target training data, model parameters, or code during the learning process, and may also attack deployed models through evasion, privacy, or other techniques. Emerging supply chain vectors, including model poisoning through fine-tuning pipelines, insecure model serialization formats, and prompt injection targeting downstream integrations, further expand the attack surface that provenance records must help address. In other words, bad actors can now compromise AI systems not just by attacking the model directly, but also by tampering with the tools, data pipelines, and third-party services that feed into the model’s development and deployment. If a model begins missing defects, misclassifying inventory, generating abnormal maintenance recommendations, or exposing sensitive operational data, provenance records help determine whether the problem came from corrupted training data, a compromised model artifact, a changed version, or ordinary model drift. Without those records, causation becomes conjecture and responsibility becomes harder to allocate. Manufacturers and supply chain managers should address AI cybersecurity transparency expressly in vendor agreements rather than relying on general security language. The following provisions may be particularly helpful: 1. Define the Required AI Bill of Materials. Contracts should specify the minimum contents of the AI bill of materials, including models, software dependencies, datasets or dataset categories, APIs, cloud services, update mechanisms, and security-relevant dependencies. Unlike traditional SBOMs, for which mature and widely adopted formats such as SPDX and Cyclone DX exists, AI-BOM standards remain nascent and are still evolving. If the vendor cannot disclose certain details directly, the contract should require an alternative such as escrow, third-party security review, or tiered disclosure under enhanced confidentiality protections. 2. Require a Cybersecurity-Focused Model Provenance Package. The vendor should document the model’s origin, training and fine-tuning history, data provenance, validation approach, security testing, and known limitations. The agreement should also include representations regarding data rights, licensing, and controls used to protect model and data artifacts from tampering. 3. Make Transparency a Living Cybersecurity Obligation. AI-BOMs and provenance records should be updated when the vendor retrains the model, changes material datasets, switches components, or modifies update pipelines. The contract should require notice of material changes before they affect production systems, especially where changes may affect cybersecurity monitoring, data exposure, vulnerability management, or incident response.

news.titleEn: The AI Dividend: Who Gets the Savings From Legal AI?
news.titleZh: AI红利：法律AI节省的成本归谁？
news.summaryZh: 过去两年，企业法务部门被告知AI将使法律工作更快、更高效、更便宜。实际上，合同审查、初稿起草、条款比较、尽职调查等工作确实大幅提速，但许多法务部门并未看到法律支出相应减少。汤森路透2026年企业法务部门报告显示，截至2025年第四季度，36%的总法律顾问预计未来一年将增加外部律师支出，仅20%预计减少。仅37%的法务部门预计外部律师支出增加（低于前一年的58%），仅32%预计律师人数增加。与此同时，律所经济依然强劲：汤森路透报告2025年第二季度计费费率同比上涨7.4%（美国通胀约2.8%），每律师利润增长8%，每权益合伙人利润增长近12%。这引发核心问题：若AI大幅提升效率，谁在获取经济收益？
news.bodyText: By Adam Nguyen, CEO, eBrevia. For the past two years, corporate legal departments have been told that AI will make legal work faster, more efficient and less expensive. Faster? Yes. More efficient? Sometimes. Less expensive? That’s still very much in question. AI is compressing work that previously took hours into minutes. Contract review, first-pass drafting, clause comparison, diligence review, playbook analysis and routine redlining are all becoming faster. In some workflows, dramatically faster. Yet many corporate legal departments are not seeing a corresponding reduction in legal spend. According to Thomson Reuters’ 2026 State of the Corporate Law Department Report, as of the fourth quarter of 2025, 36% of General Counsel said they expected to increase overall spend on outside counsel over the next year, compared with only 20% who expected to decrease it. CLOC’s 2026 State of the Industry Report tells a similar story from the legal operations perspective: only 37% of departments expected outside counsel spend to increase, down from 58% the prior year, while only 32% expected attorney headcount to increase. In other words: more work, more complexity, and less tolerance for simply adding people or sending more work outside. Meanwhile, law firm economics remain strong. Thomson Reuters reported that worked billing rates rose 7.4% year over year in the second quarter of 2025, while U.S. inflation was about 2.8%. Reuters reported that profits per lawyer rose 8% and profits per equity partner nearly 12%, while a separate Thomson Reuters Institute report found worked billing rates increased 6.5%. None of this means law firms are doing anything improper. But it does raise an important question for every corporate legal department: If AI is making legal work dramatically more efficient, who is capturing the economic benefit?
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦法律AI对法务部门和律所的经济影响，讨论效率提升与成本节省的分配问题，属于核心法律AI话题。

news.titleEn: US Law Firm Willkie Partners With OpenAI
news.titleZh: 美国律所Willkie与OpenAI达成合作
news.summaryZh: 美国大型律所Willkie宣布与OpenAI合作，共同开发覆盖法律及业务运营的AI解决方案，并在全所范围内推广ChatGPT Enterprise。此举发生在OpenAI正式推出法律垂直能力之前，OpenAI已聘请前Ironclad创始人Jason Boehmig领导该领域。合作还涉及OpenAI Codex，Willkie计划通过其AI创新组织Willkie Works将其集成到开发环境中。Willkie将使用OpenAI最新前沿模型、技术资源和企业能力，支持其AI平台组合的持续演进，并扩大先进AI能力的全所访问。Willkie此前已有创新历史，通过Wendell应用积累了经验。OpenAI的合作建立在Willkie Works基础上，该组织专注于开发专有技术并将其安全地整合到法律和业务流程中。AI正在改变法律实践，律所正拥抱这一代际转变，重新思考法律服务交付方式。借助OpenAI模型和Codex，Willkie可将专业知识和想法转化为围绕专业人士工作方式设计的工具。此次合作是Willkie AI战略的重要里程碑。
news.bodyText: Major US law firm, Willkie, is partnering with OpenAI to develop ‘AI solutions across the firm’s legal and business operations, including a firmwide rollout of ChatGPT Enterprise’. The move comes ahead of OpenAI formally rolling out its own legal vertical capabilities, which it hired ex-Ironclad founder Jason Boehmig to lead (see his comment below). The collaboration also extends to OpenAI Codex, they added, which Willkie expects to integrate into its AI development environment through Willkie Works. And it’s also expected – by AL – that OpenAI’s legal push will happen via a new ‘Codex for Legal’ capability – a bit like Claude for Legal. Willkie ‘will use the latest OpenAI frontier models, technical resources and enterprise capabilities, supporting the continued evolution of the firm’s growing portfolio of AI-powered platforms while expanding access to advanced AI capabilities across the organization’, they said. Willkie already has a long history of innovation, initially via its Wendell applications (see below). They added that the OpenAI ‘collaboration builds upon Willkie Works, the firm’s AI and innovation organization, which is focused on developing proprietary technologies and integrating them safely and securely into legal and business workflows’. Commenting on the move Thomas Cerabino, Willkie Chairman, said: ‘AI is changing the practice of law. We have been through pivotal transformations before and are embracing this generational shift, supporting our position as a leader in the AI evolution. ‘The opportunity AI presents is not simply to work faster, but to rethink how legal services are delivered, how institutional knowledge is leveraged and how clients are served. At Willkie, we are achieving this through combining exceptional legal talent with transformative technology to best meet our clients’ needs.’ Boehmig, Head of Product, Legal Vertical at OpenAI, commented: ‘With OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex, Willkie can turn its expertise and ideas into tools designed around how its professionals work and serve clients. That ability to build is genuinely new, and we’re excited to support their innovation.’ And John Elbasan, Chief Digital and Information Officer at Willkie, added: ‘This collaboration represents an important milestone in Willkie’s AI strategy. Through Willkie Works, we have invested in the people, governance frameworks and engineering capabilities necessary to transform frontier AI technologies into proprietary platforms that support legal and business workflows across the firm.’ And here are the Wilkie Wendel apps they’ve already made: Is this a big deal? Well, it’s a bit like what Freshfields did with Anthropic, although it doesn’t stop Willkie working with other LLM makers if they want to. AL sees this more as a useful step forward for both parties while we all wait for OpenAI to finalise its legal offering, which clearly will then become part of this relationship. In fact, perhaps this deal will help OpenAI to figure out what lawyers really want…?
news.relevanceReason: 文章核心内容是关于美国大型律所Willkie与AI公司OpenAI合作开发法律AI解决方案，涉及法律工作流程的AI应用，属于典型的法律AI/法律科技报道。

news.titleEn: Tomorrow – Opus 2 Webinar: AI-Native Litigation Workflows
news.titleZh: 明日直播：Opus 2网络研讨会——AI原生诉讼工作流
news.summaryZh: Opus 2与Artificial Lawyer将于7月23日（周四）联合举办一场特别直播网络研讨会，主题为“从AI辅助到AI原生：诉讼工作流及更广领域的变革”。会议时间为英国夏令时下午4点（美国东部时间上午11点）。研讨会将探讨诉讼工作真正转向AI优先方法的现实路径。多数律师和法律专业人士已在使用AI，但当前挑战在于从零散、情境化的使用转向持续、AI优先的工作流。本次会议将讨论诉讼团队如何采纳AI原生方法与思维，将安全AI嵌入律所文化及日常与复杂工作流，如案件策略、时间线创建和庭审记录管理。
news.bodyText: Join us tomorrow (Thursday) for a special live webinar with Opus 2 and Artificial Lawyer: ‘From AI-enabled to AI-native workflows in litigation and beyond.’ It will take place July 23rd, 4:00 PM BST, 11.00 AM EST, and we will explore the realities of moving to a truly AI-first approach for litigation work. RSVP here Speakers: Join the webinar to explore: RSVP here. Overview Most lawyers and legal professionals already use AI. They’re experimenting with tools, testing use cases, and automating individual tasks. Now, the challenge is moving from occasional and situational use toward consistent, AI-first workflows and expanded engagement. This shift from AI-enabled to AI-native workflows is not only an evolution in how work is done, but also how legal professionals solve challenges, deliver value, and innovate. In this webinar, the panel will share what it means for litigation teams to adopt an AI-native approach and mindset – embedding secure AI into firm culture as well as day-to-day and complex workflows like case strategy, chronology creation, and transcript management. Book your place at the live webinar on July 23 – tomorrow. —
news.relevanceReason: 文章直接聚焦于法律领域AI原生工作流的转型，涉及诉讼工作流、AI嵌入律所文化等核心法律科技议题。

news.titleEn: NetDocuments Launches Expert Witness + Plaintiff Apps
news.titleZh: NetDocuments 推出专家证人及原告应用
news.summaryZh: NetDocuments 继续扩展其 AI 工具组合，推出了一系列新应用，其中与原告工作相关的应用最为重要，包括“专家证人档案构建器”。三个新的互联应用支持原告方业务，使律所和法律团队能够将数百页医疗记录转化为结构化时间线，并生成索赔函草稿，无需使用第三方应用。此外，NetDocuments 还增加了多个商标工作相关的 AI 应用。这些应用通过其 ndMax Studio 开发，总数已达 39 个，未来还将增加。这些应用的直接目的是减少重复工作、加速关键任务并推动案件更快进展，同时保持在 NetDocuments 平台的安全和防护范围内。长期来看，法律科技生态系统正在稳步转变，缺乏基于大语言模型的能力会使公司处于不利地位。这些附加功能也有助于巩固核心文档管理系统的使用，因为应用所使用的文档将存储在该系统中。在市场上，新的 AI 驱动知识管理公司正在赢得市场份额，文档管理系统的竞争对手也在构建其 AI 能力，Box 等公司也在其存储服务之上提供代理工具，因此停滞不前并非明智之举。专家证人档案构建器是一款诉讼支持应用，可将原始专家证人材料转化为结构化、可搜索的档案。诉讼律师通常面临在时间压力下评估对方专家的挑战，往往难以获取该专家以往的证词、立场或观点变化。该应用通过自动从证词笔录和源文件中提取资历、先前意见、案例引用和聘用方历史，并揭示可用于质疑的不一致之处，从而填补了这一空白。
news.bodyText: NetDocuments is continuing its expansion drive into AI tools with a collection of new apps. For AL, the most significant ones are those related to plaintiff work, which includes an ‘expert witness profile builder’ capability. Generally, most large and established legal tech companies have sought to work with commercial law firms on the defence side of the market, and/or for the inhouse legal teams of corporates. Supporting plaintiffs widens their reach at a time when we are now starting to see a new group of ‘claimant’ legal tech companies coming to market. In this case they explained that ‘three new connected apps support the plaintiff-side practice. They enable firms and legal teams to transform hundreds of pages of medical records into a structured chronology, and to create a draft demand letter, without needing to use third-party apps.’ They cover: They’ve also added several AI apps for trademark work. Together the new range of apps, developed via their ndMax Studio, now total 39, with more to come. And you may then say: ‘But, why is a company known for its DMS offering this?’ The immediate reason for the apps is that they ‘reduce repetitive work, help accelerate key tasks, and move matters forward faster, all within the security and guardrails of the NetDocuments platform,’ they explained. The longer-term reason is that – as we’ve all seen – the legal tech ecosystem is steadily shifting. Not having LLM-based skills sets you apart – and not always in a good way. Additional capabilities also help to cement in use of the core DMS as well – as that’s where the documents used by the apps will be held. So, there is that. Moreover, in a market where we have new AI-driven KM companies winning market share and DMS rivals also building out their AI capabilities, plus companies such as Box now offering agentic tools on top of their storage services…..standing still is really not an option. — And here’s some more on how the Expert Witness app works: ‘Expert Witness Profile Builder is a litigation support app that transforms raw expert witness materials into structured, searchable profiles. Litigators routinely face the challenge of evaluating opposing experts under time pressure, often without easy access to how that expert has testified before, what positions they’ve taken, or where their opinions have shifted. This app addresses that gap by automatically extracting credentials, prior opinions, case citations, and hiring party histories from testimony transcripts and other source documents—then surfacing inconsistencies that could be used for impeachment.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要介绍 NetDocuments 推出的 AI 应用，包括专家证人档案构建器和原告支持工具，这些工具直接服务于法律诉讼和文档管理，属于法律科技领域，与法律 AI 高度相关。

news.titleEn: Firm AI Principle 4: Firm AI is built for firm growth. Every other AI is built for individual utility.
news.titleZh: 律所AI原则4：律所AI为律所增长而生，其他AI仅为个人效率而设
news.summaryZh: 专业服务公司的终极目标是增长。本系列文章提出，为律所业务端构建的智能体AI平台能够实现以往不可行的增长。管理合伙人最关心的是增长，而非成本。律所的增长受限于人员工时等吞吐量瓶颈，迫使在吞吐量、质量和成本之间权衡。律所AI通过按需扩展的智能体（而非增加人员）来缓解这些限制，且成本仅为薪资的一小部分。例如，利益冲突排查流程可连续运行，KYC流程可实时监控制裁和所有权变更，交易筛选流程可处理十倍于前的交易量，交叉销售流程可在恰当时机向合适合伙人推荐机会。这不仅是自动化或生产力提升，而是使以往不可行的业务模式成为可能，如将月均200件冲突排查提升至2000件，或年筛选300笔交易提升至3000笔。律所AI让律所规模扩大，而非仅让个人效率提升。
news.bodyHtml:
Growth is the ultimate goal for professional services firms. Our ongoing series about Firm AI makes a new case for how agentic AI platforms built for the business side of professional services firms enables growth that was previously infeasible. Today’s post covering Principle 4 demonstrates how firms will be able to overcome traditional constraints to growth.

Principle 4: Firm AI is built for firm growth. Every other AI is built for individual utility.

Practice AI lowers the cost of doing the work. Firm AI raises the ceiling on how much work the firm can win.

Managing partners do not measure themselves on cost — they measure themselves on growth. Ask the managing partner of any firm what they care about most, and the answer is always growth: of the top line, the partnership, the next fund. Every other priority reports up to it. Firms that stop growing lose partners, and then the practices those partners built.

Every firm runs into throughput governors that constrain its growth, set by how many hours its people have. A private equity manager can screen only as many deals as its analysts can get to. A law firm can process only as many conflicts as its team can clear. These limits force a constant trade-off between throughput, quality, and cost. Want to do more, faster, without dropping the bar? You cannot, because doing more has always meant adding more people.

Firm AI is not just automation or productivity. It makes possible what was previously infeasible.

Firm AI loosens those governors with agents that scale with demand instead of headcount, and without lowering the bar, because the hard calls still route to a person. And an agent costs a fraction of a salary, based on compute and token consumption. So, a conflicts clearance playbook can suddenly run continuously instead of monthly. A KYC playbook can run always-on against sanctions and beneficial ownership changes. A deal screening playbook can run the manager’s investment thesis against 10 times the volume of inbound. A cross-sell playbook can surface the right opportunity to the right partner at the right moment — turning an audit relationship into an advisory mandate, or a first-fund LP into the anchor of the next vintage.

The economic unlock here is bigger than people think, because it is not just automation or productivity. It makes possible what was previously infeasible. Imagine a conflicts team that cleared 200 matters a month and could now clear 2,000. Or a fund that screened 300 deals a year and could now screen 3,000. Firms who would have filtered out a whole range of opportunities in adjacent segments for practical reasons will now be able to vet and assess them at scale. Those are new business models. Practice AI makes individuals faster. Firm AI makes the firm bigger.

Next Up

Next week in Principle 5, we’ll talk about the how: unlocking growth with coworker agents.

In the meantime, the full argument is in the blueprint: Mind your business. Not just your practice.  

Read the Firm AI blueprint

news.titleEn: Engineering to the Power of AI: Inside Ascendion’s Global Disruption with KK
news.titleZh: AI赋能工程：深入Ascendion与KK的全球颠覆之旅
news.summaryZh: 企业技术正从被动工具转向自主智能体AI，后者能独立编排复杂工作流。本期节目探讨这一范式如何为超过30%的财富500强企业带来实际效益。Ascendion的专有工程平台AAVA™部署大量专业数字智能体，管理整个软件开发生命周期，清理遗留技术债务，自动化重复工程劳动，并在银行和医疗等受严格监管行业扩展运营。
news.bodyText:
The rapid evolution of corporate technology has brought us to a critical inflection point: the shift from passive tools to truly autonomous, Agentic AI. While the early wave of artificial intelligence focused on simple prompts and generating text; the real frontier lies in systems that can independently orchestrate complex workflows from start to finish.

In this episode, we explore how this paradigm shift is delivering concrete, bottom-line results for over 30% of the Fortune 500. The way I like to view this, is that we will be citing and discussing tangible examples in the Agentic AI era, i.e. where we are going.

So instead of just throwing linear headcount at complex coding challenges, Ascendion ’s proprietary engineering platform, AAVA™, deploys a massive constellation of specialized digital agents to manage the entire software development lifecycle. Our conversation will dive into how these autonomous networks are cleaning up legacy technical debt, automating repetitive engineering labor, and scaling operations in heavily regulated industries like banking and healthcare. So, today we’re discussing how Agents are actively reshaping corporate global digital infrastructure, right now.

For more information about Ascendion : https://ascendion.com/

news.titleEn: Inside View: Resilient foundations and AI in action at Wilkin Chapman Rollits
news.titleZh: 内部视角：Wilkin Chapman Rollits的弹性基础与AI实践
news.summaryZh: 在Legal IT Insider的《内部视角》播客中，主持人Caroline Hill与Wilkin Chapman Rollits的IT总监Ian Fowles探讨了这家英国前200强律所如何利用技术改善客户服务和内部运营，并将专业知识产品化。Fowles回顾了其法律IT职业生涯，并指出加入一家坚定投资技术的律所使他能够专注于创新而非日常系统维护。讨论强调了强大技术基础的重要性，包括云迁移、现代设备、弹性基础设施以及围绕ISO 27001、持续监控和员工意识构建的全面网络安全策略。有效的安全同样依赖于人员和流程。该律所正在使用Microsoft Copilot提高生产力、自动化重复性行政任务并支持高量法律流程。Fowles还介绍了律所基于AI的Adaptive HR平台，该平台为中小企业提供由律师法律专业知识支持的可访问HR指导。其他创新包括用于房地产工作的Orbital Witness和用于法律服务的WhatsApp商业版，以便在客户希望获取建议的地方提供更便捷的服务。
news.bodyHtml:
In this episode of Legal IT Insider’s The Inside View podcast, Caroline Hill speaks with Ian Fowles, director of IT at Wilkin Chapman Rollits, about how the UK top 200 law firm is using technology to improve client service and internal operations, as well as to productise its expertise.

Fowles reflects on his career in legal IT and explains how joining a firm with a strong commitment to technology investment enabled him to focus on innovation rather than simply maintaining day-to-day systems.

Advertisement

The discussion explores the importance of strong technology foundations, including cloud migration, modern devices, resilient infrastructure and a comprehensive cyber security strategy built around ISO 27001, continuous monitoring and staff awareness. Fowles emphasises that effective security relies as much on people and processes as it does on technology.

The conversation also examines the firm’s practical approach to AI. Wilkin Chapman Rollits is using Microsoft Copilot to improve productivity, automate repetitive administrative tasks and support high-volume legal processes. Fowles also discusses the firm’s AI-powered Adaptive HR platform, which provides SMEs with accessible HR guidance backed by its lawyers legal expertise. And he highlights other innovations such as Orbital Witness for real estate work and WhatsApp for business to make legal services more convenient and meet clients where they want to access advice.

news.titleEn: PTAB Institutes IPR2026-00276, Signaling a Strong Preliminary Obviousness Showing
news.titleZh: PTAB 对 IPR2026-00276 启动立案，表明初步的显而易见性论证有力
news.summaryZh:
专利审判与上诉委员会（PTAB）于2026年7月14日对IPR2026-00276作出立案决定，批准双方复审，认定请愿人已满足至少一项被挑战权利要求合理可能不可专利的门槛性举证要求。立案决定虽属初步且不解决实质问题，但对从业者仍具重要意义，因为它展示了委员会在IPR前端如何评估显而易见性挑战，以及何种证据支持足以使案件进入全面审理。

在立案阶段，委员会不裁决专利权利要求是否无效，而是判断请愿书是否表明至少一项被挑战权利要求有合理胜诉可能性。本案中，PTAB认为请愿人基于专家分析的现有技术组合足以证明进一步审理的正当性。对专利权人而言，关键启示在于：若答辩主要聚焦于竞争性事实叙述而非指出请愿书的具体缺陷，则质疑立案的努力往往失败。对请愿人而言，该裁决提醒：立案胜在严谨的陈述，委员会继续奖励那些清晰将专家证词与参考文献关联、预判专利权人回应并解释为何所主张组合非事后诸葛亮的请愿书。该决定未开创先例或宣布PTAB实践的重大变化，而是对35 U.S.C. § 314法定立案标准的直接适用。
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论PTAB的IPR立案决定及其对专利诉讼策略的影响，属于专利法实践，而非直接聚焦法律AI或法律科技。

news.titleEn: DOJ Seeks Clean Water Act Settlement Over 2022 Keystone Kansas Spill
news.titleZh: 美国司法部就2022年基斯通管道堪萨斯泄漏事件寻求《清洁水法》和解
news.summaryZh:
美国司法部向堪萨斯联邦地区法院提交了一份拟议同意令，以解决2022年基斯通管道破裂事件引发的《清洁水法》指控。该案针对管道系统所有者及运营商（现与South Bow关联），涉及近年来最受关注的管道泄漏事件之一。和解将解决与破裂相关的民事环境索赔及运营商的泄漏响应义务。该同意令涉及重大原油管道泄漏事件，凸显联邦政府对基础设施运营商在预防、响应和补救义务方面的持续关注。

对法律专业人士而言，此案具有多重意义：管道事故可能迅速演变为多维度执法行动，涉及联邦民事处罚、禁令救济及长期合规义务；同意令可能施加运营控制、监测、报告、培训和审计要求，重塑企业环境风险管理。诉讼律师需关注同意令如何界定因果关系、排放责任及补救措施，因其可能影响后续保险、土地所有者及监管争议。内部法律顾问应认识到事故准备不仅是技术问题，更是诉讼准备问题。合规团队需注意联邦执法对泄漏预防和响应计划的审查重点。由于同意令已提交但尚未生效，公众评论、司法审查及最终修改可能影响运营商义务范围。
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论环境执法和管道泄漏和解，涉及法律程序（同意令）和合规义务，但核心并非法律AI或法律科技，而是环境法和基础设施监管。

news.titleEn: Attorney Referral Legal Platform Vikk AI Announces $4.2M in Funding
news.titleZh: 律师推荐法律平台 Vikk AI 宣布获得 420 万美元融资
news.summaryZh: 总部位于加州长滩的人工智能法律助手及律师推荐平台 Vikk AI 宣布完成 420 万美元融资，包括 2025 年 8 月结束的 70 万美元种子前轮和近期结束的 350 万美元种子轮。投资者包括税务律师 Ronson Shamoun、人身伤害律师 Joe Samo、健康行业高管 Brad Jowell、制药高管 Cooper Collins 及其他未披露的天使投资人。该平台面向消费者，允许用户描述法律问题并获取解决方案概述，同时提供律师广告中心，律师可根据地点和执业领域向潜在客户投放广告。公司计划将种子轮资金用于持续软件开发（包括招聘更多工程师）以及提升在潜在广告客户中的知名度。Vikk AI 还计划推出律师名录和 Vikk Data Hub，后者将向律所、保险公司等企业提供关于消费者法律搜索趋势的聚合匿名数据。律师名录预计 8 月中旬上线，Vikk Data Hub 计划在 2026 年第三季度末进行初始试用。Vikk AI 由 Walid Romaya 与刘易斯与克拉克法学院教授 Tabrez Ebrahim 于 2019 年创立，最初旨在连接律师与客户，2023 年转型开发法律助手，帮助潜在客户更好地向律师阐述问题并在初步分流后实现更精准匹配。公司在完成种子前轮前为自筹资金，目前拥有 15 至 20 名员工。

# Attorney Referral Legal Platform Vikk AI Announces $4.2M in Funding

The consumer-facing platform offers an AI legal assistant and sells ads to attorneys, with plans to launch a lawyer directory and create a data hub covering legal search trends.

4 minute read July 21, 2026 at 07:00 AM

By

![Image 18](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b683f4b314e480bc994cab5d8feb663b?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Benjamin Joyner](http://www.law.com/author/profile/benjamin-joyner/)

## What You Need to Know

*   Vikk AI announced $4.2 million in funding across pre-seed and seed funding rounds.
*   The company offers a consumer-facing AI legal assistant and sells ads to attorneys.
*   Vikk AI plans to use the new funds to continue product development and grow awareness among potential customers.
