![Image 19:  Vikk AI logo](https://images.law.com/assets/35/0f/ed2fbb824b519b9e30b7cf27caf7/vikk-ai-logo-jpg767x505.jpg) Vikk AI logo
Vikk AI, a Long Beach, California-based artificial intelligence-powered consumer legal assistant and attorney referral platform, announced Tuesday that it has raised $4.2 million across a recently concluded $3.5 million seed funding round and a $700,000 pre-seed round that closed in August 2025. Investors in the company include tax attorney Ronson Shamoun, personal injury attorney Joe Samo, health executive Brad Jowell, pharmaceutical executive Cooper Collins and additional undisclosed angel investors.

Vikk AI offers a consumer-facing platform that lets users describe legal issues and receive an overview of the legal options they have to resolve them, and offers a Lawyer Ad Center, which allows lawyers to advertise to potential clients based on their location and practice area.

The company plans to use the new funds from the seed round on continued software development, including through hiring additional engineers, and increasing awareness of the company among potential advertisers.

The company also plans to release a lawyer directory and Vikk Data Hub, which will provide law firms, insurers and other enterprises with aggregated and anonymized data about consumer legal search trends. Vikk AI plans to release its legal directory by mid-August, and is aiming for an initial trial release of Vikk Data Hub around the end of the third quarter of 2026.

Vikk AI co-founder and CEO Walid Romaya told Law.com that the company aims to provide consumers with a way to triage and evaluate legal issues and to provide attorneys and firms with business from consumers who need legal assistance.

Customers “use Vikk as a first line of inquiry—‘I just got hurt in an accident, or I have a child custody issue, or a neighbor built a fence on my property,’” he said. “These are daily life issues that may never need a lawyer, but a lot of them do. ... Our mission is to provide that first assistant, triage, and then hand it over to the lawyer if the user would like to connect to the lawyer.”

Vikk AI launched its Lawyer Ad Center for beta testing in recent months and has recently released the feature for full availability, allowing attorneys and firms to advertise to users looking into legal issues on the platform.

"A lawyer who decides to join the ad center and create a profile ... they can place an actual ad, and they can also put in their ad as a sponsored ad, similar to a Google Local Services ad, when a user can actually share their specific information, their case information, and actually press on the lawyer directly,” he said. “We're a direct lead, so the users have full control of who they want to connect with.”

Going forward, the company plans to supplement the ad center with a more traditionally structured legal directory following requests from attorneys and firms. The Data Hub is designed to serve law firms and other enterprises with information about legal search trends relevant to their businesses.

“If I'm an insurance company, I want to see trends about legal matters in a certain state, and what kind of legal matters are popping that might affect me or my brand,” Romaya said. The data hub is "a terminal that you can log in and see ... live trends in real time.”

Romaya initially founded Vikk AI in 2019 with Lewis & Clark Law School professor Tabrez Ebrahim with the aim of connecting attorneys and clients. The company changed focus in 2023 to develop a legal assistant that could help potential clients better articulate their legal issues to attorneys and connect them following an initial triage to ensure a better match. Vikk AI, which was self-funded prior to the completion of the pre-seed round, currently employs a staff of between 15 and 20 people.

news.titleEn: Courtroom View Network: Learning Trial Skills By Watching Real Lawyers In Real Trials
news.titleZh: 法庭视角网络：通过观看真实律师在真实庭审中的表现学习庭审技巧
news.summaryZh: 法庭视角网络（CVN）已录制数千场庭审视频并建立索引，用户可按开场陈述、结案陈词、直接询问、交叉询问等环节检索，也可按行业、案件类型或律师姓名搜索。该平台允许用户以任意方式切分和组合视频片段，从而观察优秀律师在真实庭审中的表现。在当今庭审机会稀少的背景下，CVN提供了独特的学习途径。
news.bodyText:
Sometimes at legal conferences put on by organizations like AALL, I come across something new and innovative. Such was the case when I stumbled into a session put on by Courtroom View Network.CVN says it has videoed thousands of trials and then indexed them so you can pull up exactly what you want to see such as opening, closing, direct, cross, to name just a few.

Or you can search by industry, trial subject or even by attorney. You can literally slice and dice these videos in any way you want.

So if you want to learn a trial skill or skills, you have a chance to observe good lawyers in real trials in action.

I dont know any other platform that provides this kind of opportunity. In an age when there are so few trials to participate in or observe, this opportunity is critical.

Here’s my take on CVN for Above the Law.

news.titleEn: How Firm AI unlocks value across every stage of the private capital investment lifecycle
news.titleZh: Firm AI如何贯穿私募资本投资全生命周期释放价值
news.summaryZh: 研究表明，私募资本公司在投资全生命周期中以结构化、一致的方式应用AI能获得最大价值，但目前仅7%的公司实现了企业级AI规模化。为成功扩展AI，公司需摒弃零散的通用工具，转而采用内置Firm AI的平台。Firm AI是一种专为公司业务构建的AI类别，能理解交易、关系和投资方法的上下文，自动执行运营工作并助力公司增长而不增加人力。此类平台统一数据、执行工作流并遵守合规规则，从而在交易全生命周期安全释放价值。具体而言，平台可利用公司投资历史自动筛选和评分潜在机会，加速交易获取；通过自动提取数据并映射至交易记录，加快交易录入。在投资者关系管理方面，平台能打破数据孤岛，实现更主动高效的沟通。尽职调查阶段，平台可快速合成大量信息，节省团队时间并辅助决策。退出阶段，平台有助于识别合适买家并把握市场时机。
news.bodyHtml:
Research indicates that private capital firms get the greatest value from AI when it’s applied in a structured, consistent way across the investment lifecycle. Yet there’s a significant gap between isolated AI use cases and firmwide advantage: Only 7% of firms have scaled AI enterprise-wide.

To scale AI successfully, firms need to stop using fragmented generic point tools and start using platforms with Firm AI.

Firm AI — a category of AI built for the business of the firm — understands the context of your deals, relationships, and investment methodology. It runs operational work and grows your firm without adding headcount.

Platforms with Firm AI unify data, execute workflows, and play by your compliance rules so your firm can safely unlock value across the entire deal lifecycle — not just in isolated use cases.

Keep reading to learn about the top ways platforms with Firm AI help your firm pull ahead of its competitors by driving value at each lifecycle stage.

Origination

Identifying the most profitable opportunities before competitors is significantly easier and faster when you have a tech platform built with Firm AI since it can source and score pipeline opportunities for you using your firm’s investment history.

These platforms also speed up deal intake by automatically extracting data from teasers and CIMs, then mapping it into deal records.

Fundraising and investor relations

Investor relationships are among a private capital firm’s most valuable assets — and among the hardest to manage due to siloed data and slow manual processes. Platforms with Firm AI change that. Here’s what they can do:

  • Flag coverage gaps before they impact relationships 
  • Draft personalized emails using LP communication history  
  • Assemble reports using current portfolio data and flag variances that need human review 
  • Surface the warmest path to any contact across your firm’s network 

The result: a more effective, proactive investor relations function that creates stronger connections and drives more business.The result: a more effective, proactive investor relations function that creates stronger connections and drives more business.

Due diligence

The due diligence stage generates enormous amounts of information that investment teams need to synthesize quickly. Platforms built with Firm AI can do the heavy lifting. Here’s what they do to help:

  • Synthesize email threads, interaction history, and deal notes into a single brief on demand 
  • Auto-generate first-pass LBO models that help teams reach initial decision faster 
  • Surface deal-risk signals so professionals can focus where it matters most 
  • Expedite past-deal analysis by connecting new evaluations to past IC decisions and pass notes

This saves teams vast amounts of time, and helps them arrive at every decision point with a more complete picture than your competition.

Exit planning

A strong exit is as much about identifying the right buyers as it is about timing the market. Here’s what platforms with Firm AI do to help you achieve both:

  • Help teams find buyers by matching assets to buyer profiles using your firm’s relationship and deal data
  • Prioritize exit-buyer candidates based on deal history and market activity
  • Automate deal marketing material creation so teams can focus on positioning
  • Update deal records in real time without interrupting the flow of work

These capabilities create a more efficient, data-driven exit process that helps your firm move faster and maximize deal value.

Conversational AI: The critical capability needed at every lifecycle stage

Platforms with Firm AI also provide teams with another highly valuable feature: conversational AI. Available across every lifecycle stage, it gives your teams instant access to your firm’s intelligence through natural language.

Professionals can ask questions or make requests in plain language, then get immediate answers grounded in firm data and governed by access controls. Here are examples of what your teams can ask conversational AI to do:

  • “Summarize everything we do about the Avenrock deal ahead of Thursday’s IC.” 
  • “Identify and prioritize exit-buyer candidates for Drydale Corp. based on our deal history and market activity.” 
  • “Find companies that match the profile of our last three closed deals.” 
  • “Draft deal marketing outreach for Genrite Corp. using the latest financials and our standard template.”

Conversational AI substantially reduces time spent searching across systems, reports, and notes, and gives your firm an edge by providing professionals with critical, real-time intelligence right when they need it.

Build a bigger advantage with AI that knows your firm

There are opportunities to work faster and pull ahead of competitors at every stage of the investment lifecycle – but your firm can’t unlock them with generic AI point tools that only work for narrow use cases.

Platforms with Firm AI understand how your firm operates, governing every AI action so you can safely scale AI and grow your business without adding headcount.

Read our e-book to learn how purpose-built platforms with Firm AI can help your firm build a bigger competitive advantage.

news.titleEn: Intapp now enforces your ethical walls inside Harvey
news.titleZh: Intapp 现已在 Harvey 内部强制执行道德墙
news.summaryZh: Harvey 与 Intapp Walls 的集成现已全面上市。超过 70 家 Am Law 100 律所依赖 Intapp Walls 执行信息隔离墙，该产品已成为管理机密信息的行业标准。此前，AI 工具内部存在合规缺口，因为律所原有的道德墙在 AI 系统边界处失效，治理责任落回律师个人。Harvey 与 Intapp 的合作旨在弥合这一缺口。通过集成，律所可将现有的 Intapp Walls 政策同步至 Harvey，并在 Harvey Assistant、Vault 和 Spaces 中自动强制执行。Harvey 直接从源头继承隔离墙策略，不创建、更改或删除策略，仅在无法确认资源访问权限时予以阻止。合规团队因此获得一套权威策略，无需并行管理，确保律所记录系统与 Harvey 执行的一致性。目前，Intapp Walls 已在 Harvey、Microsoft Copilot 和 Intapp Celeste 上执行全所统一策略，更多平台正在规划中。
news.bodyHtml:
The Harvey and Intapp Walls integration is now generally available. Confidentiality risk has been one of the biggest barriers to AI adoption at law firms, and today that changes. Intapp Walls and Harvey are now integrated, letting firms sync their existing Walls policies directly into Harvey and enforce them automatically across Harvey Assistant, Vault, and Spaces. Here’s why it matters for firms deciding how far to take AI.

More than 70 of the Am Law 100 rely on Intapp Walls to enforce information barriers, and it has become the industry standard for governing confidential information. For two decades, compliance teams have configured the policies, calibrated enforcement, and earned sign-off on the infrastructure that screens lawyers from conflicting matters.

Then the firm deploys a legal AI platform, and those walls stop at the edge of the systems they were built for. Inside the AI tool, governance falls back to attorney discipline. AI has opened a compliance gap firms did not plan for, and the numbers show how wide it already is.

  • 83% of lawyers use AI in 2026
    Source: Bloomberg Law, June 2026
  • 5% of law firm leaders trust their current AI quality controls
    Source: Global Legal Post, 2026 legal sector outlook study

Earlier this year, Harvey and Intapp announced a partnership to close that gap. Today, after an early access period with a select group of firms, the integration is generally available.

What actually goes wrong

Consider a lawyer screened off a litigation matter because the firm represents the opposing party. In the document management system, the screen holds. They cannot open those files. Then they open an AI assistant, pull matter documents into a shared workspace, and invite a colleague who happens to be walled off from that matter. The information has just moved through a channel the firm’s walls never see.

The screen did its job in the DMS. The exposure reappeared one layer up. An AI-enabled lateral conflict, a privileged-information leak through a shared workspace, or an outside counsel guideline (OCG) violation that surfaces in audit becomes a partner-room event, and every new AI tool the firm adopts widens the surface where it can happen.

Native AI controls handle part of the picture. Every AI platform ships with controls for authentication and workspace permissions, and they handle those jobs well for a single tool. Ethical walls ask for something more specific: lateral-hire screens, matter-level confidentiality, waiver-driven restrictions, and controls on material nonpublic information (MNPI), enforced consistently and logged for audit across every system the firm runs. Secure a second AI tool with native controls alone and the policies begin again in a separate console, rebuilding tool by tool the fragmentation the firm spent years removing.

How Walls and Harvey work together

With the integration, firms sync their existing Intapp Walls policies directly into Harvey, where Harvey enforces them automatically across Harvey Assistant, Vault, and Spaces, the surfaces attorneys use to research, draft, and analyze every day.

Harvey inherits walls directly from the source. It never creates, changes, or deletes them. It enforces the policies Intapp Walls already manages, and when access to a resource cannot be confirmed, Harvey blocks it. For compliance teams, that means one authoritative set of policies, zero parallel administration, and full consistency between what the firm’s system of record says and what Harvey enforces.

  • Enforce your walls automatically. When a wall is created or updated in Intapp Walls, Harvey syncs it automatically. Attorneys see only the matters Walls has authorized. Firms can extend Harvey to every practice group while the walls they already validated apply from the first day, with no new round of IT configuration or compliance review.
  • Stay audit-ready from day one. Every enforcement event traces back to both systems. If a matter’s confidentiality is ever challenged, the conflicts team can produce an unbroken record showing exactly which wall policy governed Harvey’s behavior, down to the sync timestamp, giving the firm the evidence it needs for internal stakeholders, regulators, and courts.
  • Keep collaboration governed. Walls follow the work automatically. Self-maintaining walls add and remove people based on time or document activity, and matter teams can request and approve access within policy, without a ticket to compliance for every change. Sensitive matters stay protected while the firm keeps moving.

One policy layer for every AI tool

Intapp Walls enforces one firm-wide policy set across Harvey, Microsoft Copilot, and Intapp Celeste today, with additional platforms on the roadmap. Firms define a barrier once and it applies everywhere, added to each new tool through simple API configuration.

Adding the fourth AI tool looks like adding the first. As the firm’s AI footprint grows, the governed layer grows with it, and the audit trail stays in one place. Firms do not have to bet on which AI tool wins. Walls extends to whichever ones they choose.

Make firm-wide rollout certifiable

For most firms the question now is how to move from a controlled pilot to firm-wide AI. The prize is real, and firms expect AI to deliver it.

  • 240 hrs saved per lawyer each year, anticipated
  • $19,000 in value unlocked per lawyer each year, anticipated
  • 2x more likely to grow revenue for firms with a visible AI strategy
    Sources: Thomson Reuters, Future of Professionals 2025; ACEDS + Secretariat 2025 Legal AI Report.

Capturing that upside is a hard step: 88% of AI proofs of concept never reach production, and governance is often where they stall. Deployment waits on a general counsel who will certify firm-wide rollout only once the controls are provable. Intapp Walls is what makes that certification possible.

Your firm has already done the hard part. The policies exist, compliance has validated them, and they govern every other system the firm runs. Putting that same infrastructure to work inside AI tools turns firm-wide rollout into an extension of controls the firm already trusts, so the decision to expand AI access rests on walls the firm has already validated.

Activate ethical walls in Harvey with Intapp

The integration is available exclusively for Intapp Walls for AI, the cloud version of Intapp Walls — if your firm is already on it, you can activate the integration now. If you run Intapp Walls on-premises and want to learn more, contact your Intapp or Harvey representative or visit intapp.com/harvey-agentic-ai-partnership.

news.titleEn: The Insurance Challenge: AI-Assisted Pro Se Litigation and Rising Defense Costs
news.titleZh: 保险业的挑战：AI辅助的自我代理诉讼与不断上升的辩护成本
news.summaryZh: 生成式AI正重塑诉讼格局。对保险公司而言，直接担忧是AI帮助自我代理的诉讼当事人生成诉状、法律论证等文件，迫使辩护方回应。新泽西州最高法院已发布律师使用AI的初步指南，并实施相关继续法律教育要求。AI工具可在数秒内起草法律文件，降低了诉讼门槛，但自我代理当事人缺乏AI风险培训，可能提交表面光鲜但不可靠的文件。这为保险公司创造了新成本中心：看似可信的文件仍需仔细审查和回应。AI增加文件数量和复杂性，但不提升法律价值。近期案例显示AI生成文件常包含虚构权威和错误论点，如Mata案中律师因提交虚假案例受制裁。AI辅助文件可能在触及案情实质前引发法院审查和额外程序。早期实证表明，联邦民事自我代理原告比例从AI普及前的11.33%升至16.94%，AI一致性投诉引用更密集且更早被驳回，尽管缺乏实质价值，仍增加保险公司辩护成本。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Generative artificial intelligence (“AI”) is reshaping litigation. For insurers and legal operations professionals, the immediate concern is not simply that AI can help lawyers work faster; it is that AI can also help self-represented - pro se - litigants generate pleadings, filings, legal arguments, and more legal paper for defense counsel to answer. New Jersey’s courts have already acknowledged AI’s significance. The New Jersey Supreme Court issued preliminary guidance on lawyers’ use of AI in January 2024 through its Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts, and the New Jersey Judiciary later announced a technology-related Continuing Legal Education requirement for attorneys that began in 2025. Together, those developments reflect a broader recognition that AI competence now affects legal practice, court administration, and litigation risk. Most commentary has focused on lawyers’ use of AI. For insurers, however, the more disruptive development may be AI-enabled pro se litigation. Publicly available AI tools can draft complaints, motions, discovery requests, and briefs in seconds. That lowers the practical barrier to filing suit and allows self-represented litigants to submit documents that look sophisticated even when the legal analysis is weak, inaccurate, or entirely fabricated. Unlike attorneys, pro se litigants generally do not receive formal training on AI risks, verification standards, or professional duty of candor, thereby increasing the likelihood that courts and opposing parties will encounter polished but unreliable filings. The New Jersey Supreme Court’s guidance expressly warns lawyers to verify AI output, and the same concern applies with even greater force when no lawyer is involved. For people who cannot afford counsel, AI may seem like a low-cost substitute for legal representation. That accessibility has real upside, but it also creates a new cost center for insurers: filings that may appear credible on their face yet still require careful review, response, and court appearances. That is the insurance problem in practical terms. AI can increase the volume and complexity of pro se filings without improving their legal merit. The concern is not whether an AI-generated filing will ultimately fail, but how much defense work is required to test, narrow, or defeat it. Recent decisions in New Jersey and elsewhere show a familiar pattern: AI-generated filings can contain invented authorities, misstated holdings, and unsupported arguments. One example is Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), where attorneys were sanctioned for submitting fictitious cases generated by ChatGPT. Other examples, many of which involve pro se litigants, include: These decisions illustrate the operational risk: AI-assisted filings can trigger court scrutiny, verification disputes, and additional procedural steps, even before the merits are reached. The billing impact appears most clearly at the front end of a matter. Defense counsel must parse lengthy allegations, test whether cited cases are real and on point, identify procedural defects, and determine the most efficient response. Hearings may expand when the court must address citation problems, disclosure issues, or motions prompted by AI-generated overreach. Early empirical work suggests this is more than anecdotal. Indeed, among roughly 2.8 million federal filings, the federal civil pro se plaintiff rate rose from 11.33% before widespread access to generative AI to 16.94% afterward. (See The New Pro Se: Generative AI and the Surge in Federal Civil Self-Representation, Or Cohen-Sasson, Miami Law & AI Lab, University of Miami School of Law, May 28, 2026). Additionally, AI-consistent complaints were more citation-dense and more likely to be dismissed earlier in the case. Id. These more formal-looking filings can still produce more defense costs for insurers, despite a lack of merit.

news.titleEn: Alabama’s New AI Ethical Guidance and Its Impact on Legal Departments
news.titleZh: 阿拉巴马州新AI伦理指南及其对法务部门的影响
news.summaryZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会近期发布了关于人工智能伦理使用的最新指南。该指南并未创设新的伦理规则，而是阐释了律师现有职业责任如何适用于已成为日常法律实践一部分的AI工具。指南明确，AI“重新诠释”了律师在《阿拉巴马职业行为规则》下的现有义务，而非新增义务。律师必须合理了解AI工具的功能、局限及输出可能失败的方式，这属于律师胜任义务的范畴。AI生成的输出绝不应被直接采信。今年早些时候，阿拉巴马州最高法院在一起案件中驳回上诉并处以超过1.7万美元的制裁，原因是律师提交的诉状依赖AI生成的、不存在的法律权威。律师需独立审查AI生成的工作，包括核实引注、法律权威和法律结论。指南将AI视为类似非律师助理的角色，监督律师对AI辅助的工作产品负全责。律所和法务部门应制定书面AI使用政策，指定人员评估和批准AI工具，并确保未经律师独立审查的AI生成工作不会到达客户、法院或高管层。尽管指南针对执业律师，但相同的伦理原则为法务部门内部治理AI提供了实用框架。关键关注领域包括：AI可使法务部门更高效，但责任始终在人而非技术。建立明确AI政策的组织将能更好地在管理法律和伦理风险的同时实现AI的益处。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The Alabama State Bar recently released updated guidance on the ethical use of artificial intelligence. While the guidance does not create any new ethics rules, it explains how lawyers’ existing professional responsibilities apply to AI tools that are now part of everyday legal practice. Here are a few key takeaways. No. The Alabama State Bar makes clear that AI “recontextualizes” lawyers’ existing obligations under the Alabama Rules of Professional Conduct (ARPC) rather than creating new ones. Lawyers must have a reasonable understanding of what an AI tool does, what it cannot do, and how its outputs can fail. Those responsibilities fall squarely within a lawyer’s duty of competence. Virtually every set of AI ethics guidance reaches the same conclusion: AI-generated output should never be accepted at face value. By now, most lawyers are familiar with Mata v. Avianca, the widely publicized case in which an attorney filed a brief containing fictitious cases generated by ChatGPT. Alabama now has its own cautionary example. Earlier this year, the Alabama Supreme Court dismissed an appeal and imposed more than $17,000 in sanctions after an attorney submitted a brief that relied on AI-generated, nonexistent legal authority. (See Ibach v. Stewart). Whether appearing before a court or advising a board of directors, lawyers independently review AI-generated work and exercise their own legal judgment. That includes verifying citations, legal authorities, and legal conclusions against reliable legal research sources before submitting a filing or presenting advice to a decision-maker. Ultimately, the lawyer is. The guidance treats AI much like a non-lawyer assistant. Supervising lawyers remain fully responsible for AI-assisted work product, including work generated by a paralegal, legal assistant, or staff member using AI. Law firms and legal departments should implement written AI-use policies, designate individuals to evaluate and approve AI tools, and ensure that no AI-generated work reaches a client, court, or executive leadership without a lawyer’s independent review. Although the guidance is directed at practicing lawyers, the same ethical principles provide a practical framework for governing AI within legal departments. Key areas of focus include: The common thread running through the guidance, recent sanctions, and these recommended business practices is straightforward: AI can make legal departments more efficient and effective, but accountability remains with people, not technology. Organizations that build these guardrails with clear AI policies will be better positioned to realize AI’s benefits while managing legal and ethical risk.

news.titleEn: Box Targets Legal With Agentic Control System
news.titleZh: Box推出面向法律行业的智能代理控制系统
news.summaryZh: Box从云存储业务转型为智能内容管理平台，现针对法律及其他受监管行业推出新型代理AI控制系统。该系统为处理企业内容的AI代理提供安全与治理能力，帮助法律行业在合同审查、证据开示和案件准备等流程中安全使用AI，同时保护机密信息。Box通过E-Advanced计划推出政策驱动控制，限制代理的访问和操作权限。此举正值越来越多律所和法律团队采用代理工具之际，但如何控制代理、确保合规和安全成为关键问题。Box此前已与部分律所和法务团队合作，此次举措更为深入复杂，同时适用于金融服务、医疗和保险等高度监管行业。83%的组织已在关键任务中试验AI代理，必须建立适当的安全控制，确保代理有效运作而不越权访问或泄露内容。Box旨在为各类代理的安全大规模部署树立标准。
news.bodyText: Box, which has evolved from a cloud storage business into an Intelligent Content Management (ICM) platform, is targeting the legal – and other regulated sectors – with a new agentic AI control system. A spokesperson for Box told Artificial Lawyer: ‘As organisations like law firms look to deploy agents across sensitive business processes, Box is introducing a new set of security and governance capabilities designed specifically for AI agents working with enterprise content. ‘For the legal industry, this addresses the challenge of how to safely use AI for workflows like contract reviews, discovery workflows, and case preparation without compromising confidential information. With these new capabilities, firms can govern AI agents by enforcing policy-driven controls on what agents can access and act on.’ The move matters as more and more law firms and legal teams are making use of agentic tools, and the general model makers are also providing such capabilities. For example, Anthropic has a dedicated capability for agent development via Claude Managed Agents. However, how are they being controlled? What does compliance look like for them? What is the security set-up around them? Enter Box. Under its E-Advanced plan they are rolling out: It’s not the first time that Box has sought to pick up business in the legal world – it’s been working with a handful of law firms, as well as inhouse legal teams for a while. But, this is a deeper and more complex move. They are also pitching this as useful for financial services, healthcare, and insurance – in short, where there are high levels of regulatory oversight. Manoj Asnani, VP of AI Security, Privacy, Compliance & Governance Products at Box, commented: ‘83% of organizations are already experimenting with AI agents across their most critical tasks. ‘As these agentic workflows become more deeply embedded in the enterprise, it is critical to create the proper security controls to ensure agents have what they need to function effectively, without accessing, modifying, or exposing content beyond the scope of its intended task. ‘Box already provides a safe environment for organizations to apply AI to their most critical business knowledge, and with these new controls, we are creating a standard for deploying agents of any kind securely and at scale.’ And here’s a more detailed overview of what they will offer: Is this a big deal?

news.titleEn: AI Is Accelerating – Your DMS Will Determine Whether You Keep Pace
news.titleZh: AI加速发展，文档管理系统决定你能否跟上步伐
news.summaryZh: AI对法律工作的质量、效率和效果产生深远影响，而大型语言模型（LLM）的效果在结合相关数据和适当上下文时显著提升。许多律所和法律部门多年来通过文档管理系统（DMS）规范数据管理，这一基础设施在AI时代正发挥新价值。数据质量直接影响AI输出质量，律师需识别最佳工作并捕捉文档之外的信号，例如通过定制模型识别管辖区域，从而支持更精准的查询。此外，DMS中的数据需有严格的信息治理，控制访问权限、处理位置和保留期限。在AI代理可能访问数据的当下，结构化和受治理的数据至关重要，否则可能引发混乱。
news.bodyText: By Neil Araujo, CEO, iManage. In a relatively short span of time, it’s become increasingly clear that AI will have a profound impact on the quality, effectiveness, and efficiency of legal work. What has become equally evident is that the effectiveness of the large language models (LLMs) that power AI is significantly higher when you combine them with relevant data and the appropriate context. The good news here for most law firms and legal departments is they’ve had discipline around managing their data going back decades, often with a document management system (DMS) playing a central role. That long-established piece of information infrastructure – and the organizational processes that surround it – are bearing new fruit in the AI era. Better data quality translates into better AI outputs While a DMS provides a foundational layer for AI efforts, it’s not just about capturing data, but data quality. Lawyers need to be able to identify their best work and capture the signals that go beyond the document itself. A good LLM can pick up on those signals to create better outputs. Take jurisdiction, for example. It’s essential to know which country or region’s law a document is relying on, because a clause valid in one region may not be valid in another. Typically, jurisdiction wasn’t captured in any structured way – instead, it was inferred from language buried in the document. If you build custom models that are trained specifically for that one task – to identify the jurisdiction – a lawyer can then say, “Find me all share purchase agreements where the governing law is England and Wales,” and you can ask a subsequent question like: “What was the termination clause for agreements that were generated in that particular jurisdiction?” In this way, the DMS goes from capturing data to capturing data as well as signals that inform. — — Guardrails and governance safely unlock agentic workflows It’s worth stating here that guardrails matter immensely: there needs to be rock-solid information governance around the data in any DMS controlling what data can be accessed, where it is processed, and how long it lives before it is obsolete. And in the current AI era, when the “individual” who needs access to data might be an AI agent, having structured, governed data is critical – otherwise you risk chaos.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦法律领域AI应用，讨论文档管理系统如何提升AI输出质量，并涉及信息治理和AI代理工作流，核心围绕法律技术。

research.titleEn: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
research.titleZh: 先推理后翻译：利用结构化推理增强法律机器翻译
research.abstractEn: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.   In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.
research.abstractZh: 法律领域的神经机器翻译（NMT）是一项在语言和概念上要求很高的任务，这主要是由于法律语言的复杂性及其所需的高精度。最近出现的具备推理能力的语言模型为应对此类挑战开辟了新的可能性。它们补充了先前提出的其他增强翻译质量的技术，包括监督微调和强化学习。在这项工作中，我们对这些不同方法进行了比较。更具体地说，我们评估了通过不同再训练范式增强的小型语言模型，如Qwen3.5 4B、Qwen3.5 9B和Gemma 3 12B，并将其性能与前沿推理模型进行了比较。我们重点关注瑞士法律体系，该体系以其独特的多种语言法规，为推理增强模型提供了一个特别具有挑战性的测试平台。我们的结果表明，小型“基础”模型的质量可以得到大幅提升，并且带有可验证奖励的强化学习可以应用于法律领域的NMT，其翻译质量超过了监督微调。增强后的小型模型的性能接近最先进的推理模型，但仍有所不及。我们还注意到，随着模型规模的增大，再训练范式的收益递减。代码和模型可在https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL公开获取。

research.titleEn: AILQA: Evaluating AI-Driven Legal Question Answering Systems for the Indian Legal System
research.titleZh: AILQA：评估面向印度法律体系的AI驱动法律问答系统
research.abstractEn: This comprehensive study introduces an advanced Artificial Intelligence for Indian Legal Question Answering (AILQA) system tailored to the Indian legal context. AILQA leverages a variety of embedding and generative models, including recent Large Language Models (LLMs), to address the unique challenges posed by the intricate and diverse nature of Indian legal texts and to enhance the accuracy and reliability of responses to legal questions. We conducted rigorous evaluations using both lexical and semantic metrics, enriched by expert legal feedback, to ensure relevance and accuracy. Our findings underscore the effectiveness of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm in improving answer quality, particularly in complex legal domains. Additionally, we assessed performance on standardized tests such as the All India Bar Examination (AIBE), thereby providing a robust benchmark for practical applications. Under the study's evaluation protocol, some AI-generated responses received higher ratings than the available reference answers, particularly when they contained accurate and relevant supporting details. This finding is specific to the evaluated dataset and rating criteria and should not be interpreted as evidence that the models generally outperform qualified legal professionals. We also discuss the challenges encountered, such as the need for precise context and the risks of model hallucination, and propose directions for future research to further refine AI capabilities in the legal field. This study aims to pave the way for enhanced legal decision-support systems, making them more accessible and effective for legal professionals and the public alike.
research.abstractZh: 这项综合研究介绍了一种针对印度法律背景量身定制的高级人工智能印度法律问答（AILQA）系统。AILQA利用各种嵌入和生成模型，包括最近的大型语言模型（LLM），以应对印度法律文本错综复杂和多样性所带来的独特挑战，并提高对法律问题回答的准确性和可靠性。我们使用词汇和语义指标进行了严格的评估，并辅以专家法律反馈，以确保相关性和准确性。我们的研究结果强调了检索增强生成（RAG）范式在提高答案质量方面的有效性，特别是在复杂的法律领域。此外，我们评估了在全印度律师资格考试（AIBE）等标准化测试中的表现，从而为实际应用提供了稳健的基准。在研究的评估协议下，一些AI生成的回答获得了比现有参考答案更高的评分，特别是当它们包含准确且相关的支持细节时。这一发现特定于所评估的数据集和评分标准，不应被解释为模型普遍优于合格法律专业人士的证据。我们还讨论了遇到的挑战，如需要精确的上下文和模型幻觉的风险，并提出了未来研究的方向，以进一步完善AI在法律领域的能力。这项研究旨在为增强法律决策支持系统铺平道路，使它们对法律专业人士和公众都更加可及和有效。

news.titleEn: Clifford Chance pairs with Epiq Advisory and Microsoft for new knowledge management platform
news.titleZh: Clifford Chance携手Epiq Advisory与微软打造全新知识管理平台
news.summaryZh: Clifford Chance于7月20日宣布部署全新知识管理平台，该平台由Epiq Advisory for Law Firms主导设计，微软提供技术支持，历时六个月交付。平台完全基于Microsoft 365和Azure构建，目前存储超过40万份文件，支持自然语言搜索。此举打破传统第三方软件采购模式，旨在自主掌控知识管理发展路线。平台具备元数据知识检索功能，以满足客户日益复杂的保密要求。Clifford Chance于2024年2月率先向律师推广Copilot for Microsoft 365。初期推广后采用率较高，各业务团队与知识管理部门正就平台开发提出建议，未来将针对不同业务组推出更多功能。
news.bodyHtml:
By Patrick Shortall

Clifford Chance announced today (20th July) the deployment of a new knowledge management platform. The platform’s design was led by Epiq Advisory for Law Firms, the knowledge management and technology consulting arm of global alternative legal service provider Epiq, and received technical input from Microsoft.

Advertisement

Delivered in six months, the project signifies a break from the traditional model of buying third party software for legal knowledge management and retrieval. The firm’s reasoning for this is to control its own roadmap for knowledge management. The firm still uses iManage as its core document management system.

The new knowledge bank, now holding more than 400,000 of the firm’s documents and allowing natural language search, is built entirely within Microsoft 365 and Azure, which follows a historically close partnership between the firm and the technology company. Clifford Chance was one of the first firms to roll out Copilot for Microsoft 365 to its lawyers in February 2024.

Advertisement

One feature, claimed to be exclusive by Epiq, permits knowledge retrieval according to metadata, in a bid to keep pace with clients’ increasingly complex confidentiality requirements.

The firm reports strong adoption following the initial rollout and engagement between practice groups, individuals and the knowledge management team on ideas for its development.

New developments are expected to come from increased use cases or features more specific to individual practice groups. Each is expected to follow the formula of keeping things within Microsoft, keeping control, and ensuring increasingly complex client confidentiality requirements are met.

We’ll bring you more when we speak with Clifford Chance, as no spokesperson was available at the time they published the release.

news.titleEn: Law Democratized: Renee Knake Jefferson on Her Blueprint for Solving the Justice Crisis
news.titleZh: 法律民主化：蕾妮·纳克·杰斐逊谈解决司法危机的蓝图
news.summaryZh: 蕾妮·纳克·杰斐逊是休斯顿大学法律中心的法学教授和乔安妮与拉里·多尔蒂法律伦理讲席教授，其研究涉及法律伦理、司法伦理、律师监管、法律教育和司法可及性。她是《法律民主化：解决司法危机的蓝图》一书的作者，也是《入围：最高法院阴影下的女性》的合著者，美国法律研究所当选成员，曾任美国律师协会法律服务未来委员会联合报告员。2013年，她因与丹尼尔·马丁·卡茨共同创立密歇根州立大学重塑法律实验室而被《ABA期刊》评为法律叛逆者。近期，她当选美国律师协会法律教育与律师资格准入部门理事会成员。在LawNext播客中，杰斐逊与主持人鲍勃·安布罗吉深入讨论了司法可及性危机及缩小司法差距的途径，包括人们可能未意识到自身法律问题是最大障碍。他们还探讨了人工智能作为缩小司法差距工具的潜力与风险，监管改革为何未产生预期连锁效应，以及律师、法学院、监管者和创新者各自可采取的行动。杰斐逊保持乐观态度。
news.bodyHtml:
Martin Luther King famously said, “The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” My guest today quoted his words in her 2024 book, Law Democratized: A Blueprint for Solving the Justice Crisis. But now, two years after that book’s publication — at a moment when many see the rule of law under strain and speak openly of democratic backsliding — it is fair to ask: Are we still arcing toward justice?

That is the question LawNext host Bob Ambrogi put to Renee Knake Jefferson at the start of today’s conversation. Jefferson is a professor of law and the Joanne and Larry Doherty Chair in Legal Ethics at the University of Houston Law Center, and her work sits at the intersection of legal ethics, judicial ethics, lawyer regulation, legal education and access to justice.

She is also the coauthor of the acclaimed book Shortlisted: Women in the Shadows of the Supreme Court, an elected member of the American Law Institute, and a former co-reporter for the ABA Commission on the Future of Legal Services. In 2013, the ABA Journal named her a Legal Rebel for co-founding the ReInvent Law Laboratory at Michigan State together with Daniel Martin Katz. More recently, she was elected to the American Bar Association’s Council for the Section on Legal Education and Admission to the Bar, the body responsible for accrediting J.D. programs — so, as she puts it, she’s gone from offering constructive criticism from the outside to working on the inside

In her “spare time” (as if she possibly has any), she writes the Substack newsletter Legal Ethics Roundup, a weekly review of all things related to legal and judicial ethics.

In today’s conversation, Renee and Bob talk in depth about the access to justice crisis and what can be done to narrow the justice gap, including why the biggest barrier to legal help may be that people do not even recognize they have a legal problem. They also discuss the promise and peril of AI as a tool for closing the justice gap, why regulatory reform has not produced the domino effect many once predicted, and what lawyers, law schools, regulators and innovators can each do to move the needle.

Spoiler alert: Jefferson remains a glass-half-full optimist — and by the end of this conversation, you may be too.

news.titleEn: QuisLex launches AI capability framework as focus shifts from adoption to accountability
news.titleZh: QuisLex推出AI能力框架，焦点从采用转向问责
news.summaryZh: 替代性法律服务提供商QuisLex于7月20日发布了一项新的咨询框架，旨在帮助法律部门和律师事务所构建机构能力，以生成可信、可治理且可辩护的AI辅助法律工作。该框架以机构能力评估（ICA）为核心，反映了QuisLex创始人兼CEO Sirisha Gummaregula所称的法律AI成熟度的下一阶段。过去两年，法律组织主要尝试使用生成式AI工具，但现在的挑战是证明AI生成的工作可靠，且组织对其结果负责。使用AI已成为基本要求，但更大的问题是不能孤立地看待AI，需要构建背后的架构，包括内部知识、模板和业务实践，并将其提供给AI系统以提供更丰富的上下文。此外，组织还需要验证输出并建立证据，以支持基于AI生成工作所做的决策。QuisLex的新框架不针对特定技术供应商，而是评估和强化客户自身的知识、流程和治理结构。框架的第二部分是可靠性和治理，帮助组织建立工作流程和控制措施，以衡量和证明AI辅助工作的质量。
news.bodyHtml:
Alternative legal services provider QuisLex today (20 July) unveiled a new advisory framework designed to help legal departments and law firms build the institutional capability needed to produce AI-assisted legal work that can be trusted, governed and defended. 

The new offering, centred around an Institutional Capability Assessment (ICA), reflects what QuisLex founder and CEO Sirisha Gummaregula says is the next phase of legal AI maturity. While legal organisations spent much of the past two years experimenting with generative AI tools, the challenge now is proving that AI-generated work can be relied upon and that organisations remain accountable for its outcomes.   

Advertisement

“What we’re seeing in the last few months is that using AI has become table stakes now,” Gummaregula told Legal IT Insider. “Everybody is talking about ‘hey, we use AI. We are incorporating it into our workloads.’”   

QuisLex has already been active in the AI governance debate through its Five Failure Modes of Legal AI framework, launched earlier this year and submitted to organisations including the ABA, state bars and CLOC. The framework sought to move the discussion beyond hallucinations and highlight a broader set of risks associated with AI-assisted legal work.   

Advertisement

However, according to Gummaregula, client conversations quickly revealed a larger challenge. “We started realizing the bigger issue is that you can’t just look at AI using AI in legal departments or law firms by itself. It doesn’t live by itself,” she said. “You really need to build an architecture behind it in the sense that what is your internal knowledge on how you do business, what has already been codified in your templates or in your business practices? Can you make that available to the AI system that is running the work so that it has kind of richer context to that?” 

Beyond knowledge capture, Gummaregula says that organisations also need ways to validate outputs and create evidence that supports decisions made using AI-generated work. 

“Once the system really executes a work product, do you have processes that allow you to validate those findings and essentially build some kind of data, evidence data on this is the reason why I relied on this work product in case it gets questioned in the future,” she says.   

That thinking forms the basis of the new Institutional Capability Assessment. Rather than focusing on a particular technology vendor, the framework is designed to assess and strengthen the client’s own knowledge, processes and governance structures. 

“Our new offering is essentially, ‘we will help you build that framework and we are calling it the institutional capability assessment ICA for short,’” Gummaregula said. 

“What it allows clients to do is we will use whatever you have already built internally. We’ll codify it in a way that you could use that as the context, as the knowledge context for you to effectively use AI.” 

The second element of the framework is reliability and governance. QuisLex says it helps organisations build workflows and controls that allow them to measure and evidence the quality of AI-assisted work. 

“On top of the system, we will build methodologies and workflows on how somebody can kind of measure the reliability of what the work that is coming out of the AI system so that you are able to stand behind it,” Gummaregula said. 

The significance of the announcement for legal IT leaders is that QuisLex is positioning AI governance as an institutional challenge rather than a technology procurement exercise. While many organisations remain focused on selecting the right tools, Gummaregula argues that technology is only one part of the equation. 

“Clients are quite overwhelmed with the options that are out there,” she said. While QuisLex helps clients run proofs of concept and assess technologies, “it is really one piece of the puzzle in a lot of ways… a very important piece of the puzzle. But you really do need to make sure that you’re putting it in the right place, you’re giving it the right context, you’re building the appropriate controls.” 

Importantly, the framework is designed to work across different technology environments and industry sectors rather than imposing a single operating model. Gummaregula describes it as “a very organized framework” that helps organisations ask the right questions while remaining highly customised.  

“It’s not a one size fits all,” she said. “It’s a framework that allows you to ask kind of the right questions at each level and then it’s customized for that organization.”   

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of QuisLex’s thinking lies in how AI changes traditional concepts of liability. According to Gummaregula, organisations are being forced to rethink assumptions that have underpinned legal workflows for decades. 

“What does that liability look like?” she questions. “It is a completely different lens now, which is why the industry needs valid framework.” Gummaregula recently wrote an academic paper on this topic and observes: “The workflow is execution, judgment, accountability. We assume that a person who signs the contract is automatically accountable and has exercised judgment. But when you bring in an AI system, execution is by the AI system. Maybe judgment is also – you need to validate whether there was judgment. But the accountability still stays with the individual and not the system. And that changes the entire equation.   

“You really do need to look at it holistically on what does the institution needs to do to remain accountable for a work product that they may not have fully generated. Which is why evidencing worse, human judgment appropriately exercised now becomes the bigger part of the equation.” 

That shift has led QuisLex to focus heavily on how organisations remain accountable for work products that they may not have fully generated. Human judgment becomes a bigger than ever part of the equation because ultimately, accountability sits with humans. Given the evidence around cognitive surrender – people automatically relying on what their system is saying – it’s important to have plans in place. 

“Unless you’re actively thinking about it and making sure you have appropriate controls, you really may be looking at a bigger accountability issue in the future,” Gummaregula says.
news.bodyText: Alternative legal services provider QuisLex today (20 July) unveiled a new advisory framework designed to help legal departments and law firms build the institutional capability needed to produce AI-assisted legal work that can be trusted, governed and defended. The new offering, centred around an Institutional Capability Assessment (ICA), reflects what QuisLex founder and CEO Sirisha Gummaregula says is the next phase of legal AI maturity. While legal organisations spent much of the past two years experimenting with generative AI tools, the challenge now is proving that AI-generated work can be relied upon and that organisations remain accountable for its outcomes. “What we’re seeing in the last few months is that using AI has become table stakes now,” Gummaregula told Legal IT Insider. “Everybody is talking about ‘hey, we use AI. We are incorporating it into our workloads.’” QuisLex has already been active in the AI governance debate through its Five Failure Modes of Legal AI framework, launched earlier this year and submitted to organisations including the ABA, state bars and CLOC. The framework sought to move the discussion beyond hallucinations and highlight a broader set of risks associated with AI-assisted legal work. However, according to Gummaregula, client conversations quickly revealed a larger challenge. “We started realizing the bigger issue is that you can’t just look at AI using AI in legal departments or law firms by itself. It doesn’t live by itself,” she said. “You really need to build an architecture behind it in the sense that what is your internal knowledge on how you do business, what has already been codified in your templates or in your business practices? Can you make that available to the AI system that is running the work so that it has kind of richer context to that?” Beyond knowledge capture, Gummaregula says that organisations also need ways to validate outputs and create evidence that supports decisions made using AI-generated work. “Once the system really executes a work product, do you have processes that allow you to validate those findings and essentially build some kind of data, evidence data on this is the reason why I relied on this work product in case it gets questioned in the future,” she says. That thinking forms the basis of the new Institutional Capability Assessment. Rather than focusing on a particular technology vendor, the framework is designed to assess and strengthen the client’s own knowledge, processes and governance structures. “Our new offering is essentially, ‘we will help you build that framework and we are calling it the institutional capability assessment ICA for short,’” Gummaregula said. “What it allows clients to do is we will use whatever you have already built internally. We’ll codify it in a way that you could use that as the context, as the knowledge context for you to effectively use AI.” The second element of the framework is reliability and governance. QuisLex says it helps organisations build workflows and controls that allow them to measure and evidence the quality of AI-assisted work. “On top of the system, we will build methodologies and workflows on how somebody can kind of measure the reliability of what the work that is coming out of the AI system so that you are able to stand behind it,” Gummaregula said.

# AI's Potential Maximum Effect: Compliance and Beyond

In the case of AI for legal and compliance, AI is not an improvement technology—it’s the catalyst for a new way of doing things.

4 minute read July 20, 2026 at 12:31 PM

By

Jon Kessler

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

![Image 18: Jon Kessler. Courtesy photo](https://images.law.com/assets/95/fb/f2fa7acc4d4f8e625e43682805c8/jon-kessler-jpg767x505.jpg)Jon Kessler. Courtesy photo
By definition, revolutionary technologies enable the previously impossible. In the case of AI for legal and compliance, AI is _not_ an improvement technology—it’s the catalyst for a new way of doing things. The compliance function highlights how getting the most out of AI requires looking beyond the obvious use cases where AI is “simply” a workflow accelerator.

## What’s Now Possible?

Compliance consumes thousands of hours every year and has always been reactive and audit-based, for three primary reasons. First, compliance departments have finite staff with limited time. Second, those departments contend with complex technology stacks comprising numerous tools to identify risk, advise the business, and protect the company. Third, compliance is a moving target, with a steady stream of new regulations across multiple domestic and international jurisdictions. Historically, a reactive stance and sampling methodology have been the only viable approach.

This makes it understandable that compliance leaders begin by leveraging AI as way to automate manual tasks. But “faster and more frequent” is just the start. Functionally, AI is a limitless source of work hours, able to accomplish in moments what would take humans hours if not days, any time of day, on weekends and holidays. This opens the door to a new proactive compliance paradigm, built on two pillars: real-time monitoring and automated work. The first centers on AI alerting compliance staff professionals at the earliest signs of issues and taking remedial action before concerning activity becomes an actual problem. The second is about using AI to organize, analyze, and extract information, like identifying key custodians, surfacing the interactions across employees, creating interview outlines, and more.

Exemplary use cases would include:

*   Regulatory monitoring: checking regulatory websites to confirm that there are no new regulations or changes to existing ones
*   AI governance: streamlining the process to allow appropriate stakeholders to evaluate new use cases for AI workflows
*   Supplier risk management: ISO 27001 and other compliance and periodic security questionnaires for third-party suppliers and tracking certification renewals
*   Policy management and attestation: distributing new policies to employees, tracking electronic signatures, and sending automated reminders to those who haven't completed required training
*   Evidence collection and audit trails: automatically pulling logs, access records, and system configurations from cloud providers or HR platforms
*   Audit trigger: automating kickoffs for yearly, quarterly, or monthly audits

## Is My Data Ready?

In compliance, harnessing the full power of AI starts with a few crucial steps.

The first step is to centralize data that has until now been siloed across systems. Without comprehensive data consolidation, AI provides only “garbage in, garbage out” results. With it, AI makes well-informed decisions, provides useful insights, and produces reliable predictions. Importantly, as data consolidation proceeds, custom-built AI workflows address the specific, unique needs of individual practice groups, thereby reducing reliance on multiple point and SaaS solutions.

## How Do I Identify Ways to Use AI?

A second key step is reimagining workflows beyond monitoring and standard automated workflows. Those who think of AI as simply an “accelerator” for speeding up compliance workflows miss what sets AI apart. Stakeholders need to think beyond what has been possible. The right first question is, “If we had infinite staff with infinite time, what could we do that is currently impossible?” The answers will determine how to build AI workflows—not human ones with AI “bolted on”—that can, on their own, complement work autonomously.Harvesting these possibilities from the subject matter experts that do the work is a paradigm shift on how to get the most value out of this game-changing technology.

## How Do I Scale Adoption?

The third step is to encourage, and support hands on exploration of AI by those closest to the pain points of the reactive compliance. They are in the best position to apply creativity and imagination to what will have the greatest impact. They must feel safe, supported, and empowered to do so. The most impactful innovations require iteration. Frontline compliance staff need to be lauded for attempts to come up with new workflows, because those are the first steps in figuring out what will reshape the legal function, elevating both operational performance and the strategic value they deliver to the business.

Whether for compliance or any other legal function, consolidated data, novel workflows, and exploration of AI will enable legal and compliance teams to make a quantum leap forward rather than taking a mere step.

**Jon Kessler**_is VP and general manager of AI Governance and AI Advisory, Legal Solutions, Epiq._

生成式AI并未消除律所瓶颈，而是将其向上游转移：初级律师数秒内生成草稿，但高级律师需花费更多时间审查来源、重建推理并修正错误。她主张律所应从追求速度转向系统思维，将AI嵌入整个工作流程而非孤立任务，以连接信息、减少行政工作，让律师专注于客户咨询和专业判断。

中端市场律所拥有更少的工具、更紧密的客户关系和更快的变革能力，在AI转型中具备优势。她介绍了Actionstep的Trace被动时间捕获技术，该技术监控律师在实践管理、邮件和文档应用中的工作，自动生成与案件关联的计费条目，帮助律所恢复遗忘的时间并改进定价、人员配置和盈利分析。她还探讨了AI作为初级律师导师的潜力，利用机构知识提问、提示深入研究并强化律所偏好的方法，同时保留资深律师与初级律师之间的指导关系。
news.bodyText:
In this episode of The Geek in Review, Greg Lambert hosts a solo conversation with Triona Buckley, Chief Product Officer at Actionstep, about generative AI’s growing influence on mid-market law firms. Buckley challenges a common assumption about legal AI: faster task completion does not always remove friction. An associate might produce a draft within seconds, only to transfer the burden upstream to a senior lawyer responsible for reviewing sources, reconstructing reasoning, and correcting mistakes.

Buckley argues law firms should shift their attention from speed to systems. Standalone drafting and research tools address individual tasks, while system-level AI connects work across an entire legal matter. Embedded within everyday workflows, AI helps lawyers locate information, reduce administrative work, and preserve more time for client advice and professional judgment. The goal is a smoother operating model, rather than a collection of isolated tools producing faster documents.

The conversation also examines institutional knowledge, especially within firms lacking large knowledge management or innovation teams. Buckley describes an approach where AI captures decisions, context, and reasoning as lawyers work. This creates a continuously expanding record of how the firm handles matters, advises clients, and applies professional judgment. Governance still plays a central role, including clear audit trails showing whether a person or an AI agent performed each action.

Greg and Triona then explore AI as an individual tutor for junior lawyers. Remote and hybrid work have weakened the traditional apprenticeship model built around observation and informal office conversations. Drawing upon decades of firm experience, an AI tutor might question an associate’s assumptions, prompt additional research, and reinforce the firm’s preferred methods. Such systems offer structured practice while preserving the essential mentoring relationship between senior and junior lawyers.

Another major theme is the hidden cost of delayed time entry. Actionstep’s Trace passive time capture technology monitors work across practice management, email, and document applications, then presents lawyers with matter-linked, billing-ready entries. More accurate records help firms recover otherwise forgotten time while producing better data for pricing, staffing, client estimates, and profitability analysis. Those insights grow more important as clients push firms toward fixed fees and output-based pricing.

Buckley believes mid-market law firms hold several advantages during the AI transition. They often operate with fewer systems, maintain closer client relationships, and move through organizational change faster than larger enterprises. Success will still require disciplined implementation, trusted internal champions, connected data, and sustained attention to client service. Her message is optimistic but direct: firms with strong relationships, clean data, and a clear economic strategy will be better prepared for agentic AI and the changing business of law.

Actionstep’s U.S. Midsize Law Firm Priorities Report

Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering

news.titleZh: Amol Bargaje 加入 Thompson Coburn 担任首席信息官
news.summaryZh: 美国律所 Thompson Coburn 于7月20日宣布，Amol Bargaje 加入该所担任首席信息官。Bargaje 此前曾任 Mayer Brown 全球首席创新官，并在 Sullivan & Cromwell 担任同一职务。在此之前，他在 Jenner & Block 担任首席信息官超过十年。Bargaje 的领导力和创新经验将助力律所应对人工智能、新兴技术和客户数字化解决方案的持续演变。Bargaje 将指导技术生态系统的持续发展，以支持创新、运营卓越和客户服务。Bargaje 表示期待通过先进技术为律所的增长战略做出贡献。
news.bodyHtml:
Amol Bargaje has joined Thompson Coburn as chief information officer, the US firm announced today (20 July). Bargaje was previously global chief innovation officer of Mayer Brown and has held that same role at Sullivan & Cromwell. Prior to Sullivan, he was chief information officer at Jenner & Block, where he worked for over a decade.

“Amol brings a unique combination of leadership and innovation experience that will be invaluable as we navigate the continual evolution of AI, emerging technologies, and client-focused digital solutions,” said Allen Capdeboscq Jr., chief operating officer. “His track record of leading complex technology initiatives, developing high-performing teams, and aligning technology and innovation strategies with business objectives positions us well for the next phase of growth and transformation.”

Advertisement

In a statement out today, the firm said that Bargaje will guide the continued evolution of the firm’s technology ecosystem to support innovation, operational excellence, and exceptional client service.

“I am excited to work alongside Thompson Coburn’s talented attorneys and professionals,” said Bargaje. “I look forward to contributing to the firm’s growth strategy through advanced technology that supports exceptional client service and positions the firm for continued success.”

news.summaryZh: 佛罗里达南区联邦地区法院法官凯瑟琳·威廉姆斯阻止了特朗普总统针对国税局和财政部的诉讼中提出的和解方案，认定该诉讼出于“不当目的”，并将涉案律师移交可能的纪律审查。法院将审查和解协议是否基于真实法律争议，而非为获取政治或程序优势。该案凸显分权关切：联邦法院不可用于批准超出正常诉讼范围的成果。法官认为和解不能生效，因诉讼本身存在不当目的。移交纪律审查表明，律师在构建和推进案件中的行为可能面临个人后果。对企业法务和合规团队而言，此案提醒诉讼策略必须基于合法诉求、真实对抗和透明决策。涉及政府被告或政治敏感案件时，内部文件和特权决定可能成为法院评估动机的关键。短期便利的和解若被法院视为串通或虚假，可能被推翻。程序与实质同等重要，律师应预期法院对旨在制造有利裁决或绕过行政程序的案件进行严格审查。

news.summaryZh: 第39期电子取证商业信心调查显示，认为行业状况良好的受访者比例从半年前的59.38%降至38.78%，创下调查史上最大半年度降幅。然而，收入预期保持稳定，利润悲观情绪反而减弱，生成式人工智能部署率连续第四次上升，达到69.39%。调查首次纳入AI治理指标：57.14%的组织已记录AI控制措施，约30%的部署者在不一致或缺失规则下运行生产AI。45.83%的受访者无法描述其应收账款趋势，为近期最高。超过半数受访者将数据类型和数量列为首要挑战。调查于2026年4月15日至5月29日进行，共49名受访者，其中律师事务所占34.69%，软件和服务提供商占32.65%。法律和诉讼支持岗位占69.39%，战术执行专业人员占38.78%，成为最大群体。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: Business confidence in eDiscovery posted its largest half-to-half decline across the four editions reviewed, and the details matter for anyone budgeting, buying, or selling. The 39th eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey from ComplexDiscovery OÜ and EDRM finds good-conditions sentiment down over 20 points from autumn while revenue expectations hold firm and GAI deployment reaches 69.39 percent of organizations.

For cybersecurity, privacy, and eDiscovery professionals, the survey’s first governance readings are the headline inside the headline: 57.14 percent of organizations now document their AI controls, and roughly three in 10 deployers run production AI on inconsistent or absent rules. Pair that with 45.83 percent of respondents unable to describe their receivables trajectory, the highest in recent comparisons, and the operational agenda for 2H 2026 writes itself.

Watch the data-diversity number. With over half of respondents naming data types and volumes as the defining challenge, the second half of 2026 will test whether collection scoping and early-case assessment tools built for modern data can keep pace.

This complete-look overview is the culmination of a five-part series on the 1H 2026 eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey, following section reports on market sentiment and financial outlooks, impact issues, AI adoption and governance, and operational metrics.

Industry Research Beat

Confidence cools, commitment holds: full results from the 1H 2026 eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

The optimism of last autumn did not survive the spring. Six months after 59.38 percent of respondents rated eDiscovery business conditions as good, that share has fallen to 38.78 percent, and normal is once again the industry’s center of gravity.

Yet the retreat is selective. Revenue expectations held their ground, profit pessimism actually shrank, and the share of organizations deploying generative artificial intelligence (GAI) climbed for a fourth consecutive survey. The 1H 2026 eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey, the 39th edition of the benchmark conducted by ComplexDiscovery OÜ in collaboration with EDRM, captures an industry that feels less exuberant but acts no less committed.

The survey ran April 15 through May 29, 2026, and drew 49 respondents through targeted outreach to the professional networks of both organizations. The program, launched in 2016 and now in its tenth year, has collected 3,641 responses across its 39 completed editions, including this cycle’s 49. As of May 2026, the instrument spans 17 questions, expanded this cycle to add two dimensions the series had never measured: formal AI governance and the annual revenue scale of respondent organizations.

A methodological note frames everything that follows. This targeted, nonprobability sample is not designed to represent the entire eDiscovery industry; the results describe the participating respondents, and no margin of sampling error applies. With 49 respondents, one response represents about 2.04 percentage points, and changes between editions may reflect differences in sample composition as well as changes in market sentiment.

Who answered, and why it matters

Law firms supplied the largest block of respondents for the second consecutive survey, at 34.69 percent, narrowly ahead of software and services providers at 32.65 percent, a one-respondent margin. Consultancies accounted for 12.24 percent, with corporations and media or research organizations at 8.16 percent each and governmental entities at 4.08 percent. The two-survey run of law-firm leadership marks a reversal from Fall 2024, when providers made up 50.82 percent of the pool and law firms just 21.31 percent.

Function and seniority shifted as well. Legal and litigation support roles dominated at 69.39 percent, continuing a steady climb from 63.93 percent in Fall 2024, while business support functions contributed 24.49 percent and IT or product development 6.12 percent. The seniority mix tells the more consequential story: tactical execution professionals, at 38.78 percent, now form the largest tier, ahead of operational management at 32.65 percent and executive leadership at 28.57 percent. The 2H 2025 edition ran the other way, with executives and operational managers together comprising nearly 74 percent of respondents. Readers comparing cycles should weigh that shift because it may have contributed to the cooler sentiment reading.

1h2026-overview-seniority-mix

Geographically, the survey remains anchored in the United States, where 91.84 percent of respondents primarily conduct business. But the respondent base itself stretched across seven countries this cycle, with participants located in the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, South Africa, South Korea, and India alongside the American majority.

Sentiment steps back to normal

Just over half of respondents, 51.02 percent, rated current business conditions as normal, while 38.78 percent said good and 10.20 percent said bad. The good reading dropped over 20 points from 2H 2025, and the bad reading tripled from 3.13 percent.

Viewed across four cycles, a rhythm emerges. Good readings hit 54.10 percent in Fall 2024, fell to 37.66 percent in 1H 2025, surged to 59.38 percent in 2H 2025, and have now settled back to 38.78 percent. Two annual cycles are not enough to establish seasonality, and shifts in respondent composition complicate the comparison, but the repeated pattern of cooler first-half readings merits watching; one hypothesis is that the mood tracks the litigation calendar and budget cycle as much as any structural change.

1h2026-overview-conditions-trend

Expectations for the next six months reinforce the steady-state picture. A same outlook drew 59.18 percent, better drew 32.65 percent, and worse drew 8.16 percent, figures nearly identical to the 2H 2025 distribution.

Revenue holds while the mood softens

Whatever cooled the general mood did not reach the revenue line. Respondents expecting higher segment revenue in six months held at 42.86 percent, essentially unchanged from the 42.19 percent recorded in 2H 2025 and well above the 31.17 percent trough of 1H 2025. Those expecting lower revenue doubled to 12.24 percent from 6.25 percent, thinning the middle ground rather than eroding the optimists.

Profit expectations firmed. The higher-profit camp edged up to 38.78 percent from 37.50 percent, and the lower-profit camp fell to 8.16 percent from 12.50 percent, unwinding some of the margin-squeeze anxiety that colored the 2H 2025 findings. Fewer respondents now expect falling profits than falling revenue, reversing last autumn’s pattern; one reading is that cost discipline, and perhaps early AI efficiency gains, may be reaching the ledger, though the survey does not measure those drivers directly.

Data diversity takes the top seat

Increasing types of data claimed the top spot among issues expected to impact eDiscovery business over the next six months, cited by 30.61 percent of respondents, the highest reading for that issue in the last four surveys. Budgetary constraints followed at 28.57 percent, with increasing volumes of data at 22.45 percent. Together, the two data-centric issues now command 53.06 percent of the vote, up from 45.32 percent in 2H 2025; for the first time in the recent series, over half of respondents name the data itself as the defining business problem.

Down the table, the quieter findings deserve attention. Data security fell for a fourth consecutive survey, to 8.16 percent from 11.48 percent in Fall 2024, a slide that continues even as breach activity remains a fixture of the legal-technology news cycle. Lack of personnel, the top concern of the post-pandemic era, drew just 4.08 percent, and inadequate technology 6.12 percent. Practitioners planning for the second half of 2026 should read the pairing at the top literally: collections scoping, data-type triage, and early-case assessment workflows built for collaboration platforms, chat, and multimedia are where budgets and data pressures now collide.

AI moves deeper into production

Integration and deployment of large language models (LLMs) and GAI reached 69.39 percent of respondent organizations, the fourth consecutive increase in the series and up 30 points from the 39.34 percent recorded in Fall 2024. Organizations still merely considering the technology fell to 14.29 percent, active pilots stood at 12.24 percent, and just 4.08 percent reported no plans at all.

Improved service and product delivery remained the most-cited benefit at 48.98 percent, though competitive advantage rebounded to 28.57 percent, its strongest showing of the last four surveys and double its 14.06 percent low of 2H 2025. Cost savings collapsed as a rationale, drawing 6.12 percent against 18.18 percent in 1H 2025; the benefit responses suggest a shift toward treating AI as a value play rather than a cost play.

1h2026-overview-ai-deployment-trend

The barrier rankings shifted in a direction compliance officers will recognize. Results accuracy stayed on top at 30.61 percent, followed by regulatory and privacy compliance at 20.41 percent, with the skill gap and unclear ROI tied at 18.37 percent each, the former up from 8.20 percent in Fall 2024. High costs, cited by nearly a fifth of respondents two years ago, fell to 8.16 percent. The pattern suggests direct acquisition cost has become less prominent than accuracy, compliance, expertise, and return-on-investment concerns.

Governance arrives on the scorecard

The survey’s new governance question found a majority of organizations with documented rules: 42.86 percent reported a defined internal framework and 14.29 percent a formalized, monitored, and audited program, for a combined 57.14 percent. Another 28.57 percent described emerging governance applied inconsistently, 12.24 percent conceded no formal governance at all, and 2.04 percent, one respondent, marked the question not applicable. Cross-tabulating governance against adoption sharpens the picture: of the 34 organizations already integrating and deploying, 24 report documented governance, while 10, roughly three in 10 deployers, run production AI on emerging or absent rules. Deployers govern better than the full sample, but that remains a gap worth closing before regulators, clients, or opposing counsel close it for them.

1h2026-overview-governance-baseline

The other new question, on annual eDiscovery-related revenue, met the limits of self-reporting. Nearly half of respondents, 48.98 percent, said they did not know or preferred not to answer. Among the 25 who disclosed, 36 percent came in under $5 million, 24 percent between $5 million and $25 million, and 40 percent at $25 million or above, including two organizations reporting $250 million or greater.

The visibility gap widens

Reported financial visibility weakened across the survey sample. Asked about the trajectory of Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), 45.83 percent of the 48 who answered said they did not know, the weakest visibility reading in the series’ recent history. Across the 48 responses, 14 respondents, or 29.17 percent, reported increasing DSO, while one, or 2.08 percent, reported decreasing DSO. Among the 15 reporting a change, longer payment cycles outnumbered shorter ones 14 to one.

Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) told a similar story. The do-not-know share reached 39.58 percent, while the increasing share fell for a fourth straight survey, to 27.08 percent from 54.24 percent in Fall 2024. Revenue distribution across customer bases rounded out the picture, with 37.50 percent unaware of the trend and 10.42 percent reporting concentration into fewer clients. Organizations that cannot see their own receivables, recurring revenue, and concentration risk are navigating 2026 by feel; instrumenting those three metrics is a practical step toward stronger financial visibility.

1h2026-overview-visibility-trend

The 1H 2026 results describe a respondent pool that has stopped celebrating and started operating: revenue steady, AI embedded, governance half-built, and financial visibility fading just as reports of longer payment cycles multiply. When conditions read normal but 14 respondents report receivables slowing for every one reporting them speeding up, which number should leaders trust when they set budgets for 2H 2026?

news.bodyText: Editor’s Note: Business confidence in eDiscovery posted its largest half-to-half decline across the four editions reviewed, and the details matter for anyone budgeting, buying, or selling. The 39th eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey from ComplexDiscovery OÜ and EDRM finds good-conditions sentiment down over 20 points from autumn while revenue expectations hold firm and GAI deployment reaches 69.39 percent of organizations. For cybersecurity, privacy, and eDiscovery professionals, the survey’s first governance readings are the headline inside the headline: 57.14 percent of organizations now document their AI controls, and roughly three in 10 deployers run production AI on inconsistent or absent rules. Pair that with 45.83 percent of respondents unable to describe their receivables trajectory, the highest in recent comparisons, and the operational agenda for 2H 2026 writes itself. Watch the data-diversity number. With over half of respondents naming data types and volumes as the defining challenge, the second half of 2026 will test whether collection scoping and early-case assessment tools built for modern data can keep pace. This complete-look overview is the culmination of a five-part series on the 1H 2026 eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey, following section reports on market sentiment and financial outlooks, impact issues, AI adoption and governance, and operational metrics. Industry Research Beat ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff The optimism of last autumn did not survive the spring. Six months after 59.38 percent of respondents rated eDiscovery business conditions as good, that share has fallen to 38.78 percent, and normal is once again the industry’s center of gravity. Yet the retreat is selective. Revenue expectations held their ground, profit pessimism actually shrank, and the share of organizations deploying generative artificial intelligence (GAI) climbed for a fourth consecutive survey. The 1H 2026 eDiscovery Business Confidence Survey, the 39th edition of the benchmark conducted by ComplexDiscovery OÜ in collaboration with EDRM, captures an industry that feels less exuberant but acts no less committed. The survey ran April 15 through May 29, 2026, and drew 49 respondents through targeted outreach to the professional networks of both organizations. The program, launched in 2016 and now in its tenth year, has collected 3,641 responses across its 39 completed editions, including this cycle’s 49. As of May 2026, the instrument spans 17 questions, expanded this cycle to add two dimensions the series had never measured: formal AI governance and the annual revenue scale of respondent organizations. A methodological note frames everything that follows. This targeted, nonprobability sample is not designed to represent the entire eDiscovery industry; the results describe the participating respondents, and no margin of sampling error applies. With 49 respondents, one response represents about 2.04 percentage points, and changes between editions may reflect differences in sample composition as well as changes in market sentiment. Law firms supplied the largest block of respondents for the second consecutive survey, at 34.69 percent, narrowly ahead of software and services providers at 32.65 percent, a one-respondent margin. Consultancies accounted for 12.24 percent, with corporations and media or research organizations at 8.16 percent each and governmental entities at 4.08 percent. The two-survey run of law-firm leadership marks a reversal from Fall 2024, when providers made up 50.82 percent of the pool and law firms just 21.31 percent. Function and seniority shifted as well. Legal and litigation support roles dominated at 69.39 percent, continuing a steady climb from 63.93 percent in Fall 2024, while business support functions contributed 24.49 percent and IT or product development 6.12 percent. The seniority mix tells the more consequential story: tactical execution professionals, at 38.78 percent, now form the largest tier, ahead of operational management at 32.65 percent and executive leadership at 28.57 percent. The 2H 2025 edition ran the other way, with executives and operational managers together comprising nearly 74 percent of respondents. Readers comparing cycles should weigh that shift because it may have contributed to the cooler sentiment reading.
