news.titleEn: Chris Cartrett to Step Down as CEO of Aderant, Departing Legal Tech to Lead Public Safety Software Company; Former CEO Deane Price to Return on Interim Basis
news.titleZh: Chris Cartrett 将卸任 Aderant CEO，离开法律科技领域执掌公共安全软件公司；前 CEO Deane Price 临时回归
news.summaryZh: Aderant 宣布，总裁兼 CEO Chris Cartrett 将于 8 月 1 日离职，转任公共安全软件公司 ImageTrend 的 CEO。为平稳过渡，2017 至 2021 年担任 Aderant CEO 的 Deane Price 将于 7 月 20 日起出任临时 CEO，同时公司正式物色下一任 CEO。Price 自 2021 年离开后，在 Aderant 母公司 Roper Technologies 旗下担任多个高管职务，包括保险科技公司 iPipeline 的临时 CEO 及战略增长与并购顾问。Cartrett 在 Aderant 任职 12 年，于 2014 年从 Thomson Reuters 加入，历任战略与增长高级副总裁、执行副总裁，2021 年成为总裁，2022 年升任 CEO。高管团队保持不变，将继续执行 2026 年业务优先事项和长期战略。Cartrett 表示对团队成就感到自豪，并特别指出首席客户官 Josiah Chaves 和首席营收官 Aisling Fenelon 等高管将带领公司进入新阶段。
news.bodyHtml:
In a major leadership change at one of legal technology’s largest companies, Chris Cartrett will step down as president and CEO of Aderant, effective Aug. 1, the company announced today.

He is leaving the legal industry to become chief executive officer of ImageTrend, a provider of software and data analytics for emergency medical services, fire departments, hospitals, and public safety agencies.

To bridge the transition, Deane Price, who served as Aderant’s CEO from 2017 to 2021, will rejoin the company as interim CEO beginning July 20, while a formal search is conducted for the company’s next chief executive.

Since leaving Aderant in 2021, Price has held executive leadership roles across the portfolio of Roper Technologies, Aderant’s parent company, including as interim CEO of the insurance technology company iPipeline and as an advisor on strategic growth and M&A initiatives.

Cartrett’s departure ends a 12-year run at the Atlanta-based company, which develops business management and practice-of-law software used by many of the world’s largest law firms.

He joined Aderant in 2014 from Thomson Reuters as senior vice president of strategy and growth, was promoted to executive vice president in 2017, and became president in 2021 and CEO in 2022.

“It has been the privilege of my career to serve as president and CEO of Aderant,” Cartrett said in a statement announcing the change. “I am incredibly proud of what our team has accomplished and am grateful for the relationships we’ve built with our clients and partners. The opportunity to lead Aderant has been an honor, and I leave knowing the company is stronger than ever.”

In the announcement, the company emphasized continuity, saying its executive leadership team remains unchanged and that it will continue to execute its 2026 business priorities and long-term strategy “without interruption.”

Cartrett himself pointed to the depth of that bench, singling out two executives he has worked alongside for more than a decade, Josiah Chaves, who was named chief client officer last year, and Aisling Fenelon, who earlier this year became the company’s first female chief revenue officer.

“Having worked alongside leaders like Josiah Chaves and Aisling Fenelon for more than a decade — and watching them grow into the leaders they are today — gives me tremendous confidence in the future of this company,” he said. “They, along with the broader executive team, are exceptionally well positioned to lead Aderant into its next chapter.”

Chaves, Aderant’s chief client officer, returned the sentiment — invoking the company’s wolf-pack mantra in the process.

“It cannot be denied the immense impact Chris has had on Aderant and the legal community,” Chaves said. “At Aderant, our mantra is the strength of pack is the wolf, and the strength of wolf is the pack.

“Our strategy has been set by the collective leadership team with input from stakeholders across the organization and grounded in a shared vision for where the legal industry is headed and how Aderant will help law firms succeed.”

Mike Corkery, senior vice president and group executive at Roper Technologies, thanked Cartrett for his leadership, saying that under his guidance, “the company has become the clear leader in delivering solutions to help law firms run better.”

The move comes at a high point in Aderant’s trajectory. When I interviewed Cartrett on my LawNext podcast just over a year ago, in an episode recorded live at Aderant’s Momentum Global 2025 conference in Dallas, he described 2024 as a record-breaking year for the company, with 2025 on track to be even stronger.

In that conversation, he talked about the three priorities that defined his tenure as CEO: driving the company’s cloud-first transformation, embedding generative AI throughout its product suite, and doubling down on customer service.

That cloud mission was no small task for a company that is nearly 50 years old and whose customer base included many firms still running the on-premises version of its software.

I hope to speak with Cartrett later today about his decision to leave Aderant and legal tech, and will report on that conversation in a follow-up post.
news.bodyText: In a major leadership change at one of legal technology’s largest companies, Chris Cartrett will step down as president and CEO of Aderant, effective Aug. 1, the company announced today. He is leaving the legal industry to become chief executive officer of ImageTrend, a provider of software and data analytics for emergency medical services, fire departments, hospitals, and public safety agencies. To bridge the transition, Deane Price, who served as Aderant’s CEO from 2017 to 2021, will rejoin the company as interim CEO beginning July 20, while a formal search is conducted for the company’s next chief executive. Since leaving Aderant in 2021, Price has held executive leadership roles across the portfolio of Roper Technologies, Aderant’s parent company, including as interim CEO of the insurance technology company iPipeline and as an advisor on strategic growth and M&A initiatives. Cartrett’s departure ends a 12-year run at the Atlanta-based company, which develops business management and practice-of-law software used by many of the world’s largest law firms. He joined Aderant in 2014 from Thomson Reuters as senior vice president of strategy and growth, was promoted to executive vice president in 2017, and became president in 2021 and CEO in 2022. “It has been the privilege of my career to serve as president and CEO of Aderant,” Cartrett said in a statement announcing the change. “I am incredibly proud of what our team has accomplished and am grateful for the relationships we’ve built with our clients and partners. The opportunity to lead Aderant has been an honor, and I leave knowing the company is stronger than ever.” In the announcement, the company emphasized continuity, saying its executive leadership team remains unchanged and that it will continue to execute its 2026 business priorities and long-term strategy “without interruption.” Cartrett himself pointed to the depth of that bench, singling out two executives he has worked alongside for more than a decade, Josiah Chaves, who was named chief client officer last year, and Aisling Fenelon, who earlier this year became the company’s first female chief revenue officer. “Having worked alongside leaders like Josiah Chaves and Aisling Fenelon for more than a decade — and watching them grow into the leaders they are today — gives me tremendous confidence in the future of this company,” he said. “They, along with the broader executive team, are exceptionally well positioned to lead Aderant into its next chapter.” Chaves, Aderant’s chief client officer, returned the sentiment — invoking the company’s wolf-pack mantra in the process. “It cannot be denied the immense impact Chris has had on Aderant and the legal community,” Chaves said. “At Aderant, our mantra is the strength of pack is the wolf, and the strength of wolf is the pack.

news.titleEn: Exclusive: As Its Kaleidoscope Conference Returns for Year Two, 8am Trades Austin’s Cowboy Boots for the Las Vegas Strip — And Books the Savannah Bananas’ Founder As Keynote
news.titleZh: 独家：8am Kaleidoscope 大会回归第二年，从奥斯汀牛仔靴换到拉斯维加斯大道，并邀请萨凡纳香蕉队创始人担任主旨演讲嘉宾
news.summaryZh: 8am 公司宣布其第二届年度客户大会 Kaleidoscope 2026 将于 2026 年 9 月 22 日至 24 日在拉斯维加斯 Encore at Wynn 举行。大会主旨演讲嘉宾为萨凡纳香蕉队创始人兼香蕉球创造者 Jesse Cole。本届大会为期三天，设超过 25 场分组会议，分为三个主题轨道，参会者可获得 15 小时以上 CLE 学分。8am 旗下品牌包括支付平台 LawPay、律所管理平台 MyCase、人身伤害平台 CasePeer 和移民平台 Docketwise。大会核心目标仍是让客户相互连接，而非追求规模。去年首届大会约 300 人参加，超出公司预期；今年公司希望吸引更多客户、合作伙伴及潜在客户。关于从奥斯汀迁至拉斯维加斯的原因，Skinner 称是出于地理和成本考虑：客户遍布北美，而拉斯维加斯交通便利且费用较低。
news.bodyHtml:
Last September, when the company 8am — having successfully pulled off a major rebrand just three weeks earlier — then went on to pull off its first-ever customer conference in Austin, I wrote a review giving it high praise.

Although that inaugural event was modest in size, it was big in energy, as well as highly polished and professional, with the feel of a conference on the cusp of something greater.

Now we get to see whether that momentum carries into year two.

Today, 8am is releasing the details of Kaleidoscope 2026, its second annual customer conference, which will take place Sept. 22-24 at the Encore at Wynn Las Vegas.

LawSites has the exclusive on the details, including one the company had not yet revealed even on its own conference site: The keynote speaker will be Jesse Cole, the founder of the Savannah Bananas and creator of Banana Ball. The yellow-tuxedoed showman is famous for turning a struggling minor league baseball franchise into a viral global phenomenon by putting fan experience above all else.

This year’s conference will span three days and feature more than 25 breakout sessions organized into three tracks, with attendees able to earn 15 or more hours of CLE credit.

8am is the umbrella brand of an array of products that include the payments platform LawPay, the practice management platform MyCase, the personal injury platform CasePeer, and the immigration platform Docketwise.

In an interview yesterday, Nate Skinner, 8am’s chief marketing and sales officer, told me that the conference’s core purpose remains the same as it was in its debut year.

“One of our first-principle philosophies around our customer conference that we started last year was we want to create an opportunity to have our customers connect with one another,” Skinner said. “For us, it’s not about the size as much as it’s about the opportunity to create a deeper relationship with our customers, and for them to create those connections with each other.”

That said, the company is planning to grow the conference’s size. Last year’s inaugural conference drew roughly 300 attendees — a number Skinner said “overachieved” on the company’s objective — and this year the company is aiming higher, hoping to draw customers, partners and prospective customers alike.

Why Vegas?

Regular readers will recall that I ended my review of last year’s conference with a lament: The second Kaleidoscope would be in Las Vegas, a city I am not crazy about as a conference location. So I asked Skinner, Why the move from Austin, the company’s hometown?

It was a matter of both geography and math, he said. With a customer base spread across North America, any host city forces most attendees to travel. But Las Vegas has the advantage of being easy and affordable to reach from almost anywhere in the country.

Beyond that, he pointed to the concentration of legal professionals already in that vicinity — some 14,000 attorneys licensed in Nevada, including roughly 2,900 solos, plus the dense legal population of Southern California, a four-hour straight shot across Interstate 15.

The company also wanted to go somewhere different. “When we looked at all the places we could possibly go, and then you look at what everyone else is doing, [we said] let’s not do what everybody else is doing, let’s do something that’s uniquely us,” Skinner said. “There’s not a lot of legal tech conferences in Las Vegas.

“If we knock it out of the park and everybody loves it, we’ll go back,” he said. “If we don’t, and people wish they’d gone somewhere else or we did something different, we’ll adjust.”

(Those hoping for a repeat of last year’s free Tecovas cowboy boots should temper expectations. Skinner said the company leaned into the Austin theme because it was the company’s backyard. This year, there will be “some fun things” with a Las Vegas theme, but less of it. When I suggested yellow tuxedos for all attendees in honor of the keynoter, he demurred.)

Peer-Led Programming

As for the programming, Skinner said the clearest lesson from year one was that attendees most valued hearing from their peers — not from 8am executives.

“They definitely don’t want to hear from me,” he said. “They want to hear from each other.”

To that end, this year’s speaker lineup leans heavily on practicing lawyers, several of them from the more headline-grabbing corners of the profession:

  • Todd Spodek, the New York criminal defense attorney who represented Anna Delvey, the Russian-German con artist who posed as a wealthy heiress to defraud wealthy New Yorkers. Spodek will explore the ethical landmines attorneys face when a case goes viral.
  • Emily Lekahal, assistant general counsel for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, will sit down for a fireside chat on the legal strategy behind professional sports.
  • Charles Lee Mudd Jr., principal attorney at Mudd Law, will take attendees inside the surprisingly real world of space law — orbital disputes, asteroid mining, and who owns the moon.

The broader session list spans three tracks — Practice and Profession, Tech and Innovation, and Business of Law — covering everything from estate planning for the great wealth transfer, to immigration law’s unsettled landscape, to burnout, referral strategies and billing.

AI is well represented but, as was the case last year, does not dominate. Sessions include a grounded attorney’s guide to AI, a debate over AI-generated evidence in the courtroom, and a hands-on workshop connecting 8am’s MyCase to Anthropic’s Claude to surface unbilled time and collection gaps.

Skinner told me that the company thinks of a great customer conference as having three main ingredients: “A destination people don’t hate to go to, programming that is useful and meaningful, and then the third is something that draws your attention” — which is where Cole and his Savannah Bananas story come in.

The parallel between Cole’s obsession with the fan experience and how law firms should think about the client experience, Skinner suggested, is hard to miss.

A Steadier Year — Mostly

Last year, 8am put on its first-ever conference just weeks after completing a top-to-bottom rebrand. This year, the run-up to the conference has featured its own major change, a new CEO, with Jeff Hughes, a member of 8am’s board since 2024, succeeding Dru Armstrong.

I asked Skinner whether the company simply thrives on chaos.

“We do not thrive on chaos,” he said with a laugh. “We wouldn’t choose to do that again if we had the choice.” As for the new CEO: “Jeff is here and he’s great, and he’s super excited to meet our customers and get to know everybody and join us in Las Vegas.”

In a press release announcing the conference, Hughes said the event comes at a time when the industry is at an inflection point.

“Legal professionals are reimagining what a modern practice looks like, using AI and connected technology to work smarter and create better client experiences,” he said. “Kaleidoscope brings together the ideas, technology, and community to enable each of them to meet this pivotal moment with confidence.”

For his part, Skinner sees in-person events as an antidote to the relentless hype cycle around legal AI. “It’s very frothy out there,” he told me. “Half of this stuff is kind of overblown clickbait.” What customers want, he said, is for someone to tell them what is real and what is not — and they are more inclined to believe it face to face.

The Details

Kaleidoscope 2026 runs Sept. 22-24 at the Encore at Wynn Las Vegas, opening with a reception at the Encore Beach Club and closing with a party at the Intrigue nightclub.

The all-access pass is $995, but until July 31, registrants can take $400 off using the promo code FLIP at checkout. The company has also secured a room block at the Encore and Wynn at $289 per night. Registration and details are on the conference website.

Last year, Kaleidoscope’s debut proved that 8am could put on a polished, professional event whose vibe belied its modest size. If year two builds on that — yellow tuxedo or not — this conference may well cement its place on the annual legal tech calendar.

[Disclosure: I have a son who is employed at 8am — and who will be speaking there!]

news.summaryZh:
美国司法部民事司宣布，美国政府将支付约1700万美元，以解决近630名原告因红山航空燃油泄漏事件提出的索赔。该事件是近年来军方最引人注目的环境灾难之一，引发了公众对燃料储存方式、饮用水污染以及联邦政府应对社区健康和财产索赔的广泛关注。此次和解虽金额巨大，但红山事件相关的更广泛诉讼和赔偿责任仍是政府和受影响利益相关方面临的重大问题。

对诉讼律师而言，此案表明当环境损害与人身伤害、妨害及财产损失理论交织时，针对美国政府的集体索赔规模可能达到何种程度。污染事件引发的案件常涉及因果关系、医疗监测、非经济损失评估以及协调处理数百项索赔等复杂问题。此次和解可能影响相关谈判预期，尤其是原告律师可援引政府在审判前愿意支付巨额款项的先例。对企业法务和合规团队而言，红山事件是运营失败如何迅速演变为企业级法律危机的警示案例，环境事件现常同时引发侵权诉讼、监管执法、公关危机和立法监督等多重风险。

# Aderant President and CEO Chris Cartrett to Step Down, Leave Legal Tech

Cartrett, who has led Aderant since 2021, is leaving the legal technology industry to become CEO of software and data analytics provider ImageTrend.

4 minute read July 14, 2026 at 09:00 AM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b683f4b314e480bc994cab5d8feb663b?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Benjamin Joyner](http://www.law.com/author/profile/benjamin-joyner/)

## What You Need to Know

*   Aderant president and CEO Chris Cartertt is stepping down to serve as CEO of emergency response software provider ImageTrend.
*   Cartrett has been in his current position since 2021 and has been with Aderant since 2014.
*   Former Aderant CEO Deane Price will serve as interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent successor.

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

This article has been updated with comments from Aderant president and CEO Chris Cartrett and Aderant senior vice president of product management and artificial intelligence Lisa Erickson.

On Tuesday, Atlanta-based legal business management software provider Aderant announced president and CEO Chris Cartrett will be departing the company, effective Aug. 1. Cartrett is leaving to become CEO of emergency response software and data analytics provider ImageTrend.

Former Aderant CEO [Deane Price](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2021/11/10/against-the-odds-thriving-in-a-challenging-legal-tech-world/) will rejoin the company as interim CEO on July 20 to lead the company during the search for Cartrett’s permanent successor. Since her previous stint at Aderant, she has served as interim CEO of business software provider iPipeline and a mergers and acquisitions advisor to Aderant owner Roper Technologies. The remainder of Aderant’s leadership team will be unchanged following Cartrett’s departure.

Cartrett told Law.com his departure was motivated by a desire to take on a new challenge and work with emergency response personnel and leaders.

“This opportunity that got presented to me scratched an itch in a different way—the chance to move into a new space, dealing with [emergency medical services], emergency response, first responders,” he said. “It's one of those challenges that you get presented, and it felt like it was time.”

Cartrett joined Aderant in 2014, serving in roles including senior vice president of strategy and growth and executive vice president before becoming president and CEO in 2021. He said he believes Aderant is in a strong position moving forward, which he attributed to the strength of the staff and leadership team the company has assembled in recent years.

“At no time in my last 12 years have we had the level of talent inside this business that we have today,” he said. “The skill sets across the organization in every department, we really are at a unique place.”

Aderant senior vice president of product management and artificial intelligence Lisa Erickson said that following Cartrett’s departure, the company will continue focusing on incorporating AI-powered tools to help firms automate tasks in areas like intake, billing and talent management.

Looking back on his time at Aderant, Cartrett singled out the advent and rise of generative AI as a major change, noting that it fundamentally altered how the company works internally and develops software in addition to reshaping its product offerings.

He added that over his time at Aderant law firms have become increasingly sophisticated customers, requiring vendors to both improve their offerings and become comfortable moving at a quicker pace.

“We used to always joke that law firms were the laggards when it came to more progressive technologies. That is not the case today,” he said. “Every legal tech company has had to shift accordingly.”

He also said that Price’s familiarity with much of the existing Aderant staff and customer base provide stability as the company looks for a permanent successor.

“It's going to be great for the people at Aderant—somebody that they know that they can lean on, that has that established relationship,” he said. “This is really good for our customers because it's somebody who they know also understands the space, knows them.”

Aderant is owned by technology holding company Roper Technologies following a $675 million [purchase](https://www.law.com/article/almID/1202739292628/) in 2015.

Recent product developments for the company include the [launch](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/05/12/aderant-launches-new-hub-for-agentic-tools-/) of a suite of agentic artificial intelligence-powered tools housed in the Aderant Agent Center, the [introduction](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/03/18/aderant-launches-ai-powered-employee-assessment-features/) of AI-powered employee assessment features and a [partnership](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2025/12/15/harvey-partners-with-aderant-to-connect-legal-work-with-law-firm-management-/) with legal AI provider Harvey.

Aderant has also made two acquisitions in the last year, [purchasing](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2025/08/07/aderant-acquires-legal-technology-assets-of-enterprise-ai-developer-herculesai/) the legal technology assets of enterprise AI developer HerculesAI in August 2025 and [buying](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2025/10/28/aderant-acquires-law-firm-pricing-software-provider-virtual-pricing-director-/) law firm pricing software provider Virtual Pricing Director that October.

news.titleEn: Aderant’s CEO Chris Cartrett takes new role outside of legal
news.titleZh: Aderant首席执行官Chris Cartrett将离职，转任法律行业外新职
news.summaryZh: Aderant总裁兼首席执行官Chris Cartrett将于8月离职，出任ImageTrend首席执行官。ImageTrend为紧急医疗服务、消防部门、医院和公共安全机构提供软件和数据分析解决方案。2017年至2021年担任Aderant首席执行官的Deane Price将于7月20日回归担任临时CEO，同时公司正式物色Cartrett的继任者。Aderant更广泛的领导团队保持不变，但首席技术官Andy Hoyt已于6月离职。Cartrett自2014年加入Aderant，历任多个高管职务，并于2021年起担任总裁兼CEO。Aderant为上市公司Roper Technologies旗下企业，Roper在4月财报电话会议中指出Aderant“业绩惊人”，实现创纪录季度营收和新一季度预订量纪录，SaaS业务势头强劲，并推出了AI驱动的人才评估工具，继续推广Stridyn AI平台，完成创纪录的Sierra Cloud迁移。离开Aderant是个人在感兴趣领域的独特机会，他对团队成就感到自豪，并对公司未来充满信心。
news.bodyHtml:
We asked Chris Cartrett and Josiah Chaves about the new opportunity and implications for existing customers.

Aderant’s president & chief executive officer Chris Cartrett is to step down in August to take on the role of CEO at ImageTrend, which provides software and data analytics solutions for emergency medical services, fire departments, hospitals, and public safety agencies. Deane Price, who was CEO from 2017 to 2021, will rejoin Aderant as interim CEO beginning July 20th while a formal search is being conducted for Cartrett’s replacement. It opens up the most senior role at one of the most widely used technology providers in the sector.

Advertisement

Aderant’s broader leadership team remains unchanged, with the exception of its CTO, with Andy Hoyt having departed in June.
Since joining Aderant in 2014, Cartrett has served in several executive leadership roles, including senior vice president of strategy & growth; executive vice president; and president & CEO since 2021.

Aderant is owned by listed company Roper Technologies, which in an earnings call in April this year noted that it has been an “amazing few years” from Aderant. Roper’s CEO and president Neil Hunn said: “Aderant delivered a record quarter, strong revenue growth and a new Q1 bookings record. Strength was broad-based with particularly strong SaaS momentum on Sierra, Onyx and viGlobal. Aderant also launched AI-driven talent evaluation within viGlobal, continued the rollout of a Stridyn AI platform and completed a record number of Sierra Cloud migrations in the quarter.”

Advertisement

Cartrett said: “It has been the privilege of my career to serve as president and CEO of Aderant. I am incredibly proud of what our team has accomplished and am grateful for the relationships we’ve built with our clients and partners. The opportunity to lead Aderant has been an honor, and I leave knowing the company is stronger than ever. We’ve combined exceptional new talent with the deep experience and institutional knowledge that has always defined Aderant. Having worked alongside leaders like Josiah Chaves and Aisling Fenelon for more than a decade—and watching them grow into the leaders they are today—gives me tremendous confidence in the future of this company. They, along with the broader executive team, are exceptionally well positioned to lead Aderant into its next chapter.”

We asked Cartrett and Chaves about the new opportunity and implications for existing customers.

Congratulations on the new role Chris! What made you decide to leave us in legal?

This is just a unique opportunity for myself in a space that really interest me. ImageTrend is a leader in the emergency response market helping EMS, fire and hospitals make better, faster decisions to improve care. I have been at Aderant for 12 years, and in the legal space for off and on nearly 30. Aderant is killing it and the team is stronger than ever. I know the momentum at Aderant will only continue to grow. This just feels like the right time for me to move into my next chapter.

How come you’re not finding a replacement before leaving?

Aderant is a very special place. Roper and the leadership team at Aderant are being incredibly purposeful in their search. The culture at Aderant is unique. The next CEO will have to fit into the dynamic culture. Deane Price returning as interim will be a seamless transition to ensure continuity with clients and our team. The vision and strategy are sound and the team is executing. No need to rush anything.

Is there a replacement for Andy yet?

Not yet, but that is not really a concern. As I have mentioned on many occasions, we have a very talented development team with strong leaders in place. Aderant is a truly AI-native organization, not just within our products, but also in how we operate internally. The next CTO must be on par with how the team is currently performing and raise the bar even higher. There are very few people who have that skill set, so once again, the leadership team is being purposeful in their search. Finding the right CTO is more important than finding any CTO.

I’m wondering if this will be unsettling for customers – Josiah, what do you think?

Actually, clients have been very supportive of Chris’s decision. We just had another record quarter, and I have spoken with a great many of our clients about his transition. They are confident in our vision and have realized the value of what we have delivered to date. We are excited about where Aderant continues to grow. Aderant has always had a client-centric culture, and we remain committed to delivering for all of them.

We wish Chris the absolute best in his new role!

news.summaryZh: 美国联邦法院自诉案件数量持续上升，2025年自诉案件占联邦民事案件比例从2005-2022年平均11%跃升至16.8%，其中许多案件涉及生成式AI起草的诉状。麻省理工学院博士生Anand Shah与南加州大学博士生Joshua Levy于5月发布的一项待同行评审研究揭示了这一趋势。部分法院尚未察觉或认为威胁不大，但专家警告若不采取行动，积压案件将进一步加重本已疲于应对工作量增长和资金不足的司法系统。自诉案件可能累积并影响其他法庭职能，强调法院需在有限资金内创新管理流程。德克萨斯西区联邦地区法官Xavier Rodriguez表示其所在法院尚未发现自诉案件增加，但建议法院应帮助自诉人获取准确资源，例如修订自诉手册以指导其验证AI生成的法律依据。Braswell与Rodriguez共同参与司法AI联盟（JAIC），该联盟由二人与路易斯安那州第五巡回上诉法院法官Scott Schlegel于今年初创立，旨在讨论生成式AI在司法中的用例。法院需借鉴疫情期间远程视频听证的经验，通过技术采用和流程改进应对挑战，但AI工具的应用需先解决现有技术栈和伦理问题。

# Rising Pro Se Filings Push Federal Courts to Examine Case Management in the AI Era

Federal judges are rethinking their workflows and the guidance that they offer self-represented litigants to manage the rise of pro se case filings.

6 minute read July 14, 2026 at 09:45 AM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b1bb32ca30c747d2664de350bb767836?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Ella Sherman](http://www.law.com/author/profile/ella-sherman/)

## What You Need to Know

*   The percentage of U.S. federal civil cases filed by self-represented litigants has jumped from a longtime average of 11% to 16.8% in 2025, according to a study published in May.
*   Courts vary in terms of whether they are experiencing an increase in pro se complaints. 
*   U.S. Magistrate Judge Maritza Braswell of the District of Colorado said pro se cases will likely accumulate and negatively impact other court functions if the growth becomes too much for courts.

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

The number of pro se complaints filed in federal court, including those drafted using generative artificial intelligence, has risen over the past few years, presenting new challenges for overburdened courts.

The percentage of U.S. federal civil cases filed by self-represented litigants hit 16.8% in 2025, marking a jump from the 2005-2022 average of 11%, and many of these more recent pro se cases involve AI-generated filings, according to a study published in May, awaiting peer review, from Anand Shah, a doctoral candidate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Joshua Levy, a doctoral candidate at the University of Southern California.

While some courts either have not noticed this growth or do not yet see this trend as a major threat, experts say courts must act, or the mounting caseloads will add even more strain to a judiciary already fatigued by growing workloads and underfunding.

“It's the type of thing that you would only see in the data first because anecdotally, everyone's experiences are completely dispersed,” Shah told Law.com. “If we had waited for people to realize on their own, it would've just certainly been too late.”

Pro se litigants have increasingly been using gen AI to determine whether they should file a complaint, to draft the complaint and to save money where they would have hired an attorney for civil cases such as housing and employment disputes.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Maritza Braswell of the District of Colorado said pro se cases will likely accumulate and negatively impact other court functions if the growth becomes too much for courts to take on.

“An overwhelmed court would have a much harder time dispensing justice. It’s that simple. Making good decisions takes a lot more than caring and empathy,” Braswell said. “Those are important ingredients, but we need time to read the arguments, dig into the case law, listen carefully, weigh credibility, probe the evidence, manage discovery disputes, hold hearings and conferences, draft carefully reasoned opinions, improve our systems, set priorities, properly supervise our teams, train our staff and much, much more. There are so many pieces to the work we do. If our dockets were truly overwhelmed, the attention we could give each case would necessarily thin out.”

U.S. District Judge Xavier Rodriguez of the Western District of Texas, also said that, if pro se case increase continues, they could pile up. He added that he has not noticed an increase in pro se cases within his own court.

Federal courts vary in terms of whether they are experiencing an increase in pro se complaints.

Braswell said she has seen the landscape of pro se court filings shift, noting that the emergence of gen AI plays a role in that change.

“If you think about these artificial intelligence tools at everyone's fingertips, it's obvious that people are going to feel more emboldened, more comfortable with engaging with our institutions and with our systems,” she told Law.com.

Braswell added that federal courts should be thinking about this now, as she and experts cannot say for sure how long courts will have to manage this before they are completely overwhelmed.

“We have this window, and it's not big. It's a small window where we have to really step back and rethink our systems and processes and be open-minded. ... We're naturally a risk-averse profession, and when you talk about our institutions, they're naturally slow moving and for good reasons. We want to be thoughtful, deliberate, but that slow moving feature can be a hindrance and so we're going to have to be brave,” Braswell said.

Those studying and analyzing the rise of pro se cases say federal courts will eventually have to address the growing caseloads—either by somehow slowing the flow of pro se filings or by reworking their internal case management processes to handle the increased inventory.

Braswell said she favors the latter, adding that courts need to get creative with the limited funding they have.

“Having courts set up safe spaces, controlled environments where the technology can be leveraged in a more responsible way. Those are the better solutions to be thinking about, not how do we force these litigants to do something different when there's already so many barriers for them,” she said. “What tools do we need to equip ourselves with as judges and as court staff to make sure that we can dig in and do it efficiently so that we can keep up?”

Sometimes a sense of urgency can become a court’s biggest motivator.

National Center for State Courts director of technology, data and knowledge management Jason Tashea recalls courts immediately switching to a video call format to conduct remote proceedings at the start of the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. In doing this, courts were able to process high volume case types, and other process improvements followed.

“[Courts] saw the benefits during the pandemic, and a lot of the tried-and-true stuff that courts know how to do in regards to process inclusion and technology adoption. They're not particularly sexy interventions,” Tashea said.

Rodriguez said courts thinking about how to manage the rising pro se caseloads should determine whether the litigants have as much access to resources and accurate guidance as possible.

“We need to figure out some way to assist pro se filers too, before they file a document, whether most districts have a pro se handbook, and we probably need to amend our pro se handbook to give them more guidance [like,] ‘OK, if you're using AI and it generates cases or statutes, where else in the internet can you go to for reliable free checking to ensure that this case exists, stands for the proposition you believe it is standing for and that it's accurate?’” he said.

Both Braswell and Rodriguez said they could see courts potentially leveraging generative AI to manage workflows and rising caseloads in the future, but more conversations addressing courts’ existing technology stack and ethical considerations must happen well before AI adoption takes place.

Pro se litigation, technology adoption and ethics are all topics Braswell and Rodriguez are hoping to continue discussing during their ongoing [Judicial AI Consortium](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/01/28/judicial-ai-consortium-aims-to-set-the-record-straight-on-ai-in-courts-/) (JAIC), which is attended by other judges across court systems.

Braswell and Rodriguez, alongside Judge Scott Schlegel of the Louisiana Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, created the JAIC earlier this year to clarify use cases for generative AI and its role in the judiciary.

“We've got this central system, but really each federal district court does their own thing, and so, we created JAIC to create a common place where we can come together and talk about these issues. We're not trying to consensus build, we're not trying to develop policy,” Braswell said. “We're just trying to connect with each other because it's important to talk with each other about what we're seeing in our courtrooms and with self-represented litigants to work through this process together.”

news.titleEn: Superjustice or Algorithm Tyranny? How AI is Rewriting the Rule of Law with Professor Benjamin Alarie
news.titleZh: 超级正义还是算法暴政？Benjamin Alarie教授谈AI如何重写法治
news.summaryZh: 人工智能对法律体系的深远影响。AI已超越案例摘要阶段，正进入司法推理、结果预测和机构治理领域。文章将这一变革与梵蒂冈教皇通谕《Magnifica Humanitas》相类比，认为AI可能成为解决法律系统可及性差、案件积压和深度不平等的终极方案，但也引发算法暴政的担忧。核心议题是：在代码时代，问责制、公平性和正义的定义需要被重新审视。
news.bodyText:
We’ve spent years obsessing over AI benchmarks, workplace automation, and chatbot hallucinations. But while we were looking at the future of work, artificial intelligence quietly invaded the foundations of democratic society: the legal system. Today, we’re unpacking a tectonic shift with the Professor. AI isn’t just summarizing case law anymore; it’s entering the realm of judicial reasoning, predictive outcomes, and institutional governance. Is this the beginning of algorithmic tyranny, or could it be the ultimate cure for an inaccessible, backlogged, and deeply unequal legal system? Drawing striking parallels to the Vatican’s landmark papal encyclical Magnifica Humanitas , we will map out the next phase of the AI revolution. We’re moving past model capabilities and stepping into institutional adaptation. Get ready to rethink everything you know about accountability, equity, and the very definition of justice in the age of code.

# Former Kirkland, Paul Hastings Partner John Budetti Joins Hybrid Firm Norm Law

Norm Law continues its streak of Big Law hires with former Kirkland & Ellis and Paul Hastings partner John Budetti coming in as partner and co-head of global private capital funds.

2 minute read July 14, 2026 at 01:11 PM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b1bb32ca30c747d2664de350bb767836?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Ella Sherman](http://www.law.com/author/profile/ella-sherman/)

## What You Need to Know

*    Norm Law has appointed John Budetti as partner and co-head of global private capital funds.
*   Budetti brings to Norm Law his expertise on how AI is changing the structure, economics and delivery of legal work.
*   Budetti was at Paul Hastings for 18 months before separating from the firm in 2024.

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

Hybrid law firm Norm Law, affiliated with regulatory artificial intelligence company Norm Ai, announced Tuesday that it appointed John Budetti as partner and co-head of global private capital funds.

Budetti was previously a senior investment funds partner at Kirkland & Ellis, where he worked for 17 years before spending about a year and a half as partner and investment funds chair at Paul Hastings. Budetti brings to Norm Law his expertise on how AI is changing the structure, economics and delivery of legal work.

“The aim is to put tech-forward attorneys in the shoes of our clients to understand and ease their process friction points in conjunction with our top-tier legal services. I'm joining a growing core of accomplished fund and other transactional attorneys executing this together," Budetti said in a press release.

Prior to joining Norm Law, Budetti was at Paul Hastings for [18 months](https://www.law.com/americanlawyer/2024/10/17/john-budetti-paul-hastings-investment-funds-chair-departs-after-18-months/) before separating from the firm in 2024. At the time of his departure from Paul Hastings, sources told Law.com that Budetti left “to pursue personal opportunities” and would not be joining another law firm.

Budetti is one of several Big Law partners who have recently found roles at Norm Law.

Earlier this year Norm Law [appointed](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/04/21/norm-laws-hires-from-ropes--gray-sidley-discuss-their-tech-driven-transition/) former Ropes & Gray partner Bill Mone to serve as partner and head of private equity, and the firm appointed former Sidley Austin executive committee chair Mike Schmidtberger to be its chair and head of investment funds and regulatory. In May, Norm Law announced that it [appointed](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/05/29/legaltech-rundown-relativity-announces-claude-activity-integration-norm-law-announces-new-hires-and-more/) Sam Lipson, previously partner at Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, as partner and co-head of its emerging companies and venture capital (ECVC) practice.

Norm Law’s affiliated legal tech company Norm Ai has also seen a large quantity of funding since it was founded in August 2025.

Most recently, the company [announced](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/07/07/norm-ai-announces-120m-series-c-including-investment-from-fenwick-ex-kirkland-chair-/) this month that it raised $120 million in a Series C funding round led by Khosla ventures and with participation from Fenwick & West and former Kirkland & Ellis chair Jeff Hammes, as well as Blackstone, Bain Capital Ventures, Vanguard, Coatue, Craft Ventures, New York Life, TIAA and former Blackstone executive Tony James.

news.titleEn: Why AI Will Create More Legal Work, Not Less: Filevine’s Rizner and Anderson on Research, Access, and Human Judgment
news.titleZh: Filevine高管：AI将创造更多法律工作而非减少——关于研究、可及性与人类判断
news.summaryZh: Filevine首席执行官Ryan Anderson和产品经理John Rizner基于杰文斯悖论提出，AI提升效率将使法律服务惠及更多人，推动更深入的法律研究，并创造因成本高昂而被排除的工作。家庭法、移民、破产、刑事辩护和雇佣诉讼预计将率先增长。Rizner介绍了Filevine的AI平台Lois，它结合引文图谱和语义分析定位相关判例，并通过模型面板评估冲突生成结构化备忘录。引文验证分为三级：确认案例存在、判断是否支持主张、检查是否仍为有效法律。不同大语言模型对效率违约问题给出截然不同的建议，揭示了嵌入的法律和经济偏好。AI改变法律起草、律所经济和计费方式，但效率提升不会自动消除计时收费，律师可将节省的时间用于更深入的研究和更高质量的工作产品。未来将出现针对律所、律师甚至客户关系的定制化模型，但模型选择引入法理偏见和准确性风险，资深法律判断仍不可或缺。
news.bodyText:
Predictions about artificial intelligence often focus on job losses and shrinking demand for lawyers. Filevine CEO and co-founder Ryan Anderson and product manager John Rizner offer a sharply different forecast. Drawing on the Jevons paradox, they argue greater efficiency will make legal services accessible to more people, encourage deeper legal research, and create work once excluded by cost. AI might reduce the effort required for individual tasks while expanding the overall volume and ambition of legal representation.

The shift holds major implications for the access-to-justice gap. Faster drafting, research, and document review would allow lawyers to serve more clients without sacrificing professional judgment. Anderson expects family law, immigration, bankruptcy, criminal defense, and employment litigation to experience some of the earliest growth. Motions, witnesses, and legal theories once abandoned over expense become economically viable, although courts face their own capacity crisis as more disputes and arguments enter the system.

Rizner explains how Filevine’s legal AI platform, Lois, applies machine learning to one of legal research’s oldest problems: traditional citators often return different results. Lois combines citation graphs with semantic analysis to locate opinions discussing related legal doctrines even when no direct citation connects the cases. A panel of models then evaluates potential conflicts and produces a structured memo. The goal is richer legal analysis focused on the precise holding or proposition a lawyer needs, rather than a simple flag attached to an entire opinion.

Accuracy still demands disciplined human review. Filevine organizes citation verification into three levels: confirming the cited case exists, determining whether the case supports the claimed proposition, and checking whether the authority is still good law. The conversation also examines Rizner’s research into how different large language models approach efficient breach of contract. OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic models produced dramatically different recommendations, revealing embedded legal and economic preferences beneath seemingly neutral answers.

The guests also explore how AI changes legal drafting, law firm economics, and the billable hour. Filevine’s acquisition of Pincites, now Lois for Word, reflects Microsoft Word’s continuing role as the shared language of legal documents, redlines, formatting, and negotiations. Efficiency does not automatically eliminate hourly billing. Lawyers might instead use saved time to produce more thoroughly researched arguments, stronger contracts, and work product approaching senior-level depth. Firms still need incentives rewarding efficiency rather than treating faster work as lost revenue.

Looking ahead, Anderson and Rizner predict a proliferation of frontier and open-source models tailored to firms, individual lawyers, and specific client relationships. Legal teams will increasingly pair proprietary knowledge with selected models to produce highly specialized analysis. Yet model choice introduces jurisprudential bias, accuracy risks, and serious training concerns for junior lawyers. AI expands the range of available options, while experienced legal judgment decides which arguments deserve trust, which sources require verification, and which advice should reach the client.

John Rizner Slides Filevine Primary Presentation – 2026

Transcript:

**Nikki Shaver** (00:00) Hi Greg and Marlene. Ever since Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, a lot of focus has been on whether firms and legal departments should be using that in place of, or as well as, legal-specific applications like Harvey and Legora. But Anthropic is not the only big player to brush up against the legal market. Microsoft has launched its legal agent, embedded in Word and other 365 applications. OpenAI has reportedly hired someone to help build in legal. Perplexity has launched Computer for Counsel with a host of legal MCP connectors. And now it seems Amazon may also have its sights on our vertical with Amazon Quick for Legal. It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem. We’ll soon be publishing a helpful comparison of the big tech offerings for legal, with an examination of where in the legal tech stack they might be useful. Stay tuned for that on our site at legaltechnologyhub.com, or follow along on LinkedIn at Legaltech Hub. It’s a pleasure to see all of you. Until next week.

**Marlene Gebauer** (01:13) Welcome to The Geek in Review, the podcast focused on innovative and creative ideas in the legal industry. I’m Marlene Gebauer,

**Greg Lambert** (01:20) and I’m Greg Lambert. And today we are going to be digging into a fascinating and probably somewhat counterintuitive theory that’s turning the traditional panic over AI on its head. Instead of asking how many legal jobs AI will destroy, we’re actually going to explore why AI may actually trigger an unprecedented explosion of legal work, opening up massive markets that were historically priced out.

**Marlene Gebauer** (01:48) In hearing what our guests have to say about this, and to lead our conversation, we are absolutely thrilled to welcome John Rizner, product manager at Filevine. And joining John is Ryan Anderson, the CEO and co-founder of Filevine. John and Ryan, welcome to The Geek in Review.

**Greg Lambert** (02:03) Welcome, guys.

**Ryan Anderson** (02:04) Good to be here, Greg and Marlene.

**Greg Lambert** (02:05) All right, John, let’s start off with you, because we wanted to talk about the Jevons paradox, which I know a lot of our listeners have heard before. But let’s look at the big macroeconomic picture that you guys have brought to our attention as well. Many pundits out there are predicting that AI will contract the legal industry, but you guys are arguing the exact opposite of that using the Jevons paradox — the economic theory that technology makes resources cheaper and more efficient to produce, and then consumption actually skyrockets. So do you mind just talking a little bit about how the paradox applies to legal work, and how we should be prepared for that?

**John Rizner** (02:51) Yeah, totally. So I’m going to talk about it in connection with a product that I’m working on: a citator, à la Shepard’s-style citations, within LOIS. When we started off investigating our tooling, I had a number of conversations with some old law school classmates of mine that did far better in law school than I did — appellate litigators who went through the elite clerkship rounds. And I was talking with them: “If you had the ability, with large language models and new AI tooling, would you be excited to chew through fewer research materials as part of your work?” What was interesting is all of them said, actually, if I had unlimited time and unlimited resources, I would want to find more and read more, as opposed to find less and read less. If they could, they would love to boil the ocean — exhaust every possible resource in reading through opinions and relevant literature on their case before drafting or preparing anything. So I think as AI tools, especially in the legal research space, the citator space, make finding the relevant literature easier — even making more of the relevant literature an immediate delivery to the user — rather than lawyers spending less time doing research, we’re going to see lawyers spend more time doing substantive research. The difference being, instead of lawyers saying, “All right, I’ve got X amount of time, I found this handful of cases, let’s quickly draft this and get it out the door,” I think you’re going to see far more in-depth and nuanced arguments in legal work product, due to the fact that lawyers will have easier access to greater amounts of research material. And as a consequence, you’ll probably have better opinions come out of courts, because the arguments lawyers are making are going to be more nuanced, reflecting the deeper research. So I hope lawyers like doing research — I hope that’s why they went to law school — because in my view of it, you’re going to see greater and greater research, and far higher quality research, as opposed to lesser or more shallow research.

**Greg Lambert** (05:23) Yeah, that was going to be my follow-up question, on a conversation we had last week — one of the things she mentioned was: we used to get these one-page surveys or reports, and now we’re getting these 40-page surveys. And it’s not necessarily better; it’s just more. But I think your argument is that the outcome, the results, the research is actually better rather than just more research. Am I interpreting that correctly?

**John Rizner** (05:55) Yeah. So I think, at their core, and obviously we all know as part of our ethical duties, lawyers should be diving through the cases that they’re possibly looking at. And I think as these tools evolve and become more mature and can find more relevant and more on-point items for the lawyers to read, they will read the same amount, maybe even read more. But the conclusions they come to will be stronger, because they have that better picture of how the law is at that particular moment. So volume may grow, and in addition to volume growing, I think quality becomes far better in the long run.

**Marlene Gebauer** (06:38) Yeah, I think that makes sense, because AI kind of allows you to separate the wheat from the chaff, and then you can focus more deeply on the things that you need to focus on and sort of leave the other ones.

**Ryan Anderson** (06:52) Yeah, I’ll speak to that for just a moment too, from a market perspective. Two, three years ago there were a lot of predictions around what would happen to engineers, coders. Filevine employs a lot of coders — I think we will end the year with something like 400 to 450 engineers, about half of which are ML engineers, the other half your traditional coders. And there were quite a few predictions that AI would reduce the need for corporations, for tech companies specifically, to have as many engineers. The theory was that there will be so much code written, and it’ll be so much easier to write, that you won’t need as many engineers — so you’ll see some layoffs and fewer engineers hired. Well, it’s been the case at our company, and I think broadly across the industry, that the exact opposite has happened. The engineering market sort of hit a low maybe two or three years ago and has actually climbed out of that. More are being hired — not more than ever, but certainly more than the post-COVID lows. More companies are bringing on more engineers to do more work, and there’s a very logical reason for this. We definitely write 10 times more code today than we did before — it might even be more than 10 times more. But for every piece of code that we write, it has to be reviewed, it has to be QA’d, it has to be tested. And as the aperture of the product increases, the surface area for problems increases, but the ambition of the product also grows. What that has allowed us to do as a company is build a much richer, broader, more end-to-end product offering that we think is really unique, but I think it’s the same for a lot of companies. The analogy really holds true for legal. As John brought up, you’re going to have lawyers able to do research more quickly and find truth for their clients in a much broader way, and be able to zero in and find creative ways to apply the facts of their case to the law. But even consider the lawyer who says, “Instead of bringing that motion the client just didn’t want us to do because it was going to be expensive, I didn’t bring the motion to compel the deposition of that witness. We just let it go — we just didn’t do it in this case.” That happens all the time. If you talk to litigators, they’ll say their clients didn’t want to pay for witness number six, who might have had some interesting information in the case. But boy, now that you can bring that motion to compel, and it’s much easier to draft and much quicker, the opportunity costs change, and the search for truth becomes sort of superpowered. And of course, litigation in particular is a counterparty affair — what one side does, the other side is having to respond to, and then maybe bringing a counterattack themselves. So for better or for worse, I think truth will get sought out more quickly. But also, I think lawyers are going to be very busy. And honestly, I wouldn’t want to be a judge in this atmosphere — I think it is really tricky for the judiciary at this time.

**Greg Lambert** (09:47) Yeah.

**John Rizner** (09:50) And I think one other item to bring in on this truth question: it’s not like we are looking at a field where all the buried treasure has been dug up. One of the things we were looking at early on was research by Paul Hellyer and Susan Mart, two legal scholars, who had done quantitative analysis of how often, say, Lexis and Westlaw agree or disagree on a particular citation, or how often they return the same relevant opinions for a particular citation analysis. What’s really interesting is that the differences between the two could be substantial, depending on the opinions looked at. So if you’re a subscriber only to Westlaw or only to Lexis, you may be missing items that Lexis is returning but Westlaw isn’t, or vice versa. And so where AI tooling makes it cheaper and easier to apply different methodologies — so you can have your multiple citators taking different approaches at a larger scale — I think you start to discover more of those opinions that were otherwise hidden, because you were stuck with one citator and only uncovering those hidden truths via one type of methodology.

**Greg Lambert** (11:10) Ryan, I want to go back to something that you mentioned about using the engineers as a parallel path to some of the things that we’re seeing in legal. I was listening — I believe it was Adam Mosseri from Instagram — talking about how his engineering teams are made up now versus how they were pre-AI, where he was saying every project had like a baker’s dozen of people on it, ranging from engineers to project managers to researchers and data scientists. And he says now it’s essentially a team of three. Are you seeing similar things on your engineering team? And do you think there’s a parallel for how lawyers will be doing it?

**Ryan Anderson** (12:00) Yeah — and sorry, sorry to interrupt you, but yes, we are definitely seeing a reduction in what a single person can do. Let me give an example. This just happened today, about two hours ago. I was going through a new feature with our team. We were thinking through how to design an experience on our deep retrieval engine. We think we have really world-class retrieval — we think we can search through more documents than almost any product out there; we literally think we’re the best in the world at this. But you might imagine there are some UI constraints: telling the user where you are when you’re searching through millions of pages of documents can be tricky. There was some back and forth about how to do this, the team’s debating, there are about 10 people on the call, and we’re saying, “Well, how about this method to tell the user what’s going on? Here are some other methods.” And about 15 minutes into the conversation, one of the engineers goes, “Well, I actually just coded it. Does anyone want to see what I just did?” And we literally shared a screen, and he showed something — not in a production environment, but on his local machine using real live code — and said, “Here’s how I think we should do it.” It was working, and we could actually play with it right there during the meeting. I can tell you that kind of interaction never happened before. Never. We have lawyers who say, “I was exploring an argument that I didn’t think would be a good idea, but I used LOIS, and all of a sudden it found a couple cases, and it was a line of case law theory that I didn’t think applied to my case, but it does. And so we’re going to actually attack the other side in a way that we hadn’t realized at all.” When you lower the cost for exploration, for creative exploration, people become much more creative. I’ve always thought the best lawyers are actually exceptionally creative. It’s funny — lawyers don’t think of themselves as creatives. They think of artists and movie stars and musicians as creative people. But I think great lawyers are exceptionally creative, and by lowering the cost to go on a creative thread with a legal theory, you enable much more creativity. It’s very exciting.

**Marlene Gebauer** (14:09) So Ryan, when we talk about lowering costs to capture a dormant market of middle-class clients and small businesses, what specific practice areas or legal needs do you think will see the quickest influx of new work? How does Filevine view this unfolding from a macro strategy perspective?

**Ryan Anderson** (14:29) There are many great things about AI, and there are some scary things about AI. But in the legal industry, perhaps the most exciting is — we all know that getting a lawyer is actually quite a challenge. My brother, who’s our chief product officer, talks about how he needed a lawyer to help with a relatively small real estate dispute. Here’s a guy who literally leads product for a pretty significant legal tech company, has a brother who was a lawyer, and knows many, many lawyers in his day-to-day job, and he could barely get somebody to answer the phone. It is hard sometimes to find a lawyer — and that’s a well-connected guy. If you’re somebody who’s indigent, working class, maybe you don’t grow up with the same kind of privileges or connections, it can be extremely challenging to find good legal representation. And it’s pretty awesome that lawyers are going to have much more capacity now. You asked what industries: I think you’ll see a lot more in family law, a lot more immigration law, a lot more bankruptcy, and I think underrepresented criminal defendants are going to be in much better shape than they are today. In fact, a lot of those state public defenders’ offices are clients of Filevine. The Innocence Project is a client of Filevine. You’re going to be able to have more people who have meritorious claims for wrongful prosecution — or for having a lawyer who didn’t do the job they should have been doing — win their case, or at least get them a lower sentence. Many more of these cases can be taken on. It’s incredibly exciting. So I think you’ll see it across the board in those areas. The example I give is: these are lawyers, so we’ll say they have 10 hours in their workday, and it now takes two hours to draft a will instead of eight. Well, how many more people can they serve in a given day? If they could draft one will in eight hours, or maybe it was four, and now can do it in two, you’re now serving something like double the number of people during a day. You don’t even have to reduce your rates that much — maybe your rates stay the same, they might even go higher — but you’re able to serve more people, and those people wind up paying less because they’re taking less of the lawyer’s time. So it’s a very exciting world we’re going to live in. We don’t know exactly how it will all play out, but more legal customers will be served than ever before. It’s very exciting.

So I think you’re going to see a huge proliferation of models, which is going to be different, it’s going to be confusing, and it’s not, I think, the environment a lot of people expected to see even just a year ago. So that’s my big crystal ball prediction.

**John Rizner** (50:46) And the one piece I would add to that: with the proliferation of models, you’ll see, increasingly, what I like to call synthetic secondary sources. With the proliferation of models, and folks having their preferred work product — really, what some of these firms have spent decades upon decades tuning and building as their particular approach to the law — I think you’ll have tooling and models emerge where the analysis provided to a particular lawyer is so customized, where it is the specific model and specific data source coming together. If the firm name is, say, Ryan and John LLP, it is a technological marriage of our exact corpus with our exact preferred models to get our exact answer, at a scale that’s just not been achievable, because the knowledge and the style and the preferences were locked in the brains of the partner or maybe the senior associates. A crazy ability to get ultra-custom legal outputs for users.

**Ryan Anderson** (53:40) I think you’re maybe not even going far enough — it may not even be at the firm level. It might be the lawyer level, and it might even be the lawyer paired with the client. You could envision a world in which you say, “For this client, we prefer this model.” I can see that very easily being the case. We already orchestrate through multiple models just to give you a certain response to a query. So it’s going to be a world where you see a lot of models, they’re going to be used in a lot of different ways, and they’re going to become more and more specialized. It’s very exciting. Thank you both so much for the time today.

**Greg Lambert** (54:22) Yeah, you got it. John and Ryan, thank you very much. Appreciate it.

**Marlene Gebauer** (54:26) Yeah, and thanks to all of you for listening to The Geek in Review. If you’ve enjoyed the show, please share it with a colleague. We’d love to hear from you on LinkedIn and Substack.

**Greg Lambert** (54:35) And real quick — if they want to learn more, where’s the best place to reach out?

**Ryan Anderson** (54:40) Probably just hit me up on Twitter — DM me on Twitter. Ryan Filevine is my username on Twitter, and you can find me there. I guess we call it X now, right? So it’s X.

**Marlene Gebauer** (54:48) And as always, the music you hear is from Jerry David DeCicca. Thank you, Jerry, and goodbye, everybody.

news.titleEn: The Inside View: Addleshaw Goddard’s AGPT learnings and the future of build vs buy
news.titleZh: 内部视角：Addleshaw Goddard的AGPT经验与自建vs采购的未来
news.summaryZh: 在Legal IT Insider最新一期《内部视角》节目中，Addleshaw Goddard创新与法律技术总监Elliot White与编辑Caroline Hill讨论了该律所自建GenAI平台AGPT的经验，以及AI下一阶段可能促使律所重新审视某些假设。AGPT的首要目标并非创建专有工具，而是快速学习、理解技术并帮助律师培养有效使用AI的技能，结果实现了高采用率和对律师实际使用生成式AI方式的更深入理解。White对市场趋势进行了坦诚评估：尽管Addleshaw Goddard继续投资AGPT，但代理工作流的出现带来了新挑战，包括跟上快速演变的AI能力，以及律所应在多大程度上专注于自建解决方案。讨论还涉及基于代币的定价：随着供应商转向消费模式，律所需更精通为正确任务使用正确模型并理解AI赋能工作的真实成本。关于知识可移植性，White认为律所应仔细考虑知识编码的位置和方式，以便随技术平台演变保持可移植性。
news.bodyHtml:
In the latest episode of The Inside View with Legal IT Insider, Elliot White from Addleshaw Goddard joins editor Caroline Hill for a candid discussion about what the firm has learned from building its own GenAI platform AGPT, and why the next phase of AI may see law firms rethink some of their assumptions.

White is director of innovation and legal technology at Addleshaw Goddard and has been involved from the outset in the international law firm’s GenAI pilots and the build of AGPT, which is hosted in its Microsoft Azure tenancy.

Advertisement

There are lots of conversations right now about buy v build within law firms, but few have got as much experience already as Addleshaw Goddard. White explains that AGPT was never primarily about creating a proprietary tool; it was about learning quickly, understanding the technology, and helping lawyers develop the skills needed to work effectively with AI. He says the result has been strong adoption and a much deeper understanding of how lawyers actually use generative AI in practice.

What makes this podcast particularly timely is White’s honest assessment of where the market is heading. While Addleshaw Goddard continues to invest in AGPT, the emergence of agentic workflows is creating new challenges. White discusses the difficulty of keeping pace with rapidly evolving AI capabilities and raises important questions about the extent to which law firms should be focusing on building their own solutions.

Advertisement

The discussion also provides a thoughtful exploration on topics including token-based pricing. As suppliers increasingly move towards consumption models, White argues that law firms will need to become significantly more sophisticated about using the right model for the right task and understanding the true cost of AI-enabled work.

Another interesting discussion is around knowledge portability. White argues that firms should think carefully about where and how they codify their knowledge, so it remains portable as technology platforms evolve.

For law firm leaders, innovation teams and anyone trying to navigate the fast-changing legal AI landscape, this episode offers a great combination of practical experience and strategic thinking. Definitely one to watch.

You can watch the episode on YouTube below or listen on Spotify HERE.

news.titleEn: 'We're in a New Terrain': AI Bolsters Pro Se Litigation, but Judges Raise Alarms
news.titleZh: “我们进入了一个新领域”：AI助力当事人自行诉讼，但法官敲响警钟
news.summaryZh: 人工智能工具导致自行诉讼案件数量激增。然而，联邦和州法院的部分法官已对使用AI的当事人实施制裁，理由是AI产生“幻觉”及其他错误。新数据显示，AI的普及并未提高自行诉讼当事人的胜诉率。一些自行诉讼诊所（如贝勒大学法学院家庭法诊所）正在指导当事人如何有效使用AI工具，但指出AI无法处理案件中的情感因素。联邦和州法院的法官要求自行诉讼当事人遵守与律师相同的规则，发布常规命令，有时甚至对其进行制裁。

# 'We're in a New Terrain': AI Bolsters Pro Se Litigation, but Judges Raise Alarms

Many legal experts attribute skyrocketing pro se filings to artificial intelligence tools, but some judges in federal and state courts have sanctioned them over "hallucinations" and other errors caused by AI.

10 minute read July 14, 2026 at 12:58 PM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/fa0eb4371c9b77fcd6f8baa371474520?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Amanda Bronstad](http://www.law.com/author/profile/amanda-bronstad/)

## What You Need to Know

*   New data suggests that the growth of AI hadn’t improved the success rates for pro se litigants.
*   Pro se clinics, such as the Baylor Law Family Law Clinic, are working with litigants on how to effectively use AI tools, which don't account for emotional aspects of a case.
*   Judges in state and federal courts are holding pro se litigants to the same rules as lawyers, issuing standing orders or at times even sanctioning them.

news.titleEn: Briefpoint Launches Discovery Playbooks, Bringing Response Governance to the 1,000+ Law Firms That Draft Discovery on Its Platform
news.titleZh: Briefpoint 推出 Discovery Playbooks，为平台上 1000 多家律所带来发现响应治理功能
news.summaryZh: 2026 年 7 月 13 日，发现自动化平台 Briefpoint 宣布推出 Discovery Playbooks，这是一套发现响应治理功能集，可捕获律所的最佳异议和响应策略，并在诉讼律师需要时自动应用。该平台已被全美 50 个州的 1000 多家律所使用。诉讼律师经常重复回答相同的发现请求，但以往每次都需要从头开始。Discovery Playbooks 消除了这一流程：律师照常完成响应后，一键即可将其添加到律所的 playbook 中。此后，当 Briefpoint 检测到律所已回答过的请求时，会自动链接并应用保存的异议和响应策略。Playbook 条目可限定为全所范围或特定客户、司法管辖区或案件类型。辩护律所利用它在大批量案卷中强制执行一致的异议策略；原告律所一次性回答模板发现请求后可在各处重复使用；企业内部法务部门一次性编码公司立场，并在所有案件和外部律所中强制执行。
news.bodyHtml:
New featureset learns a firm’s objection and response strategy from work it has already served — then reapplies it automatically whenever a matching request appears, on any matter

 

San Francisco, California | July 13, 2026 Briefpoint, the discovery automation platform used by more than 1,000 law firms across all 50 states, today announced Discovery Playbooks, a discovery response governance feature set that captures a firm’s best objections and response strategy and brings them back automatically – where litigators need them, when they need them.

 Litigators answer the same discovery requests over and over: the same form interrogatories in every auto case, the same document demands from the same opposing counsel, the same objections a firm has served hundreds of times. Yet each new response set typically starts from scratch, with drafters digging through old work product and copy-pasting from prior matters – or improvising and drifting from the firm’s positions.

 

Discovery Playbooks eliminates that entire workflow. Attorneys respond to discovery in Briefpoint exactly as they always have. When a response is completed, a single click adds it to the firm’s playbook – no data entry or configuration required. From then on, whenever Briefpoint detects a request the firm has already answered, it links the request to the saved playbook item and reapplies the firm’s objections and response strategy automatically.

“Your best discovery response shouldn’t be trapped in a file from 2023,” said Nathan Walter, CEO and co-founder of Briefpoint. “Every firm already has winning objection language – the problem is that it lives in old documents and senior lawyers’ heads. Playbooks turns that tribal knowledge into firm policy. You do the work once, and Briefpoint makes sure it shows up every time it’s relevant, for every litigator, on every matter.”

 

One featureset, three use cases. Because playbook entries can be scoped firm-wide or to a specific client, jurisdiction, or case type, firms across the bar use Playbooks differently:

Defense firms enforce consistent objection strategy across high-volume dockets, so positions don’t vary with whoever happens to be drafting – and contradictions between matters get caught in drafting instead of surfacing in deposition.

 Plaintiff firms answer carrier boilerplate once and reuse it everywhere, reclaiming unbillable hours spent re-drafting responses to the same template discovery in every case.

 In-house legal departments encode corporate positions once and see them enforced across every matter and every outside firm to combat impeachable response variance or, at worst, bad law.

 Growing firms use playbooks to onboard: new associates draft from the firm’s tested language on day one, and partner review becomes reviewing rather than rewriting.

 

Every playbook entry carries its provenance (who added it, when it was last used, and how many times) so when a position changes, firms know exactly what the prior language said and where it has been asserted. The playbook library is searchable and filterable by document type, client, case type, and jurisdiction.

 “Preparing discovery responses takes much less time and we are able to ensure consistency throughout the firm with respect to objections and updates in the law,” said Eileen Booth, Partner at Jacobsen & McElroy, a Briefpoint customer.

 Discovery Playbooks is included in every Briefpoint plan at no additional cost and is live now for all Briefpoint accounts. A 60-second demonstration video is available at briefpoint.ai/discovery-playbooks.

 

About Briefpoint

Briefpoint is a discovery automation platform founded by Nathan Walter, a former litigator, and Chris Maffin, a former lead engineer at Relativity. Built so cases can resolve on their merits instead of their litigation budgets, Briefpoint has automated more than 186,000 discovery documents and generated more than 685,000 objections for over 1,000 law firms in all 50 states and 98 federal courts. Briefpoint is SOC 2 Type II certified, ZDR, and HIPAA compliant. Learn more at briefpoint.ai.

 

Media Contact

Nathan Walter

CEO, Briefpoint

nwalter@briefpoint.ai

news.titleEn: Intapp expands strategic partnership with Moody’s to bring counterparty intelligence directly into professional workflows via Intapp Celeste
news.titleZh: Intapp 扩大与穆迪的战略合作，通过 Intapp Celeste 将交易对手情报直接嵌入专业工作流程
news.summaryZh: Intapp 宣布扩大与穆迪的战略合作，将穆迪的信用风险、实体筛查和所有权数据集成到 Intapp Celeste 平台中。Celeste 是专为专业服务公司设计的代理型 AI 平台，用户可通过自然对话直接在工作流程中获取穆迪的金融风险情报、实体筛查结果、所有权结构和公司情报，无需切换平台。该集成基于模型上下文协议（MCP）构建，允许 AI 平台以编程方式访问穆迪的数据和分析。法律、私募资本和会计行业的客户将受益于这一整合。Intapp 客户若拥有有效的穆迪数据订阅，即可激活该集成，无需额外许可费用。
news.bodyHtml:
Celeste now surfaces Moody’s credit risk, entity screening, and ownership data at the moment of decision — through natural conversation and without disrupting the workflow

PALO ALTO, Calif. – July 14, 2026 – Deal professionals and risk teams spend significant time switching between platforms to gather counterparty intelligence — often at the precise moment a decision is in motion. Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA) today announced an expansion of its strategic partnership with Moody’s that helps reduce that friction.

Clients across the legal, private capital, and accounting verticals will benefit from new integration between Moody’s data and Intapp Celeste, Intapp’s agentic AI platform purpose-built for professional firms.

Through natural conversation, Celeste surfaces Moody’s financial risk intelligence, entity screening results, ownership structures, and company intelligence directly within the workflows professionals use every day — no context-switching required. By moving from data access to embedded intelligence, Intapp and Moody’s enable clients to unlock greater value:

  • Deal professionals can surface Moody’s counterparty risk signals, ownership structures, and financial health indicators directly within Intapp DealCloud at the moment of decision — enabling faster, better-informed deal execution.
  • Professional services firms can directly access Moody’s entity and ownership data within new business intake and conflicts workflows — accelerating client onboarding and strengthening regulatory defensibility.
  • Private capital and accounting firms can directly access Moody’s credit signals and counterparty screening during portfolio monitoring, fund diligence, and entity verification — reducing manual research and context switching while accelerating decision-making.

“Professional services firms operate in high-stakes, relationship-intensive environments where decisions carry long-term consequences,” said Helen Rider, Head of Global Sales at Moody’s. “Moody’s data has always been designed for exactly these moments — and our expanded partnership with Intapp now puts that intelligence inside Intapp’s AI-native workflows. That’s the kind of embedded intelligence that changes how professional services firms operate.”

The Celeste and Moody’s integration is built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an emerging open standard for connecting AI systems to external data sources and tools. Moody’s MCP server allows its data and analytics to be accessed programmatically by AI platforms like Celeste, enabling richer, more contextual responses grounded in structured financial intelligence.

“Celeste was designed to meet professionals in their workflow — not pull them out of it,” explained Don Coleman, Chief Operating Officer at Intapp. “Integrating Moody’s intelligence through MCP is a perfect expression of that vision. Our clients can now surface counterparty risk, credit signals, and entity data through a natural conversation with Celeste, without breaking their concentration or their process. This sets a new standard for how AI serves professional services — and marks a meaningful next chapter in our partnership with Moody’s.”

The Celeste and Moody’s MCP integration is available now to Intapp customers with an active Moody’s data subscription. Existing customers can activate the integration through their Intapp customer success team; no additional licensing is required on the Intapp side.

For more information, visit intapp.com/celeste or contact your Intapp account representative.

About Intapp

Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA) is the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries. Intapp’s vertically tailored agentic solutions are built for the specialized workflows, complex relationship networks, and professional compliance requirements of accounting, consulting, investment banking, law, private capital, and real assets firms. By applying Firm AI to core processes and data, Intapp helps partners, dealmakers, and advisors drive firm growth, manage compliance, and improve profitability. Learn why the world’s top firms trust Intapp’s industry-specific enterprise solutions at intapp.com.

Media contacts
Emily Martinez
Global Media and Communications Director
Intapp
press@intapp.com
