# Suited Announces Launch of Lateral Hiring Platform

The platform leverages generative AI as well as market and behavioral data to narrow prospects for professionals and law firms looking to fill lateral roles.

4 minute read July 08, 2026 at 08:00 AM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b1bb32ca30c747d2664de350bb767836?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Ella Sherman](http://www.law.com/author/profile/ella-sherman/)

## What You Need to Know

*   Firms using Suited were finding lateral hires more difficult to source compared with legal professionals straight out of law school.
*   Suited’s lateral hiring platform supports law firms and professionals in their search to fill lateral roles by helping narrow down and match firms with candidates and candidates with firms that fit them best.
*   The platform leverages multiple large language models to organize proprietary and public data that Suited has been gathering since its inception in 2018. 

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

Law and investment firm hiring intelligence platform Suited announced the launch of its artificial intelligence-powered lateral hiring platform Tuesday.

Suited aims to support organizations throughout the talent search process while also helping entry-level and experienced professionals evaluate career opportunities.

**What It Is:**Suited’s lateral hiring platform supports law firms and professionals in their search to fill lateral roles by helping narrow down and match firms with candidates and candidates with firms that fit them best based on a mix of public and proprietary market and behavioral data.

Users looking for jobs can set their interests and work behavior preferences, and Suited tracks relevant opportunities across the market on an ongoing basis. The platform leverages AI and a proprietary database of public and private market intelligence to generate personalized diligence briefings that show how a role aligns with the candidate’s goals or why an opportunity may not be worth pursuing.

Candidate information is not shared with a hiring firm unless the candidate gives explicit consent.

On the firm side, Suited analyzes a candidate’s experience, career path, goals and preferences to identify professionals who are most likely to succeed in a given role.

“The firm and candidate placement is really about leveraging data for both sides and helping provide more information into that ecosystem,” Suited co-founder and CEO Matt Spencer told Law.com. “So for law firms, we combine an analysis of a candidate's experience, their career trajectory, what their professional goals are, what their personal preference are around that, and then we combine that with proprietary behavioral and cognitive insights in order to identify the professionals that are most likely to thrive in any particular role.”

**Why It’s Needed:**According to Spencer, firms using the platform were finding lateral hires more difficult to source compared with legal professionals straight out of law school.

“When it's law school recruitment, sourcing isn't a problem. [Firms] know where all the candidates are, all the candidates are looking for jobs,” Spencer said. “On the lateral side, what we found is that the problem is very different. It is how do we identify, contact, engage the right candidates and ultimately get them involved in the process? And that was what we set out to ultimately do.”

**Under the Hood:**The platform leverages multiple large language models to organize proprietary and public data that Suited has been gathering since its inception in 2018. To obtain behavioral data, Suited surveys and analyzes candidates based on 13 different behavioral characteristics across three dimensions of how they work.

“How do they approach tasks and get things done? What motivates and drives them and then how do they work with others?” Spencer explained. “Candidates who have a certain pattern of behaviors who may feel like they're a mismatch and misaligned with their current firm, they're constantly swimming upstream because the way that they work is not optimal for how the firm prefers to ultimately work. That candidate could be much happier and more successful in a firm that really incentivize values and matches that candidate profile.”

**Competition:** Law firm hiring intelligence companies like [Firm Prospects](https://www.law.com/americanlawyer/2026/05/27/lateral-associate-hiring-outpaced-entry-level-hires-in-2025/) and [SurePoint Technologies](https://www.law.com/legaltechnews/2026/03/31/legal-professionals-arm-themselves-with-ai-expertise-across-practice-areas-/) also leverage data to match candidates with law firms. Spencer asserted that Suited’s behavioral data, in particular, sets it apart because that information is unique to its platform and cannot be scraped from the internet.

“[Helping] firms and candidates focus on the best opportunities for them really comes back and is underpinned by that behavioral [data],” Spencer said. “Understanding how people work, who they are at their core, their preferred working styles, what their day-to-day is like, that if you can find and facilitate an opportunity or role, a job in a firm where those things are valued, they're fundamentally just going to be happier and more successful over a longer period of time. ... That is something that can't be replicated in the market from a lateral hiring context.”

LTA Just-In-Time: Cosmo Quiz Energy Meets Legal Ops Self-Awareness

By

Stephanie Carty

posted

8 hours ago

Like

Please enjoy this feature quiz created by Stephanie Carty, Senior Practice Manager, McCarter & English.

Think you may be burned out? Take this seven-question quiz to find out!

Working in legal operations is a lot. You're juggling technology, vendors, process improvement, and attorney demands all while trying to carve out something resembling a work-life balance. Add to that a global pandemic, economic whiplash, political upheaval, and a complete reinvention of how and where we work and it's no wonder so many of us are running on fumes.

Studies consistently show that legal professionals experience burnout at rates well above the general workforce and, in legal operations, where the work is often invisible until something breaks, that pressure has nowhere to go.

But here’s the thing…. Burnout isn't just “burnout”; there is no one size fits all. Research identifies distinct profiles, and knowing which one you are experiencing is the first step toward actually doing something about it. Start by answering the following questions to learn more.

Question 1

It's Monday morning. You open your email to find 47 unread messages, three urgent pings, and a meeting invite for a recurring committee you stopped seeing value in six months ago. How do you feel?

A . Mildly overwhelmed, but I know what to tackle first. I've got a system.

B . Physically exhausted before the day even starts. I barely slept thinking about it.

C. I close my laptop, pour another coffee, and genuinely wonder if any of this matters.

D. I try to start, but I spiral…. what if I respond wrong? What if I'm already behind?

Question 2

Leadership asks you to take the lead on an overhaul of the firm's matter management workflow… again. This is the third time in two years. You...

A . Ask clarifying questions and scope it carefully. Change is part of the job.

B . Say yes, add it to the pile, and quietly calculate how many nights this will cost you.

C . Nod and think: "We'll launch this, it'll be ignored in six months, lather, rinse, repeat."

D . Wonder why they keep asking you. Have they lost confidence in your last two attempts?

Question 3

When was the last time you felt genuinely excited about something at work?

A . Recently. A project landed well/a new initiative is sparking real energy.

B . I can't remember. I'm just getting through it.

C . Months ago. I used to get excited, but now find it hard to care about most of what crosses my desk.

D . When I felt like I was actually making a difference, which feels like a lifetime ago.

Question 4

A colleague vents to you about negative impacts of firm politics, feeling frustrated by a difficult attorney, or agonizing over a failed rollout. You respond by...

A . Listening, commiserating a little, then helping them strategize.

B . Listening, but you're running on fumes and don't have much left to give.

C . Halfheartedly validating them while thinking: "Welcome to the club, this place never changes."

D . Worrying the same thing will happen to you and wondering if it's your fault when it does.

Question 5

It's 6:30 PM on a Thursday. Your to-do list has grown since this morning. You...

A . Wrap up what I can, log off, and protect my evening. The list will still be there tomorrow.

B . Keep going until I crash. Stopping feels irresponsible, even when I'm running on empty.

C . Stare at it, then close my laptop. The urgency doesn't register the way it used to.

D . Stay late trying to catch up, but feel like I'm spinning wheels and going nowhere.

Question 6

When you think about your career trajectory in legal operations, you feel...

A . Generally positive — I see growth, connection to the work, and room ahead.

B . Tired. I've given a lot, and I'm not sure how much longer I can sustain this pace.

C . Disillusioned. The profession has promise, but the day-to-day rarely reflects it.

D . Uncertain. I question whether I'm good enough at this or if anyone even sees my contributions.

Question 7

If you had to pick one phrase that best describes your relationship with work right now, it would be...

A . Busy, but fulfilled.

B . Running on empty.

C . Going through the motions.

D . Trying hard but feeling invisible.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Answer Key:

MOSTLY A's

Engaged. You're in a healthy place.

The Engaged profile is characterized by low scores on exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy. This mean you likely have energy, connection to your work, and confidence in your contributions. This doesn't mean burnout can't happen; it means your current coping strategies are working. Protect them. The biggest risk for Engaged people isn't a dramatic crash; it's a slow, unnoticed drift.

What to do next?

• Name what's working. If you have boundaries, routines, or relationships that are keeping you grounded, those aren't accidents. Identify them explicitly so you don't give them up the next time things get busy.

• Do a quarterly energy audit. Every few months, ask yourself honestly: what's energizing me, and what's draining me? Burnout is cumulative and tends to sneak up on people who thought they were fine.

• Stay connected to your "why. " Engagement is closely tied to a sense of purpose and meaningfulness at work. Keep that visible — whether it's a project you're proud of, a problem you're uniquely positioned to solve, or a colleague you're investing in.

• Mentor someone who's struggling. One of the most reliable ways to stay engaged yourself is to help someone else find their footing. It reinforces your own sense of contribution, and it builds the kind of community that buffers everyone against burnout.

• Keep learning. Research on work engagement consistently links it to growth opportunities. If your role has felt static, look for a new skill, a new committee, or a new challenge. Stagnation and disengagement are closer neighbors than most people realize.

MOSTLY B's

Overextended. You're running on fumes.

The Overextended profile is driven primarily by exhaustion and research links it most strongly to workload and resource strain. You probably still care about your work. You're just depleted. The fix isn't working harder or pushing through; it's recovery and redistribution.

What to do next?

• Audit your plate. Write down everything you're responsible for and identify what can be delegated, deferred, or dropped entirely. Not everything deserves your energy.

• Make rest a non-negotiable. Recovery isn't a reward for finishing — it's a requirement for functioning. Protect at least one hard stop per day.

• Have the workload conversation. Overextension rarely resolves itself. Name it to a manager or trusted colleague and ask specifically about rebalancing — not just venting.

• Batch your context-switching. Legal ops roles involve constant gear-shifting. Grouping similar tasks can meaningfully reduce cognitive drain.

• Watch for the "just this once" trap. Overextended people often got there through a series of reasonable-sounding exceptions. Start noticing the pattern.

MOSTLY C's

Disengaged.

You've emotionally checked out. The Disengaged profile is characterized by high cynicism only, and research found it sits closer to full burnout than the Overextended profile — which means detachment, left unaddressed, tends to deepen. The Disengaged profile is associated with low job resources such as social support, influence at work, and a sense of meaningfulness.

What to do next?

• Trace the cynicism. Is there a specific moment, project, or leadership decision that started this? Naming the source is different from just living with the feeling.

• Seek out one thing that still sparks something. It doesn't have to be your whole job; find a committee, a new initiative, a colleague whose work energizes you. Start small.

• Peer community matters. Cynicism is partly contagious, and so is engagement. ILTA communities and other professional peer groups can offer a perspective shift.

• Get honest about fit. Research links disengagement to having low social support, autonomy, and sense of meaningfulness at work. If those are structural problems with your role or firm, it's worth taking seriously.

• Consider talking to someone. A coach, therapist, or mentor who works with professionals can help you distinguish between burnout or potentially something bigger.

MOSTLY D's

Ineffective.

You're working hard but feeling invisible. The Ineffective profile reflects a loss of confidence in one's abilities, and research suggests people in this profile may respond well to interventions involving more recognition for their work. Researchers describe this as "a dull but okay work-life" — people who aren't acutely distressed but have lost the psychological connection to their work that makes it meaningful.

What to do next?

• Start a wins log. In this field, our contributions tend to become expected and often go unacknowledged. Keep a running list of what you've delivered, improved, or moved forward. Review it weekly.

• Ask for explicit feedback. Don't wait for an annual review. Ask a trusted partner, manager, or colleague directly: "What's working in how I've been showing up?" You may be further ahead than you think.

• Make your work visible. Report out on projects, even informally. A short Teams update or a monthly recap email to leadership builds the paper trail that the Ineffective profile desperately needs.(and it gives you something to go back to for your wins log!)

• Find a room where you're the expert. ILTA is genuinely good for this — presenting, contributing to content, or participating in peer discussions puts you in a context where your knowledge is seen and valued.

• Examine the structure. Sometimes the Ineffective profile is less about you and more about a role that was set up to absorb work without producing visible results. If that's the case, the problem isn't your confidence, it's your job design.

news.summaryZh:
世界杯冠军的诞生不仅取决于天赋，更在于赛前系统性的准备。顶级球队通过重复真实场景训练、数据驱动反馈和提前能力建设来提升表现。西班牙2010年凭借“tiki-taka”风格和反复演练的rondo训练夺冠；巴西2002年冠军球员从小通过室内足球积累大量触球和决策次数。德国2014年利用SAP的Match Insights平台分析训练数据，将平均持球时间从3.4秒降至1.1秒，并在意大利阿尔卑斯山进行10天高强度集训。法国2018年夺冠得益于数十年的青训体系，包括俱乐部青训营和300多名技术顾问的全国球探网络。

法律行业可借鉴这些原则：通过模拟训练增加重复练习次数，利用数据反馈精准改进技能，并提前培养抗压能力。技术使律所能够大规模实施这些策略，例如通过AI模拟训练让律师在逼真场景中反复练习，并获得即时反馈。律所应像顶级足协一样，将专业发展视为系统性工程，建立清晰的胜任标准、一致的评估和反馈机制，从而培养出深度、一致性和判断力。未来成功的律所将依靠准备而非天赋。
news.bodyText:
Every four years, the World Cup crowns a champion, and every four years, the commentariat reaches for explanations: a favorable draw, a moment of brilliance, pivotal calls or the talent of the winning squad.

Talent matters enormously, but at the top echelons of international soccer, the talent gap narrows. Every team is dangerous, and every roster is deep.

Although the drama begins when the first game kicks off, the outcome is determined by activities that begin long before the tournament. It is determined in the training sessions, the preparation camps, the data reviews, and later the tactical adjustments that shape how a squad performs when the stakes are highest.

The methods involved are not mysterious. They have been refined over decades by federations that have treated player development as a serious institutional problem rather than a matter of intuition, and the principles behind them have parallels in other fields where elite performance is studied and reproduced.

The legal profession is one such field. It has long relied on a model of attorney development based on time and exposure. Junior lawyers were given work, placed near senior lawyers, and trusted to develop judgment through some combination of repetition and proximity. That model is now under strain in ways that have become difficult to ignore: billing pressure, thinner mentoring and less tolerance for learning on a client's matter have all eroded the conditions it quietly depended on, and the conversation about what should replace it has so far produced more anxiety than direction.

The World Cup is perhaps not an obvious place to look for an answer. But it provides, on examination, a strong example of the fruits of deliberate practice techniques applied systematically at an organizational level. The way championship squads train illustrates a set of principles that translate quite well to the legal profession: repetition of realistic activity, data-driven feedback and pro-active capacity building.

## **Mastery Through Repetition Under Realistic Conditions**

Spain's 2010 World Cup win was built on continuity of style. Manager Vicente del Bosque inherited the core of a successful squad that had just won Euro 2008, and he chose to refresh it with a handful of new players rather than rebuild its identity. That identity, the vaunted "tiki-taka" style, was a single, shared way of playing: possession, patience, spacing and collective control. It was drilled, from the youth academy upward, through exercises like the rondo: the deceptively simple keep-away drill in which a ring of players must retain the ball against defenders closing them down.

So ingrained was Spain’s tiki-taka system that it survived a shock opening loss to Switzerland and carried Spain through a series of 1-0 knockout-round wins to the title, in which their astonishing 64.5% possession rate denied their opponents effective chances; it was a dominance reflected in almost every statistic except the narrow scorelines.

Brazil’s 2002 championship team provides a similar example. Long before Ronaldo, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho reached the national team, they grew up playing futsal: the fast, scaled-down indoor game that is the bedrock of Brazilian soccer development. Played on a condensed court with constant ball contact, futsal demands quick thinking, close control, fast passing, and composure in tight spaces, and it packs far more touches, decisions and transitions into an hour than full-sided play ever could.

Ronaldo, Ronaldinho and a long line of other players credit it directly for the technical skills that defined their soccer performances. The mechanism is simple: more repetitions, earlier, under conditions that mirror real performance. Without enough repetitions, even talented performers plateau. With them, decision-making accelerates, errors shrink, and execution holds up when the stakes are high.

The Spain 2010 and Brazil 2002 examples are also informative for legal skill building. The path from competent to fluent runs through repetition of the same underlying skills, performed enough times, under realistic enough conditions, that the lawyer stops thinking about mechanics and starts to focus on judgment.

Taking a deposition. Negotiating a contested deal point. Examining an adverse witness. Handling a difficult client conversation. Drafting under time pressure. Each is a complex performance task requiring judgment built through repeated execution and pushing to the edge of one’s capabilities, not just familiarity acquired through observation. The traditional model of legal training—watching senior lawyers and waiting for opportunities to surface on live matters—generates a small number of repetitions over a long stretch of time. That is an inefficient way to build expertise.

Technology has changed the possibilities for both the volume and diversity of repetitions. With simulation-based training, lawyers can now build the kind of repetition-based mastery that was previously available only to those who happened to land on the right matters at the right time.

Realistic practice opportunities can now be generated efficiently, repeated as often as needed, and used to refine specific skills until execution holds up under pressure. Legal teams can now emulate world-class soccer squads by defining the standards, committing to the repetitions, and giving the performers enough chances to make execution almost automatic.

## **Data-Driven Feedback**

Although repetition of realistic activity is a fundamental skill-building technique, doing so without data and feedback is like flying blind. Germany's preparation for the 2014 World Cup demonstrates clearly how data can be used to sharpen training in real time. Working with SAP through a platform called Match Insights, the team's coaches and analysts processed information from training and matches to produce actionable insights.

The raw volume was staggering—by Oliver Bierhoff's account, 10 players with three balls could potentially generate over seven million data points in 10 minutes, processed in real time. Each session could thus produce a read on where the squad was performing well, where it was vulnerable and which situations needed attention before the next match. Notably, the technology and data were available to every team in Brazil, but only Germany seemed to fully leverage its capabilities.

The feedback translated into specific priorities. For example, based on the data it crunched, Germany focused training efforts on a specific metric: passing speed. Analyzing past data, the team determined that players had averaged 3.4 seconds on the ball per touch at the 2010 World Cup—slow, by the standard of the sides that beat them—and set out to reduce that metric meaningfully. By the 2014 tournament, working with the Match Insights system, they had brought it down to 1.1 seconds, an indicator of a crisper and more decisive playing style.

Whether the input is seven million data points or a smaller sample size of tactical observations, the feedback loop works: Perform, get precise information about what broke down, isolate the weakness and return to the next attempt with a sharper target. In a well-designed environment, mistakes are diagnostic. They reveal where judgment is underdeveloped, where technique collapses under pressure, and where the next round of practice should focus.

The same principle applies to how lawyers are developed. The skills that matter most in legal practice can now be measured with a new level of precision. A junior lawyer does not become deposition-ready by hearing, months after the fact, that a question was too broad. They improve by taking a deposition, seeing where the witness got away from them, receiving specific feedback and trying again with a better strategy. Lawyers are now using technology to close that loop—conducting realistic practice sessions on demand, receiving structured feedback within minutes, and running the scenario again with sharper focus on what went wrong the first time. This allows professional development leaders to see, across a class of associates, where execution is strongest, where it is weakest, and where targeted training will produce the biggest return.

## **Building Capacity Before It's Needed**

Performance capacities aren’t just magically summoned when the moment demands them. Rather, they are built beforehand, deliberately, under conditions tougher than the event itself.

Before the 2014 tournament opened in Brazil, the German team (the same one that leveraged Match Insights to increase passing speed) held a 10-day camp in the Italian Alps. The camp was secluded and deliberately demanding, featuring 10 days of concentrated conditioning, away from distraction, designed to build the fitness base the team would need to sustain repeated high-intensity effort deep into matches and across a long tournament. The focus here was not on replicating match conditions, but on building the engine the match would require, in advance and under deliberately demanding conditions. That strong early foundation would enable the team to maximize its execution of more advanced skills and tactics in the games to come.

The concept scales from the body of one athlete to the structure of an entire federation. France's 2018 World Cup win is often attributed to the talent of its roster. The deeper story is the system that produced it. After decades of underachievement, the federation invested in an institutional development structure and sustained it across generations. A 1973 charter required professional clubs to run youth academies; today, that network spans dozens of club academies and regional pre-training centers, fed by a scouting operation of more than 300 technical consultants identifying promising players nationwide.

The famed Clairefontaine center is the flagship of the system, but the core value is less any single graduate than the coherent development culture it spread through every level of French soccer: consistent methods and consistent standards, applied system-wide. The result is a pipeline of elite players that has made France a consistent title contender and the envy of international soccer.

This idea of systematic capacity building not only for a specific event, but over years or even decades, also applies to legal practice. The lawyers who perform for their clients under the pressure of a daylong deposition or a marathon negotiating session are not simply those who know the most. They are the ones whose underlying capacities have been built to a level that meets the moment, no matter how intense.

The latest interactive, experiential training technologies can help individual attorneys learn to perform under realistic load, and adaptive features can increase the load and difficulty over time based on data about that individual, building the resilience and peak performance capability that leads to wins.

But individual training programs can produce uneven results without the infrastructure to support them. The firms building durable depth are treating professional development as an architecture rather than a calendar of programs—with clear competency expectations, consistent measurement across cohorts, and feedback mechanisms that surface firmwide trends to the leaders responsible for acting on them.

Technology is what makes this possible at scale. Performance data captured across practice groups, offices and experience levels can reveal patterns no single partner would otherwise see: a weakness recurring across a class of associates becomes visible, a practice group with a consistent gap can be identified and supported, the strongest performers can be recognized and stretched further.

## **A New Standard for Legal Development**

The training strategies that produce World Cup champions are not secrets. They have been studied, refined, and applied openly by federations willing to treat performance development as a serious institutional discipline. What separates the teams that win consistently from the ones that compete occasionally is the seriousness with which they apply these principles, year after year, across every level of their programs.

The legal profession has the same opportunity, and, for the first time, the same kinds of tools. Repetition under realistic conditions, structured feedback loops that turn data into actionable insights, and capacity built deliberately at both the individual and institutional level are no longer aspirational ideas for legal development. They are achievable with the technology now available to firms willing to use it. The firms that apply these principles with the rigor of championship-caliber soccer federations will build the kind of depth, consistency, and judgment that the profession has historically struggled to develop at scale.

The 2026 World Cup will produce another champion this summer. But the team that lifts the trophy will not necessarily be the most talented; rather, it will be the best prepared. The law firms that win the future will do it the same way: on preparation, not talent.

_Jeremy T. Liles is the co-founder and chief innovation officer of AltaClaro, where he leads the development of AI-powered simulation training that helps legal professionals build real-world skills through experiential learning. A multidisciplinary product leader, entrepreneur and legal technologist, he brings more than 20 years of experience spanning law, education and technology._

news.titleEn: Kalshi Takes State-Law Preemption Fight to the Second Circuit
news.titleZh: Kalshi将州法优先权争议上诉至第二巡回法院
news.summaryZh: 预测市场平台Kalshi已向美国第二巡回上诉法院提起上诉，要求审查纽约联邦法院此前拒绝其免受州博彩法执法影响的裁决。该案核心问题在于：当受联邦监管的衍生品被州官员视为赌博时，应适用哪套法律体系。Kalshi主张联邦商品法已完全覆盖其事件合约领域，限制各州将其定性为非法赌博；而纽约监管机构则坚持有权在联邦监管空间内执行州博彩限制。第二巡回法院的裁决可能为《商品交易法》框架与州赌博法之间的边界划定先例，影响选举、体育、经济等事件合约的监管格局。该案对运营方、交易所及金融科技公司具有重大商业意义，可能决定联邦授权是否足以支持全国性运营，或州级执法风险仍是核心商业约束。诉讼双方均将围绕市场诚信、消费者保护及联邦与州监管权力分配展开辩论。企业法务与合规团队需密切关注：若法院支持更广泛的联邦优先权，公司可获更强全国推广策略与执法抗辩依据；若维持原判，则需重新评估产品设计、用户准入控制、许可分析及州执法风险。此案凸显预测市场监管分类尚未明确，上诉判决可能在立法前确立规则。
news.bodyHtml:
Kalshi has opened a new appellate front in the fast-developing fight over prediction-market regulation, asking the Second Circuit to review a New York federal court decision that refused to shield the company from state gaming-law enforcement. The appeal raises a central question for event-contract platforms: when a federally regulated derivatives product looks like wagering to state officials, which legal regime controls?

The underlying suit, KalshiEX LLC v. Williams et al, puts that issue squarely before the courts. Kalshi’s position is that federal commodities law occupies the field for its event contracts, limiting the ability of states to characterize those contracts as unlawful gambling. New York regulators, by contrast, have argued for room to enforce state gaming restrictions even where the platform operates in a federally regulated space.

That dispute is not just about one company or one state. A Second Circuit ruling could help define the boundary between the Commodity Exchange Act framework and state gambling laws for a broad class of products tied to elections, sports, economics, and other real-world events. For operators, exchanges, and fintech companies exploring event-driven contracts, the case may shape whether federal authorization is enough to proceed nationally, or whether state-by-state enforcement risk remains a core business constraint.

For litigators, the appeal is worth watching as a preemption case with significant commercial implications. The court’s treatment of federal exclusivity, agency oversight, and the scope of state police powers could influence future challenges involving not only prediction markets, but also adjacent products that blend financial innovation with regulated gaming concepts. Parties on both sides will likely frame the case in terms that resonate beyond the immediate dispute: market integrity, consumer protection, and the allocation of authority between federal and state regulators.

In-house counsel and compliance teams should also pay close attention. If the Second Circuit endorses broader federal preemption, companies may gain a stronger basis for national rollout strategies and enforcement defenses. If it affirms the district court’s narrower view, businesses may need to reassess product design, user access controls, licensing analyses, and state enforcement exposure. Either way, the appeal underscores a practical reality for legal departments advising on prediction markets: regulatory classification remains unsettled, and appellate decisions are likely to set the rules before legislatures do.

With parallel debates continuing around event contracts and market oversight, this case is poised to become a key reference point for lawyers advising clients at the intersection of commodities, gaming, and emerging financial products.

news.titleEn: Judicial Conference Presses Congress for More Judges as Federal Court Funding Tightens
news.titleZh: 司法会议敦促国会增设法官员额，联邦法院资金趋紧
news.summaryZh: 联邦法院面临法官短缺和资金不足的双重压力，敦促国会授权增设地区法院和上诉法院法官席位。案件数量上升而司法能力未同步增长，导致结案时间延长、庭审日期减少、动议日程加重，并加大和解压力。资金短缺还影响书记官办公室、缓刑和审前服务、法院安保、技术等核心运作，可能造成程序延误和日程安排灵活性降低。对诉讼律师而言，需在诉讼预算中纳入更长的时间线，重新评估动议实践和庭审安排，并为客户做好案件进展缓慢的准备。法务部门应关注法院容量收紧对争议风险敞口、储备金、报告和业务规划的影响。合规团队可能面临执法行动或后续民事诉讼在联邦法院进展放缓的后果。司法会议的建议表明，这些压力并非孤立现象，而是广泛到足以需要国会干预。若国会不增加法官席位和稳定拨款，延迟和容量问题将继续成为联邦诉讼规划的核心考量。
news.bodyHtml:
The federal judiciary is signaling that two pressures are converging: too few judges and too little money. In its latest policy action, the Judicial Conference of the United States warned that funding shortfalls could worsen and urged Congress to authorize additional district and appellate judgeships. For lawyers and court users, that is more than an institutional budget debate—it is a direct statement about docket congestion, hearing availability, and the pace of civil and criminal litigation.

The request matters because judgeships are one of the clearest structural tools for addressing overloaded courts. When filings rise but judicial capacity does not, the effects show up everywhere: longer times to disposition, fewer available trial dates, heavier motion calendars, and increased pressure on settlement timing. A recommendation for new judgeships from the judiciary’s principal policymaking body suggests that these strains are not isolated, but broad enough to warrant congressional action.

The funding warning adds another layer. Even apart from staffing on the bench, constrained appropriations can affect core court operations, including clerk’s office support, probation and pretrial services, courthouse security, technology, and the day-to-day administration that keeps cases moving. For litigants, those operational limitations can translate into procedural delays and less flexibility in scheduling. For judges, they can compound already demanding caseloads.

For litigators, this development should be read as a practical case-management issue. Counsel may need to build longer timelines into litigation budgets, reassess assumptions about motion practice and trial scheduling, and prepare clients for slower resolution in especially busy districts and circuits. In-house counsel should pay attention as well: when court capacity tightens, dispute exposure can remain on the books longer, affecting reserves, reporting, and business planning. Compliance teams may also see downstream effects where enforcement actions or follow-on civil suits take longer to progress through federal court.

There is also a broader access-to-justice implication. Federal courts are handling a wide range of high-stakes matters, from complex commercial disputes to constitutional challenges and criminal cases. If judicial vacancies, insufficient judgeships, and budget pressure continue to intersect, the burden will be felt not only by institutional litigants but by individual parties waiting for decisions that can affect liberty, business operations, or legal rights.

The immediate takeaway for legal professionals is straightforward: court administration is becoming a larger strategic variable. If Congress does not respond with additional judgeships and more stable funding, delay and capacity concerns are likely to remain central considerations in federal litigation planning.

news.titleEn: The three silent hours: How Russia’s cyber war targets Ukraine’s newsrooms
news.titleZh: 寂静的三小时：俄罗斯网络战如何瞄准乌克兰新闻编辑室
news.summaryZh: 俄罗斯夏季攻势在地面受阻后，克里姆林宫将重心转向信息战。7月第一周，在导弹袭击基辅和北约峰会在土耳其举行期间，俄罗斯运营商对乌克兰电视台、新闻编辑室和数字记录系统发动了平行攻击。一次针对电视台的应用层DDoS攻击达到每分钟20万次请求，是今年最大规模之一。该攻击旨在淹没新闻网站，使乌克兰读者无法访问。自2022年全面入侵以来，该部门已挫败超过1.6万次网络攻击和事件，媒体是优先目标。攻击使用来自亚洲、欧洲和美国的僵尸网络节点，模拟真实用户流量。乌克兰安全局专家保持了网站在线。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: Russia’s summer offensive has stalled on the ground, so the Kremlin has shifted weight to the layer where it still moves freely: information. In the first week of July, as missiles hit Kyiv and diplomats gathered for a NATO summit in Turkey, Russian operators kept a parallel campaign running against the systems that carry Ukraine’s account of the war, its television stations, newsrooms and digital records. The reporting here connects a three-hour application-layer DDoS attack, a thwarted attempt to hijack a broadcaster’s voice, and Europe’s accelerating cyber support into a single story about information integrity under fire.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, the relevance is direct. Credential theft aimed at publishing rights, floods built to imitate human traffic, and disinformation synced to diplomatic calendars are not distant wartime exotica; they are the same techniques that test corporate communications, law firms and regulated institutions.

Watch two threads next: how the EU Cybersecurity Reserve performs under real load, and whether newsroom-grade defenses, tamper-evident logging and provable publishing records become a baseline expectation well beyond Ukraine.

Industry News – Geopolitics Beat

The three silent hours: How Russia’s cyber war targets Ukraine’s newsrooms

ComplexDiscovery Staff

For three hours, the weapon aimed at a Ukrainian television station made no sound at all.

It arrived as 200,000 requests a minute, a flood of counterfeit traffic engineered to drown a newsroom’s website until no reader in Ukraine could reach it.

That attack, which the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) described as one of the largest of the year, sits at the quiet center of a war usually counted in missiles and miles of front line. On the night of July 5 to 6, Russian forces launched their fourth large-scale missile and drone strike against Ukraine since June 1, hitting Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky later reported that the death toll had risen to 22. Beneath the explosions, a second campaign kept running: a contest over who controls Ukraine’s information, its newsrooms and the record of the war itself.

A strike timed for the cameras

The two campaigns are connected. The Institute for the Study of War said Russia likely timed its early-July strike package to shape perceptions ahead of the July 7 to 8 NATO summit in Turkey, where U.S. President Donald Trump was set to meet Ukrainian and European leaders. Moscow has cast itself as a willing negotiator and Kyiv as the obstacle to peace, a posture aimed less at the trenches than at the audiences watching them.

That framing carries weight because Russia’s summer offensive has bought little ground. The Institute for the Study of War has assessed in recent reporting that the spring and summer 2026 offensive failed to produce operationally meaningful gains, even as Moscow keeps shaping narratives around claimed battlefield progress. When territory stalls, the message becomes the maneuver, and the fastest way to shape a message is to control, or corrupt, the channels that carry it.

Why Ukraine’s newsrooms became targets

Since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, the SSU’s Cyber Security Department has neutralized over 16,000 cyberattacks and cyber incidents, said Brigadier General Volodymyr Karastelyov, who heads the department. Government agencies, banks and defense structures draw steady fire. So do the media, which Karastelyov named a priority target for Russian operations.

The television station attack showed the method. “The botnet generated up to 200,000 requests per minute from nodes in Asia, Europe, and the US,” Karastelyov said. The traffic hit the site’s application layer, mimicking real users to exhaust the server rather than simply flooding it with raw volume. SSU specialists kept the site online. The aim was denial: to make it harder for a Ukrainian audience to reach a Ukrainian source, creating the kind of information vacuum that invites something else to fill it.

When the goal is the byline, not the outage

Knocking a site offline is the blunt approach. Stealing its voice is the subtler one. In 2025, the SSU said, attackers struck another Ukrainian television group with a phishing campaign while probing adjacent systems, working to seize the outlet and publish propaganda under its own trusted name. Investigators caught the intrusion before the takeover succeeded.

For information governance and eDiscovery professionals, that scenario should read as both familiar and alarming. An adversary that captures a publisher’s content management system does not just steal data; it manufactures a false but authentic-looking record, signed with a legitimate credential. Separating the real article from the forgery afterward becomes a forensic exercise, one that leans on preserved logs, version history and defensible chain of custody. The strongest defense is assembled before the breach: strict access controls, tamper-evident logging and archived snapshots that let an organization prove what it published, and when.

Europe moves to shore up the defense

The institutional response has quickened. On June 10, the European Union launched EU4CyberUA, a €10 million, four-year program running from 2026 to 2029 to align Ukraine’s cyber defenses with EU standards. Days later, the Council of the European Union approved Ukraine’s entry into the EU Cybersecurity Reserve, giving Kyiv access to incident-response help from vetted private providers, coordinated through the EU Agency for Cybersecurity, during large-scale attacks.

Ukraine is also pushing defense down to the newsroom floor. The SSU and the National Council of Ukraine on Television and Radio Broadcasting ran cybersecurity training at 20 venues across 21 regions in 2026, reaching about 450 editors, journalists and technical staff. “The main aim of the joint project is not only to respond to cyber-attacks after they have already occurred, but also to build up the practical capacity of regional newsrooms to independently detect threats,” said Olha Herasymiuk, who chairs the National Council.

What the record demands of practitioners

Strip away the geography and the lesson travels. The tactics tested against Ukrainian media, credential theft aimed at publishing rights, DDoS floods engineered to pass as human traffic, and disinformation timed to diplomatic calendars, reach corporate communications teams, law firms and regulated institutions far from any front line. A DDoS built to imitate real users slips past defenses tuned only for crude volume. A propaganda takeover of a trusted account is a data-integrity incident with legal and evidentiary tails.

The practical steps are unglamorous and portable: keep tamper-evident logs, preserve the metadata that establishes authenticity, rehearse incident response before it is needed, and treat the integrity of the published record as an asset worth defending. The organizations that weather the next information operation will be the ones that can show, quickly and defensibly, what they said and what they did not.

Which returns the story to those three silent hours. The attackers blew nothing up; they tried to erase a signal and, failing that, to counterfeit one. As the fighting grinds toward another round of talks, the sharper question for anyone who manages information is not whether the next attack will land, but this: when someone tries to speak in your name, will you be able to prove they did not?

news.bodyText: Editor’s Note: Russia’s summer offensive has stalled on the ground, so the Kremlin has shifted weight to the layer where it still moves freely: information. In the first week of July, as missiles hit Kyiv and diplomats gathered for a NATO summit in Turkey, Russian operators kept a parallel campaign running against the systems that carry Ukraine’s account of the war, its television stations, newsrooms and digital records. The reporting here connects a three-hour application-layer DDoS attack, a thwarted attempt to hijack a broadcaster’s voice, and Europe’s accelerating cyber support into a single story about information integrity under fire. For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, the relevance is direct. Credential theft aimed at publishing rights, floods built to imitate human traffic, and disinformation synced to diplomatic calendars are not distant wartime exotica; they are the same techniques that test corporate communications, law firms and regulated institutions. Watch two threads next: how the EU Cybersecurity Reserve performs under real load, and whether newsroom-grade defenses, tamper-evident logging and provable publishing records become a baseline expectation well beyond Ukraine. Industry News – Geopolitics Beat ComplexDiscovery Staff For three hours, the weapon aimed at a Ukrainian television station made no sound at all. It arrived as 200,000 requests a minute, a flood of counterfeit traffic engineered to drown a newsroom’s website until no reader in Ukraine could reach it. That attack, which the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) described as one of the largest of the year, sits at the quiet center of a war usually counted in missiles and miles of front line. On the night of July 5 to 6, Russian forces launched their fourth large-scale missile and drone strike against Ukraine since June 1, hitting Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky later reported that the death toll had risen to 22. Beneath the explosions, a second campaign kept running: a contest over who controls Ukraine’s information, its newsrooms and the record of the war itself. The two campaigns are connected. The Institute for the Study of War said Russia likely timed its early-July strike package to shape perceptions ahead of the July 7 to 8 NATO summit in Turkey, where U.S. President Donald Trump was set to meet Ukrainian and European leaders. Moscow has cast itself as a willing negotiator and Kyiv as the obstacle to peace, a posture aimed less at the trenches than at the audiences watching them. That framing carries weight because Russia’s summer offensive has bought little ground. The Institute for the Study of War has assessed in recent reporting that the spring and summer 2026 offensive failed to produce operationally meaningful gains, even as Moscow keeps shaping narratives around claimed battlefield progress. When territory stalls, the message becomes the maneuver, and the fastest way to shape a message is to control, or corrupt, the channels that carry it. Since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, the SSU’s Cyber Security Department has neutralized over 16,000 cyberattacks and cyber incidents, said Brigadier General Volodymyr Karastelyov, who heads the department. Government agencies, banks and defense structures draw steady fire. So do the media, which Karastelyov named a priority target for Russian operations. The television station attack showed the method. “The botnet generated up to 200,000 requests per minute from nodes in Asia, Europe, and the US,” Karastelyov said. The traffic hit the site’s application layer, mimicking real users to exhaust the server rather than simply flooding it with raw volume. SSU specialists kept the site online. The aim was denial: to make it harder for a Ukrainian audience to reach a Ukrainian source, creating the kind of information vacuum that invites something else to fill it.

news.titleZh: 第二次请求脉搏：2025财年41项调查对2026财年的预示
news.summaryZh:
美国联邦贸易委员会和司法部于7月2日发布第48份年度哈特-斯科特-罗迪诺报告，涵盖2025财年。该财年共收到2006项交易通知，在可发出第二次请求的1944项调整后交易中，有618项（31.8%）价值超过10亿美元；FTC发出20项、司法部反垄断局发出21项第二次请求，总计41项，占调整后交易的2.1%。过去十年间，第二次请求数量稳定在每年37至66项之间，平均约51项，比率在1.6%至3.0%之间波动。2025财年的2.1%低于2024财年的3.0%。同期，执法行动为18项，占调整后交易的0.9%，为2005年以来最低。

每次第二次请求要求合并双方提供涉及产品、市场和竞争影响的文件和数据，合规通常耗时2至4个月，成本可达数百万美元，并可能将交易时间延长10个月或更久。文件量巨大，例如英国沃达丰与Three的合并调查涉及数百万份文件。在数百万份文件的审查中，人工审查成本集中在每份0.50至1美元，而生成式AI辅助审查成本多在每份0.26至0.50美元，部分低至0.11美元，价差可达七位数。2026财年截至5月的申报量比去年同期高出29%，若历史比率保持，第二次请求数量可能回升至60项左右。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: Forty-one second requests in fiscal year 2025 sounds like a quiet number until you price what each one carries: months of compliance work, millions of documents, and eDiscovery engagements that anchor entire provider practices. The FTC and DOJ released the 48th annual Hart-Scott-Rodino report July 2, and the decade of data inside it reveals a demand pulse that has held between 37 and 66 investigations per year no matter how wildly deal volume has swung.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance, and eDiscovery professionals, the pulse is a planning tool. Second requests are where information governance discipline meets a statutory clock, where collaboration data and chat platforms enter regulatory productions, and where AI-assisted review is proving itself at scale.

Watch the FTC’s monthly transaction postings through September. Fiscal year 2026 filings are running 29 percent ahead of last year’s pace through May, and if the historical rate holds, the second request count is heading back toward 60. Providers that staffed for a quiet market may need to move first.

Industry News – Antitrust Beat

The second request pulse: what FY2025’s 41 investigations signal for FY2026

ComplexDiscovery Staff

Federal antitrust regulators issued 41 second requests in fiscal year 2025, a 2.1 percent rate that lands squarely inside the narrow band the merger review process has occupied for a decade. The count matters less than the cadence. For the litigation support providers who staff these document-intensive investigations, the annual second request tally is one of the most important demand signals in the antitrust eDiscovery economy, and fiscal year 2026 filing data suggests the signal is strengthening.

The Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice Antitrust Division released their 48th annual Hart-Scott-Rodino report July 2, covering the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, 2025. Companies notified the agencies of 2,006 transactions under the HSR Act during the year. Of the 1,944 adjusted transactions in which a second request could have been issued, 618, or 31.8 percent, were valued above $1 billion; the FTC issued 20 second requests and the Antitrust Division issued 21. Transaction counts remained generally in line with the past decade, the agencies said in the report.

A narrow band across a volatile decade

The decade of data in the report’s Appendix A tells a story of stability inside apparent volatility. Reported transactions swung from a pandemic low of 1,637 in fiscal year 2020 to a record 3,520 in fiscal year 2021, then settled back to about 2,000 per year from fiscal year 2023 forward. Second request counts moved far less. Across fiscal years 2016 through 2025, the agencies issued between 37 and 66 second requests annually, averaging about 51 per year. The rate oscillated between 1.6 percent and 3.0 percent of adjusted transactions, with a 10-year mean near 2.5 percent.

That range is the pulse rate. Deal volume can double, as it did in fiscal year 2021, without doubling second request output. The fiscal year 2021 data point is instructive: transactions surged 115 percent over the prior year while the issuance rate fell to 1.9 percent, its second-lowest level of the decade, suggesting that agency capacity, enforcement priorities, and matter complexity may constrain second request output even when deal volume rises sharply. The fiscal year 2025 rate of 2.1 percent was a step down from 3.0 percent in fiscal year 2024.

Enforcement intensity tells a parallel story. The agencies took 18 merger enforcement actions in fiscal year 2025, according to the FTC’s announcement of the report. An analysis by the American Action Forum, a policy group that favors lighter regulation, calculated that figure at 0.9 percent of adjusted transactions, the lowest share since 2005.

What one second request means for a provider

Each of those 41 investigations translated into one of the largest discrete eDiscovery engagements available in the legal services market. A second request obligates both merging parties to produce documents and data covering products, markets, and competitive effects, and the parties cannot close until they substantially comply. Compliance typically takes two to four months, can cost millions of dollars, and can extend deal timelines by 10 months or longer, according to guidance published by Thomson Reuters.

Document volumes at this scale dwarf routine litigation. One global provider that markets second request services and reports over 100 completed merger deals has described, as an analogous merger-control example, a recent United Kingdom investigation involving Vodafone and Three that required collecting, reviewing, and producing millions of documents from both companies. Review economics are unforgiving at those volumes. The Winter 2026 eDiscovery Pricing Survey from ComplexDiscovery OÜ and EDRM found human review rates concentrated in the 50 cents to $1 per document range, with generative AI-assisted review most frequently reported at 26 to 50 cents per document and meaningful clustering down to 11 cents. On a review of several million documents, the spread between those price points is measured in seven figures, which explains why second requests have become the proving ground for AI-assisted review at scale.

The scope of what must be reviewed keeps widening. Second requests now routinely reach collaboration platforms, chat applications, and other emerging data sources alongside email and shared drives, a shift that rewards merging parties with disciplined information governance programs and punishes those without defensible data maps when the clock starts.

Provider economics of a 40-to-65 pulse

For litigation support providers, the historical pulse creates a market that is simultaneously small in count and enormous in revenue concentration. Forty to 65 engagements per year, split across two agencies and dozens of merging parties, means a specialized provider that captures even five or six second requests in a fiscal year has anchored a material share of its annual revenue on antitrust work. A concentrated field of specialized providers markets dedicated second request practices, and the compressed timelines reward firms that maintain standing infrastructure: pre-negotiated review platforms, tested AI workflows, and surge review capacity that can scale to hundreds of reviewers within days.

The lumpiness cuts both ways. A fiscal year like 2023, when the agencies issued 37 second requests, the lowest count of the decade, tightens competition for every engagement. A rebound year like fiscal year 2024, with 59, absorbs available capacity quickly. Providers that treat the annual HSR report as a planning document rather than a news item can calibrate hiring, platform licensing, and partner relationships against the pulse instead of against anecdote.

Fiscal year 2026 filings point higher

The forward indicator now flashing is transaction volume. Preliminary monthly data from the FTC’s Premerger Notification Program shows 1,665 transactions reported in the first eight months of fiscal year 2026: 215 in October 2025, 227 in November, 232 in December, 180 in January 2026, 188 in February, 203 in March, 185 in April, and 235 in May. That pace runs 29 percent ahead of the 1,292 transactions reported in the same eight months of fiscal year 2025, according to final figures in the annual report. Two cautions belong next to that comparison. First, fiscal year 2025’s spring months may have been depressed in part as filers adjusted to the expanded HSR form that took effect Feb. 10, 2025, so some of the year-over-year gap likely reflects a weak baseline rather than pure acceleration. Second, monthly figures are preliminary until finalized in the annual report, and they tend to revise downward: the FTC posted 1,362 preliminary transactions for the same fiscal year 2025 months that the annual report later finalized at 1,292, a 5.1 percent reduction. Measured preliminary to preliminary, the fiscal year 2026 pace runs 22 percent ahead.

October through May has historically carried about two-thirds of full-year volume. In the seven years of the past decade without pandemic or merger-wave distortions, those eight months contributed between 62.4 percent and 68.3 percent of annual transactions. Applying that range to the fiscal year 2026 data yields a full-year projection of roughly 2,440 to 2,670 reported transactions, with a central planning estimate near 2,530, which would be the highest total since fiscal year 2022. After adjusting for transactions in which a second request could not be issued, historically about 96.7 percent of the reported total, fiscal year 2026 would produce roughly 2,450 adjusted transactions. If fiscal year 2026’s preliminary counts revise downward at the same 5.1 percent rate fiscal year 2025’s did, the projection shifts to roughly 2,310 to 2,530 reported transactions, with a central planning estimate near 2,400 and about 2,320 adjusted. Either basis would make fiscal year 2026 the busiest filing year since fiscal year 2022, if the projection holds.

The second request arithmetic follows directly. At fiscal year 2025’s 2.1 percent rate, the as-posted volume implies about 51 second requests. At the decade average of about 2.5 percent, roughly 60. At the 3.0 percent rate recorded in fiscal years 2016, 2019, 2020, and 2024, about 73. On the revision-adjusted basis, those scenarios run about 49, the high 50s, and 70. Any outcome in that range would exceed fiscal year 2025’s count of 41, and the upper scenarios would surpass the decade high of 66 set during the fiscal year 2021 merger wave. This projection is a ComplexDiscovery estimate built on preliminary agency data and historical ratios, not an agency forecast, and a continuation of the current administration’s lighter enforcement posture would argue for the lower end of the range.

The form fight complicates the forecast

One wildcard sits behind the filing surge. On Feb. 12, 2026, a federal district court in the Eastern District of Texas vacated the expanded HSR premerger notification form that had taken effect in February 2025, ruling the changes arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. After the Fifth Circuit denied the FTC’s motion for a stay on March 19, the agencies returned to accepting the pre-2025 form, and client alerts from law firms including Kirkland & Ellis, Dechert, and White & Case advised merging parties that filing burdens had dropped substantially. A lighter filing burden lowers the cost of notification and may be one factor contributing to the fiscal year 2026 volume increase. The agencies opened a public comment period on the future of the premerger form March 25.

For providers, the practical takeaways sit at both ends of the process. Lighter initial filings mean less front-end document work per notification, shifting the revenue weight of merger review even further toward the second request phase. Rising notification volume expands the base to which the pulse rate applies. Providers should track the FTC’s monthly transaction postings, which update the base in near real time, and watch the comment period’s outcome, since a rebuilt form could restore front-end burdens in fiscal year 2027.

If the fiscal year 2026 projection holds and second requests climb back toward 60 or higher, will the litigation support market’s surge capacity, thinned by two quieter years, be ready when the next wave of clock-stopping demands arrives?

news.bodyHtml: It goes without saying that our court reporting systems is in crisis. There is a shortage of qualified reporters, on the one hand, and a demand to use technology to create transcripts cheaper and faster on the other. Perhaps we need new ways of thinking about the role to preserve the value court reporters bring. Here is my piece for Above the Law

news.titleEn: From Quill to Code- George Washington Debates the Patent Future of Artificial Intelligence on America’s 250th Birthday
news.titleZh: 从羽毛笔到代码：乔治·华盛顿在美国250岁生日之际辩论人工智能的专利未来
news.summaryZh: 在美国庆祝建国250周年之际，文章回顾了乔治·华盛顿作为专利制度奠基人的历史，并将其与当今人工智能引发的专利问题相联系。1790年，华盛顿签署了《专利法案》，并亲自签发了150多项专利，其中包括第三项专利——奥利弗·埃文斯的自动化磨粉机。华盛顿在1791年购买了该专利许可，升级了他在弗农山庄的磨坊。如今，人工智能系统能够起草法律文件、设计药物和创作音乐，引发了新的法律难题：当机器超越其创造者时，谁应被视为发明者——人类还是机器？文章通过历史类比，探讨了人工智能时代专利法的核心挑战。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As America celebrates its 250th year, the pulse of innovation that animated the Founders beats louder than ever. From the first patent debates to today’s courtroom clashes over artificial intelligence, George Washington’s legacy as a mill owner, pragmatic leader, and founding architect of the U.S. patent system remains strikingly relevant. Drawing on Washington’s own letters and historic drive for progress, we confront a question that now defines our technological era: When a machine surpasses its maker, who gets to claim the spark of invention, the human or the machine? Imagine a frosty December morning in 1790 in Philadelphia. President George Washington—equal parts statesman, tinkerer, and entrepreneur—stands before Oliver Evans’ astonishing automaton. This isn’t just another machine: it’s an engineering leap, grinding grain into superfine flour at a speed no human crew could match, demanding barely a touch from its operators. When Washington signs the third U.S. patent for the Evans system, he’s not just endorsing invention—he’s witnessing a technological revolution poised to transform his own fortunes and the young nation’s future. Evans’s mill was, by 18th-century standards, an automaton—a machine that could outwork skilled hands, deliver better results, and do it all with mechanical precision. Washington saw it with his own eyes and recognized its potential. Washington mill was an important source of his income as he boasted in an April 12, 1785, letter to Robert Lewis & Sons, that “my Mill [which did not at that time use the Evans system] has the reputation of turning out superfine flour of the first quality: it commands a higher price in this country and the West Indies, than any other.” Nonetheless, Washington, ever the practical visionary, purchases a patent license in 1791 and upgrades his gristmill at Mount Vernon. He sends his millwright, William Ball, to inspect a neighboring Evans system first. Then two of Evans’s brothers travel to Mount Vernon to oversee the upgrade themselves. Evans’s invention was not just an upgrade; it was Washington’s ticket to the cutting edge of quality and innovation. Washington had signed the Patent Act of 1790 into law on April 10, 1790. Under that Act, the President was required to personally sign each patent granted. Washington did so for more than 150 patents during his presidency. The first went to Samuel Hopkins of Philadelphia for a new process to make pot ash and pearl ash. The second went to a Boston candlemaker, Joseph Stacey Sampson, for a new method to aid in the manufacturing of candles. The third went to Oliver Evans for his automated mill. Fast-forward to 2026: The tools have changed, but the changes brought by innovation are ever more astonishing. Today, the “millwright” is replaced by something far stranger—a machine that thinks. AI systems now draft legal briefs, design new drugs, and compose symphonies in the blink of an eye, achieving feats that would have left even Washington speechless. As we celebrate the Semiquincentennial, the legal world faces a dilemma Washington never could have imagined: When the automaton outpaces its maker, who truly deserves the title of inventor—the human or the machine? Let’s channel Washington’s own words as we navigate today’s thorniest patent puzzles, as the questions that once kept the Founders up at night now reverberate through every courtroom and innovation lab in the age of AI. When Evans built the first automaton: The AI parallel Evans’s automated mill was the 18th-century version of AI. Evans’ described his mill as “a flour mill, which should take the grain from the wagon, and carry it through all the operations necessary to manufacture it into superfine flour…without the aid of manual labor in the attendance[.]” The mill thus became a relentless mechanical operator, replacing skilled millers one job at a time, and yet always remaining a tool, never a master. Evans’s contraption ran faster, smoother, and more profitably than any human crew. In the eyes of the law, it was revolutionary, but it still needed a human mind to claim its place in the patent record.

news.titleEn: Docusign’s Legal Tech Strategy With Jim Shaughnessy
news.titleZh: Docusign 法律科技战略：专访 Jim Shaughnessy
news.summaryZh: Docusign 年收入 32 亿美元，正加大法律科技投入。其 CLO Jim Shaughnessy 在采访中介绍，公司于 2018 年收购 CLM 公司，2020 年收购 AI 公司 SEAL，2023 年推出智能协议管理（IAM）平台，2024 年春季正式上线。IAM 是 AI 原生模块化平台，涵盖协议创建、承诺、谈判和管理，已有超过 4 万家企业订阅，占公司年经常性收入的 12%。Docusign 自研了名为 Iris 的 AI 架构，包含基于超 1 亿份客户协议（已匿名化）训练的专有模型，并结合 LLM，每日处理 100 万份协议，每份执行 50 项标准提取。公司拥有超 1100 个合作伙伴，包括 Salesforce、Perplexity、Harvey、Legora、Anthropic、OpenAI 等，旨在让客户以偏好方式与 IAM 交互。未来方向包括深化义务管理功能、开发代理（Agent）及代理治理，例如推出“代理行为证书”以解决 AI 黑箱问题。Docusign 还关注自动化谈判和智能合约的复兴，认为在低风险交易中代理间签约将逐步发展。公司上一财年研发投入 6.64 亿美元，AI 是重点领域。
news.bodyText: Docusign is a $3.2 billion revenue company and is now focusing more than ever before on its legal tech offering. In this AL interview with CLO, Jim Shaughnessy, we explore its Intelligent Agreement Management and CLM capabilities, how it’s been deploying genAI, and where it’s heading now. We also look at aspects such as Docusign providing legal customers with a ‘certificate of agentic action’ to help reduce the black box effect of AI, and we also explore the future potential for automated negotiation and a new generation of smart contracts. To watch the video please press Play. You can also go direct to the AL TV channel here. Is the primary goal to build a CLM, well, you have a CLM platform, but to build that out and to focus on CLM, is that the main goal or do you want to build into different parts ofJim Shaughnessy (02:31)I think you you we you should think about intelligent agreement management as being broader than than CLM. news.titleEn: Harvey Increases Token Use 14X in Just 6 Months
news.titleZh: Harvey 在短短 6 个月内将代币使用量提升 14 倍
news.summaryZh:
Harvey 联合创始人兼总裁 Gabe Pereyra 宣布，该法律 AI 平台处理的代币数量在过去 6 个月内增长了 14 倍，表明 AI 使用量正在激增。该数据不包括嵌入代币，也未反映 Harvey 的增长成本，据悉 Harvey 正在开发新的定价模式。当被问及律所是否会将代币成本转嫁给客户时，Pereyra 表示这可能会变得更普遍，因为律所已对其他法律科技产品进行成本转嫁。

这一增长发生在主要竞争对手 Legora 宣布采用基于代币消耗的定价体系、以及更先进的模型（如 Fable）因性能更优而成本更高的背景下。同时，客户越来越希望律所因使用 AI 而降低账单。不同代币成本不同：使用最先进模型的深度推理能力不仅消耗大量代币，且单价更高；代理工具进一步推高成本。律所倾向于选择更准确的工具，即使成本更高。法律 AI 平台可通过快速切换多个模型来控制成本，但用户是否愿意为降低成本而频繁切换模型仍是问题。代币正成为法律界的新货币，律所是否应转嫁这些成本成为焦点。
news.bodyText: Harvey’s co-founder and President, Gabe Pereyra, has announced that the number of tokens processed on the broad legal AI platform have increased by fourteen times in just the last 6 months – proof of how much AI usage is increasing. What does it all mean? AL explores. The usage data does not include embedding tokens, nor does it show the costs of this growth at Harvey, which is understood to be developing a new pricing model for customers. Interestingly, when Pereyra was asked by one poster on X about law firms passing through token costs to customers, he replied: ‘I actually think this might become more common – law firms already pass through costs for other legal tech, so not a completely crazy idea.’ So, what does all of this mean? First, it comes amid a background where main rival Legora has announced it’s moving to a pricing system that will take into account token consumption; where clearly it’s a fact that more people and more businesses in general are using AI more frequently; and where the latest models, such as Fable, are increasingly sought after because of their better performance – but in turn create higher costs. And AL is also hearing increasingly that clients want their law firms to reduce their bills because they’re using AI…! Plus, of course, we now have Claude for Legal, Codex for Legal, and Perplexity also seeking to expand its legal tech engagement. And we are seeing both law firms and legal tech companies now building open source offerings – which could reduce costs – and that includes Harvey. The fundamental issue here is that not all tokens cost the same. For example, using the most advanced models’ deepest reasoning capabilities on a very complex legal matter not just uses a lot of tokens, those tokens cost more. Agentic tools increase costs even more, as agents can tend to go back, and back again, to do the same task in order to get the best result. The problem lawyers have is that they tend to avoid risk – and that’s a good thing. But, if I say: ‘You can use A approach which is cheaper, but may make more mistakes, or B, which is expensive, but benchmarks show it performs better….which do you want?’ The lawyer will likely say B. One cannot offer a more accurate tool to lawyers and then expect them to accept a less accurate tool, aside from where the improvement is either negligible or where accuracy is not such a critical issue. Although, when is accuracy never an issue for legal work…? Now, one could argue that the legal AI platforms have an advantage over the main model providers that are doing legal as well, as you can quickly reroute calls to multiple models, from a very wide range of providers. That keeps costs down. Just getting stuck on Fable for all your Claude Legal tasks could conversely be very expensive, and will a user be ready to keep switching in and out of different Claude versions to keep costs down? Then we get to the pass through point noted above. And it’s a big one. Like the billable hour, tokens are fast becoming the new currency of the legal world today. Should law firms pass on those costs?

news.titleEn: Legatics Data Rooms Launches as VDR Alternative
news.titleZh: Legatics 数据室上线，作为 VDR 替代方案
news.summaryZh: Legatics 推出其“数据室”功能，使律所能够在单一工作流中管理交易并共享机密文件，作为更广泛交易平台的一部分，从而替代使用独立的虚拟数据室。该功能提供安全文档共享，涵盖尽职调查及任何需要受控、可审计访问交易文档的场景，且与现有交易管理平台集成。早期采用者包括 White & Case、Schoenherr 和 Hill Dickinson，已在多种交易类型中使用。传统数据室解决方案实施复杂且定价高昂，而 Legatics 提供必要功能：安全共享、精细权限、版本控制和完整审计追踪，无需额外开销。该解决方案直接与 iManage 和 NetDocuments 集成。
news.bodyText: Legatics has launched its own ‘Data Rooms’ capability, which enables law firms to manage transactions and share confidential documents within a single workflow, and as part of the wider deal platform. In short, it provides an alternative to having to use a separate VDR. AL asked the UK-based company about this and they noted: ‘We’re calling it Legatics Data Rooms rather than a VDR. The broader framing is secure document sharing – it covers due diligence and any situation where firms need controlled, audited access to documents on a transaction, all within the same platform they already use for transaction management.’ The company added that: ‘The launch reflects growing demand from leading law firms.’ Early adopters, including White & Case, Schoenherr and Hill Dickinson, are already using Data Rooms on a range of transaction types, they added. So, why do this? They explained that traditional data room solutions are often ‘complex to implement and priced for large-scale transactions, making them disproportionately expensive for everyday matters’. In this case Legatics said they provide the ‘essential functionality firms actually need: secure sharing, granular permissions, version control and complete audit trails, without unnecessary overhead’. The move comes at a time of growing debate about the wider cost of legal tech tools, in particular because of the rising cost of token use for AI solutions. Rob MacAdam, Chief Product & Strategy Officer at Legatics, commented: ‘Law firms don’t need the complexity of a general-purpose collaboration platform to run a transaction data room. ‘They need purpose-built tools that lawyers can pick up and use from day one: structured file organisation, granular access control and a reliable audit trail. And because it sits within Legatics’ broader transaction management platform, firms get true end-to-end coverage of the deal.’ They added that the solution integrates directly with iManage and NetDocuments. More about Legatics here. –

news.titleEn: Syntheia Slashes Token Costs With Novel Approach
news.titleZh: Syntheia 以创新方法大幅削减代币成本
news.summaryZh: Horace Wu 创立的 Syntheia 公司发现，通过改变合同在应用 AI 前的“切片”方式，律师可以显著降低代币成本。这种节省并非通过切换模型或使用更便宜的 LLM 实现，而是通过改变文档审查的初始条件。在交易法律工作中，LLM 阅读文档的成本通常远高于其推理答案的成本。测试中，最终答案的长度在不同方法间几乎没有变化，而输入 LLM 的文本量差异高达 30 倍。Syntheia 的研究团队针对真实信贷协议、有限合伙协议和股份购买协议，测试了两种基于结构感知文档索引技术的结构化检索方法，并与完整文档注入进行了对比。结果显示，通过聚焦最相关的内容，可以大幅减少代币使用。
news.bodyText: Horace Wu’s Syntheia has found that by taking a different approach to how a contract is ‘sliced up’ before applying AI, to put it simply, lawyers can significantly reduce their token costs. (See AL Interview below.) The token savings are therefore not gained by switching models or ‘rerouting’ to cheaper LLMs, but by changing the starting conditions of the doc review. The findings come as the debate about how to reduce rising token costs in legal tech widens across the market. The company stated that: ‘In transactional legal work, the cost of an LLM reading a document is typically far larger than the cost of it reasoning over the answer. ‘In our tests, the length of the final answer barely varied between methods, while the amount of text fed into an LLM varied by up to 30×. ‘That gap is where we can find significant savings. As AI agents increasingly decide for themselves what to retrieve and read, that matters even more. ‘Syntheia’s research team tested two structured retrieval methodologies for transactional legal text, both built on our structure-aware document indexing technology, against full document injection on a 20-question benchmark spanning real credit facility agreements, limited partnership agreements, and share purchase agreements. And here are the headline results: And, In short, by focusing on what is likely to be most relevant you can massively cut down on token use. AL Interview with Horace Wu, founder of Syntheia. What models did you use to achieve this?

news.titleEn: Oz Joins Pillsbury For Top AI Role
news.titleZh: Oz加入Pillsbury担任首席AI官
news.summaryZh: 法律AI专家Oz Benamram加入美国律所Pillsbury，担任其首位首席AI官。Benamram此前曾在Simpson Thacher和White & Case任职，并将继续运营其法律科技团体Skills group。AI最强大的作用在于增强人类专业能力，Benamram将利用AI工具简化工作流程、改进信息分析、加速知识获取，同时确保法律判断、战略思维和客户咨询仍由经验丰富的律师主导。作为首席AI官，Benamram将领导Pillsbury的AI战略、治理框架和赋能基础设施建设，与业务负责人合作推动AI解决方案的负责任部署，并负责数据科学和知识管理职能。Benamram将帮助律所负责任地利用这一变革性技术，加速创新。AI不仅能改变法律工作方式，还能扩大客户对律所集体知识和经验的获取。
news.bodyText: International man of mystery and legal AI guru, Oz Benamram, has joined US law firm Pillsbury as its first Chief AI Officer. It’s understood that the former Simpson Thacher and White & Case alumnus will keep his Skills group for legal tech going. As AL is still waiting for the firm to officially send word, AL can’t really say much, but off record Oz is very happy with the move. P.S. Pillsbury is also hiring for a bunch of other senior legal tech roles. P.P.S. as you can see, he joined the firm at the start of the year – but they’ve not done the official announcement until now. Why? No-one knows. It’s a mystery……. 🙂 …. And after a couple of strong cups of coffee Pillsbury has sent in a comment or two. As follows: ‘Consistent with the firm’s belief that AI is most powerful when used to augment human expertise, Benamram will leverage AI tools to streamline workflows, improve information analysis, accelerate access to knowledge, and support high-quality legal work while ensuring that legal judgment, strategic thinking, and client counseling remain firmly in the hands of experienced lawyers.’ Pillsbury Chair David Dekker commented: ‘Oz will help us harness this transformational tech responsibly, leverage our vast data across leading areas of practice, and accelerate innovation across the firm, all in service of delivering exceptional outcomes for those we represent.’ As Chief AI Officer at Pillsbury, Benamram will lead the development of Pillsbury’s AI strategy, governance frameworks and enablement infrastructure, partnering with practice and business leaders to support the responsible deployment of AI solutions across the firm, along with business transformation initiatives and collaboration with clients and technology partners. He will lead the firm’s data science and knowledge management functions as well, helping to ensure that Pillsbury’s collective experience, work product, and legal insights are effectively leveraged across practices and markets. Benamram added: ‘The firm understands that AI can do more than just change how legal work gets done; it can expand clients’ access to Pillsbury’s collective knowledge, experience, and judgment. I’m excited to work alongside Pillsbury’s lawyers and clients across industries and around the world to help shape a human-led AI future.’
