# The Questions That Matter When Legal Teams Choose AI

The legal teams getting value from AI are not necessarily the fastest adopters. Rather, they are the most disciplined evaluators.

5 minute read June 26, 2026 at 11:05 AM

By

Patrick Ip

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

Soon after large language models became widely available to the public, the legal profession saw its first high-profile failures in court filings. Since 2023, attorneys have faced sanctions for filing briefs that cited cases that did not exist—authorities generated by AI systems that produced confident, well-formatted references to fictional decisions.

Those incidents are not just cautionary tales about hallucinations. They underscore the need for legal teams to bring clear standards, structured evaluation, and professional judgment to AI procurement.

The central question for legal leaders is not whether an AI tool is impressive. It is whether the tool is accurate, explainable, secure, workflow-specific and measurable under real legal conditions. Having spent years building AI systems and working with legal professionals, I have seen a consistent pattern: the legal teams getting value from AI are not necessarily the fastest adopters. Rather, they are the most disciplined evaluators.

**Start With the Work, Not the Demo**

AI is already delivering real value in legal environments. It can accelerate document review, due diligence, research, intake, compliance checks, and other repetitive workflows that consume attorney time. But the strongest use cases share a common feature: they support legal judgment rather than attempt to replace it. Current systems perform best when they help lawyers gather,organize, compare, and analyze information while leaving interpretation and decision-making with trained professionals.

That distinction should drive AI procurement. A tool built for generic business writing is not the same as a tool designed for privilege, procedure, jurisdictional distinctions, evidentiary context,and the reasoning habits of lawyers.

**What the Sanctions Cases Teach Us**

The documented AI failures in legal practice share a pattern: lawyers used general-purpose tools for domain-specific legal tasks and failed to verify the output before filing it with the court. In [_Mata v. Avianca_, 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-sd-new-yor/2335142.html), a lawyer submitted a brief citing six cases generated by ChatGPT. None existed. Since then, the legal press has reported dozens of similar matters in which courts have sanctioned attorneys for filings containing AI-generated,fabricated, or defective citations.

The lesson is not that lawyers should avoid AI. It is that tools optimized for plausibility can be dangerous when accuracy, traceability, and verification are mandatory. A legal AI evaluation should therefore begin with some important questions. Does the system know when it does not know something? Can it cite source material users can inspect? Can lawyers test it on messy, incomplete, contradictory matter files rather than curated demo data? Clear answers to these questions help distinguish a legal tool that is ready for practice from one that merely promises potential.

**The Five Questions Every Legal Team Should Ask**

Before committing to any AI tool, legal teams should be able to answer five practical questions.

1.   **Was it built for the way we actually practice law?**Legal work is not generic knowledge work. And a product designed for one part of the legal market may not transfer cleanly to another. Domain specificity matters most when privilege, procedure, liability, and client trust are at stake.
2.   **How will success be measured?**Legal teams should establish baselines _before_ deployment of the AI tool, such as average review time, attorney hours, matter triage speed, error rates, staffing efficiency, and client satisfaction. Without a baseline, it will be difficult, if not impossible, to measure the improvement the AI tool delivers.
3.   **Can it be tested on real work?**Every demo is designed to succeed. The most meaningful test of an AI tool is how it performs on the legal team’s own files, including incomplete records, conflicting facts, unusual procedural histories, and edge cases.
4.   **What happens to our data?**SOC 2 compliance and encryption are baseline requirements, not the end of the inquiry. Legal teams should ask whether client or company data trains models, who can access outputs, how long data is retained, and what happens when the relationship ends.
5.   **Who owns adoption?**Technology does not create change on its own. Successful AI deployments need internal champions who understand legal workflows, attorney incentives, training, risk management, and implementation. Those internal champions will drive training, which gives lawyers the context to use AI appropriately, spot limitations sooner, and turn the tool into a reliable part of everyday work rather than a novelty.

**Purchase Decisions Require Discipline**

AI purchasing decisions being made now will shape how legal teams function for years to come:how matters are staffed, how clients are served, how lawyers manage risk, and how confidential information is protected. Those decisions should not be driven by polished demos or vague promises of efficiency. They should be governed by the same discipline legal professionals already bring to every serious matter: defined standards, real evidence, careful testing and accountability.

The call to action is simple: evaluate AI the way lawyers evaluate cases. Test the facts, challenge the assumptions, and demand evidence before acting. Legal teams that build disciplined review processes will be best positioned to successfully incorporate AI tools into their practice.

**Patrick Ip**_is the CEO and co-founder of Theo Ai, ex-Googler, and UCLA Law MLS graduate._

news.titleEn: At 3rd Circuit, Judges Press ROSS and Thomson Reuters on Fair Use, AI Training and Market Harm
news.titleZh: 第三巡回上诉法院法官就合理使用、AI训练与市场损害质询ROSS和汤森路透
news.summaryZh: 备受关注的汤森路透诉ROSS Intelligence版权案本月在第三巡回上诉法院开庭审理。由三位法官组成的合议庭就ROSS使用Westlaw判例摘要训练法律研究系统是否构成合理使用听取了辩论。法官重点询问了合理使用的第一和第四要素：使用是否具有转换性，以及是否对汤森路透版权作品的现有或潜在市场造成损害。ROSS方律师Mark S. Davies主张撤销地区法院裁决，认为使用判例摘要属于合理使用，并援引第三巡回法院近期在ASTM诉UpCodes案中的判决。汤森路透方律师Dale M. Cendali则辩称ROSS复制受保护的编辑内容以构建竞争性法律研究产品，地区法院正确驳回了合理使用抗辩。法官多次追问ROSS产品与Westlaw在用户视角下的区别，以及其是否构成商业替代品。该案因涉及AI训练与版权法的影响而受到法律科技行业广泛关注。
news.bodyHtml:
The closely watched copyright litigation between Thomson Reuters and ROSS Intelligence returned to the spotlight this month as a three-judge panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments over whether ROSS’s use of Westlaw headnotes to train its legal research system was protected by fair use.

At oral argument June 11 in Philadelphia, the three-judge panel, consisting of  Judges L. Felipe Restrepo, Tamika R. Montgomery-Reeves and Emil J. Bove,  focused much of its questioning on the first and fourth fair-use factors of whether ROSS’s use was transformative and whether it harmed an actual or potential market for Thomson Reuters’ copyrighted works.

Earlier this week, the court released the transcript of the hearing.

Representing ROSS, White & Case partner Mark S. Davies urged the court to reverse the district court’s ruling and find that its use of the headnotes was fair use.

Thomson Reuters and West Publishing, represented by Dale M. Cendali, partner at Kirkland & Ellis, argued that ROSS copied protected editorial content to build a competing legal research product and that the district court correctly rejected the fair-use defense.

The argument came in an appeal from the Delaware federal court’s rulings in a case that has drawn attention across the legal tech industry because of its implications for AI training and copyright law. Even though the case predates the current generation of generative AI tools, ROSS argued that its technology was an early example of the same broader AI transformation now reshaping legal research.

ROSS Argues Fair Use

Davies opened by invoking the 3rd Circuit’s recent decision in ASTM v. UpCodes, arguing that under that precedent, the court should summarily reverse based on fair use. He said ROSS had built a legal search platform in 2015 by adapting headnotes into questions and using them to create training materials for a system that could connect natural-language legal questions to judicial opinions.

But Judge Restrepo immediately redirected the argument to the fourth fair-use factor, asking Davies to address the effect of the use on the market. Davies responded that the copyrighted work at issue was the headnote itself and that there was no market for a single headnote or for headnotes as AI training material.

Judge Bove pressed him on whether there was, or could be, a market for AI training. Davies argued that ROSS’s use was too specific to define a market around it. ROSS did not merely take headnotes as raw data, he said, but built training memos that included questions and multiple answers, some right and some wrong, to train the model.

To let Thomson Reuters claim a lost market for that use, he argued, would be circular because any copyright owner could say it would have licensed the very use later claimed to be fair.

The judges repeatedly questioned Davies on how, from the user’s perspective, ROSS’s product differed from Westlaw. Judge Bove asked why ROSS’s system was transformative “as opposed to just a different type of legal search engine.”

When Davies focused on the internal technology, Judge Restrepo noted that ROSS was nevertheless a direct competitor to Westlaw, and Judge Montgomery-Reeves asked whether the product was aimed at serving as a commercial substitute.

Davies acknowledged that ROSS competed with Westlaw, but said copyright law was not designed to protect incumbents from competition. He described ROSS’s product as one in which a user asked a natural-language legal question and received a stream of answers in the form of quotations from judicial opinions. Because the output came from court opinions rather than generated text, he said, there was “no risk of hallucinations.”

Judge Bove continued to press for a factual description of the product, at one point telling Davies there was “a lot of dancing going on” and that he was trying to understand what ROSS planned to do and why it was materially different from Westlaw.

“Could you please describe to me what Ross’s proposed engine would have looked like, and the differences, and why it was so transformative from what happens when I log into Westlaw in the morning?” Judge Bove asked.

Davies responded that, from a user perspective, both products helped users find cases, but that ROSS operated differently internally because it used deep-learning techniques to teach the system the semantic relationships of legal language.

“The question has legal language in it, and what we have taught this machine now is how to think like a lawyer,” Davies said.

The panel also questioned Davies on the copyrightability of the headnotes themselves. Judge Montgomery-Reeves asked why headnotes that condensed and reformulated judicial language were not sufficiently original to qualify for copyright protection.

Davies argued that judicial opinions belong to the public and that the differences between the opinions and the headnotes were too slight to support protection. The judges, however, probed whether the selection and condensation of opinion language reflected editorial judgment.

Judge Bove focused on one example in which West’s editor had excerpted and condensed language from an opinion. Even if the headnote closely tracked the opinion, he suggested, the editor still made judgments about what was salient and what to include. Davies maintained that West’s editorial instructions were designed to remove creativity and track the language of the opinion as closely as possible.

Davies argued that ROSS should prevail on the second and third fair-use factors because the headnotes were factual and because ROSS copied only a small fraction of Westlaw’s total headnotes. He said ROSS used only 0.08% of Westlaw’s 28 million headnotes.

“We took so little,” He said. “We just took 0.08% is all we copied of 28 million headnotes.”

When Judge Montgomery-Reeves asked what result should follow if Thomson Reuters were ahead on factors one and four, while ROSS prevailed on factors two and three, Davies said ROSS should still win. Judge Restrepo pressed him: “If you take 2 and 3 and they take 1 and 4, you win?” Davies answered that fair use is a multi-factor test.

Judge Bove also asked Davies about Thomson Reuters’ allegations of bad faith, including communications involving Dentons and efforts by ROSS to obtain Westlaw material. (The transcript does not elaborate on how Dentons was implicated and I could find no reference to that in the parties’ redacted briefs.)

Davies said ROSS had paid for the original database and for the memos and that any license issues should be addressed in separate contract claims, not the fair-use analysis. He cited cases for the proposition that copyright is not reserved for the “well-behaved” and argued that even if there were bad-faith evidence, it should not defeat fair use.

‘A Classic Case of Substitution’

Arguing for Thomson Reuters, Cendali began by addressing the scope of the appeal. She said the district court had granted summary judgment on 2,834 headnotes, of which Judge Stephanos Bibas had found 2,430 protectable and infringed. She said the court need not go beyond that set of headnotes, although she also argued that headnotes are categorically copyrightable under long-established precedent.

Cendali then turned to fair use, framing the case as one of substitution. Citing Supreme Court authority, she said substitution is “copyright’s bete noire” and “this is a classic case of substitution” in that ROSS built and marketed a product to replace Westlaw.

She pointed to ROSS marketing materials that, according to Thomson Reuters, urged users to “choose ROSS or Westlaw,” and said that was a quintessential example of a substitute product.

Judge Bove asked Cendali to identify the relevant market for the fourth factor, noting that the parties appeared “worlds apart” on that question.

Cendali identified three forms of market harm: harm from ROSS’s product competing as a substitute for Westlaw, harm to Thomson Reuters’ ability to use its own headnotes exclusively to train its own AI products, and harm to a potential market for licensing headnotes for AI training by other AI companies.

Cendali disputed ROSS’s suggestion that Thomson Reuters had not used its headnotes for AI. She said Thomson Reuters had trained on its own headnotes years before ROSS was founded and that Westlaw’s use of AI and natural-language search predated ROSS. She also pointed to amicus briefing by Lexis as evidence that other legal research providers were developing AI products during the same period.

“So as much as they try to cast themselves as tremendous innovators, they really were latecomers,” Cendali argued.

Judge Montgomery-Reeves drew an analogy to the 3rd Circuit’s Video Pipeline case involving Disney trailers, asking whether the absence of a stand-alone market for the copied material defeated a market-harm argument.

It did not, Cendali said. She argued that, as in Video Pipeline, copied content could still harm the value of a broader platform even if it was not separately sold on its own.

On the first fair-use factor, Cendali argued that ROSS’s use was not transformative because it used Westlaw headnotes to build a competing legal research tool. Training was merely the means to an end, she said, and under the Supreme Court’s Warhol decision, the proper inquiry focuses on the purpose of the use. Here, both products served the same purpose: helping users conduct legal research.

Judge Bove asked what the record showed about the nature of ROSS’s training and technology. Cendali responded that the product ultimately returned cases and quotes, which she said was similar to what Westlaw did. She distinguished the case from disputes involving gen AI systems that produce new text, saying ROSS’s product was a legal research system for finding court opinions in response to legal topics.

Cendali also argued that ROSS took the “heart” of Westlaw’s work, even if the number of headnotes copied was small compared with Westlaw’s overall database. She said Westlaw’s editorial enhancements, including headnotes and the Key Number System, are what differentiate it from a bare collection of cases. ROSS, she said, took the question-and-answer pairs created through that editorial work rather than creating its own from the underlying opinions.

The panel also explored the relevance of cases involving intermediate copying, such as Sega, Sony and Google v. Oracle. Cendali argued that those cases did not help ROSS because they involved copying necessary to understand functional computer code or achieve compatibility. Here, she said, ROSS had access to the public judicial opinions and did not need to copy Westlaw’s headnotes to build its system.

Rebuttal: Not Merely ‘AI’ As A Label

In rebuttal, Davies returned to the technology, emphasizing that ROSS was not merely invoking “AI” as a label. He said the system used deep neural-network technology similar in kind to the systems later associated with ChatGPT and Anthropic, although he acknowledged that ROSS’s product was not generative AI.

In response to Judge Montgomery-Reeves, he agreed that ROSS did not write briefs or generate legal answers, but instead returned quotes from judicial opinions.

Davies also challenged Thomson Reuters’ market-harm evidence, arguing that the record lacked concrete proof that ROSS harmed Westlaw’s market. Judge Bove reminded him that, under precedent, ROSS bore the burden on fair use, including factor four.

Davies acknowledged the burden but argued that Thomson Reuters was better positioned to produce evidence such as subscriber numbers and customer data. He said the record included evidence that some users left ROSS and returned to Westlaw.

The argument ended with an exchange over whether the intermediate-copying cases were meaningfully analogous. Judge Bove noted that in Sega and Sony, the copying was necessary because humans could not read object code, whereas ROSS employees could read the judicial opinions and create their own training materials from them.

Davies responded that there is no strict necessity requirement for fair use and that ROSS had a legitimate purpose in building a new legal research technology under time pressure as a startup.

As the argument wrapped up, Judge Bove framed the issue more broadly, telling Davies, “I think this case is about balancing what we have and where are the red lines.”

“It’s all about balancing,” Davies agreed, “as all copyright cases are, Your Honor.”

The court did not indicate when it would rule.

news.titleEn: Start Up Corner: Caira from Unwildered – Improving access to justice
news.titleZh: 创业角：Unwildered 推出 Caira——改善司法可及性
news.summaryZh: Unwildered 成立于 2024 年，其基于 LLM 的平台 Caira 最初面向消费者提供法律助手服务，后扩展至合同审查等专业工作流。Caira 通过即时回答、起草和文件审查，帮助用户避免高昂的法律费用，月费从 15 英镑起，涵盖家庭、遗嘱认证、就业、刑事、商业、公法等多个领域。Caira 采用检索增强生成技术，针对不同司法管辖区独立检索，目前覆盖英格兰和威尔士/英国、美国、中国、印度、南非、波兰、香港、新加坡、德国、法国和瑞典。英国数据库包含超过 10,000 份法律文件，美国数据库约 50,000 份。产品包括 Caira Chat（15 英镑/月）、AI Contract Review（免费层及付费计划，15 英镑/月起）和 AI Auction Pack / Conveyancing Review（一份免费报告，付费包 30 英镑起）。Unwildered 目前为创始人主导的 lean 模式，自筹资金，未接受外部股权融资，但获得了 Microsoft for Startups、LawtechUK、Lawtech Bridge 和 FCA AI Lab Supercharged Academy 等项目的支持。
news.bodyHtml:
Unwildered was founded in 2024 and its LLM-powered platform Caira started life a consumer-facing legal assistant before expanding into specialised workflows such as contract review. Founder Hassan Luwalira talks us through strategy, investment, key achievements and – fun fact -why his earliest legal education was embarrassingly cinematic.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Legal help should be within reach. Caira helps people avoid eye-watering legal bills with instant answers, drafts and document reviews from £15/month across family, probate, employment, criminal, commercial, public law and more.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Caira is an LLM-powered legal tech platform built around retrieval augmented generation. Ask Caira a question and she retrieves relevant material from separate jurisdiction databases before answering. Each jurisdiction’s database remains distinct. Current coverage includes England and Wales/UK, the United States, China, India, South Africa, Poland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Germany, France and Sweden. Depth varies by market, but the design principle is the same: jurisdiction-specific retrieval, not generic legal autocomplete. The UK database has over 10,000 legal documents, and the US database has around 50,000. – Caira Chat (£15/month): legal answers and drafts across everyday and specialist legal problems. – AI Contract Review (free tier, then paid page plans from £15/month): upload a contract, review suggested changes, accept or reject them, download a DOCX with inline comments/redlines, and generate a counterparty email with a single click. – AI Auction Pack / Conveyancing Review (one free report, then paid packs from £30): a 40-point style risk check across the pack, highlighting missing documents, title/search/special-condition issues, and enquiry emails to the auctioneer’s solicitors. The aim is straightforward. Users should not need large prompt templates, legal engineering, demo calls or complex configuration. It should work instantly out of the box.

When were you founded?

2024. The first prototype was built in 2023; Unwildered was incorporated in January 2024.

Advertisement
By who?

Hassan Luwalira.

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Hassan Luwalira, founder and CEO. At this stage Unwildered is deliberately founder-led and lean.

Who are your target clients?

Consumers first: people dealing with separation, probate, employment problems, housing issues, disputes, property purchases, debt, contracts or official correspondence who need clarity before they can decide what to do next. We also serve SMEs and freelancers who want affordable contract and dispute support. We are seeing interest from law firms too, especially teams that want legal AI products they can use instantly without procurement theatre, large prompt libraries or complex configuration. Longer term, we see B2B2C partnerships with advice-gap organisations, financial institutions, insurers, pension providers and other trusted consumer channels.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

We started with Caira as a consumer legal chat product, then expanded into two more specialised workflows: AI Contract Review and AI Auction Pack / Conveyancing Review. The growth strategy is practical. First, win trust directly with consumers through useful, low-friction legal tech and legal content. Second, turn repeated pain points into focused products people can start using immediately: chat for ongoing legal questions, contract review for redlines and counterparty emails, and auction pack review for pre-bid risk screening and enquiry drafts. Third, expand carefully across jurisdictions, with separate databases rather than one generic knowledge base. We began with England and Wales and now support the United States, China, India, South Africa, Poland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Germany, France and Sweden. The mission is simple. We want to build the most loved legal tech product in the market: legal help that feels excellent, affordable, accessible and equitable.

Key achievements?

We built and launched the product while self-funded. Caira now spans three products: Caira Chat (£15/month), AI Contract Review (free tier, then paid page plans from £15/month), and AI Auction Pack / Conveyancing Review (one free report, then paid packs from £30). No requirement for demo calls or complex onboarding. The knowledge base has grown from a UK legal assistant into broader legal coverage across England and Wales/UK, the United States, China, India, South Africa, Poland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Germany, France and Sweden. Unwildered has been supported by Microsoft for Startups, LawtechUK, Lawtech Bridge and the FCA AI Lab Supercharged Academy. We have also taken part in policy and regulatory conversations around AI, access to justice and the information/advice boundary. Perhaps most importantly, people began using an early prototype daily, including those under significant pressure, which underscored the need to take the project forward in earnest.

Have you received investment?

No external equity investment. We are self-funded. We have had support through startup and accelerator programmes, including cloud and ecosystem support, but no institutional investment round.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Yes. The original idea was narrower: a consumer AI legal assistant, initially with a strong family-law focus. Then practical realities became apparent. Real people do not arrive with tidy, single-category legal problems. A separation can involve children, property, pensions, tax, employment, benefits and debt. A bereavement can involve probate, inheritance tax, trusts, family conflict and property. So we expanded across legal areas and then into adjacent life-event questions. The second surprise was the customer mix. We built for consumers because affordability and ease of use are existential for them. But businesses and law firms also began using the product, even though they can choose ChatGPT, Claude or more traditional B2B legal tech. This highlighted an important insight. Instant access, usability, low cost and minimal setup matter just as much to professionals. Some users do not want a platform that starts with a demo call, then an implementation project, then a prompt library they have to maintain. They want legal AI that is ready to use immediately upon access. As model inference becomes less subsidised and automated workflows become more technically complex, we think the market will increasingly value focused, ready-to-use AI solutions with retrieval, guardrails and workflow logic already built in.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Trust is the first challenge. Legal AI has to be useful without being overconfident, and affordable without feeling cheap. The information/advice boundary is another: consumers need practical help, but the regulatory framework still assumes a world of clearly separated lawyers, advisers, platforms and publishers. Regulatory recognition is also difficult. Consumers traditionally look for law firms, or enter the market through legal aid, and Unwildered is not a legal aid provider or regulated law firm. That makes trust, wording and routes to market especially important. Adoption is improving, however. We see growing numbers of users turning to AI whether they are litigants in person or already have King’s Counsel legal representation. They like that support is available 24/7, instantly, and on any device. Distribution is hard too. The people who most need affordable legal help are not always searching for “legal AI” or “legal tech” on Google. They are in WhatsApp chats, school playgrounds, GP waiting rooms, auction viewings, HR meetings and family disputes. Then there is economics. Everyone talks about AI making services cheaper, but high-quality LLMs, retrieval, document processing, evaluation and agentic orchestration all cost money. At the same time, users are becoming less patient with expensive tools that require heavy setup before they do anything useful. The market will favour solutions that are reliable, user-friendly and immediate. Legal help still has to be good. It also has to be priced for normal people and small teams.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company?

My earliest legal education was embarrassingly cinematic: Suits in 2011 and Prison Break in 2005. I loved Mike Ross because he made law feel like pattern recognition, memory and nerve; I loved Michael Scofield because he treated impossible systems as puzzles that could be mapped. Years later, after self-representing in family court, those two instincts quietly became Unwildered: make the system legible, then help ordinary people find a route through it.

# Legaltech Rundown: Filevine Launches LOIS Legal Research Tool, Eudia Partners With Microsoft—and More

An update on the legal tech market’s past week, from product launches to new partnerships.

5 minute read June 26, 2026 at 11:17 AM

By

![Image 17](https://images.law.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=contain/https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b1bb32ca30c747d2664de350bb767836?s=136&d=mm&r=g)[Ella Sherman](http://www.law.com/author/profile/ella-sherman/)

 Email

 Share

Font Size

Small Medium Large 

 Print

The fast-paced legal tech world is constantly evolving. At Legaltech News, we always try to bring you the latest news on hirings, product and feature releases, new integrations, legal tech mergers and acquisitions and more.

The Legaltech Rundown is a weekly update of legal tech happenings that might have gone under the radar.

**Berkley Research Group:**On Monday, consulting firm Berkley Research Group (BRG) announced the appointment of Jason Gu as a managing director in its AI and decision intelligence practice. Gu was previously vice president of AI at Visa and was also previously a technical lead and architect at IBM. At BRG, he will advise clients on AI strategy, governance and implementation, while also leading the development of the firm's internal AI infrastructure and reusable capabilities, according to a press release.

**Casepoint:**Legal, regulatory and compliance software provider Casepoint announced Wednesday that it reached a Blanket Purchase Agreement with the Department of Defense (DOD) to provide e-discovery software as a service, support services and training for the DOD Office of General Counsel (OGC), Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) OGC and Defense Legal Services Agency (DLSA), including 28 separate DLSA OGC offices supporting multiple offices. The Blanket Purchase Agreement will allow DOD legal agencies to more quickly procure tools to create AI-powered workflows, according to a press release.

**Centari:**Contract review platform Centari announced Tuesday the launch of Amendment Awareness and Deal Maps capabilities. Amendment Awareness helps maintain deal data related to the current state of the client's rights, and once an amendment is uploaded to an existing matter, Amendment Awareness identifies changes and updates deal profiles to reflect terms. Deal Maps generates a graph showing how agreements incorporate, modify, satisfy, replace or supersede each other to allow users to comprehend the layers of a transaction before beginning review, according to a press release.

**ClearPeople/Epiq:** On Wednesday, legal technology and services provider Epiq and knowledge management provider ClearPeople announced a partnership aimed at helping law firms and corporate legal departments modernize their knowledge infrastructure. Through the collaboration, Epiq Advisory's operational and implementation expertise combines with ClearPeople’s Atlas Fuse platform to consolidate content from Microsoft 365, iManage and other document management systems into one secure environment. The partnership covers organizations in the U.S., Canada and the UK, according to a press release.

**Dialogica/iManage:** On Thursday, legal AI platform Dialogica announced a partnership with knowledge management platform iManage. Through the integration, users can access iManage directly within Dia, Dialogica's AI assistant, allowing firms to tap into their existing document management infrastructure without leaving the platform, according to a press release.

**DocSolid**: On Monday, cloud-based information management provider DocSolid announced that Suzette Allaire has joined its advisory board. Allaire is currently chief operating and financial officer of Minneapolis-based law firm Maslon and was previously chief innovation officer at Ballard Spahr, according to a press release.

**Eudia/Microsoft**: On Thursday, legal tech startup Eudia announced a partnership with Microsoft spanning product integrations, Azure infrastructure deployment and a joint go-to-market with Microsoft's enterprise sales organization. Through the collaboration, Eudia's Expert Digital Twins, AI models built to replicate an organization's top legal experts' judgment and its suite of specialized agents, are now accessible directly within Microsoft 365 with plans to integrate with Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and PowerPoint. Eudia will also be available for purchase through the Microsoft Marketplace, according to a press release.

**Filevine:**Legal practice management provider Filevine announced Tuesday the launch of Legal Operating Intelligence System (LOIS) Legal Research, an AI-powered legal citator and validation tool. Users can search, read and navigate through precedential opinions from U.S. federal and state jurisdictions at scale, and the user can determine whether a specific passage in those opinions remains good law, expanding the capacity of verification. Users can highlight precise passages they care about, and AI-assisted analysis classifies the treatment, pulls up supporting passages and produces a consolidated memo with a treatment signal as well as a table of authorities.

**Firm Prospects/UniCourt:** On Tuesday, litigation analytics provider UniCourt announced a partnership with legal talent intelligence platform Firm Prospects. By embedding UniCourt's litigation data directly into Firm Prospects' attorney profiles, the integration aims to bring data-backed objectivity to lateral hiring and competitive intelligence. Law firms and legal recruiters using Firm Prospects can now access a candidate's verified case history, litigation relationship dynamics, co-counsel networks and opposing counsel records, replacing reliance on resumes and referrals with court-verified track records, according to a press release.

**Litify/Supio:** On Tuesday, legal AI platform Litify announced the launch of LitifyAI Instant Demands, a new capability built in partnership with personal injury startup Supio. Designed for personal injury firms, the tool automates the demand packet generation process, producing both the demand narrative and a compiled exhibit packet and leveraging Supio’s document analysis, fact extraction and initial narrative and packet drafting within the Litify platform, according to a press release.

**Reveal:**E-discovery provider Reveal announced the early access launch of Logikcull for Public Records on Tuesday. This platform centralizes request-to-disclosure automation, allowing state and local government, along with other public institutions, to address a growing number of requests under freedom of information laws. Users can submit requests through a secure portal branded for the agency. Records officers can then review, assign and monitor each request against statutory deadlines with automated reminders and a centralized record of all communications. Logikcull then supports the remaining workflow, including collection, identification and response, before sending the completed, redacted records back to the requester through the same system, according to a press release.

**U.S. Legal Services:**On Tuesday, legal access service provider U.S. Legal Services launched its AI assistant Legalia AI. Legalia provides general legal, policy information and helps users understand their options as well as connects users with a licensed attorney to give advice on a specific situation, according to a press release.

news.titleEn: FDIC Eyes Major Cutbacks to Living Wills and Deposit Insurance Charges
news.titleZh: FDIC拟大幅削减生前遗嘱与存款保险费用
news.summaryZh: 美国联邦存款保险公司（FDIC）提出一项重大监管调整，拟放宽大型银行的“生前遗嘱”义务，并将年度存款保险费用削减约40亿美元。该提案若获通过，将显著改变后2008年改革时代以来大型银行的合规要求。对于银行而言，这意味着潜在的节省和更轻的报告负担；对于监管机构、消费者权益倡导者和交易对手方，则引发关于放松危机准备要求是否会增加系统性风险的疑问。该提案涉及的两项核心变化——决议规划和存款保险评估——均具有法律意义，将改变银行多年建立的治理、文档和运营系统基线。法律顾问和合规团队需评估哪些义务可能消失，以及哪些内部控制措施在规则放宽后仍应保留。此外，费用削减直接影响资本规划、定价和战略决策，董事会和行政团队的法律顾问需将监管文本转化为实际影响分析。该提案还可能引发密集的评论期、行业游说，甚至基于行政法理论的诉讼挑战。总体而言，FDIC的提案不仅是技术性合规更新，更标志着大型银行韧性监管的重大调整，为法律部门、外部顾问和风险团队提供了重新审视十多年来银行监管假设的契机。
news.bodyHtml:
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation has proposed a notable pullback in two areas that have shaped large-bank compliance since the post-2008 reform era: resolution planning and deposit insurance assessments. If adopted, the changes would significantly ease “living will” obligations for large banks and reduce annual deposit-insurance costs by an estimated $4 billion.

Although this is not a courtroom dispute, it is the kind of regulatory shift that can drive substantial legal work across the financial sector. The proposal, reported by law360.com, would materially alter how major banking institutions prepare for failure scenarios and how much they pay into the deposit insurance system. For banks, that means potential savings and lighter reporting burdens. For regulators, consumer advocates, and counterparties, it raises familiar questions about whether easing crisis-preparedness requirements could increase systemic risk.

Resolution-planning rules were designed to ensure that large institutions could be unwound in an orderly way without destabilizing the broader economy or requiring extraordinary government support. Any rollback in that framework is legally significant because it changes the compliance baseline for institutions that have spent years building governance, documentation, and operational systems around those mandates. In-house counsel and compliance teams will need to assess not only what obligations may disappear, but also which internal controls remain prudent despite a looser rulebook.

The proposal’s assessment-related changes are equally important. Deposit-insurance premiums are a recurring cost with direct balance-sheet consequences, and a multibillion-dollar reduction could affect capital planning, pricing, and strategic decisions. Counsel advising boards and executive teams will likely be asked to translate the regulatory text into practical impacts: who benefits, what implementation timelines apply, and whether any retained obligations still create litigation or enforcement exposure.

For litigators and regulatory practitioners, the significance lies in what often follows a policy reversal. Rule changes of this scale can trigger intensive comment periods, industry lobbying, and possible legal challenges under administrative law theories if stakeholders argue the agency failed to justify its departure from prior policy. Even absent immediate litigation, firms will be watching for disputes tied to examinations, supervisory expectations, or future bank failures where prior planning standards become part of the narrative.

In short, the FDIC’s proposal is more than a technical compliance update. It signals a potentially meaningful recalibration of how large-bank resilience is regulated — and it gives legal departments, outside counsel, and risk teams an early reason to revisit assumptions that have governed bank oversight for more than a decade.

news.titleEn: What does AI governance have to do with your ethical wall programs?
news.titleZh: AI治理与你的道德墙计划有何关联？
news.summaryZh: 道德墙是律所用于隔离存在利益冲突的律师与案件的信息屏障，Am Law 200律所已建立成熟体系。AI治理正沿相同路径发展，但速度更快。2026年3月，加州律师协会职业责任与行为委员会批准对六项职业行为规则提出修订，其中Rule 5.1评注[1]新增AI使用治理要求，要求管理律师将AI政策纳入内部管理。若加州最高法院批准，缺乏AI治理文件的律所将难以证明其履行了Rule 5.1义务。纽约州法院认证规则已于6月1日生效，超过35个州律师协会已发布指引。AI治理与道德墙均旨在控制机密信息流向：道德墙针对新进律师，AI治理则确保AI工具处理案件数据时具备访问控制。2026年1月报告显示超500起AI生成内容出现在法庭文件中，法院已从罚款转向取消律师资格。71%的财富500强法务总监在律所选聘中询问AI使用情况，缺乏管控的律所正失去业务。
news.bodyHtml:
Managing partners have been running some version of this conversation for thirty years: a lateral arrives, a conflict surfaces, a screen goes up, the file gets walled. An ethical wall (also called an ethics wall) is a documented, court-recognized information barrier that separates an attorney from matters where their prior client relationships create a conflict — restricting file access, excluding the attorney from relevant discussions, and creating an auditable record of the separation. The ethical wall infrastructure at most Am Law 200 firms reflects decades of accumulated professional responsibility discipline. When a malpractice carrier or bar investigator asks how the firm handled a separation, there is a record.

That discipline did not happen by accident. It happened because the ABA Model Rules made it mandatory, regulators made it enforceable, and firms eventually built the operational infrastructure to match. The cycle took time, but the outcome is a compliance function that most chief risk officers trust.

AI governance is on the same track, moving faster, with less time to build the infrastructure before the consequences arrive. AI governance, for a law firm, means the documented policies, access controls, and audit procedures that determine which AI tools can touch which matter data — and demonstrate, when asked, that privileged information was handled consistently with the firm’s confidentiality obligations.

Why AI governance is now a Rule 5.1 obligation alongside conflicts and ethical walls

In March 2026, the State Bar of California’s Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct approved proposed amendments to six professional conduct rules. The proposals are notable for what they add to Rule 5.1, which governs the responsibilities of managerial lawyers at firms. Specifically, the proposed amendment to Comment [1] of Rule 5.1 adds governance of AI use to the list of internal policies that managing lawyers must implement, alongside the existing requirements for conflicts, calendaring, and client funds. This is a comment amendment, not a change to the black-letter rule text, but comments carry interpretive weight: they define what “reasonable efforts” under the rule actually require in practice.

This is not a standalone AI rule or an advisory opinion. It is an amendment to the enforcement framework that managing partners already operate under. If the California Supreme Court approves it, a firm without documented AI governance procedures will have a harder time demonstrating that its managing lawyers met their Rule 5.1 obligations.

California is the leading edge. New York’s court-wide certification rule took effect June 1. Over 35 state bars have issued guidance, and the pattern is consistent: AI obligations are not arriving as new categories of professional responsibility. They are arriving as sharpened applications of the obligations firms already have.

How ethical wall requirements and AI governance requirements ask the same question

The overlap with ethical wall requirements is not coincidental. Both disciplines exist to answer the same question: when privileged or confidential information moves within a firm, who controls where it goes?

An ethical wall answers that question for lateral hires. The screen separates the incoming attorney from matters where their prior representations create a conflict. It restricts file access, excludes the attorney from relevant discussions, and creates a documented record of the separation. Without it, a conflict can impute firm-wide under Rule 1.10.

The AI governance question is structurally identical. When a lawyer runs a matter file through an AI tool, where does that information go? Is it isolated within the firm’s infrastructure, or is it transmitted to a vendor’s external model? Can it surface in a response to a query on a different matter? Does the tool have access controls at the matter level, or does it operate across the firm’s full data set?

These are not IT security questions. They are privilege questions, and the California COPRAC Practical Guidance updated for 2026 says so explicitly: “Unrestricted or poorly configured agentic systems may unintentionally disclose confidential information across different matters.” The duty to configure AI tools with appropriate matter-level access controls is the governance equivalent of the duty to implement a timely ethics screen.

What the consequences look like when AI governance is missing

The stakes for getting this wrong are not theoretical. A January 2026 report documented more than 500 confirmed instances of AI-generated content appearing in U.S. court filings, and courts have moved from monetary sanctions to counsel disqualification. Outside counsel guidelines from Fortune 500 clients now routinely require explicit approval before client data is processed by any third-party tool — and 71% of Fortune 500 general counsel, according to a 2025 American Lawyer survey, are asking about AI use during panel negotiations. A firm that cannot answer those questions with documented controls is losing work to firms that can.

For a chief risk officer, this is the more immediate concern. The bar rulemaking will take time to finalize. The client-side consequence is already here.

What sound AI governance infrastructure actually requires

The firms that built sound ethical wall programs didn’t do it by writing a policy and assuming the organization would follow it. They built operational infrastructure: access controls, documented screen decisions, audit logs, notification procedures, and integration with the systems lawyers use every day. When those screens were challenged — in disqualification motions, bar complaints, or malpractice proceedings — that documentation was the difference between a defensible record and an exposed firm.

AI governance requires the same approach. A written policy is the starting point. What it cannot do on its own is demonstrate, at the matter level, that a specific AI interaction involving a specific client file was handled consistently with the firm’s confidentiality obligations — and produce that record in days, not weeks, when a GC or bar investigator asks. That requires operational infrastructure, not just intent.

The firms building that infrastructure now will be the ones that answer the bar’s questions, satisfy their clients’ OCG requirements, and retain panel work when governance becomes a selection criterion rather than an afterthought.

Specifically, the proposed amendment to Comment [1] of Rule 5.1 adds governance of AI use to the list of internal policies that managing lawyers must implement, alongside the existing requirements for conflicts, calendaring, and client funds. This is a comment amendment, not a change to the black-letter rule text, but comments carry interpretive weight: they define what “reasonable efforts” under the rule actually require in practice. This is not a standalone AI rule or an advisory opinion. It is an amendment to the enforcement framework that managing partners already operate under. If the California Supreme Court approves it, a firm without documented AI governance procedures will have a harder time demonstrating that its managing lawyers met their Rule 5.1 obligations. California is the leading edge. New York’s court-wide certification rule took effect June 1. Over 35 state bars have issued guidance, and the pattern is consistent: AI obligations are not arriving as new categories of professional responsibility. They are arriving as sharpened applications of the obligations firms already have. The overlap with ethical wall requirements is not coincidental. Both disciplines exist to answer the same question: when privileged or confidential information moves within a firm, who controls where it goes? An ethical wall answers that question for lateral hires. The screen separates the incoming attorney from matters where their prior representations create a conflict. It restricts file access, excludes the attorney from relevant discussions, and creates a documented record of the separation. Without it, a conflict can impute firm-wide under Rule 1.10. The AI governance question is structurally identical. When a lawyer runs a matter file through an AI tool, where does that information go? Is it isolated within the firm’s infrastructure, or is it transmitted to a vendor’s external model? Can it surface in a response to a query on a different matter? Does the tool have access controls at the matter level, or does it operate across the firm’s full data set? These are not IT security questions. They are privilege questions, and the California COPRAC Practical Guidance updated for 2026 says so explicitly: “Unrestricted or poorly configured agentic systems may unintentionally disclose confidential information across different matters.” The duty to configure AI tools with appropriate matter-level access controls is the governance equivalent of the duty to implement a timely ethics screen. The stakes for getting this wrong are not theoretical. A January 2026 report documented more than 500 confirmed instances of AI-generated content appearing in U.S. court filings, and courts have moved from monetary sanctions to counsel disqualification. Outside counsel guidelines from Fortune 500 clients now routinely require explicit approval before client data is processed by any third-party tool — and 71% of Fortune 500 general counsel, according to a 2025 American Lawyer survey, are asking about AI use during panel negotiations. A firm that cannot answer those questions with documented controls is losing work to firms that can. For a chief risk officer, this is the more immediate concern. The bar rulemaking will take time to finalize. The client-side consequence is already here.

news.titleEn: FTC Locks In Order Against Illuminate Over Student Data Breach
news.titleZh: FTC对Illuminate教育数据泄露案下达最终命令
news.summaryZh: 美国联邦贸易委员会（FTC）已最终批准对Illuminate Education的命令，结束了一起因数据泄露影响约1010万名学生而引发的执法行动。FTC认定Illuminate未能合理保护敏感学生信息，导致大规模泄露。此案表明，收集和存储大量儿童或学生数据的公司必须实施与风险相称的安全计划。学生记录包含个人、学术和标识信息，泄露后可能造成长期风险。在K-12环境中，法律和声誉后果因学区合同、州隐私法和公众监督而加剧。对于法律顾问和合规团队，该命令强调需重新审视供应商管理、事件响应、数据保留及技术保障措施。为教育科技客户提供咨询的律师应预期学校客户加强尽职调查和合同要求。诉讼律师应关注FTC调查结果可能成为后续民事诉讼的路线图。更广泛的启示是，儿童和学生数据在隐私执法中具有特殊地位，监管机构将其视为高风险治理问题。法律专业人士应确保安全控制、隐私承诺和董事会监督在事件发生前保持一致。
news.bodyHtml:
The Federal Trade Commission has given final approval to its order against Illuminate Education, closing out a closely watched enforcement action arising from a data breach that exposed information tied to roughly 10.1 million students. For education companies and the schools that rely on them, the case is a sharp reminder that student-data security is now firmly in regulators’ crosshairs.

According to the FTC, Illuminate failed to reasonably secure sensitive student information, resulting in a breach with sweeping impact. Final approval means the agency’s settlement terms are now locked in, and the matter stands as another example of the FTC using its unfairness authority to police data-security practices even outside the traditional consumer-tech context. The message is straightforward: if a company collects and stores large volumes of children’s or student information, the agency expects a security program commensurate with the risk.

That matters because student records often include a particularly sensitive mix of personal data, academic information, and identifiers that can create long-tail exposure long after a breach occurs. In the K-12 setting, the legal and reputational fallout can also be amplified by contractual obligations to school districts, state student-privacy laws, and public scrutiny from parents and boards.

For in-house counsel and compliance teams, the Illuminate order is a useful enforcement marker. It underscores the need to revisit vendor-management processes, incident-response planning, retention practices, and technical safeguards around access controls, patching, encryption, and network monitoring. Counsel advising ed-tech clients should also expect more diligence questions from school customers and more pointed representations and indemnity demands in procurement contracts.

Litigators should view the case as significant beyond the regulatory sphere. FTC findings and settlement allegations often become a roadmap for follow-on civil litigation, including consumer privacy suits, school district claims, and class actions alleging negligence, unfair practices, or breach of contract. Even where plaintiffs face standing or damages hurdles, an FTC action can reshape settlement leverage and narrow the range of defensible arguments about what “reasonable” security should have looked like.

The broader takeaway is that children’s and student data occupy a special place in privacy enforcement. Regulators are treating failures in this space not as routine cybersecurity lapses, but as high-stakes governance problems. For legal professionals counseling schools, software vendors, and managed-service providers, the Illuminate matter is a timely warning that security controls, privacy promises, and board-level oversight must align before an incident—not after one.

news.titleEn: AI in Insurance: The Real Test Is Readiness, Not Technology
news.titleZh: 保险业中的AI：真正的考验是准备程度，而非技术
news.summaryZh: 经过数年对生成式AI、机器学习和AI代理的实验，许多保险公司不再质疑AI是否应融入业务，而是面临更棘手的问题：试点项目是否具备规模化条件。答案通常不在于模型架构或工具的新颖性，而在于组织如何讨论AI——领导者能否将用例与具体业务成果挂钩、明确所需流程变革，并解释人类团队如何在日常工作中依赖AI输出。技术上令人印象深刻的试点若仅解决“有趣”而非重要的问题，仍可能失败。最可能规模化的AI用例是嵌入核心工作流程的，而非作为附属实验。在保险业，这通常意味着为核保、理赔或运营团队提供工具，帮助其更有效地审查、排序和决策，同时保持清晰的人类监督与问责。规模化问题同时也是治理问题。在扩展AI试点前，组织需明确AI是用于决策、推荐、总结信息还是辅助员工提速，并掌握用户信任度、何时覆盖AI建议以及可能在下游互联系统中产生的风险数据。推进过快而无治理会引发监管与运营担忧，但等待过久同样存在风险。最能适应下一阶段AI应用的保险公司，将把规模化视为准备度检验：在试点成为企业一部分之前，协调好商业价值、工作流程设计、监督、基础设施和监管预期。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! After several years of experimenting with generative AI, machine learning, and AI agents, many insurers are no longer asking whether AI belongs in the business. The harder question is whether a pilot is ready to scale. The answer usually is not found in the model architecture or the novelty of the tool. It is found in how the organization talks about AI: whether leaders can tie the use case to specific business outcomes, define the process changes required, and explain how human teams will rely on the output in day-to-day work. That distinction matters because AI can easily become a solution in search of a problem. A technically impressive pilot may still fail if it addresses an “interesting” problem rather than an important one. The AI use cases most likely to scale are the ones embedded into core workflows, not bolted on as side experiments. In insurance, that often means giving underwriters, claims teams, or operations personnel tools that help them review, prioritize, and decide more effectively, while preserving clear human oversight and accountability. For carriers, the scaling question is also a governance question. Before expanding an AI pilot, organizations need to be clear about whether AI is making decisions, recommending actions, summarizing information, or helping employees work faster. They also need data showing whether users trust the tool, when they override it, and where it may create downstream risk across interconnected systems. Moving too fast without governance creates obvious regulatory and operational concerns. But waiting too long has its own risk. The carriers best positioned for the next phase of AI adoption will be those that treat scaling as a readiness exercise: aligning business value, workflow design, oversight, infrastructure, and regulatory expectations before the pilot becomes part of the enterprise. news.titleEn: Five Eyes Issue “Call to Action” to Protect Against AI Cyber Threats
news.titleZh: 五眼联盟发布“行动呼吁”以防范人工智能网络威胁
news.summaryZh: 2026年6月22日，五眼联盟（澳大利亚、新西兰、加拿大、英国和美国）网络安全机构负责人发布题为《网络风险中的人工智能转变：领导者为何必须立即行动》的警报，呼吁组织采取行动防范网络威胁。人工智能正在迅速改变网络风险，既能提升网络防御能力，也使网络攻击更快、规模更大、更先进。网络韧性对业务连续性、市场信心和长期成功至关重要，网络风险不仅是技术问题，更是业务风险和领导责任。董事会和高管必须确保系统具有韧性，并能在实际事件中发挥作用。警报列出了领导者的关键行动，包括将网络安全纳入核心业务战略、重新审视过往决策、谨慎使用人工智能以加强防御而非仅提升效率。此外，还提出了“紧急”实际措施，建议领导者利用人工智能工具检测、监控和防御网络攻击。五眼联盟呼吁所有组织领导者审查并实施这些建议，以做好组织和社会层面的准备。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The leaders of the Five Eyes cyber security agencies, representing Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, issued an alert on June 22, 2026, entitled “The AI Shift in Cyber Risk: Why Leaders Must Act Now” urging organizations to a “call to action” to protect against cyber threats both for organizations and society as a whole. The Five Eyes are expressing urgency because artificial intelligence (AI) is quickly changing cyber risk, and organizations need to act fast to keep up. The call to action is informed by the fact that AI can improve cyber defense, but it also makes cyber-attacks faster, larger, and more advanced, including how attacks happen and how organizations can defend against them. Because of this, the Five Eyes urge that cyber resilience is critical for business continuity, market confidence, and long-term success. The Five Eyes encourage leaders to: The alert emphasizes how “success for organizations depends on getting the basics right, acting quickly, and making cybersecurity part of the core business strategy.” It stresses that cyber risk is not just a technical issue—it is a business risk and a leadership responsibility. Boards and executives must ensure systems are resilient and work under pressure. It is not enough to have controls; leaders must know those controls will work during a real incident. This may require rethinking past decisions and using AI carefully to strengthen defenses, not just improve efficiency. The alert outlines key actions for leaders, including: It also lists “urgent” practical actions: It also suggests that leaders use AI to strengthen defense against cyber-attacks. Getting ahead of cyber-attacks when threat actors are using AI requires continued preparedness and the ability to use tools to detect, monitor, and defend against them, including AI tools developed for defense purposes. If ever there was digital warfare, it is now with the proliferation of AI enhanced tools. Leaders of all organizations should review the recommendations by the Five Eyes and implement them for the preparedness of the organization and society. More Upcoming Events

news.titleEn: Consider Secure or Closed AI Systems: Recent Protective Orders Provide Guidance for Businesses Seeking to Use AI Tools Legally and Ethically
news.titleZh: 考虑使用安全或封闭的AI系统：近期保护令为企业合法且合乎道德地使用AI工具提供指导
news.summaryZh: 企业采用人工智能工具面临信息保密、安全和隐私风险。诉讼中，当事人和法官也在考虑AI工具的使用，同时需履行保护信息的义务。美国治安法官发布的两项保护令识别了某些AI工具可能对信息保密性、安全性和隐私产生负面影响的方面，并为使用这些工具的当事人设定了要求和禁令。这些保护令有助于企业理解AI工具使用中的隐私和安全风险，并确保其使用符合保护和信息管理的法律及道德义务。保护令为诉讼中各类受保护信息的披露和使用设定规则，确保信息仅用于诉讼目的、安全保管、仅向相关人员披露，并在诉讼结束后返还。在合同背景下，保密协议和数据保护协议等也规定了类似要求。某些AI工具的功能可能威胁诉讼中数据的完整性和安全性，法官将其称为“公共”或“开放”AI工具。由于这些工具可能使用输入信息训练和优化模型，因此可能无法删除或“撤回”受保护信息，导致信息在当事人控制之外被使用和披露。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! This is part of a series from Nelson Mullins' AI Task Force. We will continue to provide additional insight on both domestic and international matters across various industries spanning both the public and private sectors. Businesses looking to adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are confronting the risks that accompany these tools. One such risk is the possibility that inputting information into an AI tool may imperil the confidentiality (including privilege), security, and privacy of that information. Parties and judges involved in litigation matters are also considering the use of AI tools while taking into account various obligations to protect information and limit its use and disclosure. Two recent protective orders issued by U.S. Magistrate Judges identify and describe those aspects of certain AI tools that may negatively affect the confidentiality, security, and privacy of information, and establish requirements and prohibitions for parties seeking to use those tools. These orders may help businesses 1) understand the privacy and security risks involved in the use of AI tools; and 2) ensure that the use of AI tools is consistent with legal and ethical duties to protect and manage information. A protective order sets the ground rules for the disclosure and use of various types of protected information (typically labeling that protected information as “Confidential Information”) in discovery and at trial while protecting against unauthorized disclosure or misuse of that Confidential Information. More specifically, a protective order helps ensure that Confidential Information is 1) used only for the limited purpose of the litigation; 2) maintained securely during the litigation; 3) disclosed only to those involved; and 4) returned to the disclosing party at the end of the litigation. In the contractual context, confidentiality agreements, data protection agreements (DPAs) and other business arrangements memorialize similar requirements designed to ensure the confidentiality, security, and privacy of sensitive information, including personal information. Similarly, a protective order also allows parties to “claw back” confidential or privileged information disclosed inadvertently. Jeffries v. Harcros Chemicals Inc., 2026 WL 82018 (D. Kan. March 25, 2026) (“Harcros Chemicals”) highlights the elements of certain AI tools that can be problematic for maintaining confidentiality, security, and privacy: “the way [some] AI Tools function poses a potential threat to the integrity and security of data produced in litigation.” Judge Mitchell calls these “public” or “open” AI tools. Because these tools may use inputted information to train and improve their models, it may not be possible to delete or “claw back” protected information from those tools. research.titleEn: Legal Domain Adaptation of Modern BERT Models
research.titleZh: 现代BERT模型的法律领域适应
research.abstractEn: We investigate domain adaptation of modern BERT models in the legal domain. We further pre-train ModernBERT on all US court opinions using the masked language modeling objective. Although ModernBERT has been trained on roughly 500x more data than original BERT, we still find that this model benefits from further pre-training and domain adaptation in the legal domain: we report significant improvements compared to vanilla ModernBERT on all datasets connected to US court opinions. We find gains similar to those reported in early work on domain adaptation of BERT-like models. However, from scratch pre-training does not match the performance of further pre-training an existing ModernBERT checkpoint in our experiments. The resulting models are capable of processing sequences up to 8,192 tokens, and can be used to compute meaningful embeddings of legal passages, or could quickly rerank hundreds of legal passages for a given search query. We release all model checkpoints publicly.
research.abstractZh: 我们研究了现代BERT模型在法律领域的领域适应。我们使用掩码语言建模目标，在所有美国法院意见上进一步预训练ModernBERT。尽管ModernBERT的训练数据量大约是原始BERT的500倍，但我们仍然发现该模型在法律领域的进一步预训练和领域适应中受益：我们报告了在所有与美国法院意见相关的数据集上，与原始ModernBERT相比的显著改进。我们观察到的改进与早期关于BERT类模型领域适应的工作中报告的改进相似。然而，在我们的实验中，从头开始预训练并不比在现有ModernBERT检查点上进一步预训练的表现更好。生成的模型能够处理长达8,192个标记的序列，并可用于计算法律段落的有意义嵌入，或快速重新排序给定搜索查询的数百个法律段落。我们公开发布所有模型检查点。

research.titleEn: A Tree-of-Thoughts Inspired Hybrid Approach for Legal Case Judgement Summarization using LLMs
research.titleZh: 一种受思维树启发的混合方法：利用大语言模型进行法律案例判决摘要
research.abstractEn: In recent times, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for legal case judgement summarization. Most prior works have tried traditional extractive and abstractive summarization of case judgements. However, hybrid or extractive-abstractive techniques have not been explored much. In this work, we propose a novel tree-of-thoughts inspired extractive-abstractive summarization approach for legal judgement summarization. We conduct experiments using two popular LLMs, DeepSeek and LLama, and compare among extractive, abstractive and extractive-abstractive summarization. Our experiments show that the proposed extractive-abstractive prompt provides better summaries compared to other types of LLM prompts.
research.abstractZh: 近年来，大语言模型（LLMs）越来越多地被用于法律案例判决摘要。以往的大多数工作尝试了传统的抽取式和生成式案例判决摘要。然而，混合或抽取-生成式技术尚未得到充分探索。在这项工作中，我们提出了一种新颖的受思维树启发的抽取-生成式摘要方法，用于法律判决摘要。我们使用两种流行的大语言模型DeepSeek和LLama进行实验，并比较了抽取式、生成式和抽取-生成式摘要。我们的实验表明，所提出的抽取-生成式提示相比其他类型的大语言模型提示能提供更好的摘要。

news.titleEn: Supreme Court Reverses and Remands in No. 24-856: What the Bare Judgment Means
news.titleZh: 最高法院在第24-856号案中作出撤销原判并发回重审的裁决：简易判决的含义
news.summaryZh: 2026年6月23日，最高法院在第24-856号案中作出简易裁决：撤销下级法院判决并发回重审。目前未附具法律意见书。撤销并发回重审意味着最高法院认定原判错误，需进一步审理，其效力高于单纯的撤销判决。实务中，律师需关注发回重审的具体范围，包括哪些争点仍可辩论、哪些论点受限于授权规则，以及是否需要补充事实或修改救济措施。该裁决不自动创设广泛先例，除非后续意见书阐明新规则。目前最稳妥的理解是程序性而非实体性：原判已被推翻，案件返回下级法院依最高法院指令继续审理。从业者应密切跟踪后续程序，因为该裁决的实际影响将首先在重审中显现。
news.bodyHtml:
The Supreme Court’s June 23, 2026 disposition in No. 24-856 is notably concise: the judgment below was reversed and the case remanded. At least from the docket entry provided, the Court has not supplied an accompanying merits opinion in the materials summarized here. Even so, that procedural posture carries real significance for lawyers tracking the case and for practitioners thinking about next steps in the lower courts.

A reversal and remand means the Supreme Court concluded the lower court’s judgment cannot stand and that further proceedings are required. That is more consequential than a vacatur standing alone: reversal signals that the court below reached the wrong result, while remand leaves implementation of the Supreme Court’s directive to the lower court. The practical question for counsel is what, exactly, the remand permits or requires. That will depend on the full order and any accompanying opinion, concurrence, or dissent.

Without a written opinion in the summary provided, practitioners should be cautious about overstating the decision’s doctrinal reach. A Supreme Court reversal can announce a new rule, apply existing precedent to a particular record, or correct an error of statutory interpretation, jurisdiction, procedure, or remedy. But unless and until the Court’s reasoning is available, the safest takeaway is procedural rather than substantive: the lower court’s decision has been undone, and the case returns for further action consistent with the Supreme Court’s mandate.

Why does that matter? First, for parties in the case, remand proceedings often become the real battleground. Lawyers will need to assess what issues remain open, what arguments may be foreclosed by the mandate rule, and whether factual development, supplemental briefing, or a revised remedy is now in play. Second, for appellate practitioners, a summary reversal or short-form judgment can be an important signal that the Court viewed the error below as sufficiently clear to warrant correction without an extended merits discussion. That can influence how similarly situated litigants frame cert petitions and oppositions going forward.

It is also worth noting what this disposition does not necessarily do. A reversal and remand does not automatically create broad new precedent unless the Court’s opinion says something novel. If the decision rests on settled law applied to unusual facts, its broader impact may be limited. If, however, the eventual opinion clarifies the governing standard, burden, or remedial framework, this case could quickly become a citation target in trial and appellate briefing.

For now, the key development is clear: the Supreme Court has rejected the judgment below and sent the matter back. Practitioners should monitor the mandate and any further lower-court proceedings closely, because the operational meaning of this ruling will likely emerge there first.

View full case on Docket Alarm

news.titleEn: Jackson Lewis Wins the 2026 Litera Foundation Innovation Award for Turning Matter Data into a Firm-Wide Growth Asset
news.titleZh: Jackson Lewis 因将案件数据转化为全所增长资产荣获 2026 年 Litera 基金会创新奖
news.summaryZh: Litera 宣布 Jackson Lewis 获得 2026 年基金会创新奖，表彰其将 Litera Foundation 平台定制化，集中经验数据、提升客户响应并推动业务增长。该奖项由 Litera CEO Avaneesh Marwaha 在亚特兰大举行的 Trailblazers Summit 2026 上颁发。Jackson Lewis 在竞标中因缺乏关键案件数据，意识到问题不仅是技术性的，系统升级无法解决。团队与咨询公司合作，利用生成式 AI 根据模板从案件文档起草叙事，律师仅需审阅。此举还发现了多个有机案件数据源并纳入工作流。目前 Foundation 中超过 30,000 个案件拥有丰富档案和详细叙事，为业务拓展和律师提供可搜索的可靠数据。
news.bodyHtml:
Litera CEO Avaneesh Marwaha presented the award at the Trailblazers Summit 2026 in Atlanta

 

CHICAGO – June 25, 2026 – Litera, the legal AI platform provider that best unifies the practice and business of law, announced that Jackson Lewis P.C., a law firm with more than 1,100 attorneys in the U.S., is the recipient of the 2026 Foundation Innovation Award. The achievement recognizes outstanding innovation in how firms push Litera Foundation beyond its traditional use case, customizing it to meet their unique operational needs to centralize experience data, improve client responsiveness, and drive business growth. The award was presented by Litera CEO Avaneesh Marwaha at the Trailblazers Summit 2026, held June 9–10, 2026, at the Troutman Pepper Locke Atlanta office. 

 

“The Foundation Innovation Awards celebrate firms that are raising the bar on client value and service delivery,” said Sean Munafo, Chief Revenue Officer, Litera. “Differentiation today comes down to how effectively a firm can harness its data to clearly demonstrate where and how it creates impact for clients. Congratulations to Jackson Lewis for building a foundation that strengthens attorney performance, sharpens client engagement, and makes their value proposition clear at every interaction.”

 

When a high-profile pitch lacked key matter data, Jackson Lewis recognized that the issue was not simply technical and that a system upgrade alone would not solve it. In collaboration with Lynn Oser, founder of LKO Information Management Consulting, the Jackson Lewis Foundation team, led by Trina diNapoli, Director of Marketing & Business Development Operations and Systems, began using generative AI to draft matter narratives from case documents, guided by templates designed to shape AI responses.

 

This approach addressed one of the team’s biggest challenges: creating robust narratives that attorneys would only need to review rather than draft from scratch. The effort also revealed several organic sourcesof matter data across the firm, which the team incorporated into the workflow. As a result, more than 30,000 matters in Foundation now include enriched profiles and detailed narratives, giving business development teams and attorneys searchable, reliable client and matter data for client work, pitches, and proposals.

 

“We’re committed to continuous improvement, always moving forward, and not waiting for perfection before taking action,” said Trina diNapoli. “I understand the great potential Foundation has to inform every aspect of a law firm’s business, and we’re just getting started. I’m excited to take it to the next level, proving value every step of the way.”

 

Award finalists were evaluated by a panel of experts based on innovation, integration, and potential to inspire the broader Foundation community, including Carrie Remhof, Director of Firm Intelligence, Troutman Pepper Locke, who took home the award last year and now brings that firsthand perspective to judging this year’s finalists.

 

The Foundation user community, representing over 100 firms, recently convened at the Trailblazers Summit 2026, a peer-focused event led by Troutman Pepper Locke, featuring a series of 13 sessions led by 30 industry experts from FBT Gibbons, Sheppard, Crowell & Moring, Ropes & Gray, Cleary Gottlieb, Litera, and more. The two-day event was attended by 40 of the Am Law 100 and featured an in-person Q&A session with Litera CEO Avaneesh Marwaha, who fielded questions from Foundation customers.

 

About Jackson Lewis P.C.

Focused on employment and labor law since 1958, Jackson Lewis P.C.’s 1,100+ attorneys located in major cities nationwide consistently identify and respond to new ways workplace law intersects business. We help employers develop proactive strategies, strong policies and business-oriented solutions to cultivate high-functioning workforces that are engaged and stable and share our clients’ goals to emphasize belonging and respect for the contributions of every employee. For more information, visit: jacksonlewis.com.

 

About LKO Information Management Consulting

LKO Information Management Consulting, LLC provides consulting services to law firm administrative teams helping them to harness the power of internal and external information. We work with clients to identify information needs, harmonize the information within the organization, and develop processes for both reactive and proactive information management. We focus on strategy, process improvement, service excellence, and collaborative information aggregation and delivery.  We provide direction and support in the areas of experience management, knowledge management, client relationship management, data quality and harmonization, as well as information taxonomy.  We strive to turn information into a leveraged asset for building and running an optimized organization.  For more information, please contact us at info@lkoinfo.com.

 

About Litera
Litera is the legal AI platform provider that best unifies the practice and business of law, built on 30 years of legal expertise that no AI startup can shortcut, and engineered for the decades ahead. The company combines purpose-built legal technology with Lito, its award-winning Legal AI agent, to Raise The Bar™ for the legal profession worldwide. With AI solutions spanning legal drafting, document comparison, contract review, knowledge management, business development, and more, Litera serves over 15,000 global customers and 2.3 million daily users, including 99% of the Am Law 100. Integrated directly into Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace across devices, Litera delivers the right data, in the right place, at the right time – reducing context-switching so lawyers can practice law, not manage tools, while winningmore business, driving efficiency and the deeper client relationships that fuel sustainable growth. For more information, visit litera.com or follow us on LinkedIn.

 

Litera Press Contacts:
Jared Albert
PR & Communications Strategist
jared.albert@litera.com 

 

Tracy Wemett 

BroadPR, Inc. for Litera 

twemett@broadpr.com 

+1-617-939-3631

news.titleEn: Two upgrades come to LexBlog Platform email notifications
news.titleZh: LexBlog平台邮件通知迎来两项升级
news.summaryZh: LexBlog平台对其邮件通知系统进行了两项升级。在算法和AI时代，邮件对于维护与读者的直接关系至关重要，律师和律所长期以来依赖邮件列表进行内容分发。独立且专注的出版物具有价值，AI系统也更信任真实、权威的专家评论。升级后的邮件系统允许用户订阅同一律所的多个出版物，以满足读者在不同法律领域（如雇佣法、数据隐私、政府 advocacy）的需求。
news.bodyHtml:
In today’s world of algorithms and AI, emails are an increasingly essential part of publishing—vital for maintaining and nurturing a direct relationship with your audience.

A work isn’t truly “published” until it’s been distributed to the publication’s dedicated subscribers.

Lawyers and law firms have long relied on these lists, going back the entire 20-year lifespan of LexBlog as a company. Heck, there have been countless blogs that started as email digests. And now, as a means of cutting through the noise, they’re more important than effort.

As such, we’ve looked at ways we can improve and further modernize our platform’s email delivery setup and arrived at two quick and simple product updates.

The multi-blog email subscribe form

At LexBlog, we know there’s value in having independent and focused publications. It’s good to state with authority that “this is what this publication is about—and it is a publication!—so you know you can always come here for insight on the subject.”

We think the AI systems agree, too.

Search has always loved tightly-bound and focused entities, trusting that a site with a ton of information on a subject is a good place to send readers who type in terms related to it.

AI follows much the same pattern, trusting real and authentic expert commentary and, when possible, driving people towards it.

I thought we were talking about email?

Right, right.

While it’s valuable to have these focused independent publications, firms do want readers to know that they can subscribe to more than one of theirs—if they want.

You never know when someone’s employment law work leads to data privacy work and then, hey, they need some help with government advocacy, too.

Enter the multi-blog email subscribe form. It’s simple: subscribe to multiple firm blogs from any firm blog.

Have a look:

Independent publications on a unified publishing network. The best of both worlds.

We’ve already reached out to firms on our platform with the biggest publishing networks but if you haven’t heard from us yet and would like this on your publications, reach out and we’ll get you all set.

Full-text email notifications

This one’s just as simple but, perhaps, not as well understood. We’ll explain.

First off, the move: we’ve adjusted the email notifications our blog send to now contain the full text of the post they reference.

Before, subscribers would be notified that a new post had been published, receive a short excerpt, if anything more than the title, and have to click through to the post to actually read it.

This was industry standard for a long while. Not anymore, and we’re following suit.

Why? Having your dedicated audience read your post is more important than where they read it—and anything that makes it easier for them to read that insight is a good move in our book.

Not yours? Does it mess with some of your reporting? Is there some fine-tuning we can do, whether it’s to the emails or getting you subscriber and readership data for the emails? Is something not looking right with the emails? Or, perhaps you’re seeing something funky with a website integration using this email RSS feed?

Let us know and we’ll get everything set to your liking. We’re on the same team here.

Onward and upward.
