news.titleEn: Careers Insights: Anjelica Garcia joins Steno from Red Bull
news.titleZh: 职业洞察：安杰莉卡·加西亚从红牛加入Steno
news.summaryZh: 安杰莉卡·加西亚于四月从红牛加入Steno，担任首席人力官。Steno提供技术驱动的法庭报告和诉讼支持服务。她负责人才战略和文化塑造，确保对客户的可靠性和关怀也体现在团队管理中。她认为从红牛到法律科技的转变是自然的，因为两者都在动态行业中打造优质品牌。她强调文化基于日常体验，高绩效团队需要目标清晰、管理者能力强、反馈机制健全。她指出进入法律行业的主要挑战是深入了解行业结构和运作方式，但将其视为学习曲线而非障碍。她职业生涯的成就体现在帮助领导者成长、改善团队运作、扩大员工福利等方面。她建议尽早建立个人顾问团，以应对工作和生活的变化。她还透露Steno团队中有数十名律师，分布在销售和营销等非传统岗位。
news.bodyHtml:
Anjelica Garcia joined Steno in April from Red Bull and here she shares with Legal IT Insider her immediate thoughts and reflections on joining the legal technology sector; the culture and philosophies she brings with her; and what the biggest challenges are; her biggest achievement to date; and the one piece of advice she wish she had received.

Anjelica welcome to legal, how would you describe your new role in Steno’s leadership team?

Advertisement

I’ve recently stepped into the role of chief people officer at Steno. We provide tech-enabled court reporting and litigation support services, but at our core, we’re a people-driven business. I’m overseeing our talent strategy and helping shape our culture. I want to ensure that the same reliability and care we provide to our legal clients are baked into the way we treat our own team as we scale up.

What made you switch from Red Bull and the sports and entertainment world to legal technology?

Advertisement

On the surface, moving from Red Bull to legal technology looks like a significant shift. For me, the throughline is clear: we are building premium brands in dynamic industries. Over the past decade, sports and media have been transformed, especially in content creation, distribution, and consumption. Organisations had to rapidly adapt to change while upholding a strong identity and high standards. The true leaders in this new landscape didn’t just keep up, they set the benchmark for excellence.

Similarly, legal technology is experiencing its own transformation. There are clear changes in how legal work is getting done, alongside rising expectations around speed and quality.

What philosophies around culture and building winning teams will you bring with you?

Culture is built on the experiences people have every day at work. It is reflected in the behaviours that are rewarded, the implicit norms, and where attention is placed. The most effective organisations create environments where people find meaning in their work and feel a sense of belonging within their teams. They also foster ownership and clear pathways to building excellence in one’s craft and career.

That can happen organically in smaller environments. However, as organisations grow, it becomes more difficult. At that stage, it requires deliberate design, clarity in goals, strong manager capability, consistent feedback loops, and systems that reinforce both performance and development.

Truly high-performing teams are not just effective, they are aligned and resilient. My goal is to build an environment where both individuals and teams achieve this consistently.

Is there any crossover in terms of skills for a chief people officer in both sectors?

The core of the chief people officer role is consistent regardless of industry. It’s about building the approach, practices, and systems that allow a company to translate strategy into execution through its people. That includes organisational design, leadership development, performance management, and ensuring that incentives and ways of working are aligned with business priorities. Whether the context is consumer products, media, or legal technology, those fundamentals don’t change.
What does change is the operating environment – pace, regulatory considerations, and talent markets. The underlying discipline remains the same: understanding what the business needs, building the right structure and leadership capability, and evolving both as the company grows.

What are the biggest challenges to making the switch into the legal world?

I would say the main challenge (and my current priority) is getting a deep understanding of the industry – its structure, stakeholders, and the nuances that shape how work gets done. Legal services have their own rhythms, regulatory considerations, and long-standing ways of operating that are distinct from other sectors.

But I see that as a learning curve rather than a barrier. In fact, the advantage of coming from outside the industry is the ability to see patterns more objectively and to consider how principles around effective teams and high-performing organisations might apply in this context.

My focus so far has been on listening and learning. That is where I would start in any new role. I am spending time with people across the legal ecosystem to better understand how the work really happens, Steno’s strengths as an employer and partner, and where our opportunities lie.

How did your career to date prepare you for your current role?

My career has largely been shaped in high-growth environments where organisations needed to evolve to keep pace with the industry and their ambitions. Early on, I focused on building the foundational systems – talent management, analytics, and organizational design – that help to create clarity and consistency as a company scales.

As my career progressed, I applied those same principles in even more complex environments, supporting significant expansion across multiple lines of business and operating models.

Throughout my experience, linking performance and people through practical systems and leadership is a constant theme. That will remain at the heart of our talent and culture strategy at Steno.

What has been your biggest achievement in your career so far?

I tend not to think about any of my achievements as singular, visible milestones. A significant portion of our lives is spent at work, and what I’ve valued most in my career is the role I’ve been able to play in shaping how people feel during that time.

The impact often shows up in tangible, but ‘small’ ways – helping a leader become more effective, building systems that improve how teams operate, expanding access to benefits that support employees and their families, or creating opportunities for individuals to grow into roles they might not have otherwise had access to.

These everyday moments, though rarely visible, build strong organisations and help to move a business forward. Their lasting impact on individuals and families is what I find truly meaningful and is my greatest achievement.

Looking back, what piece of advice do you wish you had received earlier in your career?

I’m a big believer in intentionally building a personal advisory board, and I’d encourage everyone to do it earlier in their careers. It doesn’t need to be a formal structure, but a group of people you trust to help you navigate different aspects of your life and career as you move through it.

The pace of change in the working world is significant, and when you layer in different stages of life and career, it becomes difficult for any one person, whether a manager or a mentor, to be the right sounding board for everything.

Having a small group of trusted voices who understand your context and can offer a clear, direct perspective is incredibly valuable. It improves decision-making over time and gives you a level of perspective hard to build on your own.

Tell us something people don’t already know about Steno’s team?

We have dozens of lawyers across the company, in places you wouldn’t expect, like sales and marketing. Even our new SVP and head of sales, Jeff Herscott, who joined at the same time as me, comes from a BigLaw background. I always joke that we have enough legal talent here that we could go off and start our own firm.

Our thanks to Anjelica for sharing her thoughts and experiences, if you would like to be our next Career Insights guest, message caroline@legaltechnology.com
news.bodyText:
Anjelica Garcia joined Steno in April from Red Bull and here she shares with Legal IT Insider her immediate thoughts and reflections on joining the legal technology sector; the culture and philosophies she brings with her; and what the biggest challenges are; her biggest achievement to date; and the one piece of advice she wish she had received.

Anjelica welcome to legal, how would you describe your new role in Steno’s leadership team?

I’ve recently stepped into the role of chief people officer at Steno. We provide tech-enabled court reporting and litigation support services, but at our core, we’re a people-driven business. I’m overseeing our talent strategy and helping shape our culture. I want to ensure that the same reliability and care we provide to our legal clients are baked into the way we treat our own team as we scale up.

What made you switch from Red Bull and the sports and entertainment world to legal technology?

On the surface, moving from Red Bull to legal technology looks like a significant shift. For me, the throughline is clear: we are building premium brands in dynamic industries. Over the past decade, sports and media have been transformed, especially in content creation, distribution, and consumption. Organisations had to rapidly adapt to change while upholding a strong identity and high standards. The true leaders in this new landscape didn’t just keep up, they set the benchmark for excellence.

Similarly, legal technology is experiencing its own transformation. There are clear changes in how legal work is getting done, alongside rising expectations around speed and quality.

What philosophies around culture and building winning teams will you bring with you?

Culture is built on the experiences people have every day at work. It is reflected in the behaviours that are rewarded, the implicit norms, and where attention is placed. The most effective organisations create environments where people find meaning in their work and feel a sense of belonging within their teams. They also foster ownership and clear pathways to building excellence in one’s craft and career.

That can happen organically in smaller environments. However, as organisations grow, it becomes more difficult. At that stage, it requires deliberate design, clarity in goals, strong manager capability, consistent feedback loops, and systems that reinforce both performance and development.

Truly high-performing teams are not just effective, they are aligned and resilient. My goal is to build an environment where both individuals and teams achieve this consistently.

Is there any crossover in terms of skills for a chief people officer in both sectors?

The core of the chief people officer role is consistent regardless of industry. It’s about building the approach, practices, and systems that allow a company to translate strategy into execution through its people. That includes organisational design, leadership development, performance management, and ensuring that incentives and ways of working are aligned with business priorities. Whether the context is consumer products, media, or legal technology, those fundamentals don’t change. What does change is the operating environment – pace, regulatory considerations, and talent markets. The underlying discipline remains the same: understanding what the business needs, building the right structure and leadership capability, and evolving both as the company grows.

What are the biggest challenges to making the switch into the legal world?

I would say the main challenge (and my current priority) is getting a deep understanding of the industry – its structure, stakeholders, and the nuances that shape how work gets done. Legal services have their own rhythms, regulatory considerations, and long-standing ways of operating that are distinct from other sectors.

But I see that as a learning curve rather than a barrier. In fact, the advantage of coming from outside the industry is the ability to see patterns more objectively and to consider how principles around effective teams and high-performing organisations might apply in this context.

My focus so far has been on listening and learning. That is where I would start in any new role. I am spending time with people across the legal ecosystem to better understand how the work really happens, Steno’s strengths as an employer and partner, and where our opportunities lie.

How did your career to date prepare you for your current role?

My career has largely been shaped in high-growth environments where organisations needed to evolve to keep pace with the industry and their ambitions. Early on, I focused on building the foundational systems – talent management, analytics, and organizational design – that help to create clarity and consistency as a company scales.

As my career progressed, I applied those same principles in even more complex environments, supporting significant expansion across multiple lines of business and operating models.

Throughout my experience, linking performance and people through practical systems and leadership is a constant theme. That will remain at the heart of our talent and culture strategy at Steno.

What has been your biggest achievement in your career so far?

I tend not to think about any of my achievements as singular, visible milestones. A significant portion of our lives is spent at work, and what I’ve valued most in my career is the role I’ve been able to play in shaping how people feel during that time.

The impact often shows up in tangible, but ‘small’ ways – helping a leader become more effective, building systems that improve how teams operate, expanding access to benefits that support employees and their families, or creating opportunities for individuals to grow into roles they might not have otherwise had access to.

These everyday moments, though rarely visible, build strong organisations and help to move a business forward. Their lasting impact on individuals and families is what I find truly meaningful and is my greatest achievement.

Looking back, what piece of advice do you wish you had received earlier in your career?

I’m a big believer in intentionally building a personal advisory board, and I’d encourage everyone to do it earlier in their careers. It doesn’t need to be a formal structure, but a group of people you trust to help you navigate different aspects of your life and career as you move through it.

The pace of change in the working world is significant, and when you layer in different stages of life and career, it becomes difficult for any one person, whether a manager or a mentor, to be the right sounding board for everything.

Having a small group of trusted voices who understand your context and can offer a clear, direct perspective is incredibly valuable. It improves decision-making over time and gives you a level of perspective hard to build on your own.

Tell us something people don’t already know about Steno’s team?

We have dozens of lawyers across the company, in places you wouldn’t expect, like sales and marketing. Even our new SVP and head of sales, Jeff Herscott, who joined at the same time as me, comes from a BigLaw background. I always joke that we have enough legal talent here that we could go off and start our own firm.

Our thanks to Anjelica for sharing her thoughts and experiences, if you would like to be our next Career Insights guest, message caroline@legaltechnology.com

news.titleEn: The Judge Biography: Reading Between the Lines
news.titleZh: 法官传记：字里行间的解读
news.summaryZh:
法官传记有助于从初始阶段聚焦司法分析。就业历史、教育背景和专业隶属关系可以揭示有用的调查线索，并塑造律师处理州初审法院数据的方式。司法分析显示地方法院记录中的模式，而法官传记则帮助确定首先关注何处。

法官传记中的每个条目都可指向不同的调查方向。前一份工作暗示值得比较的动议类型；法学院指向值得与案卷对照的学科熟悉度；隶属关系则引发关于司法实践中的法理问题。结合州初审法院数据，法官传记不仅描述法官，还帮助识别首先需要提取哪些数据。例如，Trellis数据显示，佛罗里达州第九司法巡回法院的Luis F. Calderon法官批准即决判决动议的比率比县平均值高出近10个百分点，且在财产纠纷中，他将案件推进至审判的时间多出200多天。这些差异重塑了诉讼策略，影响成本、杠杆、和解压力及案件轨迹。
news.bodyText:
What can a judge biography tell you? A judge biography helps focus judicial analysis from the outset. Employment history, educational background, and professional affiliations can surface useful lines of inquiry and shape the questions attorneys bring to state trial court data. Judicial analytics show you patterns in local court records. Judge biographies help you decide where to look first.

At first glance, a judge biography looks straightforward: credentials, affiliations, and job titles listed in a familiar order.

But each entry can point to a different avenue of investigation.

A former job suggests which motion types are worth comparing. A law school points to subject-matter familiarity worth testing against a docket. An affiliation raises questions about jurisprudence in practice.

Used alongside state trial court data, a judge biography does more than describe a judge. It helps identify which numbers are worth pulling in the first place.

Where judicial outcomes diverge

While many cases are straightforward, doctrine inevitably runs out, leaving a judge to fill the gaps. This is especially true at the state trial court level, where legal standards are often broad, fact-dependent, and shaped by procedural discretion.

That discretion leaves measurable patterns in the data.

For example, Trellis data shows that the Hon. Luis F. Calderon of the 9th Judicial Circuit Court of Florida grants motions for summary judgment at a rate nearly 10 percentage points above the county average (left). His case timelines diverge just as sharply. In property disputes, Calderon takes more than 200 additional days to move cases to trial (right).

Differences like these reshape litigation strategy. They affect cost and leverage, settlement pressure and case trajectory.

How to read a judge biography for civil litigation

Reading a judge biography strategically means treating each entry as a hypothesis about judicial behavior — and then testing that hypothesis against docket data. The three categories below each point to a distinct set of questions worth bringing to the record.

Where has your judge worked?

Employment history is one of the most useful, and most studied , parts of a judge biography. Years in a role expose an attorney to recurring procedural environments, institutional constraints, and case-development norms. Those experiences can shape how a judge approaches litigation from the bench.

Prosecutor

A prosecutor typically works from records they didn’t build. Law enforcement develops the factual record; the prosecutor shapes it into a narrative. Over time, that dynamic can influence how judges think about evidentiary sufficiency, factual development, and dispositive motions.

Research prompts:

Pull dispositive motion data across procedural stages and examine whether outcomes cluster around moments of factual insufficiency.

Look at the plaintiff-defendant split across those motion types to test whether the judge’s expectations around record development fall more heavily on one side or the other.

Pull deposition scope rulings and examine whether the judge treats them as relevance questions or recognizes their function as testimony-locking tools.

Sole practitioner

A sole practitioner manages every stage of litigation directly, from client communication and factual development to motion practice and courtroom appearances. That experience creates firsthand exposure to the practical realities of moving a case forward without institutional support.

That background makes case pacing, discovery cost intervention, and atypical procedural demands worth closer examination.

Research prompts:

Pull case management timelines and compare them against county averages to test whether the judge moves cases faster or slower than peers—and at which procedural stages the gap appears.

Pull discovery dispute rulings and any sanctions or fee-shifting orders to examine whether the judge intervenes around litigation cost or procedural burden.

Pull the judge’s standing orders and examine whether they require pre-conference preparation that other judges in the same county don’t.

Corporate counsel

Corporate legal practice often requires evaluating legal issues alongside implementation concerns, operational realities, and business consequences. General counsel are not only trained to assess whether a position is legally sound, but also whether it works in practice.

That background makes remedies, commercial reasoning, and contractual enforcement worth closer examination.

Research prompts:

Pull rulings in commercial and business disputes and examine the written reasoning for engagement with implementation concerns, downstream effects, or administrative practices.

In cases involving injunctive or equitable relief, look at whether the judge’s orders address operational feasibility or stay tightly bound to legal standards.

Pull rulings on damages and examine whether the judge enforces contractual risk allocation as written or looks past it to equitable considerations.

Where did your judge study?

The educational background of a judge points to a separate set of questions. Geographic ties, specialized training, judicial clerkships, and public legal work each leave behind distinct professional footprints, pointing to local legal communities, academic specializations, and early judicial training. Those footprints tell you where to look in the docket before you open it.

Geographic & institutional ties

Many judges spend most of their careers in the same legal community where they trained. A judge who attended law school in the same state where they now preside may have longstanding professional relationships, deep familiarity with the informal dynamics of local practice, and roots in the same legal communities that regularly appear before the court.

That changes the unit of analysis. The question is not only how the judge behaves, but whether that behavior changes depending on who appears before the court.

Research prompts:

Pull the judge’s motion outcomes and case timelines and examine whether they cluster tightly around local court averages.

Pull motion outcomes for out-of-county counsel appearing before this judge and compare them against outcomes for local counsel on the same motion types.

Pull courtroom transcripts and examine the judge’s interactions with counsel. To what extent do they reflect familiarity, shorthand, and shared context?

Specialized academic training

Some educational backgrounds point to subject-matter familiarity that may become strategically relevant in litigation. Advanced degrees, public policy training, or academic concentrations can indicate sustained exposure to a body of doctrine, institutional framework, or technical subject matter.

That makes specialization a useful lens for asking whether a judge handles familiar subject matters differently from the rest of their docket.

Research prompts:

Pull the judge’s motion outcomes within the specialized subject area and compare them against their overall averages.

If your case touches a specialized area, pull how the judge has handled expert testimony and motions in limine in similar cases.

If the judge has no relevant specialization, examine whether technical disputes in similar cases tend to resolve procedurally rather than on the merits.

Clerkships

A clerkship offers unusually direct exposure to the internal mechanics of judicial decision-making: motion review, legal drafting, case management, and courtroom process. It also places attorneys inside specific procedural cultures and judicial chambers.

That background can shape how a judge approaches motion practice, courtroom procedure, and case management.

Research prompts:

Pull docket timelines and examine whether the judge’s ruling pace reflects the norms of the court where they clerked rather than the court where they now sit.

Pull the judge’s written rulings and examine whether the structure, depth, and procedural emphasis reflect the drafting culture of the chambers where they clerked.

Pull courtroom transcripts and examine whether the judge’s management of oral argument—how much latitude they give counsel, how quickly they intervene—mirrors the style of the judge for whom they clerked.

What memberships does your judge hold?

Professional memberships raise a different kind of strategic question. Affiliations point to the legal communities, the subject-matter conversations, and the professional environments a judge has chosen to spend time around. That context may help explain how a judge approaches judicial discretion, procedural fairness, or the practical consequences of litigation.

The Federalist Society

The Federalist Society is associated with debates around constitutional interpretation, statutory construction, and judicial restraint. If a judge lists involvement with the organization, use that as a signal to examine how interpretive questions appear in written reasoning.

Research prompts:

Pull rulings in cases involving statutory interpretation and examine whether the written reasoning treats textual and structural arguments as independently dispositive.

If your argument depends on legislative purpose or evolving standards, pull cases where similar arguments were made and examine whether the judge found them sufficient or anchored the analysis back to governing text.

Pull motion orders across case types and examine whether the reasoning stays tightly bound to record and legal text, or draws on broader policy or equitable considerations.

American Constitution Society

The American Constitution Society centers legal discussions around constitutional governance, civil rights, and the practical consequences of legal rules on access to justice. If a judge lists involvement with the organization, use that as a prompt to examine where equitable concerns appear in their motion practice

Research prompts:

Pull rulings involving equitable relief or institutional burdens and examine the written reasoning for engagement with downstream effects.

If your argument relies on doctrinal clarity alone, pull cases where similar arguments were made and examine whether the judge’s reasoning expanded to include implementation concerns.

Pull the judge’s motion practice in cases involving civil rights or institutional reform and examine whether outcomes or procedural treatment differ from the general docket.

Closing thoughts

A summary judgment grant rate tells you that a pattern exists. A case timeline tells you how a courtroom moves. A motion history tells you what happened next. But none of that tells you which numbers were worth pulling in the first place—or which ones you missed.

A judge biography changes that. It turns background information into investigative direction.

The next piece puts this into practice. We’ll use the Trellis Claude Connector to run these inquiries directly — pulling motion data, grant rates, and case timelines against the biographical questions raised here. If you want to try it before then, Trellis gives you direct access to state trial court data across thousands of jurisdictions.

FAQ

How do I connect Trellis to Claude? +

Setting up the Trellis Claude Connector takes less than a minute. In Claude, go to Settings, then Connectors. Search for Trellis and click Connect. Once connected, you can query Trellis state trial court data directly through Claude to pull judge analytics, motion outcomes, case timelines, and docket insights through natural language prompts.

What is the Trellis Claude Connector? +

The Trellis Claude Connector is an integration that allows attorneys and legal researchers to query Trellis state trial court data directly through Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant. Users can pull judge analytics, motion outcome data, case timelines, and docket insights through natural language queries without leaving their research workflow. The connector brings Trellis’s state trial court coverage directly into AI-assisted legal research.

Can Claude pull judge analytics and motion data? +

Yes. When connected through the Trellis Claude Connector, Claude can surface judge analytics, motion grant rates, case timelines, and state trial court docket data directly from Trellis. Attorneys can ask natural language questions about specific judges, motion types, or procedural patterns without manually searching through court records.

What is judicial analytics in legal research? +

Judicial analytics is the use of court data to identify patterns in how judges handle cases, including motion grant rates, procedural timelines, discovery rulings, and case outcomes. Platforms like Trellis make judicial analytics accessible at the state trial court level, where most litigation activity occurs but data has historically been difficult to access.

How do attorneys research judges before trial? +

Attorneys research judges by reviewing judicial biographies, analyzing motion outcomes and case timelines, examining written rulings, and comparing courtroom patterns against county averages. Trellis brings this information together in one platform, combining judge analytics with state trial court docket data across thousands of jurisdictions.

What motion data should attorneys review when researching a judge? +

The most useful motion data often includes grant and denial rates by motion type, plaintiff-versus-defendant outcomes, discovery rulings, sanctions, and procedural timelines. Trellis surfaces this data at the judge level and compares it against county averages so attorneys can identify meaningful deviations in judicial behavior.

How do attorneys access motion grant rates and case timelines for specific judges? +

Motion grant rates and case timelines for specific judges are available through Trellis, which aggregates and structures state trial court data across thousands of jurisdictions. Attorneys can analyze how a judge handles motions for summary judgment, motions in limine, discovery disputes, and other procedural issues before appearing in court.

What is state trial court data? +

State trial court data includes filings, motions, rulings, case outcomes, hearing activity, and procedural timelines generated in trial-level courts. Unlike appellate opinions, trial court data captures how litigation actually unfolds in practice. Trellis aggregates and structures this data across thousands of state courts to make it searchable and usable for litigation strategy and legal research.

Why does state trial court data matter for litigation strategy? +

Most litigation strategy happens at the trial court level, where judges make decisions on discovery disputes, dispositive motions, scheduling, and procedural management. State trial court data helps attorneys understand how judges handle these issues in practice. Trellis transforms fragmented trial court records into structured analytics attorneys can use before filing motions, negotiating settlements, or preparing for hearings.

What can a judge’s professional background tell you about courtroom behavior? +

A judge’s employment history, education, and professional affiliations can point to patterns in how they approach evidence, procedure, case management, and legal reasoning. A former prosecutor may evaluate factual sufficiency differently than a former corporate attorney. These signals become more useful when tested against actual motion data and case timelines in Trellis.

How do you use a judge’s employment history in litigation strategy? +

Each role in a judge’s professional background can reflect different procedural environments and litigation norms. A former sole practitioner may show sensitivity to litigation costs or procedural burden, while a former corporate counsel may focus more heavily on operational consequences in business disputes. Trellis allows attorneys to test these hypotheses against real state trial court data.

What does a judge’s law school or educational background reveal? +

A judge’s educational background can reveal geographic ties, specialized training, and professional communities that may shape how they approach litigation. Judges who trained and practiced in the same jurisdiction may show stronger alignment with local procedural norms. Trellis helps attorneys compare these signals against actual ruling patterns and motion outcomes.

How can a judge’s professional affiliations influence judicial decision-making? +

Professional affiliations can point to the legal communities and jurisprudential conversations a judge has engaged with throughout their career. Memberships associated with textualism, constitutional interpretation, or access to justice may influence how judges approach statutory interpretation or equitable arguments. Trellis helps attorneys test those theories against actual courtroom behavior and written rulings.

How does judicial analytics software work? +

Judicial analytics software aggregates court filings, motions, rulings, outcomes, and timelines, then organizes that information at the judge level to identify patterns in judicial behavior. Trellis applies this approach at scale across state trial courts, combining judge analytics with motion outcome data, case timelines, and docket-level insights.

What tools exist for researching state trial court judges? +

Most legal research platforms focus heavily on appellate opinions and provide limited visibility into state trial court activity. Trellis is purpose-built for state trial court research, offering judge analytics, motion outcome data, case timelines, docket insights, and AI-assisted legal research tools through the Trellis Claude Connector.

news.titleEn: Client Due Diligence Company Thirdfort Launches Rebuilt Platform With AI Features
news.titleZh: 客户尽职调查公司Thirdfort推出重构平台，集成AI功能
news.summaryZh: Thirdfort重构平台旨在帮助法律、房地产和会计行业的受监管实体完成客户尽职调查任务。该平台提供统一工作空间，用于身份和文件验证、企业背景调查、反洗钱筛查及资金来源分析。平台具备任务管理功能，可概览待办事项并自动升级检查；同时包含报告和活动日志，便于法律和合规团队向监管机构、保险公司及内部业务伙伴展示流程。平台新增AI功能，可扫描、提取和解释资金来源分析中的数据，并支持工程团队更轻松地集成其他尽职调查任务的AI功能。重构意味着客户可以信任AI，每个输出都显示其工作过程，有人工参与和完整审计追踪；对公司而言，可以更快地添加新功能、响应监管变化并构建更自动化的合规工作流。平台旨在让用户将整个客户尽职调查流程整合到一处，提高效率并降低警示信号被忽视的风险。重构平台还使Thirdfort能够根据客户需求和监管期望灵活添加新AI功能。合规团队面临监管要求更严格和收费人员及客户希望减少摩擦的双重压力，现有工具往往使工作更难，而重构平台从底层改变这一状况，让合规团队全面了解整个投资组合的风险。竞争对手包括ComplyAdvantage（AI驱动的欺诈和反洗钱风险检测）、EQS（收购了Convercent）、Diligent（AI驱动的尽职调查报告及增强尽职调查流程）、NICE Actimize和SymphonyAI（反洗钱软件解决方案）。
news.bodyHtml:
What It Is: Thirdfort’s rebuilt platform is designed to help regulated entities in the legal, property and accountancy sectors with customer due diligence tasks. The platform is built to provide a unified workspace for ID and document verification, know your business checks, anti-money laundering (AML) screening and source of funds analysis.

The platform features a task management function designed to provide users with an overview of outstanding actions and automatically escalate checks as required. It also includes a reporting and activity log designed to allow legal and compliance teams to demonstrate their processes to regulators, insurers and internal business partners.

The platform has also been upgraded with new artificial intelligence-powered features that are designed to scan, extract and interpret data used in source of funds analyses, and the rebuilt platform was structured to allow the Thirdfort engineering team to more easily incorporate new AI features for other due diligence tasks as they are developed.

“For our clients, [the rebuild] means AI they can trust—every output shows its workings, with a human in the loop and a full audit trail,” Thirdfort co-founder and chief product officer Jack Bidgood said in a press release announcing the launch. “For us, it means we can move faster than ever before: adding new capabilities, responding to regulatory changes and building toward a more automated compliance workflow.”

Why It’s Needed: The platform is intended to allow users to consolidate the entire customer due diligence process in a single place, allowing them to work more efficiently and lowering the chance of warning signs going undetected or unacted on.

The restructured platform is also intended to provide Thirdfort with greater flexibility to add in new AI features in response to customer demand and changing expectations and requirements from regulators.

“Compliance teams are under more pressure than ever—from regulators demanding greater rigor and from fee earners and their clients wanting less friction,” co-founder and CEO Olly Thornton-Berry said in the press release. “Too often, the tools they’re working with make that harder. We’ve rebuilt our platform from the ground up to change that, giving compliance teams full visibility of risk across their entire portfolio.”

The Competition: A number of companies offer software targeted at components of the client due diligence process. ComplyAdvantage provides AI-powered fraud and AML risk detection, and compliance software company EQS bought ethics and compliance platform Convercent in 2024.

Diligent offers a range of services from AI-powered due diligence reports to enhanced due diligence processes involving local investigators, and companies including NICE Actimize and SymphonyAI provide AML software solutions.

news.titleZh: Jylo在斯特拉斯堡开设新办公室
news.summaryZh: 伦敦创立的法律AI平台Jylo于5月19日宣布在法国斯特拉斯堡开设第二个办公室。该办公室靠近欧洲议会、欧洲委员会及欧盟主要监管机构，将作为Jylo服务其不断增长的欧洲客户群的运营基地。此举反映了各行业客户的强劲需求。斯特拉斯堡使公司处于欧洲治理中心，具备监管邻近性和文化理解力，能更好地服务客户。德国正成为Jylo的核心市场之一，其强大的专业服务行业、成熟的企业买家及对技术合作伙伴的高标准要求，使Jylo投资了针对德国的安全和隐私基础设施，包括增强的数据驻留选项和合规工具，以满足德国法律、金融和公共部门客户的期望。
news.bodyHtml:
London-founded legal AI platform Jylo today (19 May) announced the opening of a second office in Strasbourg, France. Located close to the European Parliament, the Council of Europe and key EU regulatory bodies, the new office will serve as Jylo’s operational base for its growing European client base.

Jylo says that the decision reflects strong demand from clients across various sectors, with Shawn Curran, Jylo’s co-founder & CEO commenting: “Strasbourg puts us exactly where our clients need us: at the centre of European governance, with regulatory proximity and cultural understanding to serve them properly.”

Advertisement

Germany is increasingly becoming one of Jylo’s core markets. Its strong professional services sector, sophisticated enterprise buyers, and high standards for evaluating technology partners make it a natural fit. Jylo has invested in security and privacy infrastructure tailored for Germany, including enhanced data residency options and compliance tooling built to meet the expectations of German legal, financial and public sector clients.

news.titleEn: Some Technical Questions About SCOTUS AI
news.titleZh: 关于最高法院AI的一些技术问题
news.summaryZh: 得克萨斯大学法学院教授John Greil作为客座博主，深入探讨Neal Katyal在TED演讲中描述的AI系统“Harvey”在最高法院关税案中的具体技术细节。Katyal声称Harvey是一个定制AI，基于25年来每位大法官在口头辩论中的所有提问及其所有书面意见进行训练，能够预测大法官的问题甚至部分意见。Greil提出多项技术疑问：Harvey如何将约1.2亿token的数据转化为可操作见解？系统是采用检索增强生成、微调还是预计算？它是否读取了案件书状？Harvey对首席大法官Roberts的预测具体是什么——是问题还是投票结果？这些模式是否已为最高法院律师界所知？公开信息不足以判断Harvey的实际技术实现和效果。
news.bodyText:
**[Ed. Note: Please welcome University of Texas Law [Professor John Greil](https://www.linkedin.com/in/john-greil-520a0622/) as our Guest Blogger. – GL]**

[Neal Katyal’s TED Talk](https://www.ted.com/talks/neal_kumar_katyal_what_really_won_the_trillion_dollar_supreme_court_case) detailing the role of AI in the tariffs case has drawn substantial attention in the legal world, including an [annotated](https://reason.com/volokh/2026/05/07/lets-talk-about-neal-katyals-ted-talk/) transcript; Bloomberg Law [reporting](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/katyals-boast-of-ai-role-in-tariff-win-draws-swift-blowback)the “blowback,” and David Lat providing an [on-the-record response](https://davidlat.substack.com/p/neal-katyal-tweet-ted-talk-harvey-tariffs-case-supreme-court-scotus-milbank-partner-former-acting-solicitor-general) from Mr. Katyal.

I’d like to dig into an aspect I haven’t seen receive as much attention: what exactly did the AI do to help prepare Katyal, and how did it do it? This is meant to be a bit of a deep dive for LLM nerds and those who are AI-pilled.

I approach these questions from the perspective of someone who has built AI tools for appellate argument preparation. So I’ve thought about these particular problems. [Bartolus.law](https://bartolus.law/) generates an interactive dashboard and prep report tailored to circuit panel, subject matter, and briefs. In building it, I’ve had dozens of trial-and-error lightbulbs about what has worked, and what hasn’t.

Having spent that time, there are some odd passages in the TED Talk describing what Katyal did, and what it produced that jumped out to me.

So in this post I’d like to highlight some of those passages, and try to ask some questions that would add some clarity.

**What do we know about how “Harvey Moot” works?**

In [his X post](https://x.com/neal_katyal/status/2052133764940382262?s=20) promoting the TED Talk, Katyal said:

> Harvey predicted many of the questions the Justices asked — sometimes almost word for word. Brilliant. Tireless. Occasionally insufferable.
> 
>  Here’s the catch: Harvey isn’t a person.
> 
>  Harvey is a bespoke AI I built over the last year with a legal AI company, trained on every question every Justice has asked in oral argument for 25 years, and everything they’ve ever written.

There was a bit more detail in the actual talk. From what I can tell, this is all of the meat on how it works, and how it was trained:

*   “Harvey reads the 200th tariff case the same way as he reads the first.”

*   “Harvey is an AI. A bespoke system I’d been building with a legal AI company for the last year.”

*   “I trained it on every question asked by a Supreme Court justice in the last 25 years and everything they’ve written, every opinion, every concurrence, every dissent, every separate opinion.”

*   “And in that, patterns emerged.”

*   “It predicted the contours of the very argument I would face.”

*   “Harvey taught me peripheral vision: the idea [that] if you read a lot, you can see patterns and come up with stuff and anticipate the angles of attack before it arrived.”

*   “It knew that Justice Gorsuch would ask me about the taxing power. It knew Justice Kavanaugh was going to grill me on tariffs versus embargoes. It nailed Justice Barrett’s worry about tariff refunds.”

*   “It didn’t just predict his question, it predicted a possible escape route.”

*   “Harvey even predicted Justice Gorsuch’s separate opinion, striking down the tariffs, almost verbatim.”

*   “It’s almost verbatim.” _(re: the Barrett license fee slide)_
*   “Harvey was not some god, it was our sparring partner — brilliant, tireless, occasionally insufferable — but not a god. Harvey asked the questions, we found the answers.”

*   “Justice Barrett asked a question that Harvey hadn’t predicted.”

*   “It didn’t just predict his question, it predicted a possible escape route. How the Chief Justice could vote for us and at the same time protect the institution he had spent his entire career defending.”

*   “Harvey glimpsed that narrow door, I held the door open, the Chief Justice walked through it.”
*   “A month before the argument, Harvey told me that I should expect a question from Justice Barrett about license fees.”

There’s a lot here that raises questions. Harvey describes itself as an “AI platform,” not a frontier foundation model like OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude models, or Google’s Gemini models. And it is unclear whether Katyal’s build used one model family, several, or something more bespoke.

More importantly, the talk does not explain how Harvey turned 25 years of Supreme Court data (maybe around 120 million tokens) into actionable insights. Nor are we shown the full set of outputs Harvey produced. Without that, it is hard to tell what is being described.

So here are the questions I have about the technical aspects of what Katyal described:

**1. What did Harvey actually predict from Chief Justice Roberts?**********Most of the talk is framed as preparation for the oral argument. Katyal puts up a predicted question for Justices Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett. But that’s followed with: “And the Chief Justice? It didn’t just predict his question, it predicted a possible escape route. How the Chief Justice could vote for us and at the same time protect the institution he had spent his entire career defending. Harvey glimpsed that narrow door, I held the door open, the Chief Justice walked through it, writing a six-to-three opinion, striking down the tariffs.”

“It didn’t just predict his question” implies that it actually _did_ predict his question…but this particular question is not shown to the viewer.

[![Image 1](https://www.legaltechmonitor.com/files/2026/05/Image001.png)](https://www.geeklawblog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/528/2026/05/Image001.png)

It looks like here, Katyal is not referring to a question from the Chief, but Harvey predicting that he would agree with the plaintiffs on their main theory of the case.

On this point, the Chief’s opinion for the court actually closely tracked the [D.D.C. opinion](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/pito4za5/production/c1f16cb4b55fd1408c6c6280c1ccff453bd80691.pdf) of Judge Contreras in the _Learning Resources_ case: “Nor does IEEPA include language setting limits on any potential tariff-setting power. Every time Congress delegated the President the authority to levy duties or tariffs in Title 19 of the U.S. Code, it established express procedural, substantive, and temporal limits on that authority._E.g._, 19 U.S.C. § 2132. For one example, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 authorizes the President to impose an “import surcharge . . . in the form of duties . . . on articles imported into the United States” to “deal with large and serious United States balance-of-payments deficits,” but those tariffs are capped at 15 percent and can last only 150 days without Congressional approval._Id._ § 2132(a).”

That language, unsurprisingly, closely tracks the [preliminary injunction motion](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.279804/gov.uscourts.dcd.279804.9.0.pdf#page=33) from the plaintiffs.

That injunction, as Blackman mentioned, was obtained by a trial team from Akin Gump led by Pratik Shah.

So what exactly did Harvey predict of the Chief? Any particular questions? The result? (It’s worth noting that as a “product” predicting oral argument questions and predicting outcome votes would seem to me completely different.).

If the ultimate upshot from Harvey is that “the Chief is an institutionalist,” then it’s unclear whether that comes from commentary or the corpus. That characterization is common in [legal commentary,](https://www.jurist.org/commentary/2020/07/stuart-gerson-understanding-john-roberts/) or [legal scholarship](https://scholarlycommons.law.wlu.edu/wlulr-online/vol78/iss1/4/) (and even scholarship outside [of law journals](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/00027162251324364?_gl=1*1uxo6lo*_up*MQ..*_ga*NTc5NDE4NTM5LjE3Nzg0NzQyNTU.*_ga_60R758KFDG*czE3Nzg0NzQyNTQkbzEkZzAkdDE3Nzg0NzQyNTQkajYwJGwwJGgyMDgxOTc4ODQ4)). (Another question: Did the “profiles” for the Justices include legal commentary? Or was the universe limited to the opinions and transcripts provided?)

**2. How was the system actually trained?**

According to the TED Talk, Katyal says: “I trained it on every question asked by a Supreme Court justice in the last 25 years and everything they’ve written, every opinion, every concurrence, every dissent, every separate opinion.”

That’s an interesting claim. 

Because that is a LOT of data. My estimate from Claude placed that as something like 120 million “tokens.” 

[Technical note: LLMs read text by breaking it down into “tokens.” The counts vary by model – “justice” might be one token as a common word; “unconstitutional” might be broken into “un” and “constitutional” or with current models a single token as a common enough word. “IEEPA” even though it’s shorter, probably registers as multiple tokens because it’s an unusual acronym that the underlying models weren’t trained on.]

Public frontier models now range from roughly 200,000 tokens to 1 million tokens or more, depending on the model and product tier. Consumer chat interfaces may limit the user to a smaller context window than the underlying model supports; API access or enterprise deployments sometimes expose the larger window. But even at 1 million tokens, 25 years of Supreme Court opinions and transcripts is way beyond that.

A context window is how much “stuff” the LLM can consider at one time. It’s sometimes described as like a reading desk. The desk can only fit so many papers and briefs on it, spread out and readable. Once it’s full, you need to take something off in order to add something new.

With an LLM, if you shove too much info into it, it can’t read all of it at one time. So it needs to use some process to deal with that problem.

One option is **Retrieval-Augmented Generation** – “retrieval” or “RAG.” For this, the model doesn’t actually “learn” from all the information you give it. It stores everything in a searchable index, then when you ask it a question, it tries to find the most relevant passages, and put those into the context window. In a simple vector-RAG system, the corpus is chunked, embedded, and searched for semantically similar passages. More advanced retrieval systems search the source documents in several ways, filter by metadata like court, date, Justice, or issue, rerank the best matches, and then give those passages to the model as context.

Retrieval tries to find passages that are similar to what you ask. A simple RAG setup retrieves relevant examples without estimating how representative those examples are. A better system can add metadata, classification, and aggregation to ask how often a Justice raises a category of concern in comparable cases. Retrieval is good at finding examples. But if the AI is _predicting_, that requires counting, classifying, or otherwise analyzing the whole data universe.

So which was Katyal’s system using? Simple RAG? A more sophisticated retrieval-and-analysis system? Something else entirely?

A second way is **fine-tuning.** Fine-tuning changes the model’s weights using training examples, usually prompts paired with desired outputs, so the model becomes more likely to produce the desired behavior. Not unlike a junior associate learning a task by showing her a bunch of examples: when the input looks like _this_, the answer should look like _that_. (Except the model doesn’t understand why it gives that output; it just matches the pattern.)

I think to most ears, the statement that Katyal “”trained it on every question and every opinion” connotes the idea of fine-tuning. If Harvey really fine-tuned the model, that would be a pretty impressive feat – one worth detailing. 

It would involve defining the training objective, preparing examples, deciding what the input and target output are, cleaning transcripts, separating questions from answers, tagging Justice/question metadata, handling the differences between argument transcripts and opinions, and evaluating whether the tuned model outperformed a base model plus retrieval. That is going to take significant man hours, and a fair amount of time and management. 

Fine-tuning would still have some downsides – it would likely result in a black box, where even if it were able to predict, you could probably not trace those predictions back to understand why they were made. The model’s prediction could be right, right for the wrong reasons, or wrong. And you might not be able to tell until it’s too late. 

A third possibility is**pre-computation.**That would involve someone or something going through the archive and extracting specific features from each question (and presumably from the opinions as well – again, unclear how those different types of data were incorporated). The model then works from those extracted features instead of the raw text. Given the description in the TED Talk, it doesn’t sound like Harvey was deploying this kind of human (or AI) filter on the front end – but it would be good to know if they did!

**3. What patterns emerged?**

> **“**And I trained it on every question asked by a Supreme Court justice in the last 25 years and everything they’ve written, every opinion, every concurrence, every dissent, every separate opinion. And in that, patterns emerged. It predicted the contours of the very argument I would face.”

So…what patterns emerged? What was the process for that? Can those be shared?

More importantly – are these patterns that aren’t already known to the Supreme Court bar or the general public? SCOTUS is the most studied court on earth. There are hundreds of attorneys focused on what the Justices ask and how they ask it. If Harvey was actually going to help Katyal prepare, it ought to do it better than a human could (in another context, it would be good enough if it could do it cheaper. In a multi-billion dollar case like _Learning Resources_, that’s not an issue).

To take one example from the [Bartolus dashboard](https://bartolus.law/dashboard), I can tell you that 21% of the questions in _Learning Resources_ asked about statutory text, as opposed to only 8% of questions overall in OT 2025: More importantly – are these patterns that aren’t already known to the Supreme Court bar or the general public? SCOTUS is the most studied court on earth. There are hundreds of attorneys focused on what the Justices ask and how they ask it.

To take one example from the [Bartolus dashboard](https://bartolus.law/dashboard), I can tell you that 21% of the questions in _Learning Resources_ asked about statutory text, as opposed to only 8% of questions overall in OT 2025:

[![Image 2](https://www.legaltechmonitor.com/files/2026/05/Image002-1.png)](https://www.geeklawblog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/528/2026/05/Image002-1.png)

**4. Did it read the briefs?**********The oral argument in _Learning Resources_ was on November 5, 2025. I only caught one time reference when describing the AI usage: “You know, a month before the argument, Harvey told me that I should expect a question from Justice Barrett about license fees.” So that’s about October 5.

The government filed its brief September 19. The challengers’ briefs were filed October 20.

The _Algonquin_ point featured in the Federal Circuit’s opinion, and the government distinguished it in its [opening brief](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24-1287/375365/20250919182906186_24-1287ts_Govt_IEEPATariffs_final.pdf#page=40).

news.titleEn: Some Thoughts On Harvey’s Launch of ‘LAB,’ An Open-Source, Long-Horizon Benchmark for Legal AI Agents
news.titleZh: 关于Harvey推出开源长期基准测试LAB（法律智能体基准）的一些思考
news.summaryZh:
Harvey是一家估值达110亿美元的法律AI公司，近日发布了名为“法律智能体基准”（LAB）的开源评估框架。LAB旨在衡量AI智能体在真实法律工作中执行长期任务的能力，而非此前法律AI基准测试中占主导的离散推理任务。该基准于5月6日由Harvey研究人员Niko Grupen、联合创始人Gabe Pereyra和Julio Pereyra发布，初始版本包含超过1200项任务，涵盖24个法律实践领域，依据超过75000条专家编写的评分标准进行评分。代码和部分数据集已在GitHub上公开。

LAB的每项任务围绕四个要素构建：合伙人给律师助理的简短指令、包含相关文件和无关文件的客户事项环境、可审查的法律工作产品输出，以及通过专家评分标准进行的验证。Harvey采用“全通过”评分制，即只有所有评分标准均通过才算任务完成。LAB目前没有排行榜，Harvey表示将在未来几周与研究合作伙伴合作，在排名出现前制定基线结果和提交标准化规则。LAB的24个实践领域涵盖交易、咨询、监管和诉讼工作，未来版本将扩展至企业内部法律工作及资产管理、银行等相邻专业服务领域。Harvey将LAB定位为法律智能体的可读性层，帮助律所识别智能体表现足够好的工作流程以进行委派，并据此做出部署和投资回报决策。LAB由市场参与者Harvey构建，其任务和“法律工作产品”的定义反映了Harvey团队及其研究合作伙伴的选择。LAB是迄今为止衡量法律AI智能体在律所实际委派工作中表现的最雄心勃勃的公开尝试。
news.bodyHtml:
Harvey, the legal AI company whose valuation recently hit $11 billion, recently released what it is calling the Legal Agent Benchmark, or LAB — an open-source evaluation framework designed to measure how well AI agents can perform extended, real-world legal work rather than the discrete reasoning tasks that have dominated legal AI benchmarks to date.

Announced May 6 in a post by Harvey researchers Niko Grupen, Gabe Pereyra (Harvey’s cofounder), and Julio Pereyra, the first version of LAB contains more than 1,200 tasks spanning 24 legal practice areas, graded against more than 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria. The code and a portion of the dataset are available on GitHub.

“The goal of LAB is to provide a clear picture of how agents can be deployed to support legal work in the real world,” the researchers write. “By articulating where agents can do all, some, or none of a task, LAB helps law firms measure the ROI of AI investments and where such investments can augment their teams’ work.”

Notably, Harvey is launching LAB without a leaderboard. The company says it will work with research partners over the coming weeks to produce baseline results and publish standards for normalizing submissions before any rankings appear.

“We’re intentionally launching LAB without a leaderboard because we expect the dataset to evolve over time and we want to work with the community to ensure results are clear and intuitive in how they convey agent performance,” Harvey says.

What LAB Tests

In creating LAB, Harvey says that existing legal AI benchmarks — including LegalBench, CUAD, LEXam, and Harvey’s own earlier BigLaw Bench — measure short-horizon reasoning, such as ability to read a contract, answer a question, compare cases, or analyze an argument. LAB is meant to measure something closer to the unit of work that actually gets delegated inside a law firm.

Each LAB task is structured around four elements that mirror an associate’s assignment:

  • An instruction written as a partner-to-associate request — short (averaging 50 words) and framed as what’s needed rather than how to produce it.
  • An environment built as a client matter, with a closed universe of documents that the agent must sort through. Materials include both relevant files and peripheral ones the agent has to learn to ignore.
  • An output that has to be reviewable legal work product, not just an answer.
  • Verification through expert rubrics that break the deliverable into atomic pass/fail criteria covering facts, conclusions, citations, severity ratings, recommendations, deadlines, dollar amounts, and formatting.

To illustrate the structure, Harvey uses a fictional corporate M&A example. It involves a $458 million all-equity acquisition of Crestview Software Solutions in which the agent must review a virtual data room containing eight material contracts plus adjacent documents such as a 10-K and a deferred compensation plan, identify change-of-control provisions across the matter, assess deal risk, recommend next steps, and produce a draft memorandum for the deal team and board. The rubric for that single task contains 57 criteria covering nine legal issues planted across the materials.

LAB uses what Harvey calls “all-pass” grading, meaning that a task is marked complete only if every rubric criterion passes. There is no partial credit. The rationale is that a deal memo that catches eight of 10 material risks is not 80% useful. One missed issue could blow up the transaction or surface as a problem post-closing.

The 24 practice areas in the initial release span transactional, advisory, regulatory and litigation work. Harvey says future versions will expand within those areas, add new practices, and eventually move beyond law firms to in-house legal work and adjacent professional services like asset management and banking.

Why a Benchmark?

Harvey’s thesis is that benchmarks have served as leading indicators of capability inflection points in other agentic domains — most visibly in software engineering, where benchmarks such as SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 tracked the shift that AI researcher Andrej Karpathy summarized by saying coding agents “basically didn’t work before December and basically work since.”

Harvey argues that similar benchmarks (GDPval, OSWorld-Verified, BrowseComp, FinanceAgent, and others) are now extending legibility to knowledge work, web research, financial analysis and professional services.

Harvey positions LAB as the legibility layer for legal agents. The use case Harvey describes for law firms is straightforward: identify the workflows where agents perform well enough to be delegated under a “review pattern,” identify the workflows where they don’t and need to stay heavily human-in-the-loop, and make deployment and ROI decisions accordingly.

For most firms, that may matter more than technical details. The legal industry has spent two years cycling through vendor demos and pilot programs without a shared way to answer the question every managing partner and innovation lead is being asked, which is where, specifically, can we put these things to work?

A credible, public benchmark, particularly one structured around actual deliverables rather than multiple-choice questions, could change that conversation. Of course, it could also complicate it, by revealing how far agents still are from autonomous practice in many areas.

Practical Applications of LAB

To my mind, a few practical applications of LAB jump out:

  • For law firms, LAB offers a reference point for vendor evaluation. A firm evaluating competing products could, in theory, ask each vendor to report performance on specific LAB practice areas and compare results, rather than rely on vendor demos and case studies.
  • For vendors, LAB offers a public yardstick for claims about agent capability. Harvey has acknowledged contributions from a substantial list of labs and companies (including Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Google DeepMind, Mistral, LangChain, Fireworks, Snorkel, Mercor, and Stanford LIFTLab), which suggests the major frontier labs see value in a shared evaluation context for legal agents.
  • For researchers, LAB provides a longer-horizon, domain-specific task set that they can use for evaluation, fine-tuning and post-training work.
  • For legal journalists and analysts, LAB could provide something more useful than vendor-supplied claims about their products —a way of actually putting those claims to the test.

The Bottom Line

It is worth noting that LAB is a benchmark built by a market participant. Harvey is a dominant and well-funded legal AI vendor, and the company has not been shy about its commercial positioning.

The tasks and definitions of “legal work product” within LAB reflect choices about what good legal work looks like, and those choices were made by Harvey’s team in consultation with its research partners. None of that makes the benchmark unreliable, but it is something the legal community needs to keep in mind going forward.

There is also the question of what exactly is the impact of “open source” in this context. In a post at Alt-Counsel, Houfu Ang argues that legal open source is not really a community but rather “a federation of solo-author archipelagos.”

He points specifically to projects that come from well-funded vendors such as Harvey, whose repositories are maintained almost exclusively by in-house staff in what the Open Source Initiative calls “Open Source theatre.” Virtually none of these, Ang argues, graduate from individual showcase to sustained codebase with outside contributors.

Even so, LAB is the most ambitious public attempt yet to measure what legal AI agents can actually do on the kind of work law firms actually delegate. Whether it becomes the shared yardstick Harvey wants it to be will depend on how the leaderboard rolls out, how transparently submissions are normalized, and how much room the project leaves for outside contributors to shape what gets measured.

The code and a portion of the dataset are available on GitHub .

“The goal of LAB is to provide a clear picture of how agents can be deployed to support legal work in the real world,” the researchers write. “By articulating where agents can do all, some, or none of a task, LAB helps law firms measure the ROI of AI investments and where such investments can augment their teams’ work.”

Notably, Harvey is launching LAB without a leaderboard. The company says it will work with research partners over the coming weeks to produce baseline results and publish standards for normalizing submissions before any rankings appear.

“We’re intentionally launching LAB without a leaderboard because we expect the dataset to evolve over time and we want to work with the community to ensure results are clear and intuitive in how they convey agent performance,” Harvey says.

In creating LAB, Harvey says that existing legal AI benchmarks — including LegalBench, CUAD, LEXam, and Harvey’s own earlier BigLaw Bench — measure short-horizon reasoning, such as ability to read a contract, answer a question, compare cases, or analyze an argument. LAB is meant to measure something closer to the unit of work that actually gets delegated inside a law firm.

Each LAB task is structured around four elements that mirror an associate’s assignment:

An instruction written as a partner-to-associate request — short (averaging 50 words) and framed as what’s needed rather than how to produce it.

An environment built as a client matter, with a closed universe of documents that the agent must sort through. Materials include both relevant files and peripheral ones the agent has to learn to ignore.

An output that has to be reviewable legal work product, not just an answer.

Verification through expert rubrics that break the deliverable into atomic pass/fail criteria covering facts, conclusions, citations, severity ratings, recommendations, deadlines, dollar amounts, and formatting.

To illustrate the structure, Harvey uses a fictional corporate M&A example. It involves a $458 million all-equity acquisition of Crestview Software Solutions in which the agent must review a virtual data room containing eight material contracts plus adjacent documents such as a 10-K and a deferred compensation plan, identify change-of-control provisions across the matter, assess deal risk, recommend next steps, and produce a draft memorandum for the deal team and board. The rubric for that single task contains 57 criteria covering nine legal issues planted across the materials.

LAB uses what Harvey calls “all-pass” grading, meaning that a task is marked complete only if every rubric criterion passes. There is no partial credit. The rationale is that a deal memo that catches eight of 10 material risks is not 80% useful. One missed issue could blow up the transaction or surface as a problem post-closing.

The 24 practice areas in the initial release span transactional, advisory, regulatory and litigation work. Harvey says future versions will expand within those areas, add new practices, and eventually move beyond law firms to in-house legal work and adjacent professional services like asset management and banking.

Harvey’s thesis is that benchmarks have served as leading indicators of capability inflection points in other agentic domains — most visibly in software engineering, where benchmarks such as SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 tracked the shift that AI researcher Andrej Karpathy summarized by saying coding agents “basically didn’t work before December and basically work since.”

Harvey argues that similar benchmarks (GDPval, OSWorld-Verified, BrowseComp, FinanceAgent, and others) are now extending legibility to knowledge work, web research, financial analysis and professional services.

Harvey positions LAB as the legibility layer for legal agents. The use case Harvey describes for law firms is straightforward: identify the workflows where agents perform well enough to be delegated under a “review pattern,” identify the workflows where they don’t and need to stay heavily human-in-the-loop, and make deployment and ROI decisions accordingly.

For most firms, that may matter more than technical details. The legal industry has spent two years cycling through vendor demos and pilot programs without a shared way to answer the question every managing partner and innovation lead is being asked, which is where, specifically, can we put these things to work?

A credible, public benchmark, particularly one structured around actual deliverables rather than multiple-choice questions, could change that conversation. Of course, it could also complicate it, by revealing how far agents still are from autonomous practice in many areas.

To my mind, a few practical applications of LAB jump out:

For law firms, LAB offers a reference point for vendor evaluation. A firm evaluating competing products could, in theory, ask each vendor to report performance on specific LAB practice areas and compare results, rather than rely on vendor demos and case studies.

For vendors, LAB offers a public yardstick for claims about agent capability. Harvey has acknowledged contributions from a substantial list of labs and companies (including Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Google DeepMind, Mistral, LangChain, Fireworks, Snorkel, Mercor, and Stanford LIFTLab), which suggests the major frontier labs see value in a shared evaluation context for legal agents.

For researchers, LAB provides a longer-horizon, domain-specific task set that they can use for evaluation, fine-tuning and post-training work.

For legal journalists and analysts, LAB could provide something more useful than vendor-supplied claims about their products —a way of actually putting those claims to the test.

It is worth noting that LAB is a benchmark built by a market participant. Harvey is a dominant and well-funded legal AI vendor, and the company has not been shy about its commercial positioning.

The tasks and definitions of “legal work product” within LAB reflect choices about what good legal work looks like, and those choices were made by Harvey’s team in consultation with its research partners. None of that makes the benchmark unreliable, but it is something the legal community needs to keep in mind going forward.

There is also the question of what exactly is the impact of “open source” in this context. In a post at Alt-Counsel , Houfu Ang argues that legal open source is not really a community but rather “a federation of solo-author archipelagos.”

He points specifically to projects that come from well-funded vendors such as Harvey, whose repositories are maintained almost exclusively by in-house staff in what the Open Source Initiative calls “Open Source theatre.” Virtually none of these, Ang argues, graduate from individual showcase to sustained codebase with outside contributors.

Even so, LAB is the most ambitious public attempt yet to measure what legal AI agents can actually do on the kind of work law firms actually delegate. Whether it becomes the shared yardstick Harvey wants it to be will depend on how the leaderboard rolls out, how transparently submissions are normalized, and how much room the project leaves for outside contributors to shape what gets measured.

news.bodyHtml:
Governed, auditable access to iManage content for AI replaces fragmented custom integrations, eliminates vendor lock-in, and keeps sensitive knowledge secure inside the iManage platform

CHICAGO — May 14, 2026 — iManage, the company dedicated to Making Knowledge Work™, today announced iManage MCP (Model Context Protocol) Server, a standardized, open-protocol connection that enables any artificial intelligence (AI) systems to securely access governed iManage content without custom integrations, bulk data exports, or compromising existing security, ethical wall, and compliance controls.

Findings from the iManage Knowledge Work Benchmark Report 2026  reveal a market reshaping faster than most organizations can keep up with. Nearly half of global leaders expect new legal frameworks to emerge specifically to govern AI-to-AI interactions within the decade, and two-thirds say that shift will be transformational for their business. Yet 32% cite integration complexity as one of the biggest barriers to AI adoption. iManage MCP Server resolves that tension by providing a single, standardized connection between the iManage platform and any AI system whether Harvey, Legora, ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, or a firm’s own AI agents.

“Customers are not choosing one AI tool and stopping there. They are already experimenting with multiple AI systems, and the real challenge is connecting those tools to the knowledge that matters most without creating new governance gaps or operational complexity,” said Neil Araujo, CEO of iManage. “iManage MCP Server gives organizations a governed way to do that – enabling permission-aware access to business-critical knowledge that remains governed within iManage, while giving teams the flexibility to adopt the AI tools that make the most sense for their business.”

Key capabilities of iManage MCP Server include:

  • Standardized AI Connectivity – A single MCP connection replaces a growing list of custom API integrations. Because MCP is an open, vendor-neutral standard, any MCP Compatible AI system can connect once configured. Firms add, switch, or onboard new AI tools without new IT projects and without being locked into a single vendor
  • Documents Stay in Place – Allows AI to access iManage content without bulk export of documents and negates the need for the AI tool to store a copy of the documents
  • Governed and Auditable Access – All AI access to iManage content via MCP is authenticated, permission-bound, and fully logged, respecting existing ethical walls and access controls. IT and compliance teams can approve AI adoption with confidence; legal defensibility is maintained without additional tooling
  • Richer AI, better answers – AI tools draw directly from the governed source with full context, accurate results, no data duplication

“We are already investing in AI tools across the business, but the real value comes from being able to connect those tools securely to the governed knowledge held in iManage,” said Mike Peters, Information Manager, RSM Australia. “The iManage MCP Server provides a practical pathway to do that without treating each AI use case as a bespoke integration project. For an organization managing sensitive client information, the ability to connect AI capabilities to permission-aware, governed content is an exciting development and aligns strongly with the modern way of working.”

Join iManage at ConnectLive 2026

iManage will be showcasing iManage MCP Server at ConnectLive Chicago (May 19-20) and ConnectLive London (June 9-10), the company’s annual customer conferences, where attendees can see the capabilities firsthand and explore how iManage MCP Server fits into their AI strategy.

To go deeper, iManage is hosting a dedicated launch webinar on May 28, “Your AI. Your Knowledge. Fully Governed.”, walking attendees through how iManage MCP Server works, how it fits alongside Ask iManage as part of iManage’s complete AI platform, and real-world use cases across law firms and in-house legal teams. Register here: https://event.on24.com/wcc/r/5308214/A441E63BC31FC401FFC1E2E5482A5D02.

About iManage

iManage is dedicated to Making Knowledge Work™. Our cloud-native platform is at the center of the knowledge economy, enabling every organization to work more productively, collaboratively, and securely. Built on more than 30 years of industry experience, iManage helps leading organizations manage documents and emails more efficiently, protect vital information assets, and leverage knowledge to drive better business outcomes. As your strategic business partner, we employ our award-winning AI-enabled technology, an extensive partner ecosystem, and a customer-centric approach to provide support and guidance you can trust to make knowledge work for you. iManage is relied on by more than one million professionals at 4,000 organizations around the world. Visit www.imanage.com to learn more.

 

Follow iManage via:

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/imanage

X: https://x.com/imanageinc

YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@iManage

news.titleEn: TalkingTech Podcast with Harvey: How AI Agents Are Changing Legal Work—and Why It Matters Now
news.titleZh: TalkingTech播客对话Harvey：AI代理如何改变法律工作——以及为何现在至关重要
news.summaryZh:
法律领域的人工智能正从简单自动化转向更具变革性的应用。本期播客中，Legal IT Insider编辑Caroline Hill与Harvey法律创新合伙人Tara Waters探讨了AI代理的兴起——这些工具不仅能执行指令，还能规划、推理并自主完成多步骤法律任务。代理可以接受生成尽职调查报告等目标，并自行决定如何实现，这标志着与传统软件的重大区别。这些能力已在实践中应用，Harvey平台上涌现出数百个代理用例，从检查文档与尽职调查清单的匹配等简单任务，到通过收集上下文并起草输出来生成整套法律文件等复杂工作流。尽管仍处于早期阶段，这些工具展示了法律工作如何被简化，甚至在某些情况下被根本性重新设计。

这种新水平的自主性带来了重要挑战。律师对放弃控制权持谨慎态度，尤其是当代理可能独立做出决策或采取行动时。这使得治理成为核心关注点，律所需要谨慎管理数据访问、系统集成和风险。Waters和Hill讨论了采用代理式AI的方法：建议从小处着手，先在低风险任务上测试代理，然后随着信心增长逐步扩大使用。AI代理并未消除对律师的需求，而是以不同方式增加了需求。人类监督仍然至关重要，律师负责设计、测试和验证代理输出。法律判断非但未被取代，反而在评估AI生成工作是否达到标准方面变得更加重要。展望未来，法律团队将作为律师与AI代理的混合体并行工作。
news.bodyHtml:
AI in the legal sector is moving beyond simple automation into something far more transformative. In this podcast, Legal IT Insider’s editor Caroline Hill and Harvey legal innovation partner Tara Waters explore the rise of AI agents – tools that don’t just execute instructions but can plan, reason, and complete multi-step legal tasks with a degree of autonomy. As Waters explains in this relaxed conversation and exchange of ideas, agents can take an outcome like producing a due diligence report and determine for themselves how to get there, marking a significant shift from traditional software.

These capabilities are already being put into practice. On platforms like Harvey, hundreds of agent use cases are emerging, from straightforward tasks like checking documents against due diligence lists to more complex workflows such as generating full sets of legal documents by gathering context and drafting outputs. While still in early access, these tools show how legal work can be streamlined, and in some cases, fundamentally redesigned.

Advertisement

This new level of autonomy brings important challenges. Lawyers are rightly cautious about ceding control, especially when agents can make decisions or take actions independently. This has made governance a central concern, with firms needing to carefully manage data access, system integrations, and risk. Waters and Hill discussed how to approach agentic AI adoption: the recommended approach, much like with all new technology, is to start small, testing agents on low-risk tasks and gradually expanding their use as confidence grows.

These are exciting and challenging times in equal measure, and Waters discussed how AI agents do not remove the need for lawyers, they increase it in different ways. Human oversight remains essential, with lawyers responsible for designing, testing, and verifying agent outputs. Legal judgment, rather than being replaced, becomes even more important in assessing whether AI-generated work meets the required standard.

Advertisement

Looking ahead, the conversation points to a near future where legal teams operate as hybrids of lawyers and AI agents working in parallel. What do firms need to think about right now to be ready to adapt?

As AI adoption accelerates across the legal sector, contract review is emerging as one of the most immediate and impactful use cases. However, effective AI review depends not only on technology, but on the quality and consistency of the legal knowledge underpinning it.

In this webinar, Legalfly’s senior legal solutions engineer Stephanie Adriaens will share insights into how legal teams are building the operational foundations for successful AI contract review. Drawing on real-world experience, the discussion will cover how to identify the right contracts for AI-assisted review, how to organise and centralise internal templates, and how to create playbooks that accurately reflect an organisation’s preferred clauses, fallback positions, and negotiation strategy.

Rather than focusing on technology alone, this session will explore the practical realities of preparing legal teams and contract processes for AI adoption, offering attendees actionable guidance on how to move from isolated experimentation to repeatable, trusted review workflows.
