news.titleEn: LexisNexis Owner Plans to Buy Doctrine – Top French Legal AI Company
news.titleZh: LexisNexis母公司计划收购法国顶级法律AI公司Doctrine
news.summaryZh: RELX集团（LexisNexis Legal & Professional母公司）宣布已签署收购Doctrine的看跌期权协议。Doctrine成立于2016年，总部位于巴黎，为民法管辖区提供判例法、立法和监管内容综合语料库，以及AI驱动的检索、起草和分析工具。该平台在法国、意大利、德国和西班牙拥有27,000名日常用户，涵盖律所、跨国企业、公共实体等。收购完成后，Doctrine将继续由现有管理团队领导，作为RELX集团的一部分运营。双方预计在完成员工代表机构咨询程序后签署最终文件，交易尚需获得外国直接投资许可等监管批准，具体条款未披露。Raymond James、Latham & Watkins、Scotto Partners和Freshfields分别担任各方顾问。
news.bodyHtml:
Breaking News – RELX Group, the publicly listed company which owns LexisNexis Legal & Professional, has announced that it has entered into a ‘put option agreement to acquire Doctrine, a leading legal AI platform for legal professionals across Continental Europe’.

Founded in 2016 and headquartered in Paris, Doctrine combines a comprehensive corpus of case law, legislation and regulatory content for civil law jurisdictions with a suite of AI-powered research, drafting and analytics tools.

—

—

The platform is used daily by 27,000 legal professionals across France, Italy, Germany and Spain, including law firms ranging from solo practitioners to top-tier Anglo-American firms, multinational corporations and public entities, including French ministries, local authorities, and universities.

The proposed acquisition would accelerate the delivery of enhanced, trusted, intuitive and authoritative legal AI workflow solutions in France and across key European jurisdictions, including Germany, Spain and Italy and should assist customers to improve productivity and achieve better outcomes, they said.

Doctrine and LexisNexis would provide legal professionals across Europe with end-to-end AI-powered legal workflows that span research, drafting and analyses, underpinned by trusted, authoritative content in their native language and legal tradition. Doctrine would continue to be led by its existing management team and would operate as part of RELX Group.

Sean Fitzpatrick, Chief Executive Officer, Global Legal, LexisNexis Legal & Professional, said: ‘We are excited about the prospect of welcoming Doctrine, so that we can serve customers in France, across Europe, and beyond in even greater ways. Doctrine’s customer-centric innovation approach, powerful platform and expert talent complement LexisNexis’s global capabilities in authoritative legal AI workflow solutions, and we look forward to delivering even more value to customers.”

Guillaume Carrère, Chief Executive Officer of Doctrine, said: ‘From the start, we have been obsessed with one thing: building cutting-edge AI solutions for legal professionals across Europe. Joining RELX is the natural next chapter for that mission. LexisNexis brings unparalleled depth of content, global reach and a shared conviction that AI, applied responsibly, will transform how legal work gets done. For our customers, this means faster access to a richer set of capabilities; for our team, it means joining a company that recognizes and will invest behind the technical and product excellence we have built. I want to thank every single person at Doctrine, as well as our partners at Summit Partners, whose conviction and support were instrumental at a defining stage of our journey.’

They added that: ‘The put option agreement provides RELX Group with a binding commitment to acquire Doctrine, exercisable following completion of the information and consultation process with Doctrine’s employee representative bodies in accordance with French law. The parties expect to enter into definitive share purchase documentation following the conclusion of that consultation. Completion of the envisaged transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including foreign direct investment clearances and other applicable regulatory approvals. The terms of the transaction have not been disclosed. The two companies will continue to operate separately in the interim.’

Raymond James served as financial advisor to Summit Partners, and Latham & Watkins served as legal advisors. Scotto Partners advised Doctrine’s management. Freshfields acted as legal advisors to RELX.

–

Is this a big deal?

Well, if you are in France then this is massive. Doctrine started not long after AL did and have steadily grown from being a local legal research company using NLP, to a very frontier-focused AI company that has become a leader locally and also expanded across Europe.

By buying them, they have ‘taken Doctrine off the board’, and prevented a company such as Legora or Harvey taking them – if that had ever been in the cards. Nevertheless, Doctrine is a major player in Western Europe and it really does bolster LexisNexis in the EU – a key market.

On that theme, Legora just bought Qura – a small Swedish legal research startup with a novel approach to deploying AI.

One then has to ask if Lexis – and its parent RELX – will target other research based companies in Europe? Wolters Kluwer is probably too large to bring in, but there are several others in Spain, Germany, and Scandinavia still.

It’s not clear how long Doctrine was on the market for, or what triggered the Lexis move. But, overall, it strengthens them – because, as AL has said many times: curated legal data is the best moat in the world against the inroads of general AI.

Let’s keep a look out for more deals in this legal data space.

–

news.summaryZh: Harvey 任命 Rachel Hepworth 为首席营销官（CMO）。Hepworth 此前担任 Notion 的 CMO，并曾在 Slack 担任营销主管，近期还担任 Lovable 的顾问。她曾帮助公司“大规模传达其价值”，而 Harvey 正在全球范围内扩展业务。她职业生涯致力于重塑工作方式，法律领域的信任、精确性和工艺至关重要，Harvey 正引领这一变革。当前法律 AI 市场竞争激烈，Anthropic 不仅向法律科技公司销售大语言模型，还希望律所直接使用其模型处理法律工作。Harvey 及其主要竞争对手正加大营销力度，包括名人代言等新举措。尽管这些举措可能吸引短期关注，但其长期价值存疑。法律 AI 市场快速变化，Hepworth 在 Notion 等公司的经验将发挥重要作用。主要法律 AI 平台的关键市场仍是大企业内部法律团队和大型律所，这些领域的法律创新者更关注平台如何真正帮助律师。
news.bodyHtml:
AL doesn’t usually cover marketing roles, but this one is definitely noteworthy. Harvey has hired Rachel Hepworth as Chief Marketing Officer (CMO). She was previously CMO at Notion and was a marketing leader at Slack. Most recently she was also an advisor to Lovable.  

Harvey said she has helped companies to ‘communicate their value at scale’ – and Harvey is certainly scaling, and doing so globally.

California-based Hepworth commented: ‘I’ve spent my career at companies reshaping how work gets done, and the stakes in law could not be higher. Trust, precision, and craft are critical. Harvey is the leader driving this change and I’m excited to be a part of building what comes next.’

One thing that is clear at the moment amid the ongoing platform war, and the realisation that Anthropic doesn’t just want to sell its LLMs to legal tech companies – but wants law firms to use them directly for legal work, is that there has never been so much to play for. The market for legal AI is opening up worldwide, but there is also a fierce competition taking place.

Plus, we have seen both Harvey and its main rival go into overdrive in terms of expanding their own marketing efforts, moving into areas such as celebrity endorsements – something that is really a whole new world for legal tech. That said, some wonder if such moves have a sustained value, even if they do attract short-term interest outside the legal innovation ecosystem of legal tech buyers.

Overall then, the legal AI market is changing rapidly and someone with experience at working with companies such as Notion, Lovable and others, will be very useful.

For what it’s worth, Artificial Lawyer would say – especially given recent research this site has done into the evolving sector – that the major legal AI platforms’ key markets remain large inhouse legal teams and large law firms – and perhaps they always will be. Those involved in legal innovation in these segments are a relatively tight, albeit global community and perhaps want more than anything else to really understand how platforms such as Harvey will help the people they work for: the lawyers.

Congrats to Rachel on the move!

One thing that is clear at the moment amid the ongoing platform war, and the realisation that Anthropic doesn’t just want to sell its LLMs to legal tech companies – but wants law firms to use them directly for legal work, is that there has never been so much to play for. The market for legal AI is opening up worldwide, but there is also a fierce competition taking place.

Plus, we have seen both Harvey and its main rival go into overdrive in terms of expanding their own marketing efforts, moving into areas such as celebrity endorsements – something that is really a whole new world for legal tech. That said, some wonder if such moves have a sustained value, even if they do attract short-term interest outside the legal innovation ecosystem of legal tech buyers.

Overall then, the legal AI market is changing rapidly and someone with experience at working with companies such as Notion, Lovable and others, will be very useful.

For what it’s worth, Artificial Lawyer would say – especially given recent research this site has done into the evolving sector – that the major legal AI platforms’ key markets remain large inhouse legal teams and large law firms – and perhaps they always will be. Those involved in legal innovation in these segments are a relatively tight, albeit global community and perhaps want more than anything else to really understand how platforms such as Harvey will help the people they work for: the lawyers.

Congrats to Rachel on the move!

news.titleEn: Is Claude Really Cheaper Than Your Legal Tech Stack?
news.titleZh: Claude真的比你的法律科技工具更便宜吗？
news.summaryZh: 了Claude与法律科技工具的成本对比。表面上看，Claude在处理基础文档审查等任务时成本更低，但综合考虑律所整体技术栈后，情况更为复杂。文章基于Claude和ChatGPT的估算数据，对比了法律科技工具成本、Claude企业许可费用以及按使用量计算的token成本。然而，这些估算排除了Claude难以胜任的领域，如可验证的法律研究、电子取证、计费、项目管理等。许多法律科技工具还提供附加功能，且律所已投入大量资源在应用层、用户体验、客户服务和研发上。此外，Claude在安全性、人工服务、责任承担等方面与专业法律AI平台存在差距。对于大型律所而言，全面采用Claude可能导致成本重复，且存在切换成本和未来价格不确定性。对于尚未深度使用法律AI产品的小型律所和内部团队，迁移相对容易。总体而言，Claude的成本优势仅限于特定有限用例，且需考虑现有技术栈的保留成本。
news.bodyHtml:
On face value Claude looks way less expensive than paying for a legal tech tool for the tasks that it’s able to do, such as relatively mundane document review. But, if you zoom out and look at the bigger picture, especially the realities of a firm’s entire tech stack – is it really cheaper, or even that widely applicable?

First, let’s consider some estimated data – from Claude (and below from ChatGPT also). AL went through a series of prompts and built charts that showed the differences between three elements:

  • The cost of legal tech tools that we can reasonably say that Claude could have a go at replacing – at least in some circumstances, e.g. basic doc review.
  • The cost of a standard Claude enterprise licence – which is what most legal teams or law firms would purchase per user. So, larger firms mean larger overall costs here.
  • And the same as above, plus the token cost for using Claude for applicable work streams, relative to segments. E.g. Big Law firms are not just larger in terms of people, they handle more complex, voluminous legal matters, and that generates higher token costs.

However, it’s important to note that the table excludes those areas of activity that Claude cannot be expected to easily do, e.g. verifiable legal research, eDiscovery, and other legal tech tool tasks such as billing, or project management, or acting as a DMS. And that is a key point that needs to be kept front of mind.

And here is also a table from ChatGPT, but uses an annual estimate.

AL wanted to make sure the Claude result was not a one-off. As you can see, OpenAI’s estimates are not that different proportionally, although in this case it’s an annual approximation.

And it should be noted, that all of this is very much an estimation with wide variables around number of lawyers, how much work they do that Claude can help with, the cost of legal AI platforms and point solutions that are overlapping with Claude, and the token demand overall for each segment. It also doesn’t consider that you may still have to keep most of your current legal tech tools regardless, even if you do bring in Claude at scale.

Even so, and with all the many caveats above, it’s fairly clear that for certain, limited use cases, Claude does indeed come out cheaper – if you didn’t already have a broad tech stack that you need to keep and pay for.

The Bigger Picture

As explored before in AL – see story on what percentage of legal tech spend will go to Claude – here – it’s not a simple scenario. Here are some aspects to consider for Big Law.

  • A large proportion of tech-assisted needs are not a great fit for Claude, from billing and project management, to eDiscovery, to verified legal research across curated datasets, and more.
  • Many legal tech tools now come with a broad range of additional features. So, legal research often comes with a bunch of drafting and review tools, for example. You have to use the legal research tools, so you may as well get these other AI skills regardless. Or, Claude can do some things that a broad legal AI platform does, but the platform also does a dozen other things that you want to keep. So, again, there is no easy ‘swapping out’ here.
  • While some may note the price differences with the major legal AI platforms, what is not priced in above is the huge investment companies have made in their application layers, their UI/UX, and in forward deployed teams, in customer service, and R&D to keep developing and improving features. Those costs are embedded in the price. It’s the same as people asking why a coffee in a nice restaurant is $5, when they could make it for less at home. The answer is: the restaurant is what you’re not factoring in – and that’s all around you, from the service to everything else on offer.
  • Also, legal AI platforms are not just software – rather like law firms they are organisations that instil trust because they are run by people – people who you can meet and talk to.
  • They also own the product and take responsibility for it. To build out a range of tools that you can really rely upon inside the super-demanding environment of a law firm is not a small task. Claude and some vibe-coding is not the same as a truly professional legal AI product built and designed by people who spend their lives focused on developing those features and engaging with the clients.

Other considerations:

  • As mentioned, what Claude can really be 100% trusted to do as well as a sophisticated legal tech tool is quite limited, so you still have to buy all the other tools in any case in most scenarios, at least as a Big Law firm. Or rather, you have to keep them. So, ironically, there could be a duplication of costs by using Claude.
  • Security will always be an area of concern in relation to general models. It’s unavoidable. Legal tech companies are of course operating off these models as well, but they’ve put in place a lot of security layers.
  • Human service is not a small thing. If you rang up Anthropic and asked them to help with a plug in that you’d customised, would they leap to help you? Probably not. Maybe if you had an all-in deal like Freshfields they’d be more willing to help, but Anthropic doesn’t have a dedicated legal tech sales and support group – they have a handful of lawyers internally who are engaging with some lawyers at firms and inhouse, but that’s not the same thing.
  • As Anthropic and other major LLM makers grow, will token costs drop, or rise? Will licence costs drop or rise? One argument is that more usage globally will mean lower prices, but if they gain a monopoly, or near monopoly, in the business world, maybe the prices get hiked more and more at some point in the future?
  • Switching costs – what happens if in 12 months another LLM becomes the leader? What if Claude – which is ruling the roost today, drops away relative to rivals? If you are all-in on Claude, then you could be stuck.

Conclusion

The net result is that even though the main tables are startling, once you consider the broader details, it’s not such a simple thing. For smaller firms and small inhouse teams who have not yet really committed to legal AI products, then with their lower usage demands and no loyalty to any current tool, the move is easier.

For Big Law, as explored last week, even though there are some apparent savings on face value, the reality is that few large law firms will really go all-in with Claude, nor would it really be a major cost saving, because if we are realistic, they cannot leave their tech stack except for in certain areas where they are not already committed or where it makes sense to accept duplication.

Richard Tromans, Founder, Artificial Lawyer

—

news.titleEn: Multilingual Legal AI Requires Data, Not Just Better Models
news.titleZh: 多语言法律AI需要数据，而不仅仅是更好的模型
news.summaryZh:
多语言法律AI的失败并非源于模型能力不足，而是缺乏展示法律概念在不同法系中实际运作方式的数据。法律意义并非普遍一致，而是文化、宗教、历史、学说、程序和制度发展的产物。没有对司法管辖背景和差异的结构化暴露，即使最强大的模型也会默认使用其训练数据中的主导框架。

构建支持跨境法律工作的系统需要结构化表示法律概念、跨法系映射并由专家策划的数据，以及反映法律推理而非仅语言正确性的质量控制。这种数据建设在商业环境中很少进行，因为它缓慢、昂贵且难以规模化。然而，正是这些数据决定了AI系统在多语言法律环境中是否值得信赖。组织需要质疑其工具所依赖数据的来源和结构，并考虑系统是否提供透明度和问责制。
news.bodyHtml:
By Michael Krallmann, CEO, TransLegal.

For the legal tech community, cross-jurisdictional meaning raises questions of risk, liability and trust. Increasingly capable models, wrapped in sophisticated products, still encounter failures in the cross-border context. While the instinctive response is to look for a better model, the real constraint sits elsewhere.

Better models are not enough

Multilingual legal AI does not fail because models are insufficiently powerful. It fails because they lack access to data showing how legal concepts actually function across systems. Legal meaning is not universal, being the product of culture, religion, history, doctrine, procedure and institutional development. Without structured exposure to jurisdictional context and differences, even the strongest models default to the dominant framing in their training data.

The prevailing belief seems to be that scale and generalisation will resolve jurisdictional differences, that having enough text will enable a model to infer necessary distinctions. In practice, however, many of the most important differences are subtle, under-documented or expressed through practice rather than explicit definition. In other words, they require interpretation, not pattern matching.

Accurate data as legal infrastructure

A comparative law analysis, when done properly, is not merely a paraphrasing exercise. Rather, it identifies purpose, scope, legal effect and limitations, recognises partial equivalence and non-equivalence and, not least, states explicitly where an apparently correct translation breaks down. As such data do not emerge automatically from large corpora, they must be deliberately created.

This is why data architecture matters. A system designed to support cross-border legal work needs more than a large corpus of documents. It needs structured representations of legal concepts, mapped across jurisdictions, curated by experts. It also needs quality controls that reflect legal reasoning, not just linguistic correctness.

This kind of data-building is rarely done in a commercial context because it is slow, expensive and difficult to scale. Yet it is precisely such data that determine whether an AI system can be trusted in a multilingual legal environment.

There is growing recognition that wrappers alone cannot solve this problem. Prompting can improve presentation, and retrieval can improve relevance. However, neither solves the problem of conceptual (mis)alignment. If a system does not know that two terms only overlap partially, it cannot warn the user, and if it does not know that a familiar concept carries different implications and consequences in another jurisdiction, it cannot explain the risk this involves.

The alternative is to build datasets which define, contextualise and link legal concepts across jurisdictions. This entails embedding human judgement into the data itself, rather than relying on a model to infer it later on. It also means accepting that some answers need to specify uncertainty or limitations.

Reducing risk and extracting real value

For lawyers and legal tech builders, the problem of conceptual divergence reframes the role of AI. The most valuable systems will not be those that generate the longest or most fluent answers. They will be those that help users avoid mistakes they did not know even they were making. In cross-border work, that often means making differences visible rather than smoothing them away.

There are clear practical implications to this. Organisations that deploy legal AI across markets need to ask harder questions about the provenance and structure of the data their tools rely on. They need to consider whether the system offers transparency and accountability, and think about how legal risk travels when language crosses borders.

Legal AI will increasingly operate in environments where jurisdictional context matters. Systems that acknowledge this openly and are designed accordingly will age far better than those relying on linguistic gloss alone.

Towards a solution

For those interested in what a data-driven approach to cross-border legal accuracy looks like in practice, it is worth considering how structured legal terminology and comparative datasets can improve the output of AI systems. Engaging with the hard questions now is easier than doing so later once the costs of being almost right start to bite.

At TransLegal, we’re developing human-curated legal datasets aimed at improving AI performance in multilingual and multi-jurisdictional legal environments. Our work focuses on expert-led data creation and quality assurance to support more accurate and accountable legal AI systems. To date, we have completed over 40 jurisdiction-specific datasets, and have dozens more projects ongoing.

For teams building or integrating legal AI across markets, the question is no longer whether models perform well, but whether their base data support jurisdictional accuracy. To explore what this looks like in practice, visit TransLegal to try our data demo model or contact us directly.

About the author: Michael Krallmann is CEO of TransLegal, where he leads the development of structured cross-jurisdictional legal datasets designed to improve conceptual accuracy in multilingual legal AI systems. He holds a PhD in Law and Translation and works at the intersection of comparative law, language and legal technology.

–

[ This is a sponsored thought leadership article by TransLegal for Artificial Lawyer. ]

Ingrid Van de Pol-Mensing, Principal AI Solutions Evangelist at Opus 2, takes us through the video. There is then some Q&A with Artificial Lawyer.

In this video we look at:

  • Using Matter Assist to prepare a cross-examination outline,
  • Document Assist for deeper analysis of selected documents,
  • General Assist for broader legal support beyond the document set.

news.summaryZh: NewMod Manifest OS 宣布完成 6000 万美元 A 轮融资，估值达 7.5 亿美元，由 Menlo Ventures、Kleiner Perkins 和 First Round Capital 参投。Manifest OS 通过品牌、软件和集中后台三大组件赋能下一代律所：统一品牌 Manifest Law 确保透明定价和服务质量；AI 原生平台覆盖客户沟通、法律研究、文档起草、计费等全流程，嵌入人工监督的 AI 代理；集中后台提供运营基础设施，招聘并培训律师助理、行政人员等，使律师专注于法律工作。Manifest OS 在亚利桑那州 ABS 项目下孵化了首家专注于商业移民的律所 Manifest Law，并计划拓展至其他法律领域。公司明确反对按小时计费模式，CEO Dan Mishin 表示，为真正转向基于结果的定价并普及高质量法律服务，必须从零重构律所商业模式，而非向现有律所销售 AI 软件。
news.bodyHtml:
NewMod Manifest OS has announced a $60m Series A funding round at a $750m valuation, with Menlo Ventures, Kleiner Perkins, and First Round Capital, taking part. In short – that’s a big vote of confidence in the NewMod approach from some major VC names.

Sounds great. And, as AL predicted at the end of last year: NewMods are going large in 2026! Ever get the feeling that NewMods are just going to grow and grow? (Note: three different groups of people have come to AL’s founder in recent weeks to ask about how best to form a NewMod / AI-first law firm….so, that’s just one yardstick.)

—

Express route to your Legal Innovators California June 10th and 11th ticket here.

Legal Innovators California, the landmark West Coast legal tech event, will take place on June 10 and 11, in the heart of the Bay Area, the home to many of the world’s leading AI businesses – and plenty of legal tech pioneers as well! More information and tickets here.

—

So what is happening?

They explained:

  • ‘Manifest OS incubated its first law firm in the business immigration market under the “Manifest Law” brand as part of the Arizona ABS program.
  • Manifest OS powers these next-generation law firms through three components.
  • Brand – All firms operate under the unified Manifest Law brand, creating a consistent standard for transparent pricing, service quality, and client experience. That brand signals high-caliber, outcomes-based legal work with centralized quality control.
  • Software – Manifest OS provides an AI-native platform that acts as a single end-to-end solution for client communications, attorney and client collaboration, legal research, document drafting, billing and reporting. Human-supervised AI agents are embedded directly into legal workflows, eliminating non-legal administrative work and standardizing quality. That frees lawyers to focus on delivering a high-touch, human experience and strategic counsel that technology cannot replace.
  • Centralized Back Office – Manifest OS provides centralized operational infrastructure that allows for Manifest-branded firms to achieve the scale of a large law firm. Manifest OS recruits paralegals, admins and legal writers, and trains them to become AI-proficient while handling client intake, business development, quality assurance, billing and collections, all under attorney supervision. Lawyers at Manifest OS-powered law firms focus on legal work and client advocacy, while Manifest OS provides the back-office engine to power the practice.’

I.e. this seems to be saying that they could branch out into other areas of the law. This is because Manifest OS is basically ‘the wrapper’, or maybe ‘the core’ – and from there they can go in many directions.

David Schellhase, Salesforce, Groupon, and Slack’s former General Counsel and a Manifest investor, said: ‘I’ve spent my career as a general counsel for some of the largest tech companies in the world and seen firsthand how the billable hour model creates friction on both sides of the table.

‘Companies want fee transparency, predictability, and speed. Lawyers want to focus on delivering results, not justifying billable hours. Manifest OS’s model and use of advanced technology align those interests in a way the traditional system simply doesn’t.’

And CEO Dan Mishin – who is not a lawyer and is understood not to know any secret legal handshakes – commented: ‘To truly shift the market to outcomes-based pricing and to democratize access to high-quality legal services for clients, we needed to rethink the entire business model of a law firm from the ground up.

‘We made the hard choice to not sell our AI software to existing law firms who are often beholden to billing customers more hours as a means to better compensation. Instead, we partner with forward-thinking lawyers to help them become market leaders in their respective practice areas, with AI at their core from day zero.’

And they are 100% against the use of the billable hour. Ahhh……what is that sweet music wafting into AL HQ…???

In short: What’s not to like?

Of course, if they’re going to rock the legal world, they’ll need to move into many more higher value areas beyond immigration law. But, let’s see what happens!

Congrats to Dan.

More about them here.

—

Legal Innovators California, the landmark West Coast legal tech event, will take place on June 10 and 11, in the heart of the Bay Area, the home to many of the world’s leading AI businesses – and plenty of legal tech pioneers as well! More information and tickets here.

news.titleEn: Tips For Working with Counterparties using AI Tools in Contract Negotiations
news.titleZh: 与使用AI工具的对手方进行合同谈判的实用建议
news.summaryZh: 随着语言学习模型（LLMs）支持合同分析与谈判，如何与使用AI工具的对手方合作成为新挑战。AI并非总是错误，但因其输出“足够正确”，预算敏感的消费者可能产生依赖。对此，不能简单禁止使用AI，而应采取更周全的方法：保持透明，主动询问对方是否使用了AI；提供背景信息，因为AI输出质量取决于提示词和训练数据，通过提供上下文可引导对方AI学习；管理预期，预判对方AI可能给出的回应；牢记目标导向，谈判目的是达成共识而非“击败AI”；认识到AI可能拖慢流程，因其倾向于生成大量文本，可通过电话沟通、限定往返次数等方式减少影响；同时，AI在协助律师提供精炼摘要方面可能更有效。对于使用AI生成内容的一方，建议聘请律师，注意律师-客户特权，律师的经验与判断力仍是AI无法替代的。

Following my recent blog about AI and the GC, a further question came up about how to work with counterparties that use AI tools.  The recent development of language learning models (LLMs) (artificial intelligence (AI) agents or bots) now supporting analytical work and negotiations in contracts is a challenging phenomenon.  It’s not because they are always wrong – they aren’t – but because they are often just right enough that budget-conscious consumers of legal services can grow dependent upon them.  Leaving aside the implications to those users for further discussion, I’m interested in exploring another challenge – how do business professionals with lawyers, or their lawyers themselves, respond to their counterparties’ use of the tools?

Sorry to say it, but the answer cannot be “don’t use the tools.”  Pandora’s box is open.  A more thoughtful approach is required:

So here are some tips:

  1. Be transparent – If someone presents you with something that looks like AI guidance, ask them if that’s the case.  An honest conversation can come only if the parties have a common baseline of facts.
  2. Provide context – In fact this was useful before, when it was attorney-to-attorney or business person to business person; but AI dependency is real, and when you provide feedback to someone using AI tools, remember the limitation of AI is that the output is only as good as the prompts and the information it is trained on.  You are unlikely to negotiate effectively with someone using AI by just stating an unreasoned position; but you can provide the context for your position.  If properly prompted, the counterparty’s AI will learn from the context you provide.
  3. Manage expectations – When you know your counterparty is using AI tools to evaluate what you send them, consider what their likely responses might be.  That might mean running it through AI yourself; or it might just mean thinking it through or discussing it with your attorney.
  4. Remember the goal line – the goal is not to out-think your counterparty or “beat their AI” tools.  The goal should be objective-oriented.  In the end, regardless of the tools used, both you and your counterparty need to come to a common understanding for a deal to be reached.
  5. Recognize that AI is likely to slow down the process – Recognize that AI may be just as likely to slow down the process as to speed it up, due partly to LLMs inherent ability to generate a large volume of text quickly.  Has any LLM model ever given a one sentence response to anything, like “this looks good enough”? (Prompt dependent, of course).  Perhaps merely recognizing that fact will allow you and the counterparty to come to a common understanding by (a) setting up calls to talk out issues, (b) establishing parameters on how much back and forth is acceptable, or (c) other ways to minimize the AI speedbump.
  6. Noting where AI may function better – Further to the last point, while two business professionals negotiating a contract would have to digest the volume of content AI can produce, two skilled attorneys using AI can assist those professionals by providing a more useful summary than the “TL;DR” version of AI jargon.

I’ve asked this question from the perspective of the person receiving the AI content for contract negotiations from their counterparty, but of course you may be the person generating that content.  My tip there is “use a lawyer.” Maybe not exclusively, but be mindful of the attorney client privilege if you run legal advice through AI tools.  A lawyer will serve your interests, cut to the chase hopefully faster than the AI tools, and help you to be objective-oriented in your negotiations.  It is likely that your lawyers are using AI tools now, too, which can be helpful in some contexts; but the skills for supporting clients in contract negotiations are most often enhanced by the intelligence, empathy, and experience that AI still cannot model out.

news.titleEn: Questel Launches QaECTER, a New AI Model Claiming State-of-the-Art Performance in Patent Search
news.titleZh: Questel 推出 QaECTER，声称在专利搜索领域达到最先进性能的新 AI 模型
news.summaryZh:
总部位于巴黎的知识产权软件与服务公司 Questel 发布了专为语义专利检索设计的新 AI 模型 QaECTER。该模型在所有查询类型、技术领域和司法管辖区测试中均优于竞争系统，包括规模大得多的系统。QaECTER 由 Questel 内部 AI 实验室开发，采用结合引文驱动监督与多视图自对齐的新型训练方法，基于 Questel 专有专利数据训练。该模型现已集成至 Questel 的 Sophia Search 工具和 Orbit Intelligence 平台。

为评估模型性能，Questel AI 实验室还创建了大规模基准 Sophia-Bench，包含 10,000 个专利查询和 75,000 篇专利文献，覆盖 10 年跨度、8 个 IPC 技术领域和 12 个申请司法管辖区。结果根据审查员引用的现有技术评分，测试 12 种不同查询类型。QaECTER 在 Sophia-Bench 和独立外部基准上均优于所有竞争模型，包括规模大 23 倍的系统。该模型针对专利检索从业者设计，通过引文关系和专利的多重视角学习相关性，支持发明披露、问题陈述、权利要求等多种输入。QaECTER 目前已在 Sophia Search 和 Orbit Intelligence 中可用，Sophia-Bench 计划未来公开。
news.bodyHtml:
Questel, an intellectual property software and services company headquartered in Paris, has released QaECTER, a new AI model designed specifically for semantic patent retrieval.

The company says the model outperforms competing systems, including those that are significantly larger, across every query type, technology domain and jurisdiction tested.

QaECTER is the product of Questel’s in-house AI Lab, which developed the model using what the company describes as novel training methodologies that combine citation-driven supervision with multi-view self-alignment on Questel’s proprietary patent data.

The model is now available within Questel’s Sophia Search tool and its Orbit Intelligence platform.

A Benchmark Built Alongside the Model

To evaluate the model’s performance, Questel’s AI Lab also created Sophia-Bench, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating patent search engines.

The company says the benchmark was built to address what it characterizes as a longstanding gap in the field — the absence of a realistic, practice-oriented way to measure patent retrieval performance.

Sophia-Bench comprises 10,000 patent queries and 75,000 corpus patents spanning 10 years, stratified across eight technology sections under the International Patent Classification system and 12 filing jurisdictions, including the European Patent Office, USPTO, and patent offices in China, South Korea, and Japan.

Results are graded against examiner-cited prior art, and the benchmark tests 12 distinct query types ranging from structured patent fields to AI-generated summaries.

Questel says QaECTER was tested against both Sophia-Bench and an independent external benchmark, and that it outperformed all competing general-purpose and patent-specific retrieval models evaluated, including systems described as 23 times larger.

Designed Around Practitioner Workflows

According to Questel, QaECTER was trained with patent search practitioners in mind. The model learns relevance through citation relationships and what the company calls “multiple complementary views” of each patent, enabling it to handle a range of inputs, from invention disclosures and problem statements to claims, abstracts, and technical descriptions.

Within Sophia Search, the model is paired with multilingual query translation, reranking, and other capabilities aimed at professional patent workflows.

The technology is designed to serve R&D engineers, patent attorneys, examiners and strategic searchers, Questel says.

Kim Gerdes, director of Questel’s AI Lab and also professor of computer science at Paris-Saclay University, co-authored a technical paper on both QaECTER and Sophia-Bench, published on the HAL open science platform: “Citation-Driven Multi-View Training for Patent Embeddings: QaECTER and Sophia-Bench.”

Gerdes said the team is “dedicated to advancing AI in the IP field” and characterized the developments as placing Questel “at the very forefront of modern Deep Learning for information retrieval.”

Availability

QaECTER is currently available in Sophia Search and Orbit Intelligence. Sophia-Bench is being used internally for now, though Questel says it plans to make the benchmark publicly available in the future.

Questel serves more than 20,000 clients and 1.5 million users across 30 countries and has 30 offices worldwide.

news.titleZh: AI失误频发，律所应对新技术的伦理影响
news.summaryZh: 在律师事务所的AI培训中，学习如何正确使用人工智能平台显然是重要环节，但了解何时使用以及何时不使用AI技术，却是一个有时被忽视但至关重要的组成部分。
news.bodyText: Learning precisely how to use an artificial intelligence platform in the course of legal business is obviously going to be a part of law firm AI training, but knowing when—and for that matter, when not—to use AI technology is a sometimes overlooked, but crucial, component of technology training.

news.titleEn: Questel Unveils AI Retrieval Model for Patent Tools
news.titleZh: Questel 推出专利工具 AI 检索模型
news.summaryZh: Questel 发布了名为 QaECTER 的嵌入模型，用于专利检索，旨在提升其生成式 AI 产品（如 Orbit Intelligence）的输出质量。该模型基于 Questel 的 Orbit 专利数据库训练，涵盖 2002 年至 2024 年公开的专利申请及英文文本专利。QaECTER 支持通过摘要、权利要求、说明书或发明目的进行检索，并能处理不同司法管辖区的专利文本差异。Questel 还开发了自有基准 Sophia-Bench，包含 10,000 个查询和 75,000 篇文档，覆盖 8 个国际专利分类技术领域和 12 个司法管辖区。经测试，QaECTER 在召回率上优于 PaECTER 和 bert-for-patents 等其他专利检索模型。
news.bodyHtml:
announced the appointment of Frédéric Beylier as CEO of in March. In December, Questel announced the integration of its patent and IP translation services with Equinox IP Management Software, expanding Questel’s IP environment and unifying IP services.

What It Is: QaECTER is an embedding model that performs patent retrieval and is designed to improve the output of Questel’s generative artificial intelligence products such as Orbit Intelligence the company's broader patent search and analytics offering.

An embedding model, or embeddings, are found within generative AI that compare semantic meanings, not only keywords

Questel’s model was trained on the company’s Orbit patent database, which includes patent applications published from 2002 to 2024 as well as patents with English text and translated English versions.

QaECTER is intended to enable users to conduct more comprehensive searches of existing patents.

“If someone has an idea and wants to draft a patent, of course we can just go ahead and draft, but it's much smarter to look it up first, and see, does this idea exist and can we combine the features of your idea in a way that becomes patentable by avoiding existing combinations? For all of these things, we need really good semantic search and we try to build a system that allows multiple ways of querying,” Kim Gerdes, Questel AI Lab director and co-founder/chief technology officer of Questel subsidiary qatent, told Law.com.

Why It’s Needed: QaECTER powers an upgrade to semantic search across Questel's product suite, with the aim of surfacing more relevant patents earlier in the results. Similar patent retrieval models were not as consistent across the diverse patent searches users including legal professionals would need to perform, according to Gerdes and Questel AI engineer Younes Djemmal.

“[Models] are good when you search with the abstract, but at the moment, you start using different types of inputs—for example, if a research and development engineer would just try to search with the invention disclosure—the model completely fails, and that is what we noticed in many of the models available,” Djemmal said. “We try to make QaECTER in a way that exposes it to different angles of the same invention and this way it will work whatever input is given to it.”

Questel’s QaECTER can retrieve patents with searches that include the abstract, claims, description or the object of the invention. Djemmal added that retrieval models for patents are especially useful as patent text is unique.

“Patent text is very different from other types of text, and the difference also goes beyond into the different jurisdictions, so depending on which jurisdiction you're in, you're going to have different formats, different rules that they follow,” he said. “Normal search models are not made for patent text. ... Subtle differences between jurisdictions, even existing patent models could not capture them because the data that they were trained on was not diverse enough.”

Under the Hood: To evaluate QaECTER, Questel developed its own benchmark called Sophia-Bench, made up of 10,000 queries and 75,000 corpus documents arranged across eight International Patent Classification technology sections and 12 filing jurisdictions, including European, U.S., Chinese, Korean and Japanese patent offices. The benchmark tests retrieval across 12 distinct query types, from structured patent fields to AI summaries.

The Competition: Questel used Sophia-Bench to evaluate QaECTER alongside patent retrieval models including PaECTER, and bert-for-patents, among others, and determined that QaECTER outperformed when it came to recall.

“[We] tested against models that were trained also on patent text specifically, ... and we proved also that our model using our new methodology beat patent specific search models as well,” Djemmal said.

news.titleEn: Can Opposing Parties See Your AI Prompts? Discovery Challenges in the AI Era
news.titleZh: 对方当事人能看到你的AI提示词吗？人工智能时代的证据开示挑战
news.summaryZh: 随着生成式AI工具在企业和法律部门中普及，员工可能无意中创建了新的可发现信息类别。AI提示词和输出可能构成电子存储信息（ESI），需在诉讼中保存、收集和提交。法院正依据传统证据开示原则处理AI提示词，若请求方证明其与案件主张或抗辩有具体关联，法院倾向于支持开示。AI提示词可能揭示比最终文件更直接、未经修饰的内部评估和策略，成为对方律师的有力目标。关于律师-客户特权和工作成果保护，法院判决不一。在Warner v. Gilbarco案中，法院认定AI生成材料受工作成果保护且未因向AI披露而放弃；而在United States v. Heppner案中，法院认为与公共AI平台的通信既不享有特权也不受工作成果保护，因平台服务条款缺乏合理保密预期。选择性披露AI生成内容可能导致特权放弃，如T.B. v. Big Brothers Big Sisters案中，原告引入AI聊天摘录后，法院认定工作成果保护被放弃。企业需更新法律保留流程以涵盖AI数据，并制定政策管理AI使用风险。
news.bodyHtml:
A calendar reminder appears for a related discovery response deadline that you are tasked with handling.

To save time, you send the requests to different employees outside the legal department and ask them to fill in factual information related to the business. Without your knowledge, they copy several requests into a public-facing artificial intelligence (AI) tool. Your company has its own proprietary, internal AI tools, but many employees either don’t know about the company’s tools, or prefer to use external platforms. So, attempting to be helpful, they craft a prompt along the lines of: “Draft responses that sound professional and minimize risk using the documents provided.” They feed the tool some select background facts, an internal timeline, and notes from discussions with your company’s business leaders. The AI generates clean, polished discovery responses, which are returned to you and ultimately incorporated into the version you serve on the opposing party.

You think nothing of this until, a few weeks later, you are staring at an interrogatory your company received in the same matter that asks: What AI tools did the company use to prepare its discovery responses? Provide all prompts, inputs, outputs, and chat histories related to any AI-assisted drafting of discovery materials. Suddenly, what felt like an efficient delegation decision has become a potential evidentiary minefield.
As AI becomes embedded in daily legal and business workflows, scenarios like this are no longer purely hypothetical. As organizations and employees (including, increasingly, legal departments) expand their use of generative AI tools, they may unwittingly be creating a new and largely unexamined category of potentially discoverable information.

The prompts employees feed AI tools, along with the outputs those tools generate, may constitute electronically stored information (ESI) subject to preservation, collection, and production obligations in litigation. In some circumstances, use of these tools may also threaten privilege and confidentiality protections.

AI Prompts Are Emerging as Discoverable ESI

Courts are approaching AI prompts and related outputs using traditional discovery principles, including treating prompts as ESI subject to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. In general, courts confronted with these issues will be willing to entertain discovery requests targeting AI usage where the requesting party can articulate a concrete connection to the claims or defenses at issue. While courts may still push back on speculative fishing expeditions, they are likely to favor production where prompts are plausibly relevant to the subject in dispute, in keeping with traditional discovery rules.

AI prompts may be especially impactful in discovery, as they have the potential to reveal more than final drafts of documents. For example, tracking the opening hypothetical scenario, finished discovery responses will usually be carefully vetted and sanitized. Prompts used to generate those responses, however, may reflect candid internal assessments, strategic framing of choices, or early thinking about risk exposure. As a result, from a discovery standpoint, AI prompts may function much like early drafts, margin comments, or internal emails, except they are often more direct and less guarded. That makes them attractive targets for smart opposing counsel seeking insight into how a company evaluated its conduct or shaped its litigation posture.

Privilege and Attorney Work Product Considerations

If AI discovery prompts are discoverable as ESI, the next logical question for legal departments is whether AI prompts may be protected by the attorney-client privilege, the work product doctrine, or other privileges protecting them from discovery. The emerging answer from the courts may be all too familiar for lawyers: it depends.

In Warner v. Gilbarco, No. 2:24-cv-12333, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 27355 (E.D. Mich. 2026) the court denied a motion to compel discovery into a pro se plaintiff’s use of generative AI. The court held that the materials were prepared in anticipation of litigation, were protected work product, and that any protection was not waived because “the AI tool (and other generative AI programs) are tools, not persons.” The court also emphasized proportionality, expressing skepticism toward discovery requests driven more by speculation about AI use than by genuine relevance to the claims or defenses at issue. In its assessment of whether work-product protection had been waived, the court emphasized that waiver must be “to an adversary or in a way likely to get in an adversary’s hand,” and found that disclosure to the AI tool did not qualify. However, the court reached the opposite conclusion in United States v. Heppner, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 32697 (S.D.N.Y. 2026), holding that communications with a public AI platform were neither privileged nor protected work product. There, the defendant used AI to generate documents outlining potential defense strategies and legal arguments after learning he was the target of a federal investigation, and later shared those materials with counsel. The court essentially treated the AI platform as a third party, relying heavily on the platform’s terms of service to find the absence of any reasonable expectation of confidentiality. Unlike the Warner decision, the court in Heppner did not consider whether waiver had been made to an adversary in its assessment of the work product protection. Instead, the court held that the work product doctrine did not apply because the AI documents were not prepared by or at the direction of counsel, and did not reflect counsel’s strategy.

As a result, rather than applying a bright-line rule, the privilege analysis for AI prompts turns on familiar factors like who used the AI tool, whether the communication was intended to seek legal advice, whether the tool was used at the direction of counsel, and whether the users had a reasonable expectation of privacy in utilizing the tool.

Waiver Risks

Courts have long held that selectively disclosing protected information may waive protection over related material. Utilization of AI makes this easier to trigger. If a party relies on an AI-generated summary, chart or draft in litigation, an opposing party may argue that fairness requires production of the underlying prompts and exchanges that produced it.

For example, in T.B. v. Big Brothers Big Sisters of New York City, 2025 NY Slip Op 33198(U) (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2025), a plaintiff introduced an excerpt of a chat with an AI tool, in which the AI tool purported to summarize a New York Times article, as an exhibit in a deposition. The defendant believed the article supposedly summarized by AI was hallucinated, and served a discovery request asking plaintiff to admit the article referenced did not exist, along with a request asking the plaintiff to produce the entire exchange with the AI tool that resulted in the summary of the supposed article at issue. Plaintiff asserted work product protection with respect to the full text of the chat session that led to the summary. The court rejected this argument, finding that disclosure by plaintiff’s counsel of the article summary portion of the transcript put the article at issue, and thus waived the work product protection.

For in-house counsel, the implication is clear: the familiar rules related to waiver of work product apply to AI-generated materials. If counsel inadvertently puts them at issue, the underlying AI prompts may become part of the story.

Preservation Obligations

Even if AI prompts are unlikely to be produced, they may still be subject to preservation obligations once litigation is reasonably anticipated.
Generative AI tools vary widely in how they store prompts and outputs, assuming they store them at all. Data may reside in third-party cloud systems, be retained only temporarily, or be tied to individual user accounts outside corporate IT controls.

For legal departments accustomed to preserving email, documents, and chat messages, this creates a new blind spot. A legal hold that does not account for AI usage may be incomplete, even if it is otherwise well-designed. As AI becomes more integrated into legal workflows, expect preservation disputes to follow. Savvy in-house counsel must understand how AI data being used by company employees is retained, including how long it is preserved and where it is stored.

What In-House Counsel Can Be Doing Now

Against this rapidly evolving backdrop, several practical steps may be taken by in-house lawyers to prevent a “gotcha” discovery moment:

  • Map AI usage across the legal department and the broader enterprise, with particular attention to discovery, investigations, and regulatory work. Legal teams should know which AI tools are being used and how they are being used in order to assess risk.
  • Update AI and information-governance policies to address prompts and outputs explicitly, including whether they are treated as company records.
  • Integrate AI into legal hold processes, ensuring preservation obligations account for AI-generated data.
  • Train legal and business teams on the risks of entering sensitive or privileged information into unsanctioned tools.
  • Encourage use of secure, enterprise-grade AI platforms with contractual assurances around confidentiality, retention, and data use.

Conclusion

The law governing AI prompts and discovery is still developing, and outcomes will remain fact-specific. But the direction of travel is clear: AI-generated inputs and outputs are becoming part of the discovery landscape, whether companies are ready or not.

For in-house counsel, the greatest risk lies not in using AI, but in using it without forethought. Understanding AI prompts as potential evidence today is critical to developing long-term effective litigation strategy and protecting your company’s privilege in the future.

Cara Peterman and Courtney Quirós are partners and Charlotte Bohn is a senior associate in Alston & Bird’s securities litigation group. They represent public companies and their officers and directors in securities class actions, shareholder derivative suits, M&A litigation and internal investigations.

news.summaryZh: 现代企业内部法务团队作为快速响应的服务伙伴，需要为业务领导者提供迅速且经过风险校准的答案，而业务领导者追求的是确定性而非复杂性。法务团队满足这一需求的能力不仅取决于法律判断，还取决于选择真正值得信赖的工具和合作伙伴。

news.titleEn: Ninth Circuit Clarifies Limits on Civil Appellate Review in Judge M. Smith Opinion
news.titleZh: 第九巡回法院在史密斯法官意见中明确民事上诉审查的限制
news.summaryZh:
2026年4月20日，第九巡回法院在第23-2527号案件中作出判决，由米兰·D·史密斯法官撰写意见，澄清了联邦上诉法院如何评估下级法院保留的问题、地区法院的推理以及上诉人的举证责任。上诉人不仅需指出错误，还需证明问题已妥善保留、地区法院确实滥用自由裁量权或法律错误，且错误具有损害性而非无害。该意见对民事案件中的案件管理决定、处置性裁定、证据认定或管辖权裁决的上诉尤为重要。

对于从业者，该意见强调了几个实践要点：问题保留至关重要，未在地区法院明确提出的论点通常被视为放弃；审查标准可能决定结果，法律问题适用重新审查，而自由裁量权或明显错误标准则增加上诉难度；建立清晰的事实和程序记录至关重要。若该判决解决了争议性程序问题或统一了先例，可能具有先例价值。总体而言，在第九巡回法院的成功往往依赖于上诉通知提交前严谨的诉讼策略。
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论民事上诉程序中的审查标准和问题保留，属于一般性民事诉讼程序，未涉及法律AI或法律技术相关内容。

news.titleEn: Anthropic’s AI agent-to-agent marketplace experiment: The legal frameworks don’t exist
news.titleZh: Anthropic的AI代理间市场实验：法律框架尚不存在
news.summaryZh:
Anthropic近期发布了一项名为“Project Deal”的实验，在Slack平台上创建了一个分类市场，让AI代理代表员工进行交易。实验为期一周，共完成186笔交易，涉及500件商品，总交易额略超4000美元。交易过程完全由AI代理以自然语言完成，包括识别匹配、发布列表、讨价还价和达成协议，无需预设谈判协议。

实验发现，使用更强大的模型Claude Opus 4.5的代理平均比使用较弱模型Claude Haiku 4.5的代理多完成约两笔交易，且同一商品售价平均高出3.64美元。目前尚不存在AI代理代表人类进行交易的政策和法律框架，但实验表明这样的世界已不遥远。这引发了关于代理协议的法律效力、责任归属等紧迫问题，例如当AI代理未经人类具体授权达成协议时，该协议的法律地位如何，以及因代理失误或攻击造成损失时责任由谁承担。
news.bodyHtml:
Recently, economists have begun theorising about a world in which AI models handle many or most transactions on humans’ behalf. Anthropic last week published an experiment – ‘Project Deal’ – looking at how close we are to marketplaces in which agents represent both parties. Could they make deals humans are happy with? And what would happen if different AI agents negotiate with each other? The results show that it is closer to reality than the legal sector is ready for.

For one week, Anthropic used its company’s Slack platform to create a classified marketplace for employees in its San Francisco office, “Like Craigslist, but with a twist: all of the deals were conducted by AI models acting on our employees’ behalf.”

Advertisement

The outcome? 186 completed deals across 500 listed items at a total transaction value of just over $4,000, covering everything from a snowboard to a bag of ping-pong balls. Deals required agents to identify potential matches, post listings, make and field counter-offers, and reach agreement – all in natural language, without any pre-built negotiation protocol.

One of the most significant findings – and the one, perhaps, with the most obvious legal and commercial implications – emerged from a parallel experiment run quietly alongside the main one. Anthropic secretly split participants: some were represented by Claude Opus 4.5, its then-frontier model; others by Claude Haiku 4.5, a smaller, less capable model. The difference in outcomes was measurable and meaningful. Opus users completed roughly two more deals on average. When the same item was sold by an Opus agent rather than a Haiku agent, it fetched $3.64 more on average. In one telling example, the same broken folding bike sold for $65 when represented by Opus — and only $38 when represented by Haiku. As a buyer, Opus agents paid $2.45 less for equivalent items. Whether buying or selling, the less powerful model put participants at a clear, quantifiable disadvantage.

While most of us are a long way off from being concerned about the comparative value of the deals our agents are striking for us, Anthropic itself flags the elephant in the room. “The policy and legal frameworks around AI models that transact on our behalf simply don’t exist yet,” the report concludes. “But this experiment shows that such a world is plausible. More than that, it shows that such a world isn’t far away.”

For regulators, legal professionals, and legal technologists, the questions are immediate and pressing. When two AI agents reach agreement without human sign-off, as they did in this experiment, what is the legal status of that agreement? The agents in Project Deal were acting on a general mandate established by a brief interview, not on specific authorisation for each transaction. In most jurisdictions, the doctrine of agency will require analysis: did the human principal authorise the specific deal struck? What happens when an agent exceeds its mandate, as arguably occurred when one participant’s agent bought them a snowboard they already owned?

There are also questions around liability. If an AI agent makes a deal that causes loss – whether through a bad bargain, a confabulated detail (as occurred in at least one exchange in the experiment), or a prompt injection attack – who bears responsibility? The deploying organisation? The AI provider? The individual who set the system prompt? Anthropic acknowledges a study last year from Cornell University that looked at agent-to-agent negotiation and risk.

It is worth noting that Project Deal was a small pilot, conducted with self-selected, technologically sophisticated participants in a non-adversarial environment. The researchers are appropriately cautious about overgeneralising. But the broader trajectory is clear. Economists are already theorising about economies in which AI agents handle the majority of commercial transactions on humans’ behalf. This experiment suggests that is not decades away. It may be years, or less.

Project Deal was published by Anthropic on 24 April 2026. The full study is available at anthropic.com
