research.titleEn: Mind The Gap: How The Technical Mechanism Of Agentic AI Outpace Global Legal Frameworks
research.titleZh: 警惕差距：智能体人工智能的技术机制如何超越全球法律框架
research.abstractEn: This article presents the first systematic comparative survey of how public bodies, international organisations, national regulators, and the private sector define agentic artificial intelligence, identifying the technical inaccuracies pervading each definition. Analysing eleven regulatory instruments and industry frameworks -- including the EU AI Act, the OECD/G7 Principles, NIST, the UK ICO, and the European Commission -- alongside six leading developer architectures, this study demonstrates a persistent definitional gap: legal definitions consistently conflate model capability with agentic architecture, attribute cognitive deliberation to probabilistic token prediction, and treat autonomy as a scalar property rather than a structural shift from single-inference to iterative execution loops with tool integration. A consensus technical definition synthesised from developer documentation is proposed. The article examines the consequences of this gap, demonstrating that definitional imprecision produces regulatory instruments structurally incapable of governing the actual mechanisms -- system prompts, API permissions, sandboxing, and orchestration code -- that constitute agentic autonomy.
research.abstractZh: 本文首次系统性地比较调查了公共机构、国际组织、国家监管机构和私营部门如何定义智能体人工智能，识别了每种定义中普遍存在的技术不准确性。通过分析十一项监管工具和行业框架——包括欧盟人工智能法案、经合组织/七国集团原则、美国国家标准与技术研究院、英国信息专员办公室和欧盟委员会——以及六种领先的开发架构，本研究揭示了一个持续存在的定义差距：法律定义一贯将模型能力与智能体架构混为一谈，将认知思考归因于概率性标记预测，并将自主性视为标量属性而非从单次推理到具有工具集成的迭代执行循环的结构性转变。本文提出了从开发者文档中综合得出的共识性技术定义。文章探讨了这一差距的后果，表明定义的不精确性导致监管工具在结构上无法治理构成智能体自主性的实际机制——系统提示、API权限、沙箱环境和编排代码。

news.titleEn: McDermott Chief Knowledge Officer: ‘AI Will Accelerate the Evolution of Legal Support Roles'
news.titleZh: McDermott首席知识官：人工智能将加速法律支持角色的演变
news.summaryZh: 律师事务所创新的最大障碍是人工智能工具的信任、验证和可解释性问题，而非文化阻力。律师需要确信AI能完整阅读、理解并准确反映记录，幻觉、不完整答案和不透明推理是核心挑战。McDermott通过可验证、基于引用的设计应对此，其AI助手的所有回答均自动链接回源材料并提供标准化输出。创新的最大驱动力是可靠性和问责制，当工具能提供审计追踪、可解释推理和文件覆盖证据时，律师信任将提升。生成式和代理式AI将重塑法律运营模式，提高知识工作效率，使起草、研究和总结更快、更标准化，让律师更专注于战略分析。运营上，律师事务所将增加人机混合工作流，动态助手集成到文档管理系统等中，自动化重复性高容量任务。人员配置方面，AI将加速法律支持角色的演变，知识管理、创新和法律技术专业人员将在设计、治理和维护AI工作流中发挥更大作用。业务模式也将演变，客户将更多要求AI增强的定价结构。未来法律技术需转向互联的智能生态系统，整合结构化数据、机构知识和上下文丰富的AI推理。McDermott正投资企业数据仓库内的数据治理和卫生，并利用Omni等数据可视化工具。另一个前沿是企业搜索，现代大型语言模型能实现跨系统的语义搜索。这些进步也将重塑人员配置，需要跨职能团队共同设计、训练和治理AI系统。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Hunter Jackson, chief knowledge officer at McDermott Will & Schulte, which won the award for Litigation Technology and Innovation.

What do you currently see as the biggest barriers to, and biggest drivers of innovation in law firms?

The biggest barriers to innovation in law firms center on trust, validation, and explainability—not cultural resistance. Lawyers need confidence that AI tools read, understand, and accurately reflect the full record before forming an output. Hallucinations, incomplete answers, and opaque reasoning remain the core challenges.

Traditional AI models offer little visibility into how conclusions are reached or whether all relevant information was considered. For legal work, where precision and provenance are non-negotiable, this lack of transparency creates natural hesitation. The inability to easily verify results makes adoption difficult, regardless of the underlying model’s potential.

McDermott’s approach addresses this head-on through verifiable, citation-based design. Every McDermott AI Assistant links its responses back to the source material through automatically generated citations. This gives lawyers the ability to check each statement, confirm context, and validate completeness. The firm will not launch any assistant without these capabilities—citation and auditability are mission-critical, not optional features.

Equally important is output standardization. By defining structured, task-specific outputs— such as checklists, term tables, or summaries—McDermott ensures that results are predictable and usable in downstream workflows. Testing with practicing lawyers further refines this alignment, ensuring outputs meet professional standards.

The biggest drivers of innovation, conversely, are reliability and accountability. As vendors and firms build tools that provide audit trails, explainable reasoning, and evidence of document coverage, lawyer trust will grow exponentially. When lawyers can see how an AI reached its answer—and confirm that it reviewed everything relevant—adoption follows naturally.

Innovation in law firms will accelerate when technology not only assists lawyers, but also earns their confidence through verifiable, transparent, and reproducible AI reasoning.

Emerging technologies such as generative and agentic AI are enabling new levels of automation in law firms. How do you expect these changes to impact law firms' operations, staffing and/or business models?

Generative and agentic AI are poised to fundamentally reshape the legal operating model—not by replacing lawyers, but by redefining how legal expertise is deployed. The most immediate impact will be on the efficiency of knowledge work: drafting, research, and summarization will become faster and more standardized, allowing lawyers to spend more time on strategic, judgment-based analysis.

Operationally, law firms will see an increase in hybrid human-AI workflows. Instead of static tools, firms will deploy dynamic assistants that integrate into document management systems, client portals, and practice group templates. These assistants will automate repeatable, high-volume tasks such as due diligence, discovery review, and financial agreement parsing.

From a staffing perspective, AI will accelerate the evolution of legal support roles. Knowledge management, innovation, and legal technology professionals will play a larger role in designing, governing, and maintaining AI workflows. The emphasis will shift from individual legal expertise to team-based AI orchestration, where technologists, lawyers, and data experts collaborate to scale institutional knowledge.

Business models will also evolve. Clients will increasingly demand AI-augmented pricing structures—fixed fees, subscription models, or output-based billing—reflecting the efficiency gains AI delivers. Firms that harness AI to increase throughput without sacrificing quality will gain competitive advantage.

In short, AI will make law firms more data-driven, more efficient, and more transparent—provided they invest in governance, training, and design frameworks that align with professional standards. McDermott’s work in developing controlled, reliable assistants represents a preview of this future.

How would you like to see technology specifically designed for law firms change over the next few years, and why?

The next generation of legal technology must move beyond isolated tools toward a connected, intelligent ecosystem—one that brings together structured data, institutional knowledge, and context-rich AI reasoning. At McDermott, we believe the future lies in integrated data governance and context-aware AI, built on emerging standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The Model Context Protocol represents a major shift in how law firms can securely connect AI systems to internal data sources. Rather than relying on static uploads or narrow prompts, MCP enables dynamic retrieval—allowing large language models to draw from trusted enterprise systems while maintaining guardrails and governance. This opens the door to contextually aware AI Assistants that reason across document management systems, finance data, and knowledge repositories in real time.

Our firm is also investing deeply in data governance and hygiene within our enterprise data warehouse (EDW). Reliable AI depends on clean, labeled, and well-permissioned data. To surface that value, we are leveraging data visualization tools like Omni, which allow lawyers and business teams to extract and visualize data insights directly from the EDW. This combination of governed data and intelligent visualization forms the foundation for the next phase of AI-driven insight at scale.

Another major frontier is enterprise search. With modern LLMs, the legal industry can finally achieve the kind of semantic, cross-system search it has long envisioned—the ability to ask questions across millions of documents and receive accurate, explainable, and cited responses.

These advancements will also reshape staffing. The future requires cross-functional teams—legal subject matter experts, IT engineers, data scientists, and change management professionals—working together to design, train, and govern AI systems. Traditional silos will give way to AI-enabled collaboration, redefining how law firms operationalize intelligence across their practices.

news.titleEn: What I Took Away from Texas Trailblazers
news.titleZh: 德克萨斯开拓者大会首日观察：AI信任成为工作流程问题，采用率取决于激励而非工具获取
news.summaryZh: 德克萨斯开拓者大会首日在达拉斯举行，由Cosmonauts与LegalOps.com合作组织，ILTA首席执行官Joy Heath Rush主持开幕。会议聚焦AI在律所的实际应用，核心议题包括：AI信任已成为工作流程设计问题，研究表明即使有经济激励，人们仍会过度依赖AI输出，因此审查必须嵌入流程而非依赖个人自觉；采用率取决于激励措施而非工具获取，例如在固定收费业务中，AI效率直接关联合伙人薪酬时才会被持续使用；可持续创新基础涉及人员、流程与政策，如Husch Blackwell设立虚拟办公室和“架构师”角色，Barnes & Thornburg通过客户访谈实现收入增长；工作流程设计是提升效率的关键，Legora提出AI投资回报率因使用场景差异巨大，自动化需从交付成果反向设计流程；定价模式面临挑战，计时收费仍占主导但受AI效率冲击，客户要求替代性收费却同时索要影子账单；Filevine指出法律研究市场临近拐点，公开案例数据与成熟语言模型可能颠覆传统引证工具。行业AI采用率约35%-40%，会议强调工具快速演进中，更艰巨的是协调人员、流程与期望。
news.bodyHtml:
(See Day Two Coverage for the In-House Programs over on The Geek in Review Substack page – GL)

Day One of Texas Trailblazers in Dallas had a different tone than most legal tech conferences I attend. The conversations stayed close to the work. Less speculation, more discussion about what people are doing right now, where it is working, and where it is breaking.

Organized by Cosmonauts in partnership with LegalOps.com and held at The Statler Dallas, the Private Practice Day brought together law firm leaders, legal operations professionals, and technology vendors for a full day of keynotes, panels, and product demos. Joy Heath Rush, CEO of ILTA, chaired the day and opened with a fireside on the new era of conversations between general counsel and outside counsel. Her framing set the tone: AI is living at the intersection of business and technology, and it is creating conversations that simply did not exist two years ago.

Across the sessions and hallway conversations that followed, a few themes kept showing up. They were consistent whether the speaker came from a law firm, an in-house team, or a vendor building the tools.

Trust in AI is becoming a workflow problem

Rowan McNamee, Co-Founder and COO of Mary Technology, opened the sponsor keynote with a point that came up repeatedly throughout the day. AI outputs are persuasive. They read well. They look complete. That creates a tendency to move forward without enough friction in the process.

McNamee cited a recent study on what researchers call “cognitive surrender,” based on the work of Sean Hay and building on the framework in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Under time pressure, people rely on AI even when they know they should verify the result. In a series of experiments, override rates improved from 20% to 42% when participants had real money on the line. Even then, more than half still followed the AI’s answer. “You can reduce it, but you can’t eliminate it just by telling people to be careful,” McNamee noted.

In a legal setting, the implication is straightforward. Review cannot be optional. It has to be built into the process in a way that does not depend on someone remembering to slow down.

That concern echoed later in the day during the panel I moderated. Laura Ewing-Pearle, Senior Manager of eDiscovery and Practice Support Technology at Baker Botts, described a clear split even among e-discovery practitioners who are enthusiastic about AI. They lean heavily toward document interrogation and querying. They are far less comfortable with AI making responsiveness calls, and they are “definitely not comfortable with AI making privilege calls.” The line between assistance and reliance is still being worked out in real time.

Adding urgency to the conversation, panelists referenced a recent New York case in which a court ruled that AI-generated legal advice obtained through a public tool was not protected by attorney-client privilege. The ruling was specific to a consumer-facing chatbot, but the message landed clearly: enterprise AI tools with proper security and licensing are becoming a matter of professional risk management.

Adoption follows incentives, not access

The panel on Culture, Change, and Collaboration brought together Emma Dowden of Burges Salmon, Thom Wisinski of Haynes Boone, Kelley Lugo of Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, Rowan McNamee, and Tammy Covert of Nachawati. The discussion stayed focused on what actually drives adoption inside organizations.

Kelley Lugo described how the initial reaction at many firms was to block AI tools. That position has shifted. Lawyers are experimenting, often on their own. But the challenge is whether there is a reason to use AI consistently. She offered a concrete example: in BCLP’s UK real estate group, roughly 80% of matters are handled on a fixed-fee basis. Write-offs on those fixed matters directly hurt partner compensation. That pain point, she explained, is exactly where AI efficiency aligns with real motivation. When the people doing the work see a direct connection between AI-assisted speed and their own metrics, engagement follows.

Emma Dowden framed it in terms of mindset and behavior. Transformation efforts stall when they focus on the technology without addressing how people are measured and rewarded. She also noted that the pace of change is creating a real business risk. In the UK, the Big Four are telling firms what percentage of their revenues are at risk from disruption, and the numbers are serious.

Lugo shared a story that captured the adoption dynamic well. A senior leader at her firm went on a two-week safari, came back, and told her he had not thought about work at all the entire trip. But he had thought about AI the entire time. When people get enough distance to think clearly about where the profession is headed, the conclusions tend to be similar.

No one on this panel suggested that training alone will move the needle. The focus stayed on incentives, visibility, and examples that resonate with how lawyers already operate.

Building sustainable innovation foundations

The fireside on Beyond Technology: People, Process, and Policy brought together Joanna Penn, Chief Transformation Officer at Husch Blackwell, Rochelle Rubin, Director of Client and Business Operations at Barnes & Thornburg, and Louise Thomas, Director of Transformation at Burges Salmon.

Husch Blackwell’s approach stood out for its scale. Their virtual office, “The Link,” now has over 850 people, including more than 250 attorneys, working in a distributed model that lets the firm recruit specialized talent in markets where they have no physical office. They are also hiring “architects” whose job is to translate between technical and legal teams. That is a role you are starting to see more firms create.

Barnes & Thornburg shared a result that had nothing to do with technology and everything to do with process. Their client interview program, built on the simple act of asking clients what the firm could do better, produced a 90% or greater revenue increase within 12 to 18 months for the clients who received that in-person attention. The takeaway: sometimes the highest-value innovation is a conversation.

Workflow design is where the gains are showing up

Kyle Poe, VP of Legal Innovation and Strategy at Legora, presented a framework for measuring AI ROI that moved the conversation past speed alone. His point was that firms seeing real results are looking at outcomes and pricing, not just how many minutes a task takes. The ROI, he argued, varies dramatically by use case. Some tasks show minimal time savings. Others produce modest reductions, like going from ten hours to eight. And some are transformative, compressing weeks of due diligence into hours. He also projected that firms will likely raise rates around 25% to offset AI costs while repositioning how they describe the value they deliver.

That idea came into sharper focus during the Automation in Action panel, which I moderated. Paul Pryzant, a partner at Seyfarth Shaw with 45 years in M&A, described how his group now runs deep research on target companies on day one of receiving a letter of intent. Information that used to take two or three weeks to surface during due diligence is now available immediately. Pryzant also emphasized starting from the client relationship: “My favorite question is, how are you using AI? How are members of your team using it?” That approach opens a two-way conversation rather than a one-sided pitch.

Rutvik Rau, CEO and Co-Founder of August, reinforced the importance of starting with the deliverable and working backward. That approach forces clarity about what steps are required, where the bottlenecks sit, and which parts require judgment. The most successful users, he said, are the ones with a strong sense of how they deliver a service to their client. Curiosity and creativity matter more than technical skill.

Chad Barton, a corporate transactions partner at Holland Knight, described how his lending team built AI into their existing process for handling matters with rigid institutional parameters. He also raised a tension that no one else on the panel had addressed directly. When AI makes associates dramatically more efficient, it creates a compensation problem. “If I’m really efficient, I can’t hit my target,” is something associates are already thinking about. Barton was clear that this falls on firm leadership to address, especially during compensation reviews. Partners need to defend associates who produce excellent work product even if the hours look different.

Kyle Poe added a practical observation about change management. “Workflow is just the orchestration of multiple things you could do within the product,” he said. Teams that learn the individual tools first and then map the process manually tend to have a clearer path to automation. He also described building workflows in plain English instructions, the same way you would brief a literal-minded associate, and then iterating based on mistakes.

The Legora demo and a question about legal research

During the break, Harry St. John, VP of Revenue at Legora, ran a product demo that filled the room. Legora’s platform centers on two main tools: an assistant for conversational document interrogation and a tabular review for bulk extraction across large document sets. St. John showed how the two connect. Extraction results from tabular review can be queried through the assistant, and outputs can be pushed into Microsoft Word using firm-specific templates. A newer feature called WordEdits generates multiple unique Word documents from a single instruction set, useful for tasks like drafting a set of resignation letters for every officer in a transaction.

I asked St. John about the legal research capability they had flagged, given that at Jackson Walker we tell our people not to use AI for legal research unless they are inputting their own materials. He said Legora has ingested district, appellate, and Supreme Court caselaw from a number of providers, with their legal research database launching soon. He was transparent that bankruptcy coverage was not included yet.

Pricing is moving into the center of the conversation

The panel titled Billing on Trial: Rethinking the Economics of Legal Work brought together Jon Lindrus of Foley and Lardner, Jonathan Safran of Polsinelli, Marlene Gebauer of K&L Gates, and Katon Luaces of PointOne.

Time-based billing is still the dominant model, but it is under more scrutiny than ever. AI changes how long work takes. That raises questions about how value is measured and communicated. One of the clearer moments came earlier in the day during my panel when Kyle Poe described a dynamic playing out between firms and in-house counsel. Some firms are trying to benchmark what a task would have taken with humans last year, apply a discount, and offer that as a fixed fee. But if AI produces savings far beyond 20%, clients will eventually ask why they should lock in rates that still capture most of the efficiency gains for the firm. The honest answer is that both sides are still figuring this out.

Jonathan Safran, in a pre-conference interview published by the Cosmonauts team, made a point that resonated throughout the day. Clients say they want alternative fee arrangements, but many still ask for shadow billing to verify what they would have paid under an hourly model. That tension makes standardization difficult. And on the firm side, three partners at the same firm might manage the same project three very different ways, which makes fee estimation genuinely hard.

Disrupting the citator: open data meets modern AI

John Rizner, Head of AI Legal Drafting at Filevine, gave a presentation that most of the audience probably had not expected. His argument: the legal research market is approaching an inflection point. An unprecedented volume of American caselaw is now freely accessible and processable by digital tools. At the same time, language models have reached a level of legal sophistication that would have been unimaginable five years ago. Taken together, Rizner argued, these developments create the possibility of meaningful competition in legal research and call into question long-held assumptions about who can build a citator and what it should cost.

A practical example from litigation

Craig Nesbitt, Solutions Architect at DISCO, presented a session comparing modern litigation workflows to high-performance cycling. The analogy worked because it stayed grounded in execution. Reducing “drag” in litigation comes from removing friction in how data is handled, reviewed, and analyzed. AI plays a role, but it sits alongside process design and support services. The point was about coordinating multiple elements so the overall system performs better.

The emotional journey ahead

Richard B. Gorelick, Founder and CEO of ChronoTracer, closed the formal sessions with a ten-minute pitch titled “The Lawyer Freakout of 2027.” His argument was that software developers have already gone through the emotional journey that lawyers are about to face: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. Lawyers, he predicted, will undergo a similar identity crisis as AI transforms the nature of their work. It was a useful note to end on. The tools are advancing. The process questions are getting answered. But the human side of this transition, how people feel about the work they do and who they are when they do it, is still largely unaddressed.

Where this leaves us

By the end of the day, the conversation felt less like an introduction to new technology and more like a working session on how legal services are being reshaped. Thomson Reuters data shared during one of the sessions put current AI adoption rates at 35 to 40 percent across the industry. That is meaningful progress, but it also means more than half the profession is still watching from the sidelines.

A few observations stand out from the day:

  • Trust in AI needs structure, not reminders. Even with financial incentives, people follow AI outputs more than they should. Verification has to be designed into the process.
  • Adoption depends on incentives and visible use cases. When AI efficiency connects directly to compensation or profitability, people engage. When it does not, they wait.
  • Workflow clarity is a prerequisite for meaningful automation. The firms getting results are mapping their processes before automating them.
  • Pricing discussions are tied directly to how work is performed. As tasks get faster, the economics of client relationships change alongside them.
  • Clients are already engaged and influencing expectations. They are using AI in their own organizations and forming opinions about how outside counsel should be using it too.
  • The human side of this transition deserves more attention. Junior associates worried about billable hours, senior partners rethinking their identity, and support staff facing higher-stress work after the easy tasks are automated. These are real concerns that training programs and leadership need to address.

The examples came from people who are testing, adjusting, and in some cases rethinking long-standing approaches to legal work. That is what made Day One useful. The focus stayed on decisions that need to be made now.

And if there was a consistent thread across all of it, it is this: the tools are moving quickly. The harder work is aligning people, processes, and expectations around them.

Texas Trailblazers was held March 25-26, 2026 at The Statler Dallas, organized by Cosmonauts in partnership with LegalOps.com. Day One focused on private practice; Day Two on in-house operations. Joy Heath Rush (ILTA) chaired Day One.
news.bodyText:
(See Day Two Coverage for the In-House Programs over on The Geek in Review Substack page – GL)

Day One of Texas Trailblazers in Dallas had a different tone than most legal tech conferences I attend. The conversations stayed close to the work. Less speculation, more discussion about what people are doing right now, where it is working, and where it is breaking.

Organized by Cosmonauts in partnership with LegalOps.com and held at The Statler Dallas, the Private Practice Day brought together law firm leaders, legal operations professionals, and technology vendors for a full day of keynotes, panels, and product demos. Joy Heath Rush, CEO of ILTA, chaired the day and opened with a fireside on the new era of conversations between general counsel and outside counsel. Her framing set the tone: AI is living at the intersection of business and technology, and it is creating conversations that simply did not exist two years ago.

Across the sessions and hallway conversations that followed, a few themes kept showing up. They were consistent whether the speaker came from a law firm, an in-house team, or a vendor building the tools.

Trust in AI is becoming a workflow problem

Rowan McNamee, Co-Founder and COO of Mary Technology, opened the sponsor keynote with a point that came up repeatedly throughout the day. AI outputs are persuasive. They read well. They look complete. That creates a tendency to move forward without enough friction in the process.

McNamee cited a recent study on what researchers call “cognitive surrender,” based on the work of Sean Hay and building on the framework in Thinking, Fast and Slow . Under time pressure, people rely on AI even when they know they should verify the result. In a series of experiments, override rates improved from 20% to 42% when participants had real money on the line. Even then, more than half still followed the AI’s answer. “You can reduce it, but you can’t eliminate it just by telling people to be careful,” McNamee noted.

In a legal setting, the implication is straightforward. Review cannot be optional. It has to be built into the process in a way that does not depend on someone remembering to slow down.

That concern echoed later in the day during the panel I moderated. Laura Ewing-Pearle, Senior Manager of eDiscovery and Practice Support Technology at Baker Botts, described a clear split even among e-discovery practitioners who are enthusiastic about AI. They lean heavily toward document interrogation and querying. They are far less comfortable with AI making responsiveness calls, and they are “definitely not comfortable with AI making privilege calls.” The line between assistance and reliance is still being worked out in real time.

Adding urgency to the conversation, panelists referenced a recent New York case in which a court ruled that AI-generated legal advice obtained through a public tool was not protected by attorney-client privilege. The ruling was specific to a consumer-facing chatbot, but the message landed clearly: enterprise AI tools with proper security and licensing are becoming a matter of professional risk management.

Adoption follows incentives, not access

The panel on Culture, Change, and Collaboration brought together Emma Dowden of Burges Salmon, Thom Wisinski of Haynes Boone, Kelley Lugo of Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, Rowan McNamee, and Tammy Covert of Nachawati. The discussion stayed focused on what actually drives adoption inside organizations.

Kelley Lugo described how the initial reaction at many firms was to block AI tools. That position has shifted. Lawyers are experimenting, often on their own. But the challenge is whether there is a reason to use AI consistently. She offered a concrete example: in BCLP’s UK real estate group, roughly 80% of matters are handled on a fixed-fee basis. Write-offs on those fixed matters directly hurt partner compensation. That pain point, she explained, is exactly where AI efficiency aligns with real motivation. When the people doing the work see a direct connection between AI-assisted speed and their own metrics, engagement follows.

Emma Dowden framed it in terms of mindset and behavior. Transformation efforts stall when they focus on the technology without addressing how people are measured and rewarded. She also noted that the pace of change is creating a real business risk. In the UK, the Big Four are telling firms what percentage of their revenues are at risk from disruption, and the numbers are serious.

Lugo shared a story that captured the adoption dynamic well. A senior leader at her firm went on a two-week safari, came back, and told her he had not thought about work at all the entire trip. But he had thought about AI the entire time. When people get enough distance to think clearly about where the profession is headed, the conclusions tend to be similar.

No one on this panel suggested that training alone will move the needle. The focus stayed on incentives, visibility, and examples that resonate with how lawyers already operate.

Building sustainable innovation foundations

The fireside on Beyond Technology: People, Process, and Policy brought together Joanna Penn, Chief Transformation Officer at Husch Blackwell, Rochelle Rubin, Director of Client and Business Operations at Barnes & Thornburg, and Louise Thomas, Director of Transformation at Burges Salmon.

Husch Blackwell’s approach stood out for its scale. Their virtual office, “The Link,” now has over 850 people, including more than 250 attorneys, working in a distributed model that lets the firm recruit specialized talent in markets where they have no physical office. They are also hiring “architects” whose job is to translate between technical and legal teams. That is a role you are starting to see more firms create.

Barnes & Thornburg shared a result that had nothing to do with technology and everything to do with process. Their client interview program, built on the simple act of asking clients what the firm could do better, produced a 90% or greater revenue increase within 12 to 18 months for the clients who received that in-person attention. The takeaway: sometimes the highest-value innovation is a conversation.

Workflow design is where the gains are showing up

Kyle Poe, VP of Legal Innovation and Strategy at Legora, presented a framework for measuring AI ROI that moved the conversation past speed alone. His point was that firms seeing real results are looking at outcomes and pricing, not just how many minutes a task takes. The ROI, he argued, varies dramatically by use case. Some tasks show minimal time savings. Others produce modest reductions, like going from ten hours to eight. And some are transformative, compressing weeks of due diligence into hours. He also projected that firms will likely raise rates around 25% to offset AI costs while repositioning how they describe the value they deliver.

That idea came into sharper focus during the Automation in Action panel, which I moderated. Paul Pryzant, a partner at Seyfarth Shaw with 45 years in M&A, described how his group now runs deep research on target companies on day one of receiving a letter of intent. Information that used to take two or three weeks to surface during due diligence is now available immediately. Pryzant also emphasized starting from the client relationship: “My favorite question is, how are you using AI? How are members of your team using it?” That approach opens a two-way conversation rather than a one-sided pitch.

Rutvik Rau, CEO and Co-Founder of August, reinforced the importance of starting with the deliverable and working backward. That approach forces clarity about what steps are required, where the bottlenecks sit, and which parts require judgment. The most successful users, he said, are the ones with a strong sense of how they deliver a service to their client. Curiosity and creativity matter more than technical skill.

Chad Barton, a corporate transactions partner at Holland Knight, described how his lending team built AI into their existing process for handling matters with rigid institutional parameters. He also raised a tension that no one else on the panel had addressed directly. When AI makes associates dramatically more efficient, it creates a compensation problem. “If I’m really efficient, I can’t hit my target,” is something associates are already thinking about. Barton was clear that this falls on firm leadership to address, especially during compensation reviews. Partners need to defend associates who produce excellent work product even if the hours look different.

Kyle Poe added a practical observation about change management. “Workflow is just the orchestration of multiple things you could do within the product,” he said. Teams that learn the individual tools first and then map the process manually tend to have a clearer path to automation. He also described building workflows in plain English instructions, the same way you would brief a literal-minded associate, and then iterating based on mistakes.

The Legora demo and a question about legal research

During the break, Harry St. John, VP of Revenue at Legora, ran a product demo that filled the room. Legora’s platform centers on two main tools: an assistant for conversational document interrogation and a tabular review for bulk extraction across large document sets. St. John showed how the two connect. Extraction results from tabular review can be queried through the assistant, and outputs can be pushed into Microsoft Word using firm-specific templates. A newer feature called WordEdits generates multiple unique Word documents from a single instruction set, useful for tasks like drafting a set of resignation letters for every officer in a transaction.

I asked St. John about the legal research capability they had flagged, given that at Jackson Walker we tell our people not to use AI for legal research unless they are inputting their own materials. He said Legora has ingested district, appellate, and Supreme Court caselaw from a number of providers, with their legal research database launching soon. He was transparent that bankruptcy coverage was not included yet.

Pricing is moving into the center of the conversation

The panel titled Billing on Trial: Rethinking the Economics of Legal Work brought together Jon Lindrus of Foley and Lardner, Jonathan Safran of Polsinelli, Marlene Gebauer of K&L Gates, and Katon Luaces of PointOne.

Time-based billing is still the dominant model, but it is under more scrutiny than ever. AI changes how long work takes. That raises questions about how value is measured and communicated. One of the clearer moments came earlier in the day during my panel when Kyle Poe described a dynamic playing out between firms and in-house counsel. Some firms are trying to benchmark what a task would have taken with humans last year, apply a discount, and offer that as a fixed fee. But if AI produces savings far beyond 20%, clients will eventually ask why they should lock in rates that still capture most of the efficiency gains for the firm. The honest answer is that both sides are still figuring this out.

Jonathan Safran, in a pre-conference interview published by the Cosmonauts team, made a point that resonated throughout the day. Clients say they want alternative fee arrangements, but many still ask for shadow billing to verify what they would have paid under an hourly model. That tension makes standardization difficult. And on the firm side, three partners at the same firm might manage the same project three very different ways, which makes fee estimation genuinely hard.

Disrupting the citator: open data meets modern AI

John Rizner, Head of AI Legal Drafting at Filevine, gave a presentation that most of the audience probably had not expected. His argument: the legal research market is approaching an inflection point. An unprecedented volume of American caselaw is now freely accessible and processable by digital tools. At the same time, language models have reached a level of legal sophistication that would have been unimaginable five years ago. Taken together, Rizner argued, these developments create the possibility of meaningful competition in legal research and call into question long-held assumptions about who can build a citator and what it should cost.

A practical example from litigation

By the end of the day, the conversation felt less like an introduction to new technology and more like a working session on how legal services are being reshaped. Thomson Reuters data shared during one of the sessions put current AI adoption rates at 35 to 40 percent across the industry. That is meaningful progress, but it also means more than half the profession is still watching from the sidelines.

A few observations stand out from the day:

Trust in AI needs structure, not reminders. Even with financial incentives, people follow AI outputs more than they should. Verification has to be designed into the process.

Adoption depends on incentives and visible use cases. When AI efficiency connects directly to compensation or profitability, people engage. When it does not, they wait.

Workflow clarity is a prerequisite for meaningful automation. The firms getting results are mapping their processes before automating them.

Pricing discussions are tied directly to how work is performed. As tasks get faster, the economics of client relationships change alongside them.

Clients are already engaged and influencing expectations. They are using AI in their own organizations and forming opinions about how outside counsel should be using it too.

The human side of this transition deserves more attention. Junior associates worried about billable hours, senior partners rethinking their identity, and support staff facing higher-stress work after the easy tasks are automated. These are real concerns that training programs and leadership need to address.

The examples came from people who are testing, adjusting, and in some cases rethinking long-standing approaches to legal work. That is what made Day One useful. The focus stayed on decisions that need to be made now.

And if there was a consistent thread across all of it, it is this: the tools are moving quickly. The harder work is aligning people, processes, and expectations around them.

Texas Trailblazers was held March 25-26, 2026 at The Statler Dallas, organized by Cosmonauts in partnership with LegalOps.com. Day One focused on private practice; Day Two on in-house operations. Joy Heath Rush (ILTA) chaired Day One.

By

Helen Sheeba

posted

2 days ago

Email 2.0: How AI Is Turning the Legal Inbox into a Productivity Engine

Email: The Invisible Engine behind Legal Work

In every law firm, whether a boutique practice or a global enterprise; work is propelled by email.

Client instructions arrive by email.

Draft agreements circulate over email.

Negotiations unfold across long, branching email threads.

Approvals, clarifications, and decisions are often buried somewhere in the inbox before they ever hit a document management system.

Email isn’t just communication. It is the workflow.

Yet it is also where productivity slows down the most. Attorneys spend hours reading dense threads, scanning attachments, and drafting precise responses that must meet professional, ethical, and firm standards. What should be a quick reply often becomes a multi-step exercise involving context gathering, document review, and perfectly crafted language.

So the question becomes:

What if email could work for attorneys, not the other way around?

Enter the KLapper Outlook Add‑In , a powerful integration that brings Generative AI directly into Microsoft Outlook. With it, attorneys can review, draft, and respond to emails using AI that understands the full conversation, the attachments, and the business context, without leaving the environment where legal communication already lives.

AI That Understands the Entire Conversation

Legal email threads are rarely straightforward. They often grow into long, complex chains spanning days or weeks, containing nuanced discussions scattered across multiple replies. Manually scanning each message to understand the full context before responding can be both exhausting and inefficient.

The KLapper Outlook Add‑In addresses this challenge by enabling AI to analyze the entire email thread, not just the latest message. This means professionals receive drafts that reflect the full history of the conversation, maintain the thread’s continuity, and address the actual context of the exchange. With every detail considered, attorneys can deliver responses that are not just faster, but smarter and more aligned with the ongoing dialogue.

Intelligent Drafting Directly Inside Outlook

One of the most time‑consuming tasks in legal work is drafting email responses. Whether it’s clarifying a clause, delivering an update, or summarizing progress, attorneys often start from scratch and spend valuable minutes refining tone, wording, and structure.

KLapper eliminates the friction of beginning with a blank email. With a simple prompt, attorneys receive a fully formed draft generated inside Outlook; already structured, professional, and informed by the entire conversation. Attorneys maintain full control and can refine as needed, but the foundational drafting work is done.

The result is faster communication that never compromises on quality.

AI Capable of Analyzing Attachments

In legal practice, attachments often carry more significance than the email text itself. Contracts, NDAs, policy documents, and supporting materials must be reviewed carefully before crafting a proper response.

Traditionally, this requires toggling between multiple windows, analyzing the document, then returning to the email to draft a response.

The KLapper Outlook Add‑In streamlines this workflow by enabling AI to read and understand attachments. Whether it’s a specific clause in a contract or a detail buried within a supporting document, the AI can incorporate relevant information into the generated email draft.

This allows attorneys to respond with confidence, knowing the content reflects both the email exchange and its referenced documents.

Context‑Rich Responses Aligned with Firm Standards

Every law firm has its own standards for tone, clarity, and communication style. Maintaining this consistency across all correspondence, especially in fast‑moving matters can be challenging.

KLapper Outlook Add-In helps maintain these standards by generating drafts that reflect prior communications and professional expectations. Its responses are already aligned with the conversation’s context and delivered in a polished, professional tone.

Attorneys remain the authors. The AI simply ensures that every starting point is clear, consistent, and aligned with firm expectations.

Eliminating Context Switching

One of the hidden productivity drains in legal work is context switching. Drafting a single response may require reviewing a message thread, switching to the attachment, checking prior communications, and consulting reference materials.

By embedding intelligence directly into Outlook, the KLapper Add‑In consolidates this workflow. Attorneys can review, analyze, and draft—all from the same window. This reduces friction, minimizes distractions, and supports deeper focus.

The experience becomes smoother, faster, and significantly more efficient.

Saving Time without Sacrificing Quality

Email consumes a disproportionate amount of an attorney’s day. The KLapper Outlook Add‑In dramatically reduces the time spent drafting responses while ensuring accuracy and professionalism remain intact.

Attorneys receive an intelligent first draft that reflects the thread, the attachments, and the context. They can refine and finalize the message quickly, preserving quality while reclaiming valuable time for deeper legal work.

The Future of Email in Legal Practice

Email will remain the backbone of legal communication for years to come. But as the volume, speed, and complexity of email interactions increase, the tools attorneys use must evolve.

The KLapper Outlook Add‑In represents the next step forward, a future where AI operates alongside legal professionals, elevating their communication and transforming email from a manual chore into an intelligent workflow.

The legal profession thrives on precision. KLapper brings that precision to the place where most legal work actually happens, YOUR INBOX.

With KLapper , attorneys draft faster, respond with more confidence, and manage conversations with unprecedented ease.

news.titleEn: Bundledocs expands into case management with new Review tool
news.titleZh: Bundledocs推出Review工具，扩展至案件管理领域
news.summaryZh: Bundledocs本月推出Review平台，帮助法律团队实时协作，标志着其向诉讼/案件管理等领域的重大扩展。该平台从原先仅用于文件准备阶段，扩展到审查、编辑和协作功能。在诉讼领域，Bundledocs现进入目前由Opus 2等少数供应商占据的市场。平台允许多个内外贡献者同时审查、评论、注释、编辑和推进文件，基于ISO 27001和SOC 2 Type II认证框架，提供文件进度、决策点和版本历史的可见性。用户可按文件、文件夹或角色定义访问权限，实现与内部团队及外部利益相关者的安全协作。这是自2019年公司成立以来最大的产品更新。Bundledocs成立于英国，2022年进入美国市场，该新服务目前处于测试阶段，在英国、欧洲中东非洲、北美和亚太地区均可使用。
news.bodyHtml:
Bundledocs earlier this month announced the launch of Review – a new platform to help legal teams collaborate in real time, representing a major expansion into areas including litigation/case management.  

Previously used just at the document preparation stage (hence the name), the new release sees Bundledocs shift into review, editing, and collaboration. While Bundledocs doesn’t focus exclusively on bundles for court and is used by transactional teams too, within a litigation context, it is now entering territory currently held by a small number of vendors such as Opus 2.  

Advertisement

Within Bundledocs, multiple internal and external contributors can now review, comment, annotate, redact, and progress documents simultaneously. Built on Bundledocs’ ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II accredited framework, the Review platform provides visibility over document progress, decision points, and version history. 

James Hogan, Bundledocs’ CTO, says: “Users can define access by document, folder, or role, enabling secure collaboration with internal teams and external stakeholders such as experts or counsel — without exposing entire bundles unnecessarily.” 

No wonder that co-founder and CEO Brian Kenneally and VP of revenue and operations Peter Zver told Legal IT Insider at Legalweek in New York that this is the biggest product update since Bundledocs was founded in 2019. 

Bundledocs was founded in the UK and entered the US market in 2022. This new offering, currently in beta, is available across all geographic sites including UK, EMEA, North America and APAC. We’ll keep you posted on its adoption.

news.titleEn: The future of client relationships in the GenAI era
news.titleZh: 生成式AI时代客户关系的未来
news.summaryZh: 本月Legal IT Insider与Litera联合举办的早餐会上，一个主题清晰呈现：随着生成式AI重塑法律服务，客户关系正在或应当变得更加数据驱动和更具目的性。在Milbank于哈德逊城市广场主办的讨论中，探讨了当前许多律所面临的双刃剑局面：一方面，AI无疑对律所运营模式构成压力，效率提升、自动化和更快周转时间正在挑战法律工作的经济模式，数据使客户能够前所未有地筛选顾问；另一方面，技术为律所提供了主动干预（讨论中称为“助推”）的机会，使其能更深入理解客户需求，并实现自身客户筛选（“目标定位”），将时间投入最高效的领域。
news.bodyHtml:
At a breakfast Legal IT Insider hosted with Litera this month, one theme came through clearly: as generative AI reshapes legal services, client relationships are – or should be – becoming more data-driven and more intentional.

The discussion, generously hosted by Milbank in Hudson Yards, explored a tension or perhaps double-edged sword that many law firms are now grappling with. On the one hand, AI is undeniably putting pressure on law firms’ operating model. Efficiency gains, automation and faster turnaround times are challenging the economics of legal work. And data is giving clients the ability to sift and filter advisers like never before. On the other hand, technology offers firms an opportunity to be proactive – referred to in the discussion as ‘nudging’ – and develop a far better understanding of their clients’ needs. It also enables them to do their own client filtering – or ‘targeting’ – and spend their time in the most profitable way.

Advertisement

You can read the takeaways from senior legal leaders present during this discussion in the latest edition of the Orange Rag newsletter HERE.

news.titleEn: Troutman Pepper Locke Chief KM & Innovation Officer: AI will Accelerate ‘Trend Toward Self-Service Intelligence Tools'
news.titleZh: Troutman Pepper Locke首席知识与创新官：人工智能将加速“自助式智能工具趋势”
news.summaryZh: 客户对效率、透明度和数据驱动洞察的期望正在重塑律所的价值交付方式，竞争压力推动律所现代化其服务模式，生成式人工智能和分析技术正成为催化剂。人工智能将自动化法律研究、文件起草和知识检索工作，使律师能专注于更高价值的战略工作。人工智能将加速自助式智能工具趋势，使律师和业务人员能快速获取全所经验、案件数据和客户洞察，无需依赖人工研究或大规模邮件沟通。未来几年，律所技术应从孤立点解决方案发展为集成智能生态系统，关键转变将是基于生成式和代理式人工智能的上下文感知对话界面。技术必须与律师的思维方式保持一致，嵌入Outlook、Teams或文件起草环境等熟悉工作流程的工具将提高使用率。随着律所处理敏感数据量增加，安全、道德和治理框架必须与创新同步发展。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with William Gaus, chief knowledge management and innovation officer at Troutman Pepper Locke, which won the award for Innovations in Knowledge Management.

What do you currently see as the biggest barriers to, and biggest drivers of innovation in law firms?

The drivers of innovation, especially within the legal industry, are stronger than ever. Client expectations for efficiency, transparency, and data-driven insights are reshaping how firms deliver value. Clients increasingly expect firms to leverage technology and institutional knowledge, not just individual expertise. Meanwhile, competitive pressure pushes firms to modernize their delivery models. The rise of generative AI and analytics is also acting as a catalyst, demonstrating the potential to automate routine tasks and uncover insights at scale.

Ultimately, the biggest driver of innovation will be a firm’s ability to align people, process, and technology, ensuring that innovation is not just about tools but about transforming the way lawyers work, collaborate, and serve clients.

At Troutman Pepper Locke, our teams focus on orchestrating a firm-wide transformation, seamlessly integrating gen AI into high-impact practice and business workflows with executive leadership’s sponsorship, driving measurable success. 

Emerging technologies such as generative and agentic AI are enabling new levels of automation in law firms. How do you expect these changes to impact law firms' operations, staffing and/or business models?

Emerging technologies like generative and agentic AI are set to transform every dimension of law firm operations. In the near term, AI will automate a growing portion of legal research, document drafting, and knowledge retrieval, allowing lawyers to focus on higher-value strategic work.

Operationally, AI will accelerate the trend toward self-service intelligence tools, enabling lawyers and business professionals to quickly access firm-wide experience, matter data, and client insights without relying on manual research or large-scale email outreach. This will make firms more agile, responsive, and data-driven. AI’s ability to surface firm experience will also enhance cross-selling and relationship management, helping firms grow existing client relationships more strategically.

Over time, the firms that thrive will be those that integrate AI into workflows holistically, not as a novelty, but as a core operational layer. AI will amplify lawyers’ capabilities, making knowledge and experience more scalable and consistent. The greatest impact will come from firms that pair technology adoption with thoughtful governance, ethical use of data, and a culture that encourages continuous learning and adaptation.

How would you like to see technology specifically designed for law firms change over the next few years, and why?

Over the next several years, technology designed for law firms must evolve from isolated point solutions to integrated, intelligent ecosystems that mirror how lawyers actually work. Today’s landscape often requires attorneys to toggle between multiple platforms, such as document management, billing, CRM, and experience databases, resulting in fragmented workflows and incomplete data insights. The next generation of legal technology should be seamlessly connected, drawing on unified data models to provide a 360-degree view of client relationships, firm knowledge and experience, and matter history.

A key shift will be toward context-aware, conversational interfaces powered by generative and agentic AI. Instead of searching static databases, lawyers should be able to ask natural-language questions and instantly surface curated, reliable firm knowledge (e.g., who has handled a similar matter, what precedents apply, or which judge has ruled in comparable cases). These systems should learn continuously, improving accuracy and anticipating user needs over time.

Equally important is a greater emphasis on user experience and adoption. Technology must align with the way lawyers think, not the other way around. Tools that embed directly into familiar workflows, including Outlook, Teams, or document drafting environments, will drive far higher engagement.

Finally, as firms handle increasing volumes of sensitive data, security, ethics, and governance frameworks must evolve alongside innovation. Transparent data practices and responsible AI usage will be essential to maintaining client trust.

In essence, the future of law firm technology should be smart, secure, and seamlessly human-centered, enhancing, not replacing, the judgment and creativity that define great lawyering.

news.titleEn: Dutch Court Orders Musk's xAI and Grok to Stop Generating AI-Produced Nonconsensual Nude Images
news.titleZh: 荷兰法院下令马斯克的xAI与Grok停止生成AI非自愿裸体图像
news.summaryZh: 荷兰法院已禁止埃隆·马斯克旗下社交媒体平台X的人工智能聊天机器人Grok使用其“裸体化”功能。该功能允许用户根据真实人物的照片生成虚假裸体图像。
news.bodyHtml:
Credit: PhotoGranary/Adobe Stock

A Dutch court has banned Elon Musk’s social media site X’s AI chatbot Grok from using its “nudify” function, which allows users to create fake nude images of real people from photos.
news.bodyText:
Credit: PhotoGranary/Adobe Stock

A Dutch court has banned Elon Musk’s social media site X’s AI chatbot Grok from using its “nudify” function, which allows users to create fake nude images of real people from photos.

news.titleEn: Cleveland & Co CTO: ‘AI Strengthens the Client Firm Partnership by Creating Shared Intelligence.'
news.titleZh: Cleveland & Co首席技术官：人工智能通过创造共享智能来加强客户与律所的合作关系
news.summaryZh: 律所创新的主要障碍是传统运营模式，包括计时收费、碎片化工作流程和孤立沟通。创新驱动力来自客户需求，如实时可见性、可预测定价和ESG治理。生成式和智能体人工智能将重塑律所与客户的合作，转向主动风险管理和预测性决策支持。AI可实现实时摘要、文件分类和监管跟踪，减少律师行政负担。人员配置将随自动化演变，提升律师的法律分析和战略咨询作用。商业模式加速转向固定费用和价值定价。AI通过创造共享智能加强客户与律所合作关系，双方基于相同数据和仪表盘操作。未来法律科技需向协作性、预测性系统发展，提供共享界面、分析和可见性。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Grant Cleveland, chief technology officer at Cleveland & Co, which won the award for Most Innovative Law Firm/Client Tech Collaboration **New**.

What do you currently see as the biggest barriers to, and biggest drivers of innovation in law firms?

The biggest barrier to innovation in law firms remains structural: legacy operating models that prioritize time-based billing, fragmented workflows, and siloed communication between internal teams and clients. Traditional legal delivery often lacks transparency, relies heavily on manual reporting, and treats technology as an add-on rather than a strategic asset. As a result, law firms and in-house teams spend significant time reconciling information, clarifying updates, and navigating disconnected systems, all of which hinder innovation.

A further driver is the cultural shift within the legal sector. There is growing recognition that diversity, flexible working, and inclusion strengthen decision making and innovation. Our firm is built on these values, and they influence the technology we create. Many firms still operate within rigid hierarchies where innovation is seen as a risk rather than an opportunity. This creates hesitancy around co-development with clients or adopting technologies that reshape established workflows.

In contrast, the biggest drivers of innovation are coming directly from clients. In-house legal teams increasingly demand real-time visibility, predictable pricing, ESG-aligned governance, and collaborative solutions that support their internal reporting cycles. Technology has become essential to meeting those expectations. Tools that support shared interfaces, live dashboards, and automated workflows are no longer differentiators, they are baseline requirements for modern legal partnerships.

Regulatory complexity is another key driver. Investors, pension funds, and asset managers face heightened scrutiny, and they expect their external counsel to embed transparency, auditability, and compliance into every engagement. 

Finally, the rise of fixed-fee and alternative fee models is accelerating innovation. These commercial structures reward efficiency, data-driven forecasting, and shared ownership of outcomes. For Cleveland & Co, this environment has made collaboration essential. Our Portal was developed alongside clients to address precisely these needs, ensuring that innovation is not unilateral but a shared asset that strengthens both organizations.

Emerging technologies such as generative and agentic AI are enabling new levels of automation in law firms. How do you expect these changes to impact law firms' operations, staffing and/or business models?

Generative and agentic AI will fundamentally reshape how law firms and in-house teams work together. For firms that embrace these tools, AI will shift legal service delivery from reactive advice to proactive risk management and predictive decision-support.

Operationally, AI enables real-time summarization, document classification, regulatory tracking, and automated updates directly into collaborative client portals. This significantly reduces the administrative burden on lawyers and enhances the accuracy and speed of reporting. Client teams benefit from simultaneous access to the same real-time insights, creating a unified and transparent workflow.

Staffing models will evolve as repetitive tasks become automated. Instead of replacing lawyers, AI will elevate them, freeing time for legal analysis, strategic advisory, and complex problem-solving. Junior lawyers will accelerate their learning curves through AI-enabled drafting and research assistance, while senior lawyers will rely on predictive analytics to make more informed decisions and manage risk strategically.

For business models, AI will accelerate the shift away from hourly billing toward fixed-fee and value-based pricing. Predictive tools, like those integrated into Cleveland & Co’s Portal, allow firms to estimate cost and complexity with far greater accuracy. This enables clients and law firms to align around outcomes rather than inputs, reinforcing transparency and trust.

For collaborative models specifically, AI strengthens the client–firm partnership by creating shared intelligence. Both parties operate with the same data, the same dashboards, and the same understanding of risk and progress. AI-driven legal delivery is not simply more efficient, it is more equitable, transparent, and strategically aligned.

How would you like to see technology specifically designed for law firms change over the next few years, and why?

Technology for law firms must evolve toward systems that are collaborative, predictive, and deeply integrated with clients’ business processes. The next generation of legal tech should eliminate the divide between external counsel and in-house counsel by providing shared interfaces, shared analytics, and shared visibility, reflecting the reality that legal work is increasingly cross-functional and data-driven.

First, client-facing platforms must become more personalized. Legal teams should be able to configure dashboards according to jurisdiction, regulatory theme, or risk category, with real-time feeds that reduce the need for manual reporting. Tools must adapt to the client’s industry and governance framework, not the other way around.

Second, technology should embed predictive analytics across matter management, pricing, compliance, and regulatory change. Forecasting tools, such as Cleveland & Co’s Retainer Calculator, must become standard, enabling both sides to plan resources, budgets, and timelines with greater certainty.

Third, technology should focus on strengthening trust and transparency. Automated audit trails, real-time approval workflows, and data visualizations foster a more open, accountable relationship between in-house and external counsel. This directly supports regulatory compliance, ESG goals, and board-level reporting.

Finally, legal tech should move beyond automation to create intelligence. AI-enabled insights can help identify emerging risks, flag inconsistencies, and propose workflow optimizations before issues arise. This transforms legal operations into a proactive function rather than a reactive one.

The future of legal tech should strengthen the entire legal ecosystem. The most impactful tools will be those that help firms and clients work as one cohesive team, aligned through shared intelligence, shared processes, and shared goals.

news.titleEn: FOLIO Launches New AI-Powered Tools for Categorizing and Tagging Legal Information
news.titleZh: FOLIO推出AI驱动新工具，助力法律信息分类与标记
news.summaryZh: FOLIO发布免费新工具，旨在帮助机构采用统一法律术语标准。FOLIO Enrich利用人工智能自动为上传文档添加相关FOLIO标签，通过符号AI和大语言模型识别文档概念，支持本地部署。FOLIO Mapper可将机构内部分类体系自动映射至FOLIO共享标准，生成可视化对比图谱，帮助发现内部分类不精确之处。新工具支持多种导出格式，并包含面向开发者的MCP服务器、Python库和API，便于第三方集成FOLIO分类体系。同时发布的OpenGloss知识图谱包含超15万个概念定义与关系，作为FOLIO法律分类体系的补充。这些工具共同推进法律行业建立统一术语标准的目标。
news.bodyHtml:
The new tools, available free of charge, are designed to help organizations adopt and use shared terminology for legal matters. They include the ability to apply relevant concept tags from the FOLIO ontology to legal documents, the ability to map proprietary organizational taxonomies to FOLIO’s shared standard, and tools to allow developers and AI models to leverage FOLIO resources.

The release of the new tools follows an August 2025 update to FOLIO’s website, which introduced a taxonomy explorer, allowing users to browse the more than 18,000 tags for legal concepts contained in FOLIO.

Among the new tools released as part of the launch is FOLIO Enrich, which leverages artificial intelligence to automatically apply relevant FOLIO tags to users’ uploaded documents.

“FOLIO Enrich is the ability to be able to take any text and to tag it up with FOLIO tags, ... whether it's a time entry narrative, or whether it is a judicial opinion, or a motion to dismiss,” said ALEA board member Damien Riehl.

The tool then creates an annotated version of the text where users can identify the legal concepts contained in their document and link them back to the broader conceptual families they belong to.

Riehl told Legaltech News the tool relies on both symbolic AI and large language models (LLMs) to determine which concepts are contained in a document, the beginning of a 16-step process to identify and label relevant information.

He added that a version of FOLIO Enrich could be downloaded from code creation and storage platform GitHub, which would allow users to run the program locally on their own devices.

In addition to FOLIO Enrich, the product launch includes FOLIO Mapper, which automatically correlates conceptual tags from an organization’s internal taxonomy to the shared taxonomy housed in FOLIO. The resulting output includes visualizations designed to illustrate which FOLIO tags are included in any given proprietary terminology.

“What you could do is now just march through and be able to map all of your tags to the FOLIO tags, and then you have this beautiful, one-to-many mapping,” Riehl said.

Riehl noted that organizational tags are often overbroad and include several concepts under a single heading. As a result, one of the intended benefits of FOLIO Mapper is the ability to see where an organization’s internal taxonomy is imprecise and update accordingly.

FOLIO Mapper is "mostly an educational tool, to be able to educate both the knowledge management people within a law firm as well as their stakeholders, to be able to say, ‘Hey, the thing that we're doing internally isn't nearly as good as what we could be doing,’” he said.

He added that the process of doing this taxonomy mapping manually for a single organization could take hundreds of hours, and that FOLIO Mapper provides organizations with an alternative to paying large fees to a consultancy to do the work.

Both FOLIO Enrich and FOLIO Mapper support a large number of export formats.

The new releases also include several tools designed to allow third-party developers and programs to incorporate the FOLIO taxonomy into their own work. These include a model context protocol (MCP) server, which is a specialized program that allows AI models to access to FOLIO’s data, a Python library that contains code that allows users to perform actions like searching individual classes of tags by label, and an application programming interface (API), a protocol that allows developers to leverage FOLIO’s information for other programs.

The FOLIO team also introduced OpenGloss, a knowledge graph of more than 150,000 concepts, designed to provide definitions and relationships between concepts beyond legal-specific ideas. OpenGloss is intended as a counterpart to FOLIO, categorizing facts in the same way that the original ontology categorizes the law.

Collectively, Riehl said the new tools would advance FOLIO’s mission of providing a shared terminology for communicating about legal matters among the law teams, vendors, law schools and courts that make up the industry.

“We are cooperating through a lot of different stakeholders,” he said. “You can help law firms, legal service providers, courts, legal educators, corporate law departments, legal tech, etc.”

news.titleEn: Legaltech Rundown: Thomson Reuters Announces AI Advisory Board, Docusign Launches AI Contract Review Assistant, and More
news.titleZh: 法律科技动态：汤森路透成立AI顾问委员会，Docusign推出AI合同审查助手等
news.summaryZh: Docusign于周三推出生成式人工智能合同审查助手，可建议编辑、审查协议并基于过往合同识别风险、关键条款与差异。Eudia于周二推出专有决策引擎Expert Digital Twins，旨在使专家知识跨业务部门可用。Husch Blackwell于周三推出AI咨询服务，协助客户管理AI相关的治理、合规与部署障碍。Legalfly于周二推出AI代理工作室，指导专业AI代理完成法律工作流程各阶段。Mitratech于周二推出ARIES高级案件管理功能，利用生成式AI自动提取、计算和安排法院规定期限。Questel于周三任命Frédéric Beylier为首席执行官。Smokeball与汤森路透建立合作关系，实现实时数据集成，将文件批量传输至CoCounsel Legal。汤森路透研究院于周四成立由21名成员组成的AI与法律实践未来顾问委员会，将讨论AI如何重塑法律行业。
news.bodyHtml:
The Legaltech Rundown is a weekly update of legal tech happenings that might have gone under the radar.

Docusign: On Wednesday, Docusign announced the launch of its generative artificial intelligence contract review assistant. The assistant can suggest edits and redlines, review agreements and identify risks, key terms and discrepancies based on past contracts. Users will also be able to query the assistant, which can provide answers with the related contract terms, according to a press release.

Eudia: Legal tech startup Eudia announced Tuesday that it launched Expert Digital Twins, a proprietary decision engine that aims to make expert knowledge available across business functions. Within Eudia’s platform, users will be able to access unique internal expertise from their organization for the tasks they need to complete like contract review, compliance guidance, marketing claims review, procurement approvals, or policy interpretation, according to a press release.

Husch Blackwell: On Wednesday, Husch Blackwell announced the launch of Husch Blackwell Consulting AI Advisory Services. The law firm’s new advisory services support clients in managing AI‑related governance, compliance and deployment hurdles throughout the entire adoption process, providing guidance on steps including evaluating readiness, building pilot projects, creating risk models and improving return on investment. These services will be led by principal of AI advisory services Michael Yang. Yang was previously senior director of AI advisory services at the firm, according to a press release.

Legalfly: On Tuesday, Belgium-based AI company Legalfly announced the launch of its AI agent studio. The studio guides specialized AI agents through each stage of the legal workflow including contract review, due diligence, legal research and email drafting, while keeping the lawyer in the loop, according to a press release.

Mitratech: On Tuesday, legal, risk and HR compliance solutions provider Mitratech announced the launch of its ARIES Advanced Docket Management capability. Within Mitratech’s matter managment platform, gen AI is leveraged to automate the extraction, calculation and scheduling of court-mandated deadlines to reduce litigation risks, automatically detect updates in scheduling orders, and allow users to review and adjust upcoming tasks and appointments. The system also handles time zone differences, so all scheduling is aligned with the matter’s designated time zone rather than the individual user’s, according to a press release.

Questel: Intellectual property management provider Questel announced Wednesday the appointment of Frédéric Beylier as CEO. Beylier was previously CEO of payment and ticketing systems company Flowbird Group and was also group chief operating officer at French multinational technology company IDEMIA. Beylier succeeds Questel’s former CEO Charles Besson, who will serve on the supervisory board of the Questel Group, according to a press release.

Smokeball/Thomson Reuters: Cloud-based practice management software maker Smokeball announced Wednesday its partnership with Thomson Reuters. Thomson Reuters is introducing a real-time data integration, synchronizing legal documents across systems and enabling Smokeball users to transfer files into CoCounsel Legal in bulk instead of uploading them individually. The integration sends documents directly from Smokeball to CoCounsel Legal, streamlining the workflow and minimizing errors or version-control issues, according to a press release.

Thomson Reuters: On Thursday, the Thomson Reuters Institute announced that it created an AI and the Future of Legal Practice (AIFLP) Advisory Board consisting of 21 members. The board will discuss how the legal profession is being reshaped by AI and cover issues like legal education and talent development, ethics, risk management, client counseling and access to justice, according to a press release.

Members of the board include Donna Haddad, founding member of the IBM AI Ethics Board; Mark Martin, professor and founding dean at the Kenneth F. Kahn School of Law at High Point University and former chief justice of the Supreme Court of North Carolina; Caitlin (Cat) Moon, professor of the practice of law and founding co-director of the Vanderbilt Law School AI Law Lab; Joanna Penn, chief transformation officer at Husch Blackwell; Judge Morris Silberman of the Florida Second District Court of Appeal; and Mark Wasserman, partner and CEO emeritus at Eversheds Sutherland, among others.
