AI That Listens Like a Lawyer: Courts Are Exposing the Gap Between What AI Notetakers Promise and What Their Contracts Permit. Purpose-Built Legal Conversational Intelligence™ Tools, Such as Querious®, Offer Attorneys a Defensible Path Forward.

A gap exists between how general-purpose AI notetakers are marketed to legal professionals and what their terms of service permit. As courts and regulators begin to test that gap, Legal Conversational Intelligence™ platforms, such as Querious ® , offer attorneys a defensible alternative built from the ground up to align architecture, contractual terms, and professional obligations.

Hilary Bowman, Querious , CEO & Founder, Author

William Love, Managing Partner of EsqLove, Editor

Attorney-client conversations are critical moments that raise legal issues, uncover factual inconsistencies, and even trigger disclosure obligations. Key words surface in the flow of dialogue and context can be extraordinarily difficult to reconstruct after the conversation.

This reality makes live conversation one of the most valuable and untapped use cases for AI in legal practice. Unlike tools that support research, drafting, and data analysis behind the scenes, AI in a live client conversation is a highly visible application of the technology.

Until recently, attorneys who recognized this opportunity faced an uncomfortable choice: adopt general-purpose AI notetakers that were never designed for the legal profession or go without. Today, a new category of purpose-built technology, Legal Conversational Intelligence™, offers attorneys a third path that is designed to advance both productivity and professional responsibility through real-time insights during a conversation and secure note-taking after the conversation.

The following is a side-by-side analysis of these two categories of tools from functional, design, contractual, legal, and ethical perspectives.

1. What is the purpose of the product?

General-purpose AI notetakers are designed to capture everything that happens in a conversation. Tools like Otter.ai, Fireflies.ai, Fathom, and Granola automatically join scheduled meetings, record audio and video,¹ generate real-time transcripts, and produce post-meeting summaries. They are inexpensive, require no prompting, and integrate with Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. For professionals outside of law, these tools deliver meaningful productivity gains. For attorneys, they raise questions about privilege, consent, confidentiality, and biometric privacy that the tools were not designed to address.

During a conversation, Querious accesses audio in real-time, analyzes it, and delivers to attorneys real-time insights about potential legal issues, follow-up questions, and relevant legal content. After the conversation, Querious generates a summary email and detailed notes, including a draft billing entry. Querious is on par with the cost of general-purpose AI notetakers. The product integrates into all major virtual meeting platforms, as well as legal-specific practice management tools such as Clio and Smokeball. Whether it’s an intake, advisory or strategic conversation, this product opens up new possibilities for attorneys to brainstorm and capture critical details in real-time during every key legal conversation.

General-purpose AI notetakers typically create and store full audio recordings and transcripts on the vendor’s cloud infrastructure, often indefinitely by default. Deleted content may remain in a trash folder for weeks before permanent removal.² When speaker recognition features are used to distinguish between participants (a process known as speaker diarization), the resulting voice-derived data may constitute biometric identifiers under state privacy laws.³

Querious processes meeting audio and by default, filters personally identifiable information (“PII”) such as names, phone numbers, and identification numbers, before the content reaches an AI model.⁴ The conversational data is then analyzed by a handful of privately deployed LLMs.⁵ Querious neither creates, nor stores, complete audio files or verbatim transcripts of the conversation.⁶ Any interim speaker diarization is deleted upon conclusion of the conversation.⁷ After a conversation ends, Querious generates the post-meeting summaries and billing entries. Any partial audio or transcript files created during the analysis process is deleted. By default, the attorney’s summaries are retained for sixty days, unless the attorney sets a shorter time period in their profile.⁸

3. Can the product use my conversational data to train AI?

At least one major vendor of a general purpose AI notetaker explicitly reserves the right to use machine learning on user content and usage data for testing, tuning, and improving its algorithms.⁹ Others grant themselves licenses to use de-identified or aggregated customer data to train and improve their products.¹⁰ These permissions are often buried in dense contractual language that bears little resemblance to the vendor’s marketing, which typically emphasizes privacy and security.

The claim that data is “de-identified” before training deserves scrutiny. Vendors rarely offer technical explanations of how de-identification takes place. Both courts and regulators have grown skeptical of such assurances. For example, the FTC has taken an aggressive position on “hashing,” which is a method that “us[es] math to turn [personal data] into a number (called a hash) in a consistent way.”¹¹ The FTC warned that “hashes aren’t ‘anonymous’” and “staff will remain vigilant to ensure companies are following the law and take action when the privacy claims they make are deceptive.”¹²

Querious’s architecture differs in several respects. The terms of service certify that production and training data pipelines are physically and logically separated at the network level.¹³ Thus, it is technically impossible for client communications to enter training pipelines.¹⁴ Querious uses privately deployed AI model instances that are isolated from the public internet.¹⁵ As a result, the conversational data is never routed to publicly accessible AI platforms. Querious’s agreements with third-party AI providers contractually prohibit those providers from using client data for training and require processing through private, isolated instances.¹⁶

4. Does the product support compliance with wire-tapping laws?

General-purpose AI notetakers that record meeting audio may expose attorneys to liability under federal and state wiretapping statutes.¹⁷ Fifteen states require all-party consent to record a conversation, including California, Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania.¹⁸ If any meeting participant is located in an all-party consent jurisdiction, that state’s law may apply and an AI tool that records by default, without prompting the host to obtain consent from each participant, could trigger liability for the attorney who enabled it.

In contrast, Querious’s default settings are designed to support compliance with all-party consent requirements. For example, when Querious joins a virtual meeting, the default bot image visible to every participant in the meeting clearly states that the tool is being used to analyze audio and if you do not consent to the meeting, to tell the organizer to remove it or exit the meeting. A similar default text message is pushed to the meeting chat visible to all participants with a similar message regarding consent. Querious also enables users to customize the bot image, including adding their own logo and editing the disclaimer language to meet their specific needs and risk tolerance. Similarly, Querious and its “instant meeting” feature runs off a device during an in-person meeting, the attorney cannot start the audio analysis and note-taking process until the attorney has checked a box acknowledging that all participants in the conversation have been informed that Querious is being used and the participants have consented to its use.

5. Does the product support compliance with biometric privacy laws?

General-purpose AI notetakers that distinguish between speakers by analyzing vocal characteristics face growing exposure under state biometric privacy laws. In Cruz v. Fireflies.AI Corp. and Basich v. Microsoft Corp. , plaintiffs allege that speaker diarization creates voiceprints without the written notice, informed consent, or publicly available retention and destruction policy the statute requires.¹⁹ With the Illinois Biometric Privacy Act having statutory damages of $1,000 to $5,000 per violation and over twenty additional states now classifying biometric data as sensitive personal information, the compliance landscape extends well beyond Illinois.²⁰

Querious addresses biometric privacy compliance directly in its architecture, terms of service and dedicated compliance documents.²¹ From an architecture perspective, Querious by default does not distinguish between speakers and it automatically applies a personally identifiable information (“PII”) filter that removes names, phone numbers, identification numbers etc. from the conversation data before privately deployed LLMs analyze it.²² When speaker diarization is enabled, Querious analyzes voice characteristics to cluster audio segments by speaker. Speaker labels in the output are derived from the meeting platform’s participant metadata, not from biometric identification. Querious does not create a mapping between voice characteristic data and participant identity. Once a conversation ends, this ephemeral speaker-differentiation data is deleted and does not persist as a voiceprint that is created, stored, or carried across conversations.

Even if the analysis of conversational data by Querious would constitute biometric data ( i.e., a voiceprint) and implicate certain state privacy laws, Querious reminds the attorney to collect consent from all participants of the conversation. Why the OpenAI Hiring Surge Signals a Crisis of Professional Control

The management problem in AI is no longer whether the models are improving. They are. The management problem is whether the working surface is becoming more dependable or less.

That is why the recent OpenAI hiring story on its plan to nearly double its workforce to 8,000 by late 2026 deserves closer attention than it seems to have received. At first glance, it looks like an ordinary growth story of a leader scaling to meet demand.

But this expansion carries a second, more sobering meaning.

For years, the public narrative of AI has been one of radical labor efficiency. The story was simple: systems get better, labor requirements go down. The machine does more; the human does less. Yet, the leading company in the field is currently planning to hire another 3,500 workers.

This does not disprove the story of AI capability. It does, however, signal that the LLM we think we are buying is only the core of a much larger, increasingly human-governed machine.

The Rise of the Managed System

If the most advanced AI products require growing layers of human labor, what exactly is the user buying?

The answer is that the user is not buying a model. They are buying a managed system. The model is only one component. Around it sits a structure of tuning, evaluation, policy, interface design, memory, and routing.

OpenAI’s current hiring surge is not focused on “pure science” alone. According to reports, OpenAI’s hiring push aimed mainly at product development, engineering, research, and sales, along with customer-facing technical ambassadorship roles. These roles suggest the prioritization of enterprise integration over the arrival of AGI. These are specialists whose job is to sit between the model and the customer, manually stitching the intelligence into the enterprise.

This matters because we still use the phrase “model drift” as though the difficulty lies in one place. That is no longer an adequate description.

If an AI tool begins to behave differently, the change may not be in the model at all. It may be in the wrapper. It may be in the safety layer. It may be in the routing logic. This is Systemic Drift. When the surface changes without attribution, a professional cannot build a dependable workflow. It is no longer a technical annoyance; it is a management failure.

Intelligence Inside a Bureaucracy

More hiring means more human governance. More human governance means more opportunity to tune, shape, constrain, and redirect the output. While this often makes the product “better” for a mass audience (smoother, safer, more polite), it also means the product becomes less like an instrument and more like the organization that created the system it becomes.

An organization has priorities like commercial goals, legal concerns, brand anxieties, and cost discipline. Soon, the user is no longer dealing with intelligence alone. They are dealing with intelligence inside a bureaucracy.

The problem is no longer just that LLMs drift. The entire AI tool surface drifts.

Professional users do not merely want a good answer. They want diagnostic power. They also want to know whether a change in output came from the model, the context window, or the product team’s latest idea about how the tool should behave. Without that, it’s impossible to distinguish between improvement and interference.

The Commercial Corridor

Commercial pressure will intensify this tendency. With Anthropic reportedly gaining enterprise traction faster than OpenAI, there’s a strong pressure to productize. OpenAI has expressed concerns about competition from Google. OpenAI looks less like a pure AGI lab and more like it wants to become the enterprise control plane for applied AI.

The economic logic is plain: a commercial system is rewarded for efficient closure. This creates a “managed corridor” that’s nicely lit, frictionless, and heavily signposted with a slight smell of ozone. It feels like help, but it functions as a wall, except that it is a wall that drifts, wobbles, and moves.

This is why the OpenAI hiring story matters. It tells us that the future of AI is not simply smarter models. It is larger governance structures wrapped around smarter models. These structures shape what the user can see, what they can reproduce, and most importantly, what they can no longer notice changing. And they are created by the vendor, not the user.

The Professional Standard of Care

There is a reasonable objection to my perspective. Most users don’t care which layer changed or who changed it as long as the system works. For the mass market, this is what success looks like.

But the issue is not the average user. The issue is whether the serious knowledge worker can build durable methods on top of such systems. A tool can become more helpful to the mass market while becoming less dependable for the user who needs stable procedures and exacting authorship. This is a core issue in agentic AI.

When behavior changes and no one can say why, how is a professional supposed to maintain a standard of care?

This is why the interest in local models is growing. Not because they are always stronger, but because a weaker system you can inspect, version, and control is more valuable than a stronger system arriving through shifting layers of invisible mediation.

This is management, not romance.

The standard question in AI has been: Which model is best? The question for the next phase must be: How much of the system do I actually control?  What OpenAI appears to be building is not just a better model company, but something closer to an enterprise control plane for applied AI. It is signalling where it believes control should lie.

If you ignore the fact that the instability is now systemic, you may still get very good answers. However, you will be getting them from a system you understand less each month. For anyone whose work depends on method, that is a dangerous bargain. You aren’t operating the tool. You are a passenger.

And the passenger seat might seem like a comfortable place to sit. That is, right up to the moment you need to know who is driving.

news.titleEn: What Does the White House AI Framework Mean for Free Speech?
news.titleZh: 白宫人工智能框架对言论自由意味着什么？
news.summaryZh: 白宫人工智能框架包含保护言论自由的条款，其中第四章呼吁国会禁止政府向开发者施压进行意识形态驱动的内容审核，并要求建立联邦申诉机制处理公民认为政府机构施压审查生成式人工智能工具信息的情况。框架还要求国会优先于州法律，使人工智能开发者免于为第三方使用其模型从事非法行为承担连带责任，这与《通信规范法》第230条类似。然而，框架也包含可能限制言论自由的条款，例如要求对部分生成式人工智能功能进行年龄验证，且未涉及大规模监控可能抑制生成式人工智能作为表达技术使用的问题。年龄验证可能侵犯未成年人言论自由，并影响不愿提供身份信息的成年人的有效言论权。
news.bodyHtml:
But other provisions could place limitations on the ways users interact with those tools, with elements of the framework cutting both in favor of and against speech rights.

Of particular note, Section IV of the framework, “Preventing Censorship and Protecting Free Speech,” urges Congress to ban government pressure on developers to perform ideologically driven content moderation. It also asks the legislature to create a means of redress within the federal government to address instances when citizens think federal agencies applied pressure to censor or dictate the information provided by gen AI tools.

John Coleman, legislative counsel for AI and free expression at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), said these protections were designed to bar the government from coercing private companies to remove content or disassociate from certain parties.

“Americans should have a clear way to challenge government-driven censorship,” he said. “I think anti-jawboning protections, ... or even going further with prohibitions, would be a step in the right direction for targeting government when they are pressuring or coercing platforms like AI [in ways] that end up shaping or suppressing thoughtful speech.”

The framework’s treatment of third-party liability is another strong suit in the eyes of some speech advocates. The document urges Congress to preempt state laws that would expose AI developers to liability for the use of their models in illegal conduct by third parties.

Jay Sabin, an attorney at Brach Eichler, noted that this mirrors Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users, He said the creation of a similar shield for developers fit with the Trump administration’s broader regulatory approach to AI.

“[Section] 230, because of its indemnification provision, allowed website operators to not be legally responsible for what's on the website,” Sabin said. “There are exceptions, ... but in the main, the federal initiative from the White House is, like with 230, we want this to be an unregulated space.”

Although the avoidance of third-party liability may appear to primarily benefit AI developers, some speech advocates believe it to be an important protection for free expression more generally because efforts from developers to avoid the illegal use of their platforms could prove over-broad and preclude legitimate uses. They also worry that the use of third-party liability can be a way to outsource regulation to less accountable for-profit bodies.

While important elements of the framework appear protective of free expression, Coleman said FIRE saw some cause to worry in the inclusion of proposals to require age verification to access some gen AI capabilities and in the framework’s failure to address mass surveillance and the dampening effect it may have on the use of gen AI as an expressive technology.

Age verification requirements can both impinge on the speech rights of minors and dampen the effective speech rights of adults who do not wish to provide identifying information, while the existence of a mass surveillance regime can make people reluctant to engage in legal expressive acts.

More broadly, Coleman noted, there is a risk legislators might overlook speech issues when regulating gen AI, given the greater attention typically given to safety concerns in specific realms.

“Oftentimes, legislators are thinking about AI as a technology and in a particular context, whether it's consumer protection, child safety,” he said. “If you are regulating the output, you are limiting the user's available ability to receive information and the developer’s right to share information. ... [Speech issues] come up in legislatures requiring disclosures or disclaimers, whether that's a warning label telling users that this content was generated by AI or risk assessments.”

news.titleEn: Demand for Legal Engineers Skyrockets in the AI Age
news.titleZh: AI时代法律工程师需求激增
news.summaryZh: 法律工程师的角色自21世纪初就已存在，最初涉及与技术特定业务领域合作。如今，特别是在生成式AI推动下，该角色正从后台支持转向法律服务交付的核心。专家将其类比为变革管理者和创新官，负责AI整合与流程变革。法律工程师直接与律师合作，将法律判断转化为可重复的技术驱动工作流程。在律所，他们常作为技术试验团队的一部分评估技术可行性；在法律科技公司，则更接近法律科技产品经理，兼具法律与技术专长，协助构建解决方案。部分替代性法律服务提供商认为律师已承担相关职责，无需另设“法律工程师”头衔。无论是否采用该称谓，律所、替代性法律服务提供商和供应商都将增加聘用能衔接法律与技术、确保律师了解AI影响的专业人士。
news.bodyHtml:
“What you're seeing in terms of the rise of legal engineers is really the operationalization of law in an AI-enabled environment. ... The difference now is that, particularly with generative AI, these professionals are moving to the center of legal service delivery instead of really being more of a back-office position,” Morgan, Lewis & Bockius chief AI and knowledge officer Colleen Nihill told Legaltech News.

Experts have likened the current, gen AI-era legal engineer role to existing ones like change manager and innovation officer that navigate AI integration and changing internal processes. In some ways, the legal engineer title is a rebrand of such roles for the AI age.

“I see the legal engineer role being one where they're working directly alongside attorneys on client matters, helping translate legal judgment into repeatable technology-enabled workflows at scale,” Nihill said.

The role of the legal engineer has existed since the early 2000s, according to the American Bar Association. Nihill said the legal engineer went through many variations, though it initially entailed working alongside the first technology-specific practice areas. Nihill held such a role when she first arrived at Morgan Lewis as administrative officer, a position that landed her within the intersection of law, technology and design.

“We've had [an e-data practice] for a very long time. They were one of the first practice groups at our firm that really started to combine process design, technologists and the practice of law in a different way,” she said. “When I was charged with working with our practice groups in a different title at the time, I realized that any kind of change wasn't going to come just from technology alone, and it really required professionals who had strong credentials and discipline in process design, and then also pairing that with legal expertise.”

Today’s legal engineers wear many hats, and for legal tech companies, the role seems most similar to that of the legal technology product manager—typically a professional with both legal and technical expertise who helps software developers ideate and construct solutions for lawyers and other legal professionals.

“[The legal engineer is] a repackaged notion of those roles in the AI age. ... The demands of a product manager five years ago look different, demands of a customer success person five years ago look different, same for an engineer in a more technical space. If you update all of those to 2026, all of those J.D.s, and then smash them together, that's the legal engineer,” said Sarah Johansson, head of legal product at AI litigation prediction platform Theo AI.

Legal engineers at legal tech companies versus legal engineers at law firms operate differently these days, according to Jackson Lanning, head of product at Theo AI.

“From law firms, it's almost a part of a tech trial team that's asking someone to go in and help explore tech and see if it's viable for certain workstreams. For vendors, it seems much more of the creation capacity of you're actually asking someone to help build from the ground up and someone who can go in there, understand the workflows, but be able to layer on top of that foundation that engineers help build,” he said.

As the legal engineering role becomes more relevant, it is not gaining traction everywhere. Some alternative service providers (ALSPs) prefer not to use the term as the role is still not clearly defined, according to QuisLex CEO Sirisha Gummaregula.

She said that if a legal engineer is also a lawyer, they should identify as a lawyer first as they are not developing the technology systems by themselves. Instead, they are trying to comprehend and navigate the technology systems.

“[At QuisLex] we have not created a nomenclature like that because of the belief that, as lawyers, this is a role that we have already owned and the role that we already are responsible for. ... Any legal process that we do, we need to understand where is the data coming from? What systems is it passing it through? How is it transforming? ... What aspects of those end results do I as a lawyer need to validate and stand behind? Those responsibilities are my own as a lawyer,” Gummaregula said. “In that process, I'm not a data expert in the true sense, right? I'm not a technical expert in the true sense. I have not built the system.”

Whether organizations use the title “legal engineers” or not, law firms, ALSPs and vendors are likely to hire more professionals that can bridge the gap between law and technology as well as ensure lawyers are well informed on AI’s impact.

"At the core of it, you're sitting in as the expert that has managed this end-to-end process, whatever it may be for years and you know what can go wrong and what can go right, and you need to be in charge, in the lead, really driving that, and then working with a straightforward technologist that can say, ‘Hey, I'm not getting this result in the way that I want it. What is happening? This is what would be helpful.’ And a technologist will work with you on that, but I don't think you need to become a legal engineer to do that,” Gummaregula explained.

news.titleEn: The hidden risk in your independence process
news.titleZh: 独立性流程中的隐藏风险
news.summaryZh: 许多会计和咨询公司依赖电子表格、邮件线程、年度认证和提醒邮件来管理独立性，这种方法在小型公司尚可维持，但随着合伙人增加、服务扩展、上市公司审计业务增多以及复杂项目增加，便会迅速失效。人工控制容易出错，难以跟上投资变化、客户渠道演变和监管要求调整。当监管机构询问如何执行独立性时，仅靠发送提醒邮件无法构成有效辩护。好消息是，连接的AI解决方案能够提供公司数据、业务渠道和员工财务利益的透明度，使公司能够从被动风险管理转向持续独立性合规。
news.bodyHtml:
Your firm’s independence record may be spotless — but is your independence process built to keep it that way? 

Too often, accounting and advisory leaders assume that strong policies are enough to protect their firm from independence risk. But independence failures rarely stem from flawed policy. They usually stem from processes that can’t scale. 

Many firms still rely on spreadsheets, email threads, annual attestations, and reminder emails to manage independence. That approach may suffice when a firm is small — but it breaks down quickly as the firm adds partners, expands services, pursues more public company audits, and navigates more complex engagements. 

What once felt manageable becomes fragile. Manual controls — already prone to human error — struggle to keep pace with changing investments, evolving client pipelines, and shifting regulatory expectations. And when regulators ask how independence is enforced, “We send reminder emails” isn’t a defensible answer. 

The good news? A connected AI solution can provide visibility into your firm’s data, pipeline, and employees’ financial interests — enabling a shift from reactive risk management to continuous independence compliance.

news.titleEn: [Educational Webcast] Meaningful Transparency in AI: What Privacy Laws Actually Require
news.titleZh: [教育网络研讨会] AI中的实质性透明度：隐私法实际要求
news.summaryZh: 随着AI融入商业运营，监管机构和消费者日益关注组织如何以清晰、准确且法律上可辩护的方式解释AI使用。从州消费者隐私法规到新兴的全球AI框架，隐私法律和监管指南正形成共同期望：透明度必须具有实质性，而非仅技术性或愿景性。HaystackID即将举办的网络研讨会将探讨监管机构对“实质性透明度”的定义，包括组织何时及如何在隐私通知、消费者披露和内部治理文件中披露AI使用、自动化决策及数据处理实践。研讨会由HaystackID®数据保护官Christopher Wall主持，与会者将学习如何将复杂AI系统转化为易懂、准确且符合法律要求的披露。专家小组将讨论常见陷阱——如过度笼统的表述、不一致的披露以及技术现实与公开声明之间的错位——并就建立能经受监管审查同时维护消费者信任的AI透明度计划提供指导。
news.bodyHtml:
Meaningful Transparency in AI: What Privacy Laws Actually Require

As AI becomes embedded across business operations, regulators and consumers are increasingly focused on how organizations explain the use of AI in clear, accurate, and legally defensible ways. From state consumer privacy statutes to emerging global AI frameworks, privacy laws and regulatory guidance are converging on a common expectation: transparency must be meaningful, not merely technical or aspirational.

HaystackID’s upcoming webcast will explore what regulators mean by “meaningful transparency,” including when and how organizations must disclose AI use, automated decision-making, and data processing practices in privacy notices, consumer disclosures, and internal governance documentation.

Event Details

Moderated by HaystackID® Data Protection Officer Christopher Wall, attendees will learn how organizations can translate complex AI systems into disclosures that are understandable, accurate, and aligned with legal requirements. Expert panelists will discuss common pitfalls—such as over-generalized language, inconsistent disclosures, and misalignment between technical reality and public statements—and offer guidance on building AI transparency programs that withstand regulatory scrutiny while maintaining consumer trust.

+ Original Date: Wednesday, March 25, 2026

news.titleEn: AI in consulting firms: Institutional intelligence will determine who wins
news.titleZh: 咨询公司中的AI：机构智能将决定胜负
news.summaryZh: 未来三年，咨询行业的分水岭将不在于是否采用人工智能，而在于利用AI加速个人产出与强化机构决策之间的差异。专注个人生产力的公司推进更快，提案发送更迅速，内部流程更高效，但交叉销售渗透率基本不变，风险冲突仍会延迟显现，利润压力事后持续出现。投资机构智能的公司行动更审慎，它们将关系数据、项目历史和管理流程整合为统一系统，12至24个月内将更早识别扩展机会、结合情境评估风险、在利润受损前干预交付问题。这一选择决定了AI在公司的实际作用，只有后者能形成长期优势。战略问题不在于AI是否带来益处，而在于公司能否利用AI规模化提升决策质量而不增加风险。
news.bodyHtml:
AI in consulting firms will separate along one line

Over the next three years, the divide the consulting industry will not be between those that adopt artificial intelligence and those that do not. It will be between firms that use AI to accelerate individual output and firms that use it to strengthen institutional decision-making.

Firms that focus on individual productivity will move faster. Proposals will go out more quickly. Internal workflows will feel more efficient. Yet cross-sell penetration will remain largely unchanged, conflict risk will still surface late, and margin pressure will continue to appear after the fact.

Firms that invest in firm intelligence will move more intentionally. They will spend time connecting relationship data, engagement history, and governance workflows into a unified system. Within 12 to 24 months, those firms will begin to operate differently and identify expansion opportunities earlier, evaluate risk in context, and intervene on delivery issues before margin erodes.

That choice determines what AI actually does inside the firm. Only one of those compounds into long-term advantage. The strategic question is not whether AI benefits your firm. It is whether your firm can use AI to make better decisions at scale without increasing risk.

See how your firm can connect client, risk, and engagement data to make better decisions at scale.

news.titleEn: AI in accounting firms: Protecting client confidentiality at scale
news.titleZh: 会计师事务所中的AI应用：规模化保护客户机密
news.summaryZh: 多数企业已在环境中建立某种治理机制，但现有控制措施需适应AI生成与整合信息的新方式。生成式AI通过分析信息集合生成回应，依赖结构化元数据模式和访问控制来确定可处理的信息。当结构、元数据、访问和治理控制不一致时，业务信息可能面临负面暴露风险。利用自动化技术为AI整理业务背景，可通过无限方式捕获企业知识，提高计费人员效率并优化专有知识。治理问题已从应用文档安全转向执行知识边界控制。控制谁能打开文件的时代已结束，现在还需控制“什么”能打开文件。实现此控制级别需要自动化引擎来实施治理，保护企业免受AI在环境中访问内容的影响。近期网络研讨会中，专业服务公司的技术与风险负责人描述了这些问题如何在Microsoft 365等企业系统中显现，包括AI回应受多个业务工作区存储材料影响的情况，揭示了企业先前未考虑的治理漏洞。
news.bodyHtml:
Building on Microsoft 365 to support AI safely

Most firms have some form of governance in their environments. The challenge is how those controls extend to keep pace with the way AI now generates and synthesizes information.

Generative AI behaves the way we instruct it to. Instead of retrieving a specific file, it analyzes collections of information to generate a response. Because it doesn’t have hands to organize information, it relies on patterns of structured metadata and access control to determine which information it can process for analysis.

When the structure, metadata, access, and governance controls are inconsistent, engagement information is subject to negative exposure. Using automation to curate engagement context for AI introduces unlimited ways of capturing firm knowledge to increase fee earner efficiency and optimize proprietary knowledge that is now available in the world of AI.

The governance question has shifted from applying document security to enforcing knowledge boundaries. The age of controlling who can open a file is over. We must now control “What” can open a file, as well. To harness this level of control, automated engines are needed to implement governance that protects firms from what AI has access to in their environments. Otherwise, it will consume any information it can locate and access.

In a recent webinar discussion, technology and risk leaders from professional services firms described how these issues are already emerging in firm systems like Microsoft 365. Several possibilities involve AI responses influenced by material stored across multiple engagement workspaces, revealing governance gaps firms had not previously considered.

These scenarios and the controls firms are implementing are explored in more detail in the webinar recording.

news.titleEn: NewMod General Legal Hits $11.5m Funding in 3 Months
news.titleZh: 新商业模式律所General Legal三个月内融资1150万美元
news.summaryZh: 人工智能原生律所General Legal宣布，自三个月前正式推出以来，已通过种子轮和预种子轮融资1150万美元，本轮融资由Audacious Ventures领投。该律所专注于商业合同业务，通过Slack等平台为客户提供服务，对每份合同收取500美元固定费用，承诺数小时内完成审核，且不按小时计费、无隐藏费用或最低消费门槛。其律师均为美国持证律师，使用人工智能平台辅助工作，但所有协议均由经验丰富的人类律师最终审核。服务范围包括主服务协议、数据处理协议、保密协议等各类标准商业合同，并可协助起草新协议。该律所主要面向早期初创公司，属于Y Combinator孵化项目。
news.bodyHtml:
NewMod, AI-native law firm General Legal has announced it has hit $11.5m in Seed and pre-Seed funding since launching officially just three months ago.

Co-founder, Ryan Walker, who previously was CTO at Casetext and then a VP at Thomson Reuters, said: ‘I’m so proud to announce that General Legal – the AI native law firm for commercial contracts – has raised a combined $11.5m Seed and Pre-Seed round led by Audacious Ventures!

‘Our elite commercial attorneys live in your Slack and turn contracts lightning fast, for a fraction of the cost of traditional outside counsel.’

So, what is this all about? Well, see their rate card below – which is an eye-opener. Then read some of the answers to their FAQs.

And as you can see, they will handle your work via a private Slack channel, take just hours, and charge a flat rate of $500 per contract. How many Big Law firms would be able to do that with their current business model?

..

Some illustrative FAQs and answers:

‘We’re a law firm that hires only highly-qualified, US barred attorneys. Our attorneys are trained to use our AI platforms to accelerate their work but all agreements handled by our firm are reviewed by an experienced human attorney.

‘We can help with any standard commercial agreements, including MSAs, DPAs, NDAs, vendor agreements, TOSs EULAs, and more.

‘Our lawyers work where you work. Many of our clients use Slack and our lawyers can work with you or your legal team directly in your Slack. We can also support you over email, video-conference, or phone.

‘For our flat review price, our firm will support your contract through every turn all the way to signature. Our lawyers can even join a negotiation with the other side. We don’t bill by the hour, there are no surprise fees, and no minimums.

‘We’re happy to draft new commercial agreements.’

–

Is this a big deal?

One conversation that keeps coming up with AL, at least among folks focused on the frontier of the legal tech market, is NewMods / AI-native law firms. And understandably so. Their combination of putting AI at the core of the business, but also adding skilled lawyers around the ‘means of legal production’ creates what AL has been hoping to see since this site started. I.e. lawyers really using AI as it’s meant to be used, not as a little helper on the side of your work, but right in the centre of it, in a way that allows its full capabilities to be leveraged.

Naturally, to do so means dropping the time-based approach to billing. Time to value for clients is thus rapid and the costs are – relatively – far less than what Big Law currently charges.

General Legal, as with many others now, such as Soxton which has already pioneered the area of helping startups, is focused on early-stage companies. And that makes sense. Those companies are new to having legal needs, maybe don’t have a legal team internally, and are cost-sensitive as they’re running on VC money.

But.…..! AL is sure that once they get going, the legal market segments they will approach will expand. In fact, while General Legal says on its website that it’s for those ‘in the growth stage’, its offer of handling MSAs and NDAs could be useful for companies of any size.

And finally, there is the fact that this Y Combinator cohort startup – one of several NewMods in this Winter’s group to get backing from the legendary investor and incubator – is only a few months old and already has some solid capital to help it grow.

More about General Legal here.

Note: ‘NewMod’ is an AL term, which stands for New Business Model Law Firm. This site tends to prefer this over AI-native, or AI-first in this context, because the term AI-native is getting used very broadly and AI-first doesn’t really tell us what is going on at a commercial level. So, NewMod refers specifically to a new business model approach, (i.e. no hourly bills and not shaped in the traditional way), plus it’s the AI that makes that possible – rather than the other way round.

—

news.titleEn: Legora Partners With Jus Mundi For Arbitration Needs
news.titleZh: Legora与Jus Mundi达成合作以满足仲裁需求
news.summaryZh: Jus Mundi与Legora建立合作伙伴关系，将Jus AI工具集成至Legora的生成式人工智能平台，以协助处理国际仲裁需求。该集成将于今年晚些时候全面推出。合作核心功能包括：在Legora平台内直接调用Jus Mundi的AI进行仲裁情报查询、将权威仲裁情报整合至Legora工作流程，以及通过一键访问功能直接链接至Jus Mundi的完整文档进行深度分析。用户现可通过Legora查询Jus AI，获取基于Jus Mundi仲裁文档库（涵盖国际裁决、条约、机构规则、出版物及与全球100多家领先仲裁机构的独家合作数据）的完整、带引证的答案。此次合作旨在将专业AI融入从业者工作场景，Jus AI专为仲裁构建，具备独特的推理能力和对国际争议语境的理解，已获仲裁从业者质量验证。集成使从业者能在其AI工作流程中直接获取领先的仲裁情报。
news.bodyHtml:
Jus Mundi and Legora have formed a partnership that will integrate the Jus AI tool within the wider genAI platform to help with international arbitration needs. It will roll out in full later this year, they added.

Sounds useful, and it is one of a growing number of data-focused partnerships that Legora – and its main rival Harvey – have done across the market since launching. They’re calling it ‘an agent to agent integration’, but it’s probably simpler just to think of this as access to very useful arbitration data that you can get to via Legora.

They added that the key features are:

  • ‘Call Jus Mundi’s AI inside Legora: Query Jus Mundi’s specialized arbitration intelligence without switching platforms or losing context.
  • Integrate authoritative arbitration intelligence into Legora workflows: Build workflows grounded in Jus Mundi’s expert content.
  • One-click access to trusted sources: Citations link directly to full documents on Jus Mundi for deeper analysis.’

So, now within Legora, you can ‘query Jus AI to receive comprehensive, citation-backed answers grounded in Jus Mundi’s collection of arbitration documents, including international awards, treaties, institutional rules, publications, and exclusive data from partnerships with more than 100 leading arbitration institutions worldwide’.

Jean-Rémi de Maistre, CEO and Co-Founder of Jus Mundi, commented: ‘This partnership is about bringing specialized AI where practitioners work. We built Jus AI from the ground up for arbitration. It reasons differently, it understands the context of international disputes, and arbitration practitioners have validated its high quality. Legora’s platform brings research, review, and drafting into one collaborative workspace, and together we are making Jus AI’s unique capabilities accessible within workflows lawyers already use.’

Gabrielle Persson, VP Content & Partnerships at Legora, added: ‘Arbitration lawyers work with some of the most complex legal information in the profession. By integrating Jus AI with Legora, we are enabling practitioners to access leading arbitration intelligence directly within their AI workflows.’

As ever access to quality legal data is key….!

—

And, if the above was interesting, wait until you see these events:

There will be more news about the conference and key speakers as we get closer to June.

Look forward to seeing you there!

Richard Tromans, Founder, Artificial Lawyer and Legal Innovators conference Chair.

news.titleEn: Steno Raises $49m, Hits $150m Total Funding
news.titleZh: Steno完成4900万美元C轮融资，总融资额达1.5亿美元
news.summaryZh: 法庭记录与诉讼支持公司Steno已完成4900万美元全股权C轮融资，由Savano Capital Partners领投，First Round Capital、The Legal Tech Fund等现有投资者跟投。该公司自2018年成立以来总融资额已达1.5亿美元。新资金将用于三倍扩大扩张投资、开发新一代诉讼技术套件、进军新市场并提升在AmLaw 200律所中的渗透率。Steno最初专注于法庭记录服务，后通过AI技术拓展平台功能，其核心产品Transcript Genius是AI驱动的笔录分析工具。该工具通过解决实际工作流程摩擦显著提升了用户留存率，新投资将用于推出大幅改进的差异化产品。公司已重新定义笔录分析、推出首个现代法庭记录专业人员职业管理市场，并通过Steno Connect简化远程诉讼。公司计划超越简单自动化，构建数据驱动AI与专家诉讼支持相结合的统一平台。生成式AI的精准语言理解能力正在加速改变证言与取证领域，Steno计划利用大语言模型技术实现最大增长。
news.bodyHtml:
Steno, the court reporting and litigation support company, has raised $49m in an all equity C round, following $46m raised in 2024. The round was led by Savano Capital Partners with continued participation from First Round Capital, The Legal Tech Fund, and other strategic investors.

Since it started back in 2018, the Los Angeles company has now raised $150m in total, which includes both equity and debt financing.

The new injection of capital will ‘allow Steno to triple investments in [its] expansion and the development of the next evolution of its litigation technology suite’.

It added that there are ‘thousands of firms now utilizing Steno every month’, and ‘the funding will be used to enter new markets and significantly increase penetration within the AmLaw 200’. I.e. larger law firms.

The company – as with others in this space – started with a focus on court reporting, and developed a services team, but then evolved as AI offered new opportunities to quickly analyse that material, with now the company’s platform growing outward with LLM-based features. Key to this has been Transcript Genius, its AI-driven analysis tool.

Or, as Greg Hong, CEO of Steno, commented: ‘When we released Transcript Genius, our revolutionary AI-powered transcript analysis tool, it was a game-changer for the industry, driving unprecedented user retention by solving real workflow friction. Today’s investment allows us to release a vastly improved, differentiated offering that stays ahead of anything else in the market.’

‘Because we operate as both a world-class services provider and a tech company, we have a unique advantage: we live inside litigation workflows every day. That hybrid position allows us to build AI capabilities that software-only companies simply cannot replicate.’

Prabhdeep Singh, COO of Steno, added: ‘Today’s investment marks a major milestone in Steno’s journey as we work to combine personalized service with the latest technology. We’ve already redefined transcript analysis with Transcript Genius, launched the first modern marketplace for court reporting professionals to manage their careers, and made remote litigation easier with Steno Connect.

‘Now, we’re finding new ways for lawyers to work with testimony and case data. Our goal is to expand beyond simple automation, providing a unified platform where data-informed AI and expert litigation support work together to solve the complex challenges law firms face daily.’

Is this a big deal?

AI has clearly changed many parts of the legal tech world, and the field of testimony and depositions has been especially turbo-charged with the acute language understanding provided by genAI. Steno has been quick to adapt to what LLMs can offer and, given the funding they’ve now received, are planning to leverage this for maximum growth.

—

More about Steno here.

news.titleEn: AI-First ‘Keith’ Bags £2m For Property Work
news.titleZh: AI优先的‘Keith’为房产交易业务融资200万英镑
news.summaryZh: AI优先的新型法律服务机构Keith专注于英国住宅房产交易（产权转让）业务，已融资200万英镑。该公司由联合创始人Andy Shovel、Pete Sharman和Sam Tucker创立，前英国产权转让协会主席Eddie Goldsmith担任战略顾问兼非执行董事。Keith将提供与传统律所相同的产权转让服务，但通过AI自动审核信函和文件，所有操作均通过预设工作流程管理。客户可通过电子邮件、短信或电话随时联系Keith，实时跟踪交易进度，并通过在线平台直接签署文件或上传信息。AI负责审查产权文件、分析房产搜索结果、处理往来信函并起草回复，但所有输出均需经合格产权转让律师审核批准。公司目前使用Anthropic的Opus和Sonnet模型，并计划通过API与搜索提供商、土地注册局和英国税务海关总署等外部服务对接。本轮投资方包括欧洲风投机构Backed、Breega和Notion。
news.bodyHtml:
There is another NewMod, AI-first ‘law firm’ in town. In this case it’s called Keith and will focus on residential property sales in the UK, (AKA conveyancing). It has just raised £2m.

AL asked its co-founder Andy Shovel – who previously launched a vegan sausage company – all about it, (see below). It’s understood that Keith won’t be regulated by the SRA, but instead the plan is to be regulated by the official body for conveyancers in the UK, the CLC.

Also a co-founder is Pete Sharman, who previously created the plant-based food brand THIS, with Shovel. Then there is Sam Tucker who is Keith’s third founder; previously he started hybrid scheduling platform Common Surface and now oversees product at Keith. Eddie Goldsmith, former Chairman of the UK Conveyancing Association and founder of a market-leading conveyancing firm in the 90s, is a strategic advisor and non-exec Director, they added.

AL Interview with Andy Shovel

Can you please set out what it will offer in terms of conveyancing?

Keith will be a law firm offering all the same conveyancing services you’d expect from any other – handling both purchases and sales of residential property. However, behind the scenes we’ll be running the process very differently: AI automatically reviews correspondence and documents and every action is managed through pre-defined workflows. For clients, rather than lengthy email chains and time spent on hold waiting to speak to a conveyancer, they’ll be able to instantly speak to Keith via email, text or phone, track real-time progress on their transaction, see exactly what they need to do next, and complete tasks like signing documents or uploading information directly through our online platform – all available 24/7, not just during office hours.

What will the AI do, what will lawyers do?

AI handles the heavy lifting across the transaction: reviewing title documents, analysing property search results, processing incoming correspondence, and drafting responses. It flags issues, extracts key information, and makes recommendations – but a qualified conveyancer always reviews and approves before anything goes to the client or the other side. The result isn’t fewer lawyers, it’s dramatically more efficient ones – focused on judgment calls and client care rather than admin. Clients will also be able to speak to Keith, our AI agent, who can securely provide details about their transaction and answer conveyancing questions.

Which LLMs are you using?

Initially we were mostly using models provided by OpenAI; however, in recent months we have found Anthropic’s Opus + Sonnet models to perform better.

How will it be managed?

The AI will be managed our team of lawyers, and with strict guardrails in place to make sure that it only completes in-scope work, and has a low threshold for human referral, when there is any doubt.

What will you charge?

This is still TBC but we plan to come in around the lower end of the market.

Given that one of the biggest challenges with house sales is the human factor and the Land Registry data, how will Keith speed things up?

Currently conveyancers are often overwhelmed and it can take days for simple tasks to reach the top of their to do list. Keith will be able to immediately action tasks, requests or enquiries – and because AI can review documents and process information in seconds rather than hours, the work itself gets done faster and more accurately too. Secondly, it’s often unclear who needs to act and what is holding up the process. At Keith, we’ll make it clear who needs to act when and be able to handhold through every step of the process. Clients get a much better experience – guided step by step through what they need to do, with forms pre-filled from information we already hold so they’re never duplicating work. Today, conveyancers juggle multiple different portals and systems for each external service. At Keith, everything is centralised in one platform. We’ll interact with most external services such as Search Providers, Land Registry and HMRC via API. Also, you’ll be able to call and speak to Keith 24 hours a day. Keith is a much more sophisticated client service agent than 99% of people will have ever experienced.

And, has the £2m already been invested into your new company?

Yes we closed the funding round earlier this year. We’re pleased to be working with several leading European VCs: Backed, Breega and Notion.

—

So, there you go. There is no stopping NewMods / AI-first firms now. As predicted by AL at the end of 2025, there will be more and more of them this year, in the UK, in the US, and elsewhere. AI has simply made their arrival totally logical and the best way for many work streams to be handled.

More here about Keith.

—

And, if the above was interesting, wait until you see these events: 

A Legal Tech Conference For All of Europe

Legal Innovators Europe – Paris – June 24 and 25.

There will be more news about the conference and key speakers as we get closer to June.

Look forward to seeing you there!

Richard Tromans, Founder, Artificial Lawyer and Legal Innovators conference Chair.

Note: the conferences are organised by Cosmonauts – please contact them with any queries. 

If you would like to be a speaker at Legal Innovators Europe, especially if you are at a law firm or inhouse legal team in Europe – whether based in France, Belgium, Spain or Germany, or beyond…..then please contact Phoebe at Cosmonauts:  phoebe@cosmonauts.biz

Note: if you are a legal tech company, please contact Robins: robins@cosmonauts.biz or Anjana anjana@cosmonauts.biz

–

And if you’re in the US and looking for the next major event to join after Legal Week, then see you in California this June!

Legal Innovators California, the landmark West Coast legal tech event, will take place on June 10 and 11, in the heart of the Bay Area, the home to many of the world’s leading AI businesses – and plenty of legal tech pioneers as well! More information and tickets here.

research.titleEn: Can Small Models Reason About Legal Documents? A Comparative Study
research.titleZh: 小型模型能否推理法律文件？一项比较研究
research.abstractEn: Large language models show promise for legal applications, but deploying frontier models raises concerns about cost, latency, and data privacy. We evaluate whether sub-10B parameter models can serve as practical alternatives by testing nine models across three legal benchmarks (ContractNLI, CaseHOLD, and ECtHR) using five prompting strategies (direct, chain-of-thought, few-shot, BM25 RAG, and dense RAG). Across 405 experiments with three random seeds per configuration, we find that a Mixture-of-Experts model activating only 3B parameters matches GPT-4o-mini in mean accuracy while surpassing it on legal holding identification, and that architecture and training quality matter more than raw parameter count. Our largest model (9B parameters) performs worst overall. Chain-of-thought prompting proves sharply task-dependent, improving contract entailment but degrading multiple-choice legal reasoning, while few-shot prompting emerges as the most consistently effective strategy. Comparing BM25 and dense retrieval for RAG, we find near-identical results, suggesting the bottleneck lies in the language model's utilization of retrieved context rather than retrieval quality. All experiments were conducted via cloud inference APIs at a total cost of $62, demonstrating that rigorous LLM evaluation is accessible without dedicated GPU infrastructure.
research.abstractZh: 大型语言模型在法律应用中展现出潜力，但部署前沿模型引发了关于成本、延迟和数据隐私的担忧。我们通过测试九个模型在三个法律基准（ContractNLI、CaseHOLD和ECtHR）上使用五种提示策略（直接提示、思维链提示、少样本提示、BM25检索增强生成和稠密检索增强生成），评估了参数少于100亿的模型是否能作为实用替代方案。在每种配置使用三个随机种子进行的405次实验中，我们发现仅激活30亿参数的专家混合模型在平均准确率上与GPT-4o-mini相当，同时在法律判决识别方面超越它，并且架构和训练质量比原始参数数量更重要。我们最大的模型（90亿参数）整体表现最差。思维链提示策略被证明高度依赖任务，能改进合同蕴含推理但会降低多项选择法律推理的表现，而少样本提示策略成为最持续有效的策略。比较BM25和稠密检索在检索增强生成中的表现，我们发现结果几乎相同，表明瓶颈在于语言模型对检索上下文的利用而非检索质量。所有实验均通过云推理API进行，总成本为62美元，证明无需专用GPU基础设施即可进行严谨的大型语言模型评估。

news.titleEn: Foley & Lardner's Director of Innovative Tech: 'Truly Agentic, AI-driven Workflows Will be Transformative'
news.titleZh: Foley & Lardner创新技术总监：'真正自主的AI驱动工作流程将带来变革'
news.summaryZh: 律师事务所的创新由客户对更快、更透明、注重价值的法律服务期望驱动，促使律所采用人工智能、分析工具和云技术来简化工作流程。领导力与实验文化、专门创新团队和持续培训对律师利用新工具至关重要。然而，法律专业人士对变革的抵触、组织复杂性、保密担忧和风险规避可能阻碍进展。生成式人工智能和自主人工智能正在改变律所工作方式，自动化法律研究、合同审查和文件起草等常规任务，使律师能更专注于战略工作和客户关系。业务专业人员和律师角色可能转变，初级律师和业务专业人员将更专注于审查人工智能结果并提供专家建议。有效运用人工智能的律所将吸引更多客户和人才，但需要强大的人工智能政策、持续培训和对负责任使用的承诺。从基本自动化转向真正自主的AI驱动工作流程将带来变革，使日常实践中的任务管理更高效。技术供应商应优先考虑用户友好界面和互操作性，确保人工智能能力成为平台的基本价值而非昂贵附加项。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Charlotte Logullo, director, innovative technology and research at Foley & Lardner, which won the award for Best Use of Artificial Intelligence.

What do you currently see as the biggest barriers to, and biggest drivers of innovation in law firms?

Innovation in law firms is driven by client expectations for faster, more transparent, and value-focused legal services, prompting adoption of AI, analytics, and cloud technologies that streamline workflows and enhance responsiveness. Leadership and a culture of experimentation are essential, with dedicated innovation teams and ongoing training helping lawyers leverage new tools and adapt to evolving market dynamics. Strategic planning, robust governance, and partnerships with tech vendors and clients further accelerate solution development and business model innovation.

However, significant barriers persist: resistance to change remains strong among legal professionals accustomed to established workflows, and organizational complexity can slow coordinated adoption. Confidentiality concerns and risk aversion often hinder collaboration and the inclusion of non-lawyer professionals, while a narrow view of innovation—focused solely on technology rather than holistic problem-solving—can limit progress. Successful law firms overcome these obstacles by aligning innovation with strategic goals, fostering open-minded leadership, and continuously improving processes. Ultimately, innovation flourishes where technology, leadership, culture, and client-centricity intersect, enabling law firms to deliver higher-quality work with greater speed, efficiency, and confidence.

Emerging technologies such as generative and agentic AI are enabling new levels of automation in law firms. How do you expect these changes to impact law firms' operations, staffing and/or business models?

Generative and agentic AI are changing how law firms work by automating routine tasks including components of legal research, contract review, and document drafting. This allows lawyers to spend more time on important strategic work and building client relationships. With AI handling repetitive jobs, law firms can work faster and provide services more efficiently.

Business professional and attorney roles will likely shift, as junior lawyers and business professionals focus more on reviewing AI results and giving expert advice, while technology skills become more valuable. Firms that use AI effectively will attract more clients and talented professionals, while those that do not may fall behind. For these changes to succeed, law firms need strong AI policies, ongoing training, and a commitment to using AI responsibly and securely. In the end, AI should aid law firms to become quicker, more accurate, and more flexible in their work.

How would you like to see technology specifically designed for law firms change over the next few years, and why?

As law firm technology evolves, the shift from basic automation to truly agentic, AI-driven workflows will be transformative, enabling routine tasks such as document review, contract analysis, and legal research to be managed with minimal human input and delivering new efficiencies across daily practice. Rather than simply speeding up repetitive work, these advancements empower legal professionals to focus on strategic, client-centered activities while AI proactively anticipates client needs and provides actionable insights directly within familiar workflows.

Secure, real-time collaboration platforms, intuitive document management, and integrated analytics are becoming indispensable, as they support teamwork across practice groups and with clients, all while upholding strict confidentiality standards.

To promote widespread adoption, technology providers must prioritize user-friendly interfaces, seamless interoperability, and flexible configuration options so firms can tailor solutions to their strategic goals and practice specialties — moving away from one-size-fits-all offerings. As agentic AI becomes more mainstream and readily available, legal technology vendors should view AI capabilities as a fundamental value-add to their platforms, not as a separate expensive add-on, ensuring that pricing reflects AI’s role in enhancing the efficiency and overall value of legal services rather than capitalizing on novelty. Ultimately, these advances will drive better client engagement by improving transparency and providing quicker turnaround for routine matters, helping law firms become faster, more accurate, and more adaptable in a competitive market.

news.titleEn: Legora launches Legal AI Scholars Program with nine US law schools
news.titleZh: Legora与九所美国法学院合作推出法律人工智能学者项目
news.summaryZh:
Legora宣布正式启动法律人工智能学者项目，将其企业平台引入斯坦福大学、康奈尔大学、西北大学普利兹克法学院、加州大学洛杉矶分校等九所美国法学院的课程体系。该项目为合作院校提供与商业部署相同的Legora平台，并配备专门的教师培训与课程开发支持。项目旨在让毕业生入职律所时已熟练掌握专业级人工智能工具，从而降低培训成本并提升工作效率。

该项目启动于Legora完成5.5亿美元D轮融资两周后，此轮融资使其估值从去年10月的C轮融资后增至55.5亿美元。Legora在美国的扩张正在加速，计划在休斯顿和芝加哥设立新办公室，目标在2026年底前拥有超过300名美国员工。该平台主要基于Anthropic的Claude构建，定位为对抗通用人工智能层的专业解决方案。康奈尔大学法学院院长Jens David Ohlin将其与该校新成立的法律与人工智能中心的目标相联系，西北大学法学院院长Zachary Clopton则强调人工智能熟练度对未来行业领导者的必要性。Legora表示计划在未来数月将该项目扩展至其他关键司法管辖区的法学院。
news.bodyHtml:
By Neil Cameron, lead analyst

Legora has announced the Legal AI Scholars Program, a formal initiative placing its enterprise platform inside the curricula of nine US law schools including Stanford, Cornell, Northwestern Pritzker, and UCLA. The founding cohort also includes University of Chicago, University of Texas, Vanderbilt, Boston University, and University of San Francisco.

Advertisement

The program gives participating institutions access to the same platform Legora deploys commercially, alongside dedicated faculty training and curriculum development support. The pitch to schools is straightforward: graduates who arrive at firms already fluent in professional-grade AI tools reduce training costs and accelerate productivity from day one.

I have some personal history here. In the early 1980s I was involved in placing LexisNexis into UK law schools – at the time a similarly disruptive proposition, the idea that students should encounter professional research tools before they qualified rather than after. The logic was sound then and it is sound now. But that experience also left me with a lasting frustration: law schools remain stubbornly selective about which practical competencies they take seriously. Knowledge management, client relations, matter management – the infrastructure of actual legal practice – have never been adequately embedded in legal education. They are still not. AI training is unambiguously necessary. But it does not fill those gaps, and the risk is that it becomes the latest shiny addition to a curriculum that remains structurally incomplete.

On the AI training itself, two things matter above all others, and they are related. The first is that students learn to be the master of AI in legal research, not its servant – understanding what the tool is doing, why, and what it cannot do. The second is developing the discriminatory judgment to recognise when the AI is taking them somewhere wrong. These are not instinctive skills. They require deliberate teaching. Hallucination in a legal research context is not an abstract problem; it is a professional liability exposure. The students who emerge from this programme fluent in Legora but unable to interrogate its outputs critically will be more dangerous, not less, than those who never used it.

The announcement lands two weeks after Legora closed a $550 million Series D, tripling its valuation from October’s Series C to $5.55 billion TechCrunch and cementing its position as the principal European-origin challenger to Harvey in the US market. The round was led by Accel, with participation from Benchmark, Bessemer, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Redpoint, Y Combinator, and a clutch of new investors including Bain Capital, Menlo Ventures, and Salesforce Ventures.

The timing of the scholars programme is not incidental. Legora’s US expansion is accelerating rapidly – new offices in Houston and Chicago follow its New York and Denver presence, with a target of more than 300 US employees by end of 2026 Legora – and embedding its platform in elite law schools is an obvious pipeline play. Students trained on Legora become advocates within the firms that hire them. It is a customer acquisition strategy that doubles as a legitimacy signal, and at this valuation, Legora can afford both.

The platform itself warrants a note. Legora is built primarily on Anthropic’s Claude and positions itself explicitly against the generalist AI layer. When Anthropic launched a legal plugin for Claude earlier this year, CEO Max Junestrand’s public response was pointed: there is a material difference, he argued, between a plugin and a production-grade, matter-centric, collaborative platform embedded in firm workflows. Roughly 80% of legal tasks are theoretically within reach of current AI models, yet observed daily adoption in legal practice sits at around 15% – one of the widest gaps of any professional sector. Legora’s entire commercial thesis is built on closing that gap through workflow integration rather than capability alone.

The scholars programme fits that thesis. Law schools are not just a recruitment channel – they are where professional norms and tool expectations are formed. Getting Legora into the hands of students at Stanford and Cornell before they encounter Harvey at the firms that recruit them is a long game, but a rational one.

news.bodyText:
Legora has announced the Legal AI Scholars Program, a formal initiative placing its enterprise platform inside the curricula of nine US law schools including Stanford, Cornell, Northwestern Pritzker, and UCLA. The founding cohort also includes University of Chicago, University of Texas, Vanderbilt, Boston University, and University of San Francisco.

The program gives participating institutions access to the same platform Legora deploys commercially, alongside dedicated faculty training and curriculum development support. The pitch to schools is straightforward: graduates who arrive at firms already fluent in professional-grade AI tools reduce training costs and accelerate productivity from day one.

I have some personal history here. In the early 1980s I was involved in placing LexisNexis into UK law schools – at the time a similarly disruptive proposition, the idea that students should encounter professional research tools before they qualified rather than after. The logic was sound then and it is sound now. But that experience also left me with a lasting frustration: law schools remain stubbornly selective about which practical competencies they take seriously. Knowledge management, client relations, matter management – the infrastructure of actual legal practice – have never been adequately embedded in legal education. They are still not. AI training is unambiguously necessary. But it does not fill those gaps, and the risk is that it becomes the latest shiny addition to a curriculum that remains structurally incomplete.

On the AI training itself, two things matter above all others, and they are related. The first is that students learn to be the master of AI in legal research, not its servant – understanding what the tool is doing, why, and what it cannot do. The second is developing the discriminatory judgment to recognise when the AI is taking them somewhere wrong. These are not instinctive skills. They require deliberate teaching. Hallucination in a legal research context is not an abstract problem; it is a professional liability exposure. The students who emerge from this programme fluent in Legora but unable to interrogate its outputs critically will be more dangerous, not less, than those who never used it.

The announcement lands two weeks after Legora closed a $550 million Series D, tripling its valuation from October’s Series C to $5.55 billion TechCrunch and cementing its position as the principal European-origin challenger to Harvey in the US market. The round was led by Accel, with participation from Benchmark, Bessemer, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Redpoint, Y Combinator, and a clutch of new investors including Bain Capital, Menlo Ventures, and Salesforce Ventures.

The timing of the scholars programme is not incidental. Legora’s US expansion is accelerating rapidly – new offices in Houston and Chicago follow its New York and Denver presence, with a target of more than 300 US employees by end of 2026 Legora – and embedding its platform in elite law schools is an obvious pipeline play. Students trained on Legora become advocates within the firms that hire them. It is a customer acquisition strategy that doubles as a legitimacy signal, and at this valuation, Legora can afford both.

The platform itself warrants a note. Legora is built primarily on Anthropic’s Claude and positions itself explicitly against the generalist AI layer. When Anthropic launched a legal plugin for Claude earlier this year, CEO Max Junestrand’s public response was pointed: there is a material difference, he argued, between a plugin and a production-grade, matter-centric, collaborative platform embedded in firm workflows. news.titleEn: Harvey reaches $11bn valuation with $200m new funding round
news.titleZh: Harvey完成2亿美元新一轮融资，估值达110亿美元
news.summaryZh:
Harvey于3月25日宣布完成2亿美元新一轮融资，本轮融资由现有投资者GIC和红杉资本共同领投，估值达到110亿美元。参与本轮融资的现有投资者还包括Andreessen Horowitz、Coatue、Conviction Partners、Elad Gil、Evantic和Kleiner Perkins。这笔投资将用于扩展客户在Harvey平台上运行的智能代理，并扩大全球范围内支持客户的嵌入式法律工程团队规模。

Harvey在宣布融资的博客中披露，目前有超过25,000个定制智能代理在Harvey平台上运行，执行并购、尽职调查、合同起草和文件审查等工作。客户越来越多地部署长期智能代理来处理复杂用例的多步骤工作流程，例如基金组建。客户还在共享空间内部署智能代理，以便在法律团队及其外部合作伙伴之间安全协调工作。Harvey的法律工程师与客户合作，构建并持续改进运行其工作的智能代理。
news.bodyHtml:
Harvey today (25 March) announced $200 million in new funding co-led by returning investors GIC and Sequoia. The round values Harvey at $11 billion and includes participation from existing investors Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction Partners, Elad Gil, Evantic, and Kleiner Perkins. Harvey says that the investment will be used to expand the agents customers run on Harvey and grow the embedded legal engineering teams supporting them globally.

“AI isn’t just assisting lawyers. It’s becoming the system through which legal work gets done,” said Winston Weinberg, CEO and co-founder of Harvey. “The law firms and in-house teams leading the way are building agents that execute complex workflows so lawyers can focus on judgment, strategy, and outcomes.”

Advertisement

In a blog post noting the raise today, Harvey said that more than 25,000 custom agents operate on Harvey, executing work across M&A, due diligence, contract drafting, and document review. Customers are increasingly deploying long-horizon agents that handle multi-step workflows over extended periods for complex use cases such as fund formation. They are also deploying agents within Shared Spaces to securely coordinate work across legal teams and their external partners. Harvey’s legal engineers work alongside customers to build and continuously improve the agents that run their work.

Pat Grady, a partner at Sequoia, said: “Co-leading three rounds in the same company is rare for Sequoia and reflects conviction that has only grown stronger since we first partnered at the Series A. More than 100,000 lawyers around the world run their most critical work on Harvey, and we believe it’s positioned to become one of the most important companies of the next decade.”

news.titleEn: Relativity's IPO Gamble: Can It Succeed Where Many Legal Tech Companies Have Struggled?
news.titleZh: Relativity的IPO赌注：能否在众多法律科技公司挣扎的领域取得成功？
news.summaryZh:
法律科技公司上市后的表现普遍不佳，许多公司股价大幅下跌，部分还面临财务不当行为的诉讼指控。例如，仅今年2月，Anthropic为Claude推出法律插件后，法律科技公司股价在一周内下跌约12%至20%，这反映了投资者因人工智能颠覆而撤离软件公司的趋势。在此背景下，Relativity计划进行首次公开募股（IPO），其动机引发关注。支持者认为该公司拥有可持续业务、正收益、高于同行的盈利能力，以及约15%以上的复合年增长率、典型的SaaS利润率和强大的AI叙事。Relativity近年通过严格定价、推动客户从服务器环境转向云端以优化云增长故事，并重塑品牌定位为“法律数据智能”服务商，以扩大投资者吸引力。

然而，挑战依然存在。作为一家成立数十年的传统公司（原名kCura），Relativity可能被视为缺乏灵活性，其生成式AI产品aiR Suite被部分观点认为是“附加式”AI，而非从零构建。尽管公司曾成功应对从本地部署到云端的范式转变，但在当前市场，SaaS公司普遍面临股价压力。财务方面，Relativity作为私营公司未披露详细数据，仅知2021年Silver Lake投资时估值36亿美元。公开法律科技公司中，DISCO和Intapp等持续净亏损，LegalZoom和Nuix虽有盈利但股价远低于发行价，且Nuix和DISCO均卷入法律或财务丑闻，KLDiscovery则因债务问题被债权人控股。这些案例因独特问题难以作为市场基准，而Intapp在营收规模上可能与Relativity最具可比性，其股价表现相对较好，市值约20亿美元。
news.bodyHtml:
For legal tech companies that have gone public, the results have not been rosy—many have suffered significant stock drops, while a few have been hit with lawsuits alleging financial improprieties.

In February alone, AI developer Anthropic’s launch of a legal plug-in for Claude resulted in legal tech companies seeing their share prices drop by around 12% to 20% over the span of a week, part of a larger, ongoing trend of investors pulling away from software companies in the face of artificial intelligence disruption.

Given the track record of many legal tech companies navigating the whims of Wall Street, why would Relativity want to join the crowd?

For one thing, past isn’t always prologue—and not all legal tech companies are made equal.

Some see Relativity’s situation as unique, with the company on stronger footing than those whose stocks have significantly underperformed since their public debut.

But a lot will depend on how Relativity can market itself to investors, at least some of whom may be wary of backing a legacy software-as-a-service (SaaS) company in a market where disruption by newer AI-focused startups is on everyone’s mind.

Bucking the Trend?


For Mike Bryant, a partner at investment firm Knox Capital and a board member at HaystackID, the proposed IPO makes sense given Relativity’s sustainable business.

“Where Relativity is different than everything else out there, … they have positive earnings,” he said. “They have a structurally more profitable business than any of their public peers by a lot.”

Bryant explained, “When you bring a business like this that is a category leader that has good growth rates, I would estimate at 15% plus compounded annual growth rates, typical SaaS margins, very likely showing a lot of stickiness in their base in terms of gross revenue retention, and a very strong AI narrative with deep domain expertise, ... I think the institutional investors will welcome an asset like this into the public markets.”

In fact, Bryant notes that recent moves by Relativity may make the company a more attractive prospect for Wall Street.

“As someone that is a practitioner, an investor and an operator in this field, some of Relativity’s behavior over the last couple of years makes more sense now. They've been very strident around pricing, very parochial about moving their clients from their server environment to the cloud environment to make for a cleaner story when they go to the public markets. You want a very clean story around your pure cloud growth, SaaS growth—having the two environments is not ideal.”

Relativity is also positioning itself as more than just an e-discovery company with its recent brand refresh, which included new language and a visual identity to emphasize how the company serves the broader “legal data intelligence” community beyond just e-discovery.

Zach Abramowitz, founder of Killer Whale Strategies, said Relativity will likely emphasize this broader appeal to investors. “‘We sell to government, we sell to Big Four, we sell to corporate, we sell to major corporations, and we sell the law firms’—They might go in that direction, which positions them away from being legal tech and focuses them as a necessary compliance or regulatory tool.”

Still, other aspects of Relativity’s identity may be harder to position for Wall Street. Its status as a legacy company that has been around for decades—previously under the name kCura—may be seen as a drawback. Despite Relativity's launch of its generative AI aiR Suite, some believe younger, more nimble startups are better equipped to the meet the AI moment.

“Relativity was not built from the ground up with the assumptions about AI capabilities that you would build an e-discovery company with if you were starting today,” Abramowitz said.

He added, “The question I have is, is that fruit of the wilting flower … that flower is not going to last the way it would if it were still planted in the ground. … And I think it's very possible to argue right now that Relativity’s success with AI is AI that is bolted on. And ultimately, there will be providers that will so completely transform discovery and the technology behind discovery that paying Relativity’s current fees, and having a product that has some of the quirks that Relativity’s product has, will just be unthinkable.”

The company, however, has a record of adapting to the moment. “Relativity has endured at least one massive paradigm shift during its lifetime, going from on-prem to the cloud, and, quite frankly, I think they navigated that about as well as you could,” Abramowitz said. “Where there were companies like Everlaw and DISCO and Logikcull that said they were going to sink Relativity, because Relativity was not built cloud-first, Relativity very much survived that. And I could understand a narrative today that says that Relativity is, in fact, adapting with AI.”

At the end of the day, however, Relativity is still a SaaS company, and in today’s market, that may count against it—no matter how different it is from other software providers. “It is very, very possible that Relativity will get labeled with all of the other SaaS stocks. Right now, the market. … It hasn't been kind to any SaaS stocks,” Abramowitz said.

No Easy Comparisons


As a private company, Relativity does not disclose its finances, and its Form S-1 filing to the SEC remains, for the time being, confidential.

To date, Relativity has only announced one public investment, from private equity firm Silver Lake in 2021, which valued the company at $3.6 billion. At the time, its then CEO Mike Gamson told Legaltech News that the impetus behind the investment was to help Relativity scale.

Several legal tech public tech companies—including e-discovery DISCO and legal tech provider Intapp—have struggled with profitability, reporting net losses for each year since their IPO. A few, however, have bucked the trend. Online marketplace LegalZoom and Australian e-discovery company Nuix have had profitable years, though their current stock prices—like almost all other public legal tech companies—are fractions of their initial listing price.

Comparisons between these companies and Relativity are not straightforward. Bryant argued that LegalZoom, which heavily focuses on the compliance needs of small business customers, is such a different company than Relativity that it is not comparable.

Meanwhile, all public e-discovery companies have run into legal or financial issues. Nuix was hit with allegations that it omitted information in its IPO and market disclosures, while DISCO faced federal and state class action lawsuits alleging that it violated securities laws and misled investors. In addition, KLDiscovery, which went public through merging with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) in 2019, struggled publicly with mounting, unsustainable debt levels, before reaching a deal with creditors, which now own most of the company’s equity.

Given the unique experience of these few public e-discovery companies, they may not provide a benchmark for others in the market. Nuix and DISCO “are two companies that have had that have had a serious amount of scandal follow them, and so it's sort of hard to figure out how legal technology companies will do when they hit the market. We don't have a huge sample size. We can talk about other verticals, but just to say ‘legal tech’ is a little bit unclear,” Abramowitz said.

For Bryant, however, there is at least one potential public company comparable to Relativity—Intapp, which he said may be similar in the size of its revenue and financials. Intapp’s stock price has fared better than other public legal tech providers—which is hovering just under the company’s $26 initial listing price.

“Their largest hit [on a] share price basis really was since the dislocation in the market associated with the last couple months. Outside of that, it's still got a $2 billion market cap, and it's not too dissimilar in terms of—again Relativity is private company, I don't know exactly their metrics—but they're, I suspect, close to [that], or I would say bigger.”
