news.titleEn: How Two Litigators Spent Five Years in Stealth Building What They Say Is the Most Comprehensive Litigation Platform on the Market
news.titleZh: 两位诉讼律师如何用五年时间秘密打造他们口中市场上最全面的诉讼平台
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Syllo由Jeffrey Chivers和Theodore Rostow于2019年创立，致力于构建统一诉讼平台。由于多年研发无近期产品，风险投资不愿资助，两人通过运营诉讼业务维持公司，早期投资者为理解长期愿景的律师和高净值人士。公司技术基础与卡内基梅隆大学工程师合作构建。Syllo自称是市场上最广泛的诉讼技术工具，功能涵盖电子取证、代理式人工智能文档审阅、案件构建与事实管理及诉讼代理，覆盖电子取证参考模型并延伸至案件策略和庭审准备。2024年2月，公司开始向客户部署代理式人工智能文档审阅系统，该系统能协调多个大型语言模型自主执行文档审阅任务。2025年3月，Syllo与七家律所的25名律师及电子取证从业者联合卡内基梅隆大学发布白皮书，报告系统在活跃诉讼中常规估计召回率超过93%，平均召回率97.8%，中位估计精确度85.9%，平均估计精确度79.7%。昆鹰律师事务所的审判团队曾在并购执行案件中使用Syllo处理超过7万份文档并赢得诉讼。公司客户主要面向大型律所，擅长处理复杂的重大诉讼。2024年，Syllo与全国就业律师协会建立合作伙伴关系。公司此前一直处于秘密运营状态，前五年没有销售人员。2023年10月，公司获得由Venrock领投的3000万美元成长轮融资，此后员工数量在四个月内翻倍，新增约30人，并即将聘请销售主管。2024年2月，公司聘请Alexis Mitchell担任高级人工智能顾问。
news.bodyHtml:
At the recent Legalweek conference in New York, I sat down with the cofounders of Syllo, a legal technology company that has taken a uniquely ambitious approach to developing technology for litigators.

Rather than focus on any one segment of the litigation process, they have built a unified, AI-powered litigation workspace that spans the entire lifecycle of a case, from raw data collection through trial.

The company is the brainchild of Jeffrey Chivers, its chief executive officer and head of product, and Theodore Rostow, its chief operating officer and chief strategy officer. The pair cofounded the company in 2019 after meeting while clerking in federal court.

Chivers, a Harvard computer science graduate who went on to earn his law degree at Georgetown and litigate at Sullivan & Cromwell, says he brings a technologist’s instincts to the practice of law.

Rostow, a Yale Law School graduate who practiced at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, had been immersed in legal technology and AI since 2014, writing about automation, structured and unstructured data, and deep learning while still in law school.

The Monastic Period

Part of what makes their story unusual – and what may make it instructive for anyone watching the trajectory of legal technology – is how they chose to build the company.

Rather than follow the conventional startup playbook of building a narrow point solution and expanding from there, Chivers and Rostow decided from the outset to build the entire infrastructure for a unified litigation platform.

That meant years of foundational work on plumbing and architecture before any meaningful user interface existed on top of it.

“We basically decided we are going to build the unified platform,” Chivers told me. “And we didn’t build one thing or another thing and then add other things on. We actually built out the entire infrastructure of the entire unified platform, which did almost nothing.”

That approach came at a cost. No venture capital firm wanted to fund a multi-year R&D project with no near-term product to show.

To keep the lights on, Chivers and Rostow ran a litigation practice alongside the company for more than three years. Their initial investors were lawyers and high-net-worth individuals who understood the long-term vision – people who, as Chivers put it, “knew a ton about the legal industry and could really understand the long-term value proposition.”

The company’s early philosophy, Rostow said, was simple: “We want the risk to be placed entirely on, ‘Can we actually build this thing?’ If we build it, it’s definitely the right thing.”

The technical foundation was built in collaboration with engineers from Carnegie Mellon University, including Jamie Callan, professor at CMU’s Language Technologies Institute, who collaborated with the company on its agentic AI document review research.

What Syllo Actually Does

Today, Syllo describes itself as the broadest litigation technology tool on the market. Based on the capabilities that Chivers and Rostow walked me through, but which I have not yet seen demonstrated, that claim  is at least plausible.

The platform encompasses:

  • E-discovery, including raw data ingestion, load file ingestion, search, threading, deduplication, redaction, and production.
  • Agentic AI document review, which automates responsiveness review, issue coding, privilege review, confidentiality review, and PII/PHI review and redaction. The system can apply an unlimited number of issue codes across data sets of any size.
  • Case building and fact management, including exhibit management, transcript management, pretrial document stamping, and deposition preparation.
  • A litigation agent that can draw on everything across the platform for dialogue-based work, analysis, and work-product generation.

That combination of features means that Syllo covers not just the EDRM (Electronic Discovery Reference Model), but extends beyond it into case strategy, trial preparation and document generation.

The company competes, depending on the use case, with e-discovery platforms such as Relativity, Everlaw, DISCO and Reveal; with e-discovery services companies such as Consilio, Epiq and FTI; with case-building tools such as Opus 2; and with AI legal assistants such as Harvey and CoCounsel.

Chivers acknowledged that some firms have trouble grasping that broad competitive positioning. “You could imagine we go in and tell a firm, use Syllo instead of using Relativity, Opus 2 and CoCounsel or Harvey. That is really hard for a law firm to accept.”

Why the Unified Approach?

By no means would Syllo be the first legal tech company to attempt to unify the litigation stack. Both LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters have tried it over the years through various acquisitions and product combinations, and many e-discovery providers today are pushing their products farther to the right of the EDRM into case management and trial preparation.

But Chivers sees those attempts as largely having failed, and he  attributes those failures partly to the different kinds of software engineering required by each domain.

E-discovery involves forensically sound data processing, complex metadata handling and constantly evolving technical standards. Case management involves more lawyer-facing workflow and strategic tools. Building both under one roof requires distinct engineering competencies and a single data environment that connects them.

It is precisely that single data environment, Chivers argued, that makes AI maximally effective.

“What I think people are starting to appreciate more,” he said, “is that to get the most out of AI and agentic AI involves structured data. It involves extremely clean data. It involves very elaborate context management by the system itself.”

The way Syllo was built, he added, “was exactly what is needed to get the most out of AI.”

The practical implications are significant, he said. Because Syllo houses everything from the raw collected data through to case strategy, its AI agent can draw on the entire factual record when generating analysis or work product, not just the subset of data a lawyer has manually fed into a standalone AI tool.

Agentic Document Review

While Syllo was built as a full-lifecycle platform, the feature that it first brought to market was its agentic AI document review system, which the company began deploying with clients in February 2024.

The system coordinates multiple large language models that autonomously manage and execute document review tasks based on user-defined guidelines, the company says. It dynamically allocates more powerful models to complex documents and simpler models to straightforward ones, and it can handle an unlimited number of issue codes without the prompt-overload problems that plague more linear applications of AI to large data sets.

In March 2025, Syllo and a group of 25 litigators and e-discovery practitioners from seven law firms published a white paper, in collaboration with Carnegie Mellon’s Callan, documenting how the system performs in active litigation.

The paper reported that the system routinely achieves estimated recall above 93 percent, with an average recall of 97.8%. The median estimated precision was 85.9%, and the average estimated precision was 79.7%.

In one example discussed in the white paper, a Quinn Emanuel trial team used Syllo in a merger enforcement case where the firm was retained just weeks before trial. The team used Syllo for outgoing and incoming document review, deposition preparation and case strategy across more than 70,000 documents. Quinn Emanuel won the trial, and the team was named AmLaw Litigators of the Week in March 2025.

Chivers told me the agentic document review capability was what initially drew many AmLaw 100 firms to the platform. “Firms will come in and think Syllo is good at document review, and that’s why they want to work with us,” he said. “And then they’ll onboard the case and realize, ‘Oh, Syllo is an entire platform for all this stuff.’”

Clients and Market Position

Syllo’s customer base skews heavily toward the larger-firm market. The company counts multiple Am Law 100 firms among its users, including Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman (which announced a multi-year integration of the platform last year), and Ballard Spahr.

Its sweet spot, Chivers and Rostow said, is complex, high-stakes litigation – think antitrust MDLs, environmental litigation, complex bankruptcy, patent cases – where the sheer volume and complexity of the factual record can be overwhelming.

Syllo has also been expanding beyond Big Law. In 2024, it announced a partnership with the National Employment Lawyers Association (NELA) to make its platform available to the organization’s 4,000-plus members, many of whom are plaintiffs’ employment lawyers at smaller firms.

From Stealth to Scale

For much of its existence, Syllo operated in near-total stealth, bound by NDAs with its law firm clients. The company had no salespeople for its first five years and, as recently as late last year, employed only three.

That is changing. Last October, the company announced a $30 million growth funding round led by Venrock, with participation from Two Seas Capital and strategic investors. Venrock partner Nick Beim said the company’s software represents “a step-function improvement in capabilities for the industry.”

Since the funding round, the company has been growing rapidly. Chivers told me that Syllo has roughly doubled its headcount in just the past four months, adding approximately 30 people, and was about to bring on a head of sales.

In February, the company announced the hiring of Alexis Mitchell as senior AI consultant. Mitchell previously held key data science and linguistic roles at Epiq, Opus 2, OpenText, Recommind, Autonomy and H5. That hire came alongside a broader talent expansion drawing from companies such as Meta, SpaceX, Amazon, Sony, Google and OpenAI.

“On the product side, we are now at a decisive lead moment,” Rostow told me. “The question is how, over the next year and a half, does that lead dramatically widen, even as hundreds of millions of dollars and dozens of billions of dollars are poured into the space.”

Whether Syllo can translate its technical breadth into sustained commercial growth in a market that traditionally rewards specialization remains to be seen.

But after five years of building in stealth, a successful funding round, and a growing roster of elite law firm clients, they appear to be well-positioned to give it a shot.

news.titleEn: Orange Rag Legaltech Clinic: “How should firms go to market to select the best compliance technology?”
news.titleZh: 《Orange Rag》法律科技诊所：律所应如何选择最佳合规技术？
news.summaryZh:
本月法律科技诊所专家小组成员为娜塔莉·库伯勒，她是伦敦咨询公司Alt-V Law的董事总经理兼联合创始人。其客户经常寻求帮助以选择合适的合规系统。

合规技术已成为全球律所最具战略意义的投资领域之一。监管要求不断提高，客户尽职调查日益复杂，律所面临压力需在整个运营模式中展示更强、更可审计的控制措施。这些技术高度专业化，可协助律所进行身份识别、利益冲突和金融犯罪检查，并管理客户尽职调查、风险评估和持续监控以支持监管报告。其最新研究已识别出超过109种合规技术。
news.bodyHtml:
This month our expert legal tech clinic panellist is Natalie Kuebler, managing director and co-founder of London-based consultancy Alt-V Law, whose clients regularly ask for help in selecting the right compliance system.

Kuebler says: “Compliance technology has become one of the most strategically important investment areas for law firms globally. Regulatory expectations are increasing, client due diligence is increasingly complex, and firms are under pressure to demonstrate stronger, more auditable controls across the operating model. Technologies are highly specialised and help firms perform identity, conflicts and financial crime checks, and manage client due diligence, risk assessment and ongoing monitoring to support regulatory reporting. Our latest research identifies more than 109 compliance technologies.”

Advertisement

For her in-depth advice, see the February edition of the Orange Rag here: https://www.flipsnack.com/86D6B577C6F/the-orange-rag-february-2026/full-view.html?p=6

news.titleEn: American Arbitration Association AGC: AI Isn't Just About Time, Cost Savings, But Improving Outcomes
news.titleZh: 美国仲裁协会副总法律顾问：人工智能不仅关乎节省时间与成本，更在于改善结果
news.summaryZh:
法律科技市场正进入关键一年，生成式人工智能将从新奇事物转变为可衡量的竞争优势。能够展示人工智能如何改善结果、加快解决速度并降低客户成本的法律机构和争议解决组织将脱颖而出，而未能负责任整合人工智能的机构将面临重大竞争风险。客户将不仅期望人工智能使用的透明度，更要求价值证明。生成式人工智能将继续扩展至各行业主流平台，涵盖法律研究、文书起草、运营、风险管理和工作流系统。随着技术更可靠地嵌入日常工具，法律行业将面临更大压力，需要现代化那些仍依赖人工且成本高昂的流程。

法律科技买家正从谨慎好奇转向战略需求，关注重点不仅是人工智能节省多少时间或成本，更在于其如何改善结果和增强决策。生成式人工智能减少资源差距的潜力正在改变市场动态，使小型机构和自我代理方能够获得以往需要大量资金和人力投入的工具。买家将期望人工智能直接嵌入工作流程而非作为附加组件购买，同时要求可解释性、数据治理和人工监督功能以维护道德标准和公众信任。法律系统的文化仍是创新的主要障碍，但各行业趋势表明，采用负责任治理人工智能的组织正在效率、透明度和成本可预测性方面取得实质性进展。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Kelly Turner, vice president, associate general counsel at American Arbitration Association, which won the award for Innovations in Arbitration/Mediation Technology.

The legal tech industry has grown significantly over the past few years, with many new entrants and offerings. How do you see the market evolving in the next 12 months and why?

The legal tech market is entering a decisive year in which generative AI (gen AI) becomes a measurable competitive advantage rather than a novelty. Law firms and dispute resolution organizations that can demonstrate how AI improves outcomes, speeds time to resolution, and reduces client costs will differentiate themselves. At the same time, those that fail to integrate AI responsibly will face significant competitive risk. Clients will increasingly expect not just transparency regarding AI use, but evidence of value.

Gen AI will continue to expand across mainstream platforms across industries—not only in legal research and drafting, but also in operations, risk management, and workflow systems. As technology becomes more reliable and deeply embedded in everyday tools, the legal sector will face growing pressure to modernize processes that remain manually intensive and expensive.

We also expect a rise in AI-driven access-to-justice tools. The combination of guided user experiences and domain-specific gen AI models will better equip individuals and small businesses to understand their rights, prepare filings, and navigate dispute processes without prohibitive cost. As these tools improve, they will begin to rebalance long-standing resource disparities. In the coming year, AI will move from “nice to have” to a determinant of fairness, efficiency, and competitiveness in legal services.

How have you seen legal tech users and buyers’ behavior, demands and/or preferences evolve over the past few years, and how do you predict it will change in the near future?

Legal tech buyers—law firms, in-house teams, public institutions, and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) organizations—are shifting from cautiously curious to strategically demanding. Importantly, the question is not just how much time or cost AI saves, but how AI can improve outcomes and enhance decision-making.

There is also an interesting dynamic fueled by gen AI’s potential to reduce resource disparities: smaller firms and self-represented parties now have access to tools that once required significant investment in terms of dollars and people.

These dynamics are already emerging in practice. Gen AI is beginning to level the playing field, particularly in research, drafting, and dispute submission. We see this in governed tools like the AI Arbitrator, where AI supports case analysis and efficiency while a human arbitrator retains full decision authority.

Buyers will expect AI to be embedded directly into workflows rather than purchased as add-ons. They will also demand explainability, data governance, and human oversight—capabilities that protect ethical standards and public trust. Vendors will need to show not only how their products automate tasks, but how they enhance fairness, resolution quality, and access.

What do you see as the biggest barriers to and drivers of innovation in the legal industry right now?

The legal system’s culture remains the primary barrier to innovation. Traditional law firm business models, particularly the billable-hour model, can disincentivize efficiency, and ethical guardrails can make risk-averse professionals hesitant to adopt emerging technologies. Additionally, many legal professionals lack the technical literacy needed to evaluate or govern advanced AI tools confidently. 

However, the trend seen across finance, health care, construction, and other industries is clear: organizations that harness responsibly governed AI are achieving meaningful gains in efficiency, transparency, and cost predictability. Legal services will not be exempt from this market reality. Clients will demand outcome-based value and faster resolution cycles coupled with lawyers’ judgment—pressures that will drive innovation more forcefully than internal motivation alone.  

This is where responsible frameworks become essential. Models like the AI Arbitrator—where AI supports analysis and efficiency while a human arbitrator retains full decision authority—illustrate how governance, transparency, and ethical safeguards can coexist with innovation. These frameworks increase trust, address regulatory concerns, and serve as proof points for how the legal profession can modernize without compromising its principles.  The next wave of innovation will come not from experimentation alone, but from governed AI that respects ethics, enhances outcomes, and expands access to justice.

At the same time, those that fail to integrate AI responsibly will face significant competitive risk. Clients will increasingly expect not just transparency regarding AI use, but evidence of value.

Gen AI will continue to expand across mainstream platforms across industries—not only in legal research and drafting, but also in operations, risk management, and workflow systems. As technology becomes more reliable and deeply embedded in everyday tools, the legal sector will face growing pressure to modernize processes that remain manually intensive and expensive.

We also expect a rise in AI-driven access-to-justice tools. The combination of guided user experiences and domain-specific gen AI models will better equip individuals and small businesses to understand their rights, prepare filings, and navigate dispute processes without prohibitive cost. As these tools improve, they will begin to rebalance long-standing resource disparities. In the coming year, AI will move from “nice to have” to a determinant of fairness, efficiency, and competitiveness in legal services.

How have you seen legal tech users and buyers’ behavior, demands and/or preferences evolve over the past few years, and how do you predict it will change in the near future?

Legal tech buyers—law firms, in-house teams, public institutions, and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) organizations—are shifting from cautiously curious to strategically demanding. Importantly, the question is not just how much time or cost AI saves, but how AI can improve outcomes and enhance decision-making.

There is also an interesting dynamic fueled by gen AI’s potential to reduce resource disparities: smaller firms and self-represented parties now have access to tools that once required significant investment in terms of dollars and people.

These dynamics are already emerging in practice. Gen AI is beginning to level the playing field, particularly in research, drafting, and dispute submission. We see this in governed tools like the AI Arbitrator, where AI supports case analysis and efficiency while a human arbitrator retains full decision authority.

Buyers will expect AI to be embedded directly into workflows rather than purchased as add-ons. They will also demand explainability, data governance, and human oversight—capabilities that protect ethical standards and public trust. Vendors will need to show not only how their products automate tasks, but how they enhance fairness, resolution quality, and access.

What do you see as the biggest barriers to and drivers of innovation in the legal industry right now?

The legal system’s culture remains the primary barrier to innovation. Traditional law firm business models, particularly the billable-hour model, can disincentivize efficiency, and ethical guardrails can make risk-averse professionals hesitant to adopt emerging technologies. Additionally, many legal professionals lack the technical literacy needed to evaluate or govern advanced AI tools confidently.

However, the trend seen across finance, health care, construction, and other industries is clear: organizations that harness responsibly governed AI are achieving meaningful gains in efficiency, transparency, and cost predictability. Legal services will not be exempt from this market reality. Clients will demand outcome-based value and faster resolution cycles coupled with lawyers’ judgment—pressures that will drive innovation more forcefully than internal motivation alone.

This is where responsible frameworks become essential. Models like the AI Arbitrator—where AI supports analysis and efficiency while a human arbitrator retains full decision authority—illustrate how governance, transparency, and ethical safeguards can coexist with innovation. These frameworks increase trust, address regulatory concerns, and serve as proof points for how the legal profession can modernize without compromising its principles.  The next wave of innovation will come not from experimentation alone, but from governed AI that respects ethics, enhances outcomes, and expands access to justice.

news.titleEn: Relativity Announces Proposed IPO, Following Brand Refresh, Startup Investments
news.titleZh: Relativity宣布拟进行IPO，此前已完成品牌焕新及初创企业投资
news.summaryZh:
其拟议的首次公开募股将涉及A类普通股，但“拟发行股票数量及价格区间”尚未确定。该公司拒绝就拟议IPO置评。

此次IPO计划宣布前，Relativity近期完成了品牌焕新，采用新的语言和视觉标识以强调其服务范围已超越电子取证，延伸至更广泛的“法律数据智能”领域。公司还通过去年十月成立的创新投资部门Rel Labs，首次公开投资了两家法律科技初创企业Patlytics和Advocacy。本月早些时候，Relativity还宣布了其生成式人工智能套件aiR的最新更新，其中aiR for Case Strategy已在Relativity One Government平台全面上线。
news.bodyHtml:
Relativity noted in a press release that its proposed IPO—the filings related to which are not yet public—would be of Class A common shares, with “the number of shares to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering” not yet determined.

Relativity declined a request for comment on the proposed IPO.

The announcement of a proposed IPO follows the company’s recent brand refresh, with new language and visual identity to emphasize how Relativity serves the broader “legal data intelligence” community beyond just e-discovery. The move to go public also comes after the company made its first public investments in two legal tech startups—Patlytics and Advocacy—through its investment and innovation arm Rel Labs, which the company launched in October.

Earlier this month, Relativity also announced the latest update for its generative artificial intelligence aiR suite, with the general availability for aiR for Case Strategy in Relativity One Government.

news.titleEn: Preparing Every Student for an AI-Powered Future
news.titleZh: 为每位学生迎接人工智能驱动的未来做好准备
news.summaryZh:
生成式人工智能的迅速兴起使美国教育体系陷入“被动应对的困境”。在华盛顿特区举行的SCSP AI+教育会议上，由AiEDU首席执行官Alex Kotran、哈佛大学CEPR执行主任Christina Grant博士和主持人Eva Doug组成的小组探讨了一个关键转变：必须超越简单的“人工智能素养”，从根本上重新设计人类智能和学生准备度的衡量方式。

人工智能正朝着代理能力发展，传统技术素养定义已过时。学生需要持久技能：沟通、协作和高阶计算思维。Christina Grant博士提出，人工智能应作为教师的副驾驶，减轻导致职业倦怠的管理和诊断负担。小组还强调标准化测试存在数据不匹配问题，当前激励结构阻碍了培养持久技能的项目式学习。会议为现代学生提出三大支柱：完成困难任务、成为专家学习者、掌握人际摩擦能力。人类能力是当前唯一的真正差异化因素，教育应成为国家竞争力的主要引擎。
news.bodyHtml:
The rapid onset of generative AI has left the American education system in a state of “reactive whiplash.” At the recent SCSP AI+Education conference in Washington, DC, a panel featuring Alex Kotran (CEO of AiEDU), Dr. Christina Grant (Executive Director at Harvard’s CEPR), and moderator Eva Doug explored a critical pivot: we must move past simple “AI literacy” and toward a fundamental redesign of how we measure human intelligence and student readiness.

From a technologist’s perspective, the discussion wasn’t just about putting tablets and LLMs in classrooms; it was about change management at a civilizational scale.

Beyond Literacy: The Shift to Agentic Capabilities

Early in the conversation, Alex Kotran made a provocative point that resonates with anyone watching the trajectory of Silicon Valley. We are already moving past the “prompt engineering” phase. As AI moves toward agentic capabilities, where models don’t just answer questions but execute complex, multi-step goals, the traditional definition of technical literacy becomes obsolete.

“We don’t talk about cell phone literacy… AI skills to us felt like, is that really going to be it? So, we made this bet on, well, what is the human advantage actually going to be?” – Alex Kotran

For the technologist, this is the “Abstraction Layer” argument. Just as we no longer need to know assembly language to build a website, students won’t need to be “AI experts” to use AI. Instead, they need durable skills: communication, collaboration, and high-level computational thinking.

The Teacher as a “Facilitator of Knowledge”

One of the most inspiring visions came from Dr. Christina Grant, who addressed the dwindling satisfaction of teachers. She argued that AI shouldn’t replace the teacher but act as a co-pilot that offloads the administrative and diagnostic “noise” that leads to burnout.

Imagine an English teacher in a classroom where an AI is “listening” in real-time, not to surveil, but to provide immediate feedback on how to pivot a lesson based on student questions.

“The tools could really create teachers… a facilitator of knowledge to do something that humans do well. How do you think? How do we collaborate?” – Dr. Christina Grant

In this model, the classroom becomes a “fluid environment” where the loop between school and home is closed. No more “Johnny saying there’s no homework,” because the data flow is transparent and continuous.

The Assessment Crisis: Measuring What Matters

The panel hit a significant nerve regarding standardized testing. As a technologist, I see a massive data mismatch: we are using industrial-era metrics (multiple-choice tests) to measure students entering an era of infinite information.

Kotran noted that while AI can now solve most math and writing tasks, this doesn’t make those subjects irrelevant, it actually raises the bar. If the AI can provide the answer, the student must now possess the “meta-cognitive” skills to understand the why and the how.

The challenge is that our current incentive structures, school funding tied to test scores, actively discourage the project-based learning that builds these durable skills. We need a “wholesale system alignment” that rewards innovation rather than rote memorization.

A New Compass for Parents: “Do Hard Things”

For parents worried about which career paths remain “safe,” the panel offered a refreshing, if challenging, perspective. The “doctor, lawyer, engineer” trifecta is no longer a guaranteed ticket to the middle class.

Instead, the panel suggested three pillars for the modern student:

  1. Accomplish Hard Things: Whether it’s sports, a trade, or a difficult project, the ability to persevere through friction is a signal that AI cannot replicate.
  2. Become an Expert Learner: In a world where tools change every six months, “lifelong learning” isn’t a cliché; it’s a survival requirement.
  3. Master Human Friction: As AI reduces friction in technical tasks, the ability to navigate office politics, lead a team, and manage human emotions becomes the ultimate differentiator.

“The children of the future will need to be durable. They will need to know how to pivot. They will need to know how to stay ahead of the learning curve.” – Dr. Christina Grant

The Technologist’s Takeaway

We are entering an era where human capacity is the only true differentiator, for now. As software stocks fluctuate and technology becomes a commodity accessible to everyone from Goldman Sachs to a rural high schooler, the “winner” isn’t the one with the best model. It’s the one with the best-trained humans capable of leveraging that model.

For policymakers, the “low-hanging fruit” is clear: stop treating AI as a threat to be managed and start treating education as the primary engine of national competitiveness. We cannot afford to be afraid; we were, as Dr. Grant put it, “designed to be in this moment.”

For more information, please visit the following:

Website: https://www.josephraczynski.com/

Blog: https://JTConsultingMedia.com/

Podcast: https://techsnippetstoday.buzzsprout.com

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/joerazz/

news.titleEn: Emma Legal CEO, CMO: Trust Remains a ‘Central Obstacle' to AI Innovation
news.titleZh: Emma Legal CEO与CMO：信任仍是AI创新的“核心障碍”
news.summaryZh: 法律科技市场成熟，AI从创新转向基础设施。通用AI无法满足复杂法律工作，专用工具提供可靠见解并降低风险。AI重塑并购经济，缩短尽职调查周期，使大型律所处理小型事务，客户期望提高。初级律师转向高阶分析，专用工具扩大审查范围并保持律师控制。买家更挑剔，关注工具可靠性、工作流契合和验证负担减少。基础模型改进，差异化在于能力转化为实际流程。律师期望透明度、可解释性和可定制工具。未来竞争优势来自用例优化和生态系统集成。信任仍是核心障碍，早期生成式AI过度承诺使律师谨慎；欧洲合规门槛高，美国需自行定义治理框架。基础模型改进、客户期望和AI经济变化加速创新。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Rick van Esch, co-founder and CEO of Emma Legal, and Joost Verhaard, founding CMO of Emma Legal, which won the award for M&A and Transaction Innovation.

The legal tech industry has grown significantly over the past few years, with many new entrants and offerings. How do you see the market evolving in the next 12 months and why?

The legal tech market is moving into a more mature phase, and the next 12 months will likely be defined by grounded, intentional adoption rather than experimentation. AI is shifting from an innovation project to part of the operational fabric of legal work.

Precision over generalization: Across the industry, there’s a growing acceptance that generic AI cannot meet the depth or nuance required in complex workflows like legal due diligence. As discussed during our recent panel, “horses for courses” captures the emerging consensus: workflow-specific tools consistently produce more reliable insights and reduce verification burdens. This distinction will become more pronounced.

Shifting deal economics and expectations: AI is subtly reshaping M&A economics. Shorter diligence cycles and clearer scoping make smaller matters more viable for large firms. At the same time, clients are raising expectations, speed is no longer sufficient; richer insight is now the benchmark. This will influence how firms evaluate technology and structure deal teams.

Evolving junior roles and risk management: With AI absorbing low-value review, juniors are moving sooner into higher-order analysis, provided firms support them with structured training. Specialized tools also reduce risk by widening the volume of material that can be reviewed while keeping lawyers firmly in control of judgment.

Taken together, these trends suggest a steady transition: legal AI becoming normalized, embedded, and expected. Not as a headline innovation, but as infrastructure for modern legal practice.

How have you seen legal tech users and buyers’ behavior, demands and/or preferences evolve over the past few years, and how do you predict it will change in the near future?

Legal tech buyers have become far more discerning in recent years. Early generative AI created excitement but didn’t meet lawyers’ expectations for precision or reliability, which reset the market’s sense of what “good” looks like. Today, buyers are focused less on novelty and more on whether a tool delivers dependable outputs, aligns with existing workflows, and reduces verification burden.

As foundation models have improved, the field has effectively leveled. Access to strong AI is no longer a differentiator on its own; the differentiation now lies in how well vendors translate that capability into real legal processes. Lawyers increasingly expect transparency, explainability, and tools they can tailor to their preferred way of working, not generic systems or black boxes.

In the near future, we can expect this trend to deepen. Baseline AI quality will continue to rise, while competitive advantage will come from use-case optimization and broader eco-system integrations: solutions that fit naturally into legal reasoning and elevates the quality of advice. The market is shifting from “AI as innovation” to “AI as infrastructure,” and buyers are choosing tools that support how they already think, work, and deliver outcomes for clients.

What do you see as the biggest barriers to and drivers of innovation in the legal industry right now?

Innovation in the legal industry today sits at the intersection of rising capability and persistent structural hesitation. The dynamics are similar across markets, but the barriers and drivers differ in emphasis between the U.S. and Europe/UK.

Barriers—Trust remains the central obstacle. Early generative AI overpromised and underdelivered for legal use, particularly in precision and explainability. That experience made lawyers far more selective: tools must now be transparent, verifiable, and adaptable to existing workflows. Anything that feels like a black box meets resistance.

In Europe, regulation adds weight. The EU AI Act and strict data-protection regimes raise the compliance threshold but also push the market toward more rigorous, explainable systems. Limited access to large-scale tech funding can slow adoption.

In the U.S., the challenge is different: a fragmented regulatory environment leaves firms to define their own AI governance, which creates caution in high-stakes practice areas.

Drivers—At the same time, several forces are accelerating the pace of innovation. Foundation models have improved dramatically, leveling the technical field and shifting competition from “model performance” to “workflow performance.” This is where much of the meaningful differentiation will happen.

Client expectations are another catalyst. Faster delivery is no longer the benchmark; richer insight, clearer visibility into risk in a know workflow defines quality now. Recent peer discussions reinforced this shift: purpose-built tools consistently outperform generic platforms in e.g. M&A, echoing the “horses for courses” view gaining traction across firms.

Finally, the economics of AI are changing. Shorter diligence cycles and more predictable scoping make previously unattractive matters viable again, nudging firms toward tools that help them operate with greater confidence and efficiency. In the near future, innovation will be driven less by novelty and more by thoughtful integration, AI that fits how lawyers already think, work, and advise.

news.titleEn: Clearbrief CEO: AI Focus Will Shift to Accountability, Verification Requirements
news.titleZh: Clearbrief CEO：AI焦点将转向问责与验证要求
news.summaryZh: 未来12个月法律科技市场将由问责与验证要求主导。追踪法律AI在提交诉状中产生幻觉的数据库已收录600余条记录，相关制裁包括3万美元罚款乃至律所退出重要客户代理。2025年沃兹沃思诉沃尔玛案（摩根与摩根代理）和科尔斯诉埃里森案（涉及明尼苏达州总检察长专家证词）成为分水岭事件，使提交前验证成为强制要求。大型律所合伙人正在制定全所政策，要求每次提交前进行引证核对。伊利诺伊州最高法院2025年1月的指导方针采取“支持AI”立场，同时强调律师有责任确保引用权威来源准确且非生成式AI工具“幻觉”产生。泰夫律师事务所在相关新闻稿中提及使用Clearbrief的责任AI确保诉状准确性。法律技术研究证实，生成式AI的“验证负担”可能超过效率收益——中间步骤和最终输出的验证成本常超出节省时间，使律所对AI部署高度审慎。Clearbrief通过自动化验证解决此矛盾，使安全层比人工核对更快。汤森路透研究显示71%客户要求明确AI如何影响计费，59%期望律所使用AI同时要求效率带来成本效益。市场将日益需求能同时验证法律与事实引证的工具。买家优先级已从效率显著转向风险缓解，用户寻求能预防错误并识别诉讼制胜机会的工具。行业研究显示95%法律专业人士预计五年内生成式AI将成为组织工作流核心，使带验证记录的引证核对成为基础合规设施。
news.bodyHtml:
As part of our awards series, we asked our winners about what they see as the biggest barriers and drivers of innovation, the impact of emerging technologies, and how they believe the market will change in the near future.

Here’s our Q&A with Jacqueline Schafer, CEO of Clearbrief, which won the awards for Litigation Technology and Litigation Technology and Technology for Good.

The legal tech industry has grown significantly over the past few years, with many new entrants and offerings. How do you see the market evolving in the next 12 months and why?

The next 12 months will be defined by accountability and verification requirements. A database tracking legal AI hallucinations in filed pleadings has over 600 entries, with sanctions ranging from $30,000 in fees to firms withdrawing from major client representation. High-profile 2025 cases (Wadsworth v. Walmart involving Morgan & Morgan, and Kohls v. Ellison involving an expert declaration for Minnesota's Attorney General) created a watershed moment where verification before filing is becoming mandatory.

BigLaw partners are instituting firm-wide policies requiring cite-checking before every filing. As an Am Law 20 firm partner noted, firms need "the safety layer" for AI implementation in high-stakes matters. Court guidance is accelerating this shift. The Illinois Supreme Court's January 2025 guidance takes a "pro-AI" stance while emphasizing that lawyers have a duty to ensure cited authority is accurate and not "hallucinated" by generative AI tools. Taft mentioned Clearbrief in its press release on this guidance, noting the firm uses Clearbrief's responsible AI to ensure accuracy in pleadings.

Legal technology research confirms that the “burden of verification” with gen AI can outweigh efficiency gains—verification costs for intermediate steps and final outputs often exceed the time saved, making firms highly selective about AI deployment. Clearbrief solves this paradox by automating verification itself, making the safety layer faster than manual checking. This aligns with client expectations: Thomson Reuters research shows 71% of clients want clarity on how AI affects billing, while 59% expect firms to use AI while demanding cost benefits from that efficiency. The market will increasingly demand tools that verify both legal and factual citations. Tools verifying only case law leave firms exposed to sanctions for unsupported factual statements.

How have you seen legal tech users and buyers’ behavior, demands and/or preferences evolve over the past few years, and how do you predict it will change in the near future?

Buyer priorities have shifted dramatically from efficiency to risk mitigation. Firms that previously evaluated tools based on time savings are now savvy about measuring the time spent on validating the resulting work product. Users are looking for tools that can prevent mistakes and identify opportunities to win in litigation. Our Add Fact Cite button, part of Clearbrief's patented cite-checking tech, finds the best evidence to support your own statements in Word while finding contradictory evidence to dispute opposing counsel’s statements. This dual capability is what gives our cite-checking tools a strategic impact beyond proofreading.

Users also demand comprehensive coverage. As Kristina Bakardjiev, Director of Legal Practice Innovation at Cozen O’Connor noted, the strongest safeguard is AI where "every factual assertion and legal citation is independently checked, and the system generates a clear validation record." Tools that verify only case law without checking factual citations leave firms exposed.

Industry research shows lawyers prefer innovative technology 'within the confines of the application they already know'. Clearbrief's Microsoft Word integration addresses this core adoption barrier while providing the verification layer that makes AI deployment defensible. Thomson Reuters and other industry studies indicate 95% of legal professionals expect gen AI to become central to organizational workflows within five years, making cite-checking with documented validation baseline compliance infrastructure.

There's growing demand for audit trails. Partners need documented proof they satisfied ethical obligations before signing. Tools that flag issues without tracking how those issues were resolved fail to provide the validation record courts are demanding. Users want trusted verification inside their drafting environment. Clearbrief's integration with LexisNexis and Fastcase/vLex means cases display automatically in Word without requiring lawyers to switch to separate research platforms. Looking ahead, cite-checking with documented validation will become baseline compliance infrastructure, similar to how conflict checks became mandatory before taking on new matters.

What do you see as the biggest barriers to and drivers of innovation in the legal industry right now?

The biggest barrier is the trust deficit created by hallucinated citations. High-profile 2025 sanctions demonstrate that even sophisticated users at elite firms can submit fake citations when using generative AI without proper verification. The subtlety of AI errors compounds the challenge. Gen AI mistakes can be so subtle the human eye easily misses them, such as replacing a single number in a citation so it appears to be from the court's own jurisdiction rather than another circuit. Partners signing pleadings prepared by junior associates on tight deadlines are especially at risk when a single filing can contain hundreds of citations to both facts and law.

Professional responsibility requirements create challenges. The Illinois Supreme Court guidance (effective January 1, 2025) makes clear that lawyers must ensure cited authority is accurate and not hallucinated by AI. Taft mentioned Clearbrief in its press release on this guidance, demonstrating how firms are addressing these requirements from a compliance perspective.

Fear of sanctions does drive rapid adoption of tech that can ensure accuracy. Sanctions range from $30,000 in fees to requiring firms to withdraw from representing major clients. Firms are choosing Clearbrief as they pursue what one AmLaw 20 leader called "the safety layer" for AI implementation.

news.titleEn: A Wander Among Web Browsers
news.titleZh: 在网页浏览器间的漫游
news.summaryZh:
作者受丹麦同行影响，持续减少对美国技术的依赖，将网络使用分散至多个浏览器以限制数据追踪。工作环境中默认使用Google，但作者主要使用Microsoft Edge，并扩展使用Firefox、Brave、LibreWolf和Vivaldi等替代浏览器。浏览器本身并非核心问题，关键在于追踪数据控制，因此作者优先使用支持关键追踪拦截扩展的浏览器。

主要扩展包括：NoScript用于禁用JavaScript以阻断追踪；电子前沿基金会的Privacy Badger用于禁用出现的追踪功能；gorhill的UBlock作为辅助工具。浏览器普遍转向Chromium基础，使Chrome扩展兼容Edge和Vivaldi。作者通过Thunderbeam-Lightbeam演示追踪拦截效果，显示启用扩展后第三方请求显著减少。作者还调整默认搜索引擎，使用自定义Google搜索链接（UDM=14和PWS=0参数）减少AI和个人化影响，并建议使用VPN地理伪装。Edge因支持工作和个人双配置文件而受青睐，但多数浏览器也支持多配置文件。作者使用Brave专门访问YouTube并屏蔽广告，但对其商业模式持保留态度。LibreWolf作为Firefox分支，默认关闭隐私侵犯功能，已取代Firefox成为主要备用浏览器。Vivaldi作为非开源的Chromium浏览器，集成电子邮件、日历和RSS等个人信息管理功能，可通过Microsoft Store安装。作者计划最终放弃Edge和Chrome，主要使用Vivaldi和LibreWolf，并保留Brave隔离视频流量。
news.bodyHtml:
Reading Time: 8 minutes

I have been watching some online colleagues in Denmark engage in a massive withdrawal from US-based technology. #DanmarkSkifter It has encouraged me to continue along this path myself. Years ago I started to spread my internet use across web browsers to try to silo some of their knowledge about me. Even though I tend to be adversarial with any web browser, I have been slowly trying to move away from anything Google or Microsoft.

That can be hard when you are in a corporate environment. Our corporate default is Google, so I just ignore it. I can do that because our operating system is Microsoft Windows and the Microsoft app store is enabled. I tend to use Microsoft Edge at work. I have expanded my alternate browser use so that I also have, in addition to Chrome and Edge, I use Mozilla’s Firefox, Brave, and more recently Librewolf and Vivaldi.

Lockdown

The reality is that the browser isn’t really the key problem. It’s the tracking, so the first thing I focus on when I use a web browser is to cauterize the outflow of tracking data. This means that I can only use web browsers that support my key tracking blocking extensions:

  • NoScript is the first one. It turns off JavaScript unless you proactively turn it on. Most of the web functions just fine without it and, where it doesn’t, you can toggle on — temporarily or permanently — support for a specific part of a website. Since most tracking seems to be loaded up by JavaScript, this really eliminates the need for a dedicated ad blocking extension. Once you have your primary browser set up, you can export/import the block settings to other browsers to avoid having to re-train each one.
  • Electronic Fronter Foundation’s Privacy Badger. This is for trimming around the edges. Sometimes you have to turn on a JavaScript for functionality. I use Privacy Badger to disable any tracking that appears, allowing the functionality without the diminishment of privacy.
  • I still load up a copy of gorhill’s UBlock but it’s largely just a belt-and-suspenders tool. Google’s customized take on the Chromium web browser breaks some of the UBlock functionality so I wouldn’t use it by itself.

One big shift among web browsers is to the Chromium base: Google Chrome uses it. So does Microsoft Edge and Vivaldi. It means that any developer’s extension designed for Chrome should work on Edge and Vivaldi as well. In a pretty common “information technology lockdown” approach, our corporate IT has blocked the Google Chrome web store within the corporate network but cannot block the Microsoft extensions store. Also, if you have your web browser profile’s synchronized across desktop devices (home and office, say), the addons will synchronize even if you can’t reach the web store. Blocking extensions is a bit of a mug’s game.

You might not think it would matter but if you spin up a copy of Thunderbeam-Lightbeam and have tracking on, the difference is significant. I showed this to my legal tech students recently. Same web browser, same websites (CNN, National Post, Washington Post, ABA, LexisNexis). First, without any adversarial add-ons, showing all of the third-party tracking and requests going on:

and then with those add-ons, listed above, active:

Now I can move among my web browsers with some certainty that I’m not trailing a load of digital exhaust. The one other tweak I make is to the default Google search engine. I try not to use Google but students will use it whether they realize it or not. I taught them this simple hack to add a custom Google search engine so that, if they wanted to, they could see what Google offers them without AI or personalization:

https://google.com/search?q=%s&udm=14&pws=0

The UDM= impacts artificial intelligence results. The PWS impacts personalization. Search engines are pulling IP address to over-ride search keywords to localize results. I’ve tinkered with obfuscation here but the best bet is to flip on a VPN and pop out somewhere else on the internet, geographically, to be certain.

Pick Your Poison

I don’t really mind switching between apps. I find that a custom search is actually far easier than trying a search in different web browsers. The personalization or skewing of results is happening outside of the web browser. So the choice of a particular web browser starts to become one of what other functionality it offers.

Microsoft Edge has been useful because I have a work profile and a personal profile built into the web browser. This means I can toggle between them — or have them both open at the same time — to help me focus on one or the other. State universities don’t want you engaged in personal business at work. I’m also a firm believer that work is 9 to 5 and I do not want my web activity to be tied to work email notifications or other nonsense like that. I already think about work nearly 24/7, I don’t need it available at my finger tips.

Most web browsers support multiple profiles, though, so there’s no reason to use Edge if your only need is alternative profiles. We are also a Microsoft 365 shop, though, and it feels like the integration is better with Edge than it would be with other Chromium-based web browsers, excepting for perhaps Google. But since Google is my last choice for web browsing, Edge has been a good primary choice. I log in to both my Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 (work and personal) accounts on Edge. It’s the one place where I give up the most privacy in order to get the greatest integration.

Although I use Google Workspace for mail and for Drive (and occasionally for Docs when some other academic shares one), I do not log in to any other OAuth-powered Google sign in. My Google and Microsoft accounts are not linked to any other websites unless I cannot avoid it. If there is a choice for an email and a password on a site, even if it supports OAuth, I create a new account.

Brave

I have a copy of Brave installed as well at home and I use it for the sole purpose of accessing YouTube content. For privacy and content reasons, I have turned off my YouTube watch history. The privacy reasons speak for themselves, but they feed into the content reasons: I don’t want YouTube recommending stuff to me. I think we can seek the impact algorithms on sites like X (skew conservative; PDF) or Meta properties have on their users. I can subscribe to channels I want to follow since I’m logged in with my Google account and I can do searches. That is plenty for my very limited openness to video content.

The benefit of Brave is that it combats YouTube advertising. I haven’t seen a YouTube ad in years. Since I proactively block all youtube.com and googlevideo.com URLs on other browsers, I leave the blocking add-ons off Brave. I don’t use Brave’s search or leave YouTube, so I have no non-YouTube history in the browser. Brave is marketed as privacy first but I find them to be sketchy and I’m not a fan of any business running on ad revenue.

Firefox and LibreWolf

They have also introduced an AI component to their browser and I am trying to avoid artificial intelligence under the hood. That’s one reason that I have left Mozilla’s Firefox. For decades, my web browser setup was to use Google Chrome as my primary and Firefox as my alternate. The shift to Microsoft Edge came about only when Microsoft finally dropped its own browser engine — the one that had powered Internet Explorer — and so the extension or add-on functionality was modernized.

But Firefox, as much as it has been a constant companion through my research life, is also headed down the road of AI. The original infusion of artificial intelligence came without much choice on the part of the browser operator. They have started to mitigate that, providing opt-out choices in recent builds. But Mozilla, the Firefox owner, has dumped a lot of resources into its own Mozilla.ai. Their latest CEO says that they’re going to be doubling down on re-building trust but I’m leery. It is too easy to put AI into web browsers and they are too key to how professionals, and professional researchers especially, get their work done. I don’t want my work training LLMs.

Enter LibreWolf. It’s a fork of Mozilla’s Firefox and so it runs the same engine and feels exactly like Firefox. But it is, like Brave, privacy first. It is designed to proactively remove privacy-invading features of Firefox as well as having privacy default settings. This includes turning off DRM and disabling Google “Safe Browsing”, which is a way of running content requests through Google’s systems and capturing browsing habits and IP addresses.

In very short order, LibreWolf replaced Firefox for me. It had become my primary backup web browser until I started playing with Vivaldi. The web browser, not the composer.

Vivaldi

Initially, I had started using Vivaldi because I was unhappy with my webmail app. As I tell my law practice technology students, start with the problem. The problem was that the webmail app, hosted by my web host, was clunky and lacked a lot of functionality. I had started to use an email app on my phone to get around that. But I really wanted a strong, web-based — so I could access it anywhere, not just on a device-based app — email client. When I learned about Vivaldi, I was intrigued.

And put off. Unlike Firefox, Chromium, and LibreWolf, Vivaldi is not open source. It is free and is European, so that gives me some confidence if only because it is subject to European privacy laws. Like it’s fellow Scandinavian originating web browser, Opera, it is Chromium-based like Edge and Google Chrome. This means that it is making similar balances of privacy and Google-centric functionality.

As an email client in a web browser, it is pretty great. It can support a calendar as well as RSS feeds and is a nice little personal information manager (PIM) all on its own. If you’ve got an IMAP or POP3 email account, and can configure SMTP, you’re good to go. The RSS feed function is a bit iffy. I think that it is a good RSS news reader if you don’t have any need to filtering or customization. As someone who generates feeds using XPath, it lacks functionality for me.

I was sick recently, though, and that gave me a lot of time to mope around. This included sitting wrapped up in a blanket at my computer. While I was there, I started to explore Vivaldi more as an alternative to Microsoft Edge. For one thing, as I had learned when I added it to my work computer, Vivaldi is in the Microsoft Store. This meant I could install it without needing admin rights to a PC. Since it was Chromium-based, I could also load in my normal privacy extensions.

The more I played around with it, the more I liked the merger of web browsing and PIM functionality. I will eventually be dumping my Google Mail account and it will be nice to have email in my web browser without using webmail (think Horde, Roundcube, etc.) and having to log in and keep a tab open. Vivaldi’s email function is set and forget.

Many of my web browser tabs are in fact pinned apps: a window with a music player in it, a tab for my password manager, for my note-taking app. Vivaldi’s PIM functionality meant that all of my web-based apps could be in a single web browser. You can pin a tab in Vivaldi just like you can in any other web browser, so I have my default tabs open up on start.

They have done a good job of providing a balance of security under the hood. Unlike LibreWolf, Vivaldi still relies on Google Safebrowsing. But you can toggle it off if you want to. LibreWolf also turns off DNS over HTTPS (DoH, which is unfortunate because of Homer Simpson). But I use a Cloudflare secure DNS that protects against malware in the same way that Safe Browsing does, with a block list, and so I am happy to use DoH and disable Google’s hook. To use this, you change your web browser’s DNS setting to Custom and drop in the URL that works for you:

  • Cloudflare DoH blocking malware: https://security.cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query
  • Cloudflare DoH blocking malware and adult content: https://family.cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query

You can create multiple profiles like on other browsers and also multiple workspaces, just like on Microsoft Edge (but not on Google Chrome from what I can tell). These are niche. Windows users familiar with Task View, and creating virtual desktops of icons and apps that you can swap between for productivity (instead of having EVERY app open on the same screen at once) will understand the value of workspaces. You can create a set of tabs and put them on a workspace, then toggle to (or mouse wheel scroll) between tab sets.

I’m still determining if this is easier than just having all the apps on one tab bar. I have 10 default pinned tabs but rarely have more than 20 total tabs open. I know some people have dozens of tabs open all the time. I’m not sure I need two or more workspaces but I know some people would probably find them useful for managing their open tabs.

I had started with four web browsers in play: Edge, Firefox, Brave, and very occasionally Chrome. I had shifted to Edge, LibreWolf, Brave, and Chrome. But it looks like the best arrangement for me going forward will be to dump Edge and Chrome, and stick with Vivaldi and LibreWolf. Every other Chromium-based web browser seems to be trying to create an artificial intelligence-powered or -infused version of itself and I am not interested in being part of those experiments. For now, I’ll keep Brave if only to isolate that video traffic. I am also going to start playing with a user-agent switcher (although you can add a custom user-agent within Vivaldi natively) to see if I can get around any “Better with Edge” or “You Must Use Chrome” website developers.

I’ve tinkered with obfuscation here but the best bet is to flip on a VPN and pop out somewhere else on the internet, geographically, to be certain.

I don’t really mind switching between apps. I find that a custom search is actually far easier than trying a search in different web browsers. The personalization or skewing of results is happening outside of the web browser. So the choice of a particular web browser starts to become one of what other functionality it offers.

Microsoft Edge has been useful because I have a work profile and a personal profile built into the web browser . This means I can toggle between them — or have them both open at the same time — to help me focus on one or the other. State universities don’t want you engaged in personal business at work. I’m also a firm believer that work is 9 to 5 and I do not want my web activity to be tied to work email notifications or other nonsense like that. I already think about work nearly 24/7, I don’t need it available at my finger tips.

Most web browsers support multiple profiles, though, so there’s no reason to use Edge if your only need is alternative profiles. We are also a Microsoft 365 shop, though, and it feels like the integration is better with Edge than it would be with other Chromium-based web browsers, excepting for perhaps Google. But since Google is my last choice for web browsing, Edge has been a good primary choice. I log in to both my Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 (work and personal) accounts on Edge. It’s the one place where I give up the most privacy in order to get the greatest integration.

Although I use Google Workspace for mail and for Drive (and occasionally for Docs when some other academic shares one), I do not log in to any other OAuth-powered Google sign in . My Google and Microsoft accounts are not linked to any other websites unless I cannot avoid it. If there is a choice for an email and a password on a site, even if it supports OAuth, I create a new account.

Although I use Google Workspace for mail and for Drive (and occasionally for Docs when some other academic shares one), I do not log in to any other OAuth-powered Google sign in . My Google and Microsoft accounts are not linked to any other websites unless I cannot avoid it. If there is a choice for an email and a password on a site, even if it supports OAuth, I create a new account.

I have a copy of Brave installed as well at home and I use it for the sole purpose of accessing YouTube content. For privacy and content reasons, I have turned off my YouTube watch history. The privacy reasons speak for themselves, but they feed into the content reasons: I don’t want YouTube recommending stuff to me. I think we can seek the impact algorithms on sites like X ( skew conservative ; PDF ) or Meta properties have on their users. I can subscribe to channels I want to follow since I’m logged in with my Google account and I can do searches. That is plenty for my very limited openness to video content.

The benefit of Brave is that it combats YouTube advertising. I haven’t seen a YouTube ad in years. Since I proactively block all youtube.com and googlevideo.com URLs on other browsers, I leave the blocking add-ons off Brave. I don’t use Brave’s search or leave YouTube, so I have no non-YouTube history in the browser. Brave is marketed as privacy first but I find them to be sketchy and I’m not a fan of any business running on ad revenue .

They have also introduced an AI component to their browser and I am trying to avoid artificial intelligence under the hood. That’s one reason that I have left Mozilla’s Firefox. For decades, my web browser setup was to use Google Chrome as my primary and Firefox as my alternate. The shift to Microsoft Edge came about only when Microsoft finally dropped its own browser engine — the one that had powered Internet Explorer — and so the extension or add-on functionality was modernized.

But Firefox, as much as it has been a constant companion through my research life, is also headed down the road of AI. The original infusion of artificial intelligence came without much choice on the part of the browser operator. They have started to mitigate that, providing opt-out choices in recent builds . But Mozilla, the Firefox owner, has dumped a lot of resources into its own Mozilla.ai . Their latest CEO says that they’re going to be doubling down on re-building trust but I’m leery. It is too easy to put AI into web browsers and they are too key to how professionals, and professional researchers especially, get their work done. I don’t want  my work training LLMs.

Enter LibreWolf . It’s a fork of Mozilla’s Firefox and so it runs the same engine and feels exactly like Firefox. But it is, like Brave, privacy first. It is designed to proactively remove privacy-invading features of Firefox as well as having privacy default settings . This includes turning off DRM and disabling Google “Safe Browsing” , which is a way of running content requests through Google’s systems and capturing browsing habits and IP addresses .

In very short order, LibreWolf replaced Firefox for me. It had become my primary backup web browser until I started playing with Vivaldi . The web browser, not the composer .

Initially, I had started using Vivaldi because I was unhappy with my webmail app. As I tell my law practice technology students, start with the problem. The problem was that the webmail app, hosted by my web host, was clunky and lacked a lot of functionality. I had started to use an email app on my phone to get around that. But I really wanted a strong, web-based — so I could access it anywhere, not just on a device-based app — email client. When I learned about Vivaldi, I was intrigued.

And put off. Unlike Firefox, Chromium, and LibreWolf, Vivaldi is not open source. It is free and is European, so that gives me some confidence if only because it is subject to European privacy laws. Like it’s fellow Scandinavian originating web browser, Opera, it is Chromium-based like Edge and Google Chrome.  This means that it is making similar balances of privacy and Google-centric functionality.

As an email client in a web browser, it is pretty great. It can support a calendar as well as RSS feeds and is a nice little personal information manager (PIM) all on its own. If you’ve got an IMAP or POP3 email account, and can configure SMTP, you’re good to go. The RSS feed function is a bit iffy. I think that it is a good RSS news reader if you don’t have any need to filtering or customization. As someone who generates feeds using XPath , it lacks functionality for me.

I was sick recently, though, and that gave me a lot of time to mope around. This included sitting wrapped up in a blanket at my computer. While I was there, I started to explore Vivaldi more as an alternative to Microsoft Edge. For one thing, as I had learned when I added it to my work computer, Vivaldi is in the Microsoft Store . This meant I could install it without needing admin rights to a PC. Since it was Chromium-based, I could also load in my normal privacy extensions.

The more I played around with it, the more I liked the merger of web browsing and PIM functionality. I will eventually be dumping my Google Mail account and it will be nice to have email in my web browser without using webmail (think Horde , Roundcube , etc.) and having to log in and keep a tab open. Vivaldi’s email function is set and forget.

Many of my web browser tabs are in fact pinned apps: a window with a music player in it, a tab for my password manager, for my note-taking app. Vivaldi’s PIM functionality meant that all of my web-based apps could be in a single web browser. You can pin a tab in Vivaldi just like you can in any other web browser, so I have my default tabs open up on start.

They have done a good job of providing a balance of security under the hood. Unlike LibreWolf, Vivaldi still relies on Google Safebrowsing. But you can toggle it off if you want to. LibreWolf also turns off DNS over HTTPS (DoH, which is unfortunate because of Homer Simpson ). But I use a Cloudflare secure DNS that protects against malware in the same way that Safe Browsing does, with a block list, and so I am happy to use DoH and disable Google’s hook. To use this, you change your web browser’s DNS setting to Custom and drop in the URL that works for you:

Cloudflare DoH blocking malware: https://security.cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query

Cloudflare DoH blocking malware and adult content: https://family.cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query

You can create multiple profiles like on other browsers and also multiple workspaces, just like on Microsoft Edge (but not on Google Chrome from what I can tell). These are niche. Windows users familiar with Task View , and creating virtual desktops of icons and apps that you can swap between for productivity (instead of having EVERY app open on the same screen at once) will understand the value of workspaces. You can create a set of tabs and put them on a workspace, then toggle to (or mouse wheel scroll) between tab sets.

I’m still determining if this is easier than just having all the apps on one tab bar. I have 10 default pinned tabs but rarely have more than 20 total tabs open. I know some people have dozens of tabs open all the time. I’m not sure I need two or more workspaces but I know some people would probably find them useful for managing their open tabs.

I had started with four web browsers in play: Edge, Firefox, Brave, and very occasionally Chrome. I had shifted to Edge, LibreWolf, Brave, and Chrome. But it looks like the best arrangement for me going forward will be to dump Edge and Chrome, and stick with Vivaldi and LibreWolf. Every other Chromium-based web browser seems to be trying to create an artificial intelligence-powered or -infused version of itself and I am not interested in being part of those experiments. For now, I’ll keep Brave if only to isolate that video traffic. I am also going to start playing with a user-agent switcher (although you can add a custom user-agent within Vivaldi natively) to see if I can get around any “Better with Edge” or “You Must Use Chrome” website developers.

news.summaryZh:
Syllo是一家由两位前诉讼律师Jeffrey Chivers和Theodore Rostow于2019年共同创立的法律科技公司。两人在联邦法院担任书记员时相识，Chivers拥有哈佛计算机科学和乔治城大学法学学位，曾在Sullivan & Cromwell从事诉讼业务；Rostow毕业于耶鲁法学院，曾在Simpson Thacher & Bartlett执业，自2014年起深耕法律科技与人工智能领域。

公司采用独特开发路径，放弃传统创业模式，直接构建覆盖整个诉讼生命周期的统一AI驱动工作平台。为此进行了多年底层架构开发，期间因缺乏短期产品难以获得风投支持，创始人通过运营诉讼业务维持公司运转，早期投资者为理解长期愿景的律师和高净值人士。平台技术基础与卡内基梅隆大学工程师合作构建，包括语言技术研究所教授Jamie Callan。Syllo平台涵盖电子取证、代理式AI文档审阅、案件构建与事实管理、诉讼代理四大功能模块，覆盖电子取证参考模型并延伸至案件策略、庭审准备和文件生成领域。其代理式AI文档审阅系统于2024年2月首次部署，采用多大型语言模型协调架构，2025年3月与七家律所25名专业人士发布的白皮书显示系统平均召回率达97.8%。客户群体以大型律所为主，包括Quinn Emanuel、Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman、Ballard Spahr等，2024年与全国就业律师协会建立合作。公司前五年处于保密运营状态，2025年10月获得由Venrock领投的3000万美元成长轮融资，随后团队规模四个月内翻倍，近期聘请Alexis Mitchell担任高级AI顾问，并从Meta、SpaceX等公司招募人才。
